stem: A 54-year-old woman has persistent MCP and PIP synovitis despite 20 mg weekly oral methotrexate and folate. Adherence is confirmed, renal function is normal and she has troublesome nausea after each dose. Which adjustment is the most appropriate before declaring methotrexate ineffective?

options.A: Switch to subcutaneous methotrexate
options.B: Use methotrexate daily
options.C: Add long-term prednisolone alone
options.D: Stop all DMARDs
options.E: Switch immediately to cyclophosphamide

explanation: Subcutaneous methotrexate can improve tolerability and exposure; optimise methotrexate before moving to an alternative mechanism, with disease activity reassessed. Before switching mechanism, verify weekly dosing, folate prescription, adherence and disease activity. Splitting the weekly oral dose or using subcutaneous administration can improve gastrointestinal tolerability and bioavailability; monitor blood counts, liver tests and renal function. Persistent synovitis despite an optimised trial warrants treat-to-target escalation. The early arthritis modules emphasise assessing both swollen joints and function when judging response; persistent power-Doppler synovitis can help distinguish inflammation from non-inflammatory pain.

stem: A 62-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis develops progressive exertional dyspnoea, bibasal crackles and a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function tests. High-resolution CT demonstrates a probable UIP pattern. Which comorbidity most strongly influences the safety discussion before a new biologic is prescribed?

options.A: Primary hyperparathyroidism
options.B: Raynaud phenomenon
options.C: Interstitial lung disease
options.D: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition
options.E: Carpal tunnel syndrome

explanation: RA-associated interstitial lung disease requires integrated respiratory-rheumatology assessment and treatment selection based on pulmonary disease. RA-associated ILD should trigger joint rheumatology-respiratory assessment, including baseline and serial FVC and DLCO. UIP morphology can carry a poorer prognosis. Treatment choice must balance articular control against pulmonary disease, infection risk and progression; the presence of ILD is not in itself an automatic ban on every biologic. The course highlights crackles, exertional hypoxaemia and falling diffusion capacity as clues to inflammatory connective-tissue-disease lung involvement; HRCT pattern and serial physiology are complementary.

stem: A man receiving adalimumab for severe psoriatic arthritis develops blurred vision, optic neuritis and new periventricular demyelinating lesions on MRI. What is the most appropriate change to his arthritis treatment?

options.A: Continue adalimumab unchanged and simply observe the visual symptoms
options.B: Start infliximab immediately as an alternative anti-TNF agent
options.C: Increase the adalimumab dose or frequency to treat a presumed flare
options.D: Add a second TNF inhibitor to intensify disease control
options.E: Stop the TNF inhibitor and seek neurological evaluation

explanation: Suspected demyelinating disease is a major concern with TNF inhibition; choose a non-TNF approach after specialist assessment. New optic neuritis and MRI demyelination while using a TNF inhibitor require urgent neurology review and investigation for demyelinating disease. Do not substitute another drug from the same TNF-inhibitor class without specialist assessment; choose a non-TNF mechanism once the neurological diagnosis is clarified. The immunology module links TNF signalling to host defence and immune regulation; a new neurological syndrome during targeted therapy requires reassessment of drug-related and independent causes.

stem: A 33-year-old man has inflammatory back pain, raised CRP, active sacroiliitis on MRI and persistent high disease activity despite adequate trials of two NSAIDs and a structured exercise programme. What is the most appropriate next therapeutic strategy?

options.A: Start long-term high-dose oral glucocorticoids as first-line axial treatment
options.B: Continue a further six-month course of antibiotics for presumed infective sacroiliitis
options.C: Add oral methotrexate specifically to treat the isolated axial symptoms
options.D: Offer intra-articular methotrexate injections into the sacroiliac joints
options.E: Consider a biologic or targeted therapy for active axial spondyloarthritis

explanation: Persistent active axial disease after conventional measures may justify targeted treatment; conventional DMARDs lack proven efficacy for isolated axial inflammation. Confirm persistent objectively active axial disease, adequate NSAID trials, physical therapy and alternative explanations for pain. Biologic selection is influenced by psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, uveitis, infection screening and local access criteria. Conventional synthetic DMARDs do not reliably improve isolated axial inflammation. The axial spondyloarthritis modules distinguish active inflammatory lesions from chronic structural damage; symptoms, CRP and sacroiliac MRI should be interpreted together.

stem: A 41-year-old woman with axial spondyloarthritis has recurrent anterior uveitis and active spinal disease despite NSAID therapy. Which biologic class and formulation is generally preferred when recurrent uveitis is an important comorbidity?

options.A: Etanercept specifically, considered equally effective against uveitis
options.B: Monoclonal-antibody TNF inhibitor
options.C: Rituximab monotherapy, targeting circulating B lymphocytes
options.D: Abatacept, a selective T-cell costimulation blocker
options.E: Anakinra, a short-acting interleukin-1 receptor antagonist

explanation: Monoclonal TNF inhibitors have more favourable evidence for recurrent uveitis than etanercept in axial spondyloarthritis. When recurrent anterior uveitis coexists with axial disease, monoclonal TNF inhibitors such as adalimumab or infliximab are commonly preferred over etanercept. Review previous uveitis treatment with ophthalmology and screen for TB and viral hepatitis before starting a biologic. An episode of anterior uveitis may present with unilateral pain, photophobia and redness. Ophthalmological confirmation is important because extra-musculoskeletal disease changes biologic selection.

stem: A 47-year-old man with active psoriatic arthritis has severe chronic plaque psoriasis, dactylitis and several swollen peripheral joints despite methotrexate. Which treatment mechanism directly addresses both prominent skin disease and peripheral arthritis?

options.A: Thrombin inhibition
options.B: Acetylcholinesterase inhibition
options.C: IL-17 pathway inhibition
options.D: Osteoclast activation
options.E: Dopamine agonism

explanation: IL-17 inhibitors treat both psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis; other biologic choices depend on uveitis and IBD comorbidity. IL-17 inhibition can address both joint and extensive skin psoriasis. An IL-23-pathway agent is another appropriate class for prominent cutaneous disease, and concomitant IBD or uveitis may alter selection. Screen for infection and review dermatology input rather than selecting solely on tender-joint count. The course describes dactylitis as a combined inflammatory process involving digits and peri-tendinous tissues, while enthesitis and nail disease increase the likelihood of psoriatic arthritis.

stem: A 52-year-old man with psoriatic arthritis and active Crohn disease requires escalation beyond conventional treatment. Which option is least suitable because it may worsen his bowel disease?

options.A: Gastroenterology-led Crohn therapy
options.B: An appropriate IL-23-pathway agent
options.C: Monoclonal TNF inhibitor
options.D: A bowel-effective biologic
options.E: IL-17 inhibitor

explanation: IL-17 inhibition is generally avoided in active inflammatory bowel disease; coordinate joint and bowel treatment. IL-17 blockade can induce or worsen inflammatory bowel disease and is generally avoided in active Crohn disease. Prefer an agent effective for both joints and gut after discussion with gastroenterology; monoclonal TNF inhibitors are a common choice, while the specific IL-23 agent matters because bowel approvals differ. Always ask specifically about bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain and known bowel inflammation before prescribing an IL-17 inhibitor for spondyloarthritis or psoriatic arthritis.

stem: A 28-year-old man has asymmetric oligoarthritis, conjunctivitis and inflammatory heel pain three weeks after microbiologically confirmed Campylobacter enteritis. Joint aspirate shows inflammatory sterile fluid. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Gonococcal septic arthritis
options.B: Osteoarthritis
options.C: Rheumatoid arthritis
options.D: Calcium pyrophosphate arthritis
options.E: Reactive arthritis

explanation: An antecedent gastrointestinal infection followed by sterile peripheral arthritis and enthesitis supports reactive arthritis. Reactive arthritis usually appears days to weeks after gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection and is frequently asymmetric with enthesitis or extra-articular inflammation. Exclude a septic joint when clinically indicated. Initial management centres on NSAIDs and local measures; persistent disease may require a DMARD. The course contrasts reactive arthritis with septic or disseminated gonococcal infection: preceding infection is supportive, but a new hot joint still requires consideration of aspiration.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with an acutely swollen knee has synovial fluid showing positively birefringent rhomboid crystals and a white cell count of 48,000/microlitre. She is febrile and diabetic. What is the most important additional test on the aspirate?

options.A: Anti-CCP antibody testing on the aspirate
options.B: Gram stain and bacterial culture
options.C: Rheumatoid factor measurement on the synovial fluid
options.D: Serum urate level alone, assuming this confirms gout
options.E: HLA-B27 typing from a peripheral blood sample

explanation: Crystal identification does not exclude concomitant septic arthritis, particularly with systemic features. CPP crystals establish crystal deposition but cannot exclude concomitant bacterial infection. Send Gram stain and culture, including appropriate blood cultures if febrile. A high synovial leukocyte count and immunometabolic risk factors strengthen the need for urgent septic arthritis assessment. On polarised microscopy, CPP crystals are commonly rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent; monosodium urate crystals are needle-like and strongly negatively birefringent.

stem: A 69-year-old patient presents with first acute monoarthritis of the wrist; radiographs show chondrocalcinosis and aspiration reveals weakly positively birefringent crystals. Which underlying metabolic disorder is a recognised association worth assessing in recurrent or atypical CPPD?

options.A: Wilson disease, given the chondrocalcinosis on imaging
options.B: Addison disease, because of the recurrent acute arthritis
options.C: Type 1 diabetes, as a presumed CPPD association
options.D: Hyperparathyroidism
options.E: Hypoparathyroidism, due to low circulating parathyroid hormone

explanation: CPPD may accompany hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis, hypomagnesaemia or hypophosphatasia. CPPD associations include hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis, hypomagnesaemia and hypothyroidism. Investigations should be proportionate to age, recurrence and atypical distribution. Consider both calcium/phosphate/PTH and iron indices when the presentation suggests a secondary cause. Chondrocalcinosis may also occur with osteoarthritis or asymptomatic CPP deposition. A younger patient or unusual distribution particularly strengthens the case for secondary metabolic testing.

stem: A 45-year-old man with gout and chronic kidney disease has recurrent flares and tophi despite taking 100 mg of allopurinol daily; serum urate is 510 micromol/L. What is the most appropriate long-term strategy?

options.A: Aim for a maintenance serum urate above 500 micromol/L
options.B: Stop allopurinol permanently because of his chronic kidney disease
options.C: Treat flares only with a prolonged course of oral antibiotics
options.D: Titrate urate-lowering treatment towards a target with monitoring
options.E: Change to aspirin monotherapy for long-term urate control

explanation: Allopurinol can be started low and carefully titrated in CKD; aim below 360 micromol/L, and consider below 300 with tophi. NICE NG219 recommends treat-to-target urate-lowering therapy with dose adjustment guided by monthly urate testing. Aim below 360 micromol/L, and consider below 300 micromol/L in tophaceous or persistently symptomatic gout. CKD calls for lower starting doses and careful titration, not automatic permanent withdrawal. Hyperuricaemia alone does not diagnose gout, and serum urate can fall during a flare; treatment decisions should account for clinical burden, crystal evidence and long-term urate targets.

stem: A 59-year-old man taking allopurinol for tophaceous gout presents with a typical flare. He is afebrile with no concern about infection. What should usually happen to established urate-lowering therapy during the flare?

options.A: Replace it with high-dose aspirin until the flare settles
options.B: Continue allopurinol while treating the flare
options.C: Change to probenecid for one week during the flare
options.D: Stop allopurinol until all joint pain has fully resolved
options.E: Double the dose immediately without review

explanation: Do not routinely interrupt established urate-lowering therapy during gout attacks; provide appropriate flare treatment. Stopping established allopurinol during a flare risks subsequent urate fluctuation and poorer long-term control. Treat acute inflammation with a suitable NSAID, low-dose colchicine or corticosteroid, adjusting for renal function, comorbidities and interactions. Review urate control after the episode. The crystal arthropathy section stresses that treating inflammation and dissolving urate deposits are distinct goals: continuing background urate lowering does not replace acute-flare therapy.

stem: A 36-year-old woman is starting urate-lowering treatment for frequent gout attacks. She asks about preventing early flares during titration. Which accompanying approach is appropriate when not contraindicated?

options.A: Routine high-dose antibiotic prophylaxis for six weeks
options.B: Avoid all anti-inflammatory agents throughout titration
options.C: Long-term cyclophosphamide to prevent further flares
options.D: Daily intravenous methylprednisolone during titration
options.E: Low-dose colchicine prophylaxis during initiation and titration

explanation: Flare prophylaxis, commonly low-dose colchicine, reduces mobilisation flares when urate-lowering therapy begins. Starting urate-lowering treatment can mobilise deposits and precipitate early flares. NICE NG219 recommends considering colchicine while achieving target urate; if unsuitable, other anti-inflammatory prophylaxis may be considered. Tailor colchicine to kidney function and interacting drugs, and explain its temporary preventive purpose. Counselling should explain that mobilisation of stored urate after initiating treatment can transiently increase flares even while the long-term therapeutic strategy is working.

stem: A 72-year-old patient has severe acute knee pain, fever, CRP 220 mg/L and turbid aspirate. Gram stain is negative but the cell count is 110,000/microlitre with 94% neutrophils. What is the most appropriate next action?

options.A: Wait two weeks and simply repeat the CRP before acting
options.B: Label this presentation as osteoarthritis and discharge
options.C: Inject corticosteroid into the knee immediately, before culture results
options.D: Urgent management for suspected septic arthritis while cultures are pending
options.E: Exclude infection outright because the Gram stain is negative

explanation: A negative Gram stain cannot exclude septic arthritis; urgent microbiological sampling, antibiotics and drainage planning are required. A negative Gram stain does not rule out septic arthritis. Obtain synovial cultures and blood cultures before antibiotics where this does not delay critical treatment; urgent orthopaedic/infectious disease review, antimicrobial therapy and drainage assessment are indicated. Never inject intra-articular steroid into an infected joint. The joint infection module cautions that inflammatory and septic synovial-fluid white-cell counts overlap; neither a threshold nor a negative Gram stain reliably rules out infection.

stem: A 66-year-old man has recurrent haemarthroses and disproportionate ankle arthropathy. Ferritin and transferrin saturation are elevated; hand radiographs show hook-like osteophytes at the second and third MCP joints. Which diagnosis best explains the arthropathy?

options.A: Reactive arthritis following a preceding infection
options.B: Rheumatoid arthritis with atypical joint distribution
options.C: Ochronosis secondary to alkaptonuria
options.D: Primary hyperoxaluria with calcium oxalate deposition
options.E: Hereditary haemochromatosis

explanation: MCP hook osteophytes, iron overload and atypical joint involvement suggest haemochromatosis arthropathy. Haemochromatosis arthropathy commonly involves MCP joints and can mimic inflammatory arthritis or CPPD. Hook-like osteophytes and high transferrin saturation are clues. Genetic testing and liver assessment may be appropriate; venesection treats iron overload but established arthropathy may persist. The course identifies second and third MCP disease with characteristic hook osteophytes as a clue to haemochromatosis arthropathy, often accompanied by CPP crystal deposition.

stem: A 43-year-old man reports alternating buttock pain, waking in the second half of the night, and improvement on exercise. Pelvic X-ray is normal but CRP is raised. Which investigation is most useful if axial spondyloarthritis remains suspected?

options.A: A routine CT scan of the lumbar spine alone
options.B: Hand ultrasonography looking for synovitis
options.C: Repeating the plain pelvis X-ray again the next day
options.D: Dual-energy X-ray bone densitometry
options.E: MRI of sacroiliac joints using inflammatory sequences

explanation: MRI can detect active sacroiliitis in non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis when plain films are unrevealing. MRI sacroiliac joints using inflammation-sensitive sequences helps identify active sacroiliitis when plain films remain normal. Imaging findings must be interpreted alongside clinical pattern and alternative causes of marrow oedema, including mechanical loading and postpartum changes. Inflammatory back pain features improve the pre-test probability but are not diagnostic; MRI bone-marrow oedema may also reflect mechanical stress, so imaging needs clinical correlation.

stem: A 48-year-old woman with erosive RA develops new gait instability, hand clumsiness and hyperreflexia. Cervical movement provokes paraesthesia. What is the most urgent investigation?

options.A: MRI of the cervical spine with urgent spinal assessment
options.B: A plain chest radiograph alone
options.C: Routine DEXA bone densitometry only
options.D: An elective outpatient foot ultrasound
options.E: Simply repeating the rheumatoid factor test

explanation: Signs of cervical cord compromise in RA require urgent MRI and specialist evaluation. Neurological deficit in RA with suspected cervical instability warrants urgent cervical spine MRI and specialist spinal assessment; immobilisation precautions may be appropriate. Atlantoaxial subluxation and pannus can threaten the cord, and plain flexion-extension radiographs alone cannot assess neural compression. Longstanding erosive disease may damage the transverse ligament and cervical joints; clinical signs of myelopathy take priority over reassuring appearances on earlier plain radiographs.

stem: A 57-year-old woman with poorly controlled seropositive RA develops neutropenia, recurrent infections and splenomegaly. What is the most likely syndrome?

options.A: Behcet syndrome
options.B: Schnitzler syndrome
options.C: RS3PE
options.D: Adult-onset Still disease
options.E: Felty syndrome

explanation: The triad of longstanding RA, neutropenia and splenomegaly suggests Felty syndrome; exclude LGL leukaemia and other causes. Felty syndrome classically combines established RA, neutropenia and splenomegaly. Check infections, medication toxicity and other causes of cytopenia; large granular lymphocytic leukaemia is an important mimic requiring haematological evaluation, sometimes with flow cytometry and clonality testing. Neutropenia in RA requires a broad differential including medication toxicity, infection, hypersplenism and clonal lymphoproliferative disease, not just Felty syndrome.

stem: A 62-year-old man with RA develops progressive neutropenia and splenomegaly. Peripheral smear shows increased large granular lymphocytes. Which investigation best distinguishes an alternative haematological cause from Felty syndrome?

options.A: Serum urate level, assuming this represents a gouty flare
options.B: Anti-dsDNA antibody testing for lupus activity
options.C: HLA-B27 typing, assuming underlying axial disease
options.D: A plain hand radiograph alone looking for erosions
options.E: Peripheral blood flow cytometry with T-cell clonality testing

explanation: T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukaemia can mimic Felty syndrome and requires haematological immunophenotyping/clonality assessment. T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukaemia can coexist with rheumatoid arthritis and neutropenia. Peripheral blood immunophenotyping and T-cell receptor clonality testing help distinguish it from Felty syndrome; haematology input is appropriate, especially with severe neutropenia or recurrent infections. Large granular lymphocyte disorders may feature chronic neutropenia and autoimmune arthritis; peripheral blood flow cytometry and molecular clonality testing assess this important mimic.

stem: A 37-year-old man develops abrupt, recurrent attacks of painful MCP swelling lasting two days with complete return to normal function between attacks. Anti-CCP is strongly positive. Which is the most likely clinical syndrome?

options.A: Palindromic rheumatism
options.B: Septic arthritis
options.C: Established destructive rheumatoid arthritis
options.D: Osteoarthritis
options.E: Polymyalgia rheumatica

explanation: Brief self-limited attacks with symptom-free intervals suggest palindromic rheumatism; anti-CCP positivity predicts RA risk. Palindromic rheumatism produces self-limited episodes with return to baseline between attacks. Anti-CCP positivity increases the likelihood of later persistent RA, so follow for sustained synovitis and radiographic progression. Hydroxychloroquine may be considered for frequent attacks after assessment. The episodic, fully reversible nature of palindromic rheumatism distinguishes it from persistent RA synovitis; ACPA positivity modifies future-risk counselling.

stem: A 51-year-old woman with RA continues to have a high DAS28 and elevated CRP after six months of verified optimal csDMARD treatment. Which principle should direct subsequent treatment selection?

options.A: Treat only once radiographic erosions become visible
options.B: Accept persistent moderate disease activity indefinitely
options.C: Treat-to-target escalation to achieve remission or low disease activity
options.D: Use analgesics alone instead of disease-modifying treatment
options.E: Monitor disease activity annually only

explanation: Active RA warrants systematic reassessment and escalation towards remission or low disease activity. Treat-to-target requires regular objective disease-activity assessment, timely treatment adjustment and a shared remission or low-activity target. The 2025 EULAR RA update incorporates comorbidity and safety considerations, including JAK-inhibitor risks, when choosing the next mechanism. Treat-to-target assessments should document swollen and tender joint counts plus inflammatory markers and patient assessment, while avoiding escalation based on non-inflammatory pain alone.

stem: A 44-year-old patient with longstanding seronegative peripheral arthritis has recurrent painful oral ulcers, genital ulcers and posterior uveitis with retinal vasculitis. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Relapsing polychondritis
options.B: Behcet syndrome
options.C: Primary Sjogren syndrome
options.D: Psoriatic arthritis
options.E: Sarcoid arthropathy

explanation: Recurrent mucosal ulcers with retinal vasculitis strongly support Behcet syndrome. Behcet syndrome is a clinical diagnosis; there is no single diagnostic blood test. Retinal vasculitis is organ-threatening and requires urgent ophthalmological assessment and systemic immunosuppression tailored to severity. Recurrent oral ulcers alone are insufficient to establish the diagnosis. Behcet disease is a variable-vessel vasculitis; ocular, neurological and vascular disease carry greater organ-threatening implications than isolated mucocutaneous lesions.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with severe destructive RA has red eyes with deep, boring ocular pain and scleral tenderness. Vision is reduced. What is the most concerning ocular complication?

options.A: Allergic conjunctivitis
options.B: Necrotising scleritis
options.C: Dry-eye syndrome
options.D: Simple episcleritis
options.E: Presbyopia

explanation: Severe painful scleritis in RA may threaten vision and signal systemic vasculitis; urgent ophthalmological assessment is needed. Scleritis typically causes severe deep ocular pain and may threaten sight, whereas episcleritis is usually more superficial. Urgent ophthalmology referral is required. Necrotising scleritis can indicate severe systemic RA-associated vasculitis and may require systemic immunosuppression. The eye-symptoms module distinguishes superficial episcleritis from deep scleritis by severity of pain and potential visual risk; scleral inflammation merits urgent specialist assessment.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with SLE develops rising urine protein-creatinine ratio, haematuria with casts and declining complement despite few systemic symptoms. Which investigation most directly classifies renal disease to guide induction treatment?

options.A: Skin biopsy
options.B: HLA-B27 testing
options.C: Plain renal radiograph
options.D: Anti-Ro titre alone
options.E: Kidney biopsy

explanation: Renal biopsy defines lupus nephritis class and activity/chronicity, guiding treatment decisions after contraindications are assessed. Proteinuria, active urinary sediment and falling complement support possible lupus nephritis, but histology determines class, activity, chronicity and relevant mimics. The ACR 2024 guideline recommends prompt biopsy when lupus nephritis is suspected unless contraindicated; treatment intensity should be pathology-guided. Urinary protein quantification, blood pressure, creatinine, sediment and complement trends inform suspicion, but kidney biopsy supplies the proliferative versus membranous histological distinction.

stem: A woman with active proliferative lupus nephritis is already receiving hydroxychloroquine and glucocorticoids. Which drug is an established induction treatment backbone?

options.A: Etanercept, used as induction therapy for nephritis
options.B: Sulfasalazine, as an induction immunosuppressant
options.C: Allopurinol, to reduce inflammatory renal injury
options.D: Colchicine, for its anti-inflammatory renal effect
options.E: Mycophenolate mofetil

explanation: Mycophenolate is an established treatment backbone for active class III/IV lupus nephritis. The 2024 ACR guideline conditionally recommends combination (triple) therapy comprising glucocorticoids plus either a mycophenolic-acid analogue and belimumab, a mycophenolic-acid analogue and a calcineurin inhibitor, or low-dose cyclophosphamide and belimumab followed by mycophenolate. Treatment selection depends on the kidney biopsy, proteinuria, renal function, extrarenal activity and patient factors.

stem: A 24-year-old with SLE taking 400 mg hydroxychloroquine daily weighs 48 kg and has eGFR 40 mL/min/1.73 m2. Which long-term safety concern needs particular attention?

options.A: Ototoxicity caused by concurrent low-dose folate supplementation
options.B: Retinal toxicity due to high weight-adjusted dose and renal impairment
options.C: New rheumatoid nodules related to hydroxychloroquine
options.D: Permanent neutrophilia from chronic hydroxychloroquine use
options.E: Rapid urate nephropathy secondary to hydroxychloroquine

explanation: Hydroxychloroquine target dosing around 5 mg/kg actual weight/day requires individualisation; impaired renal function increases retinal risk. Retinal toxicity risk is associated with daily dose per actual body weight, renal impairment and duration of exposure. At 48 kg, 400 mg daily greatly exceeds the commonly advised 5 mg/kg/day threshold. Reassess dose and ensure risk-adapted ophthalmic monitoring. The lupus modules distinguish the benefits of continuing hydroxychloroquine from dose-dependent retinal toxicity; renal impairment and duration of exposure increase screening importance.

stem: A 31-year-old with SLE is in partial remission but requires prednisolone 12.5 mg daily for persistent arthritis and rash despite hydroxychloroquine. Which longer-term strategy aligns with contemporary lupus recommendations?

options.A: Stop hydroxychloroquine routinely once remission is reached
options.B: Add steroid-sparing immunomodulatory therapy and reduce prednisolone
options.C: Maintain prednisolone 12.5 mg indefinitely without review
options.D: Use continuous low-dose antibiotics as steroid-sparing therapy
options.E: Replace prednisolone with high-dose aspirin long term

explanation: EULAR and ACR emphasise minimising chronic glucocorticoid exposure, using immunomodulatory agents to enable tapering. Long-term oral glucocorticoids carry cumulative infection, metabolic, cardiovascular and bone risks. The 2025 ACR and 2023 EULAR lupus recommendations support early steroid-sparing escalation when activity persists; choose agents according to manifestations and pregnancy plans, while maintaining hydroxychloroquine when suitable. Persistently requiring moderate-dose glucocorticoids suggests inadequate disease control and cumulative toxicity risk; steroid-sparing treatment should be assessed against objective disease activity.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has three early miscarriages and persistently positive lupus anticoagulant. She is now pregnant, with no prior thrombosis. Which is the usual antithrombotic strategy for obstetric APS?

options.A: Low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin
options.B: Dual antiplatelet therapy alone, without anticoagulation
options.C: No treatment despite confirmed antiphospholipid syndrome
options.D: Full-dose warfarin continued throughout the pregnancy
options.E: Rivaroxaban as a direct oral anticoagulant

explanation: Obstetric APS generally requires aspirin plus prophylactic heparin during pregnancy, with individualised postpartum planning. Pregnancy management for obstetric APS generally combines low-dose aspirin with prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin, with antenatal surveillance. Women with previous thrombosis usually require therapeutic anticoagulation instead. Confirm laboratory persistence and discuss postpartum thromboprophylaxis. Pregnancy management depends on whether antiphospholipid antibodies are associated with obstetric events, prior thrombosis, or neither; review medication safety and maternal-fetal surveillance.

stem: A woman with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis has rapid skin progression and a new blood pressure of 190/110, acute kidney injury and microangiopathic haemolysis after recent high-dose glucocorticoids. What is the urgent treatment priority?

options.A: An elective renal biopsy performed before any treatment
options.B: Stopping all antihypertensive medication immediately
options.C: Starting NSAIDs and continuing to observe
options.D: Escalating high-dose prednisolone further
options.E: Start an ACE inhibitor promptly with specialist monitoring

explanation: Scleroderma renal crisis is an emergency requiring rapid ACE inhibition; glucocorticoids increase risk. Scleroderma renal crisis is defined by rapidly developing hypertension, AKI and often microangiopathic haemolysis. ACE inhibition is urgent even if creatinine initially rises; monitor potassium, renal function and blood pressure closely and involve nephrology. High-dose glucocorticoids are a recognised risk factor. Abrupt hypertension, acute kidney injury and microangiopathic haemolysis are classic scleroderma renal crisis clues; normal baseline blood pressure does not eliminate risk.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis develops increasing exertional dyspnoea, falling DLCO and basal inspiratory crackles. Which investigation is most appropriate for assessing suspected interstitial lung disease?

options.A: A plain wrist radiograph
options.B: High-resolution CT chest
options.C: Diagnostic arthroscopy of the knee
options.D: Whole-body bone scintigraphy
options.E: A serum urate level

explanation: HRCT is central to assessing systemic-sclerosis ILD alongside pulmonary function testing and multidisciplinary review. HRCT characterises the pattern and extent of SSc-associated ILD; PFTs including FVC/DLCO provide complementary baseline and surveillance data. ACR/CHEST suggests monitoring PFTs every 3-6 months during the first year of SSc-ILD, adjusted for stability and severity. Systemic sclerosis lung disease assessment relies on HRCT and serial FVC/DLCO, because symptoms and auscultation alone may underestimate interstitial involvement.

stem: A 46-year-old patient with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis has progressive dyspnoea, normal spirometry and disproportionately reduced DLCO. Echocardiography suggests elevated pulmonary arterial pressure. What is required to confirm pulmonary hypertension haemodynamics?

options.A: Right-heart catheterisation
options.B: A chest radiograph alone
options.C: A serum ACE level
options.D: An ultrasound of the left ankle
options.E: Repeating the ANA alone

explanation: Right-heart catheterisation confirms and characterises pulmonary hypertension, differentiating pre-from post-capillary disease. Right-heart catheterisation establishes haemodynamic pulmonary hypertension and discriminates precapillary disease from left-heart or other causes. Echocardiography is a screening assessment, not definitive classification. Systemic sclerosis patients require ongoing cardiopulmonary surveillance. A disproportionate fall in DLCO with relatively preserved lung volumes should raise suspicion of pulmonary vascular disease, while also prompting evaluation for concomitant ILD and other causes.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has proximal muscle weakness, mechanic’s hands, Raynaud phenomenon and ILD; anti- Jo-1 is positive. Which unifying syndrome is most likely?

options.A: Muscular dystrophy with secondary Raynaud phenomenon
options.B: Antisynthetase syndrome
options.C: Polymyalgia rheumatica with incidental lung findings
options.D: Sarcoidosis presenting with myopathy
options.E: Inclusion-body myositis with coincidental ILD

explanation: Antisynthetase antibodies with myositis, ILD and characteristic hands support antisynthetase syndrome. Antisynthetase syndrome may feature myositis, ILD, inflammatory arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, fever and mechanic’s hands. ILD can precede muscle disease, so HRCT and full PFT assessment are important. Autoantibody subtype informs phenotype but does not replace organ assessment. Mechanic hands, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon and ILD together form an antisynthetase-spectrum presentation; myositis may be subtle or clinically absent.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with dermatomyositis is positive for anti-TIF1-gamma and has progressive weight loss. Which additional assessment has particularly high priority?

options.A: HLA-B27 typing as the priority investigation
options.B: Routine urate estimation only
options.C: Risk-stratified malignancy screening
options.D: Immediate joint replacement surgery
options.E: Screening for haemochromatosis alone

explanation: Anti-TIF1-gamma adult dermatomyositis is associated with increased cancer risk; screening should be risk-adapted. Adult dermatomyositis has a malignancy association, particularly with anti-TIF1-gamma. Follow current international risk-stratified cancer screening recommendations, with age-appropriate and enhanced investigations when indicated by high-risk phenotype, symptoms and local protocol. Myositis-specific antibodies help identify clinical phenotypes and malignancy risk, but screening intensity must be tailored to age, symptoms and the full antibody profile.

stem: A 48-year-old woman with inflammatory myopathy has rapidly progressive ILD, painful palmar papules and minimal muscle weakness. Anti-MDA5 is strongly positive. What is the greatest immediate threat?

options.A: Rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease
options.B: Carpal tunnel syndrome from the papular skin changes
options.C: Hyperparathyroidism presenting with weakness
options.D: Secondary osteoarthritis of the hands
options.E: Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia

explanation: Anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis is associated with potentially fulminant ILD requiring urgent specialised management. Anti-MDA5 disease is strongly linked to rapidly progressive ILD even when overt myositis is minimal. Arrange immediate respiratory/rheumatology multidisciplinary evaluation, oxygenation assessment and HRCT/PFTs as feasible. Treatment often requires rapid combination immunomodulation rather than routine observation. Anti-MDA5-associated dermatomyositis may have little measurable muscle weakness despite severe lung involvement, making respiratory trajectory and oxygen requirement especially important.

stem: A 56-year-old woman with sicca symptoms, positive anti-Ro and parotid enlargement develops purpura, low C4 and monoclonal gammopathy. Which serious complication must be excluded?

options.A: Osteoid osteoma
options.B: B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma
options.C: Osteonecrosis of femoral head
options.D: Reactive arthritis
options.E: Ankylosing spondylitis

explanation: Persistent salivary swelling, purpura, low complement and monoclonality are lymphoma risk features in Sjogren disease. Persistent gland enlargement, palpable purpura, low C4, cryoglobulinaemia or monoclonal gammopathy raise concern for B-cell lymphoma in Sjogren disease. Investigate with imaging and tissue sampling of suspicious lesions, rather than attributing enlarging glands to uncomplicated sicca disease. Sjögren disease accompanied by persistent salivary gland enlargement, low complement, purpura or cryoglobulins calls for assessment of systemic activity and lymphoproliferative complications.

stem: A 71-year-old woman has new temporal headache, scalp tenderness and transient monocular visual loss. ESR is 92 mm/h; temporal artery ultrasound cannot be organised today. Which immediate step is most appropriate?

options.A: Begin high-dose glucocorticoids urgently and arrange rapid assessment
options.B: Wait for temporal artery biopsy before starting any treatment
options.C: Repeat the ESR again in four weeks’ time
options.D: Give only paracetamol for symptom control
options.E: Start methotrexate monotherapy without glucocorticoids

explanation: Visual ischaemic symptoms in suspected GCA require immediate treatment without waiting for imaging or biopsy. Suspected GCA with amaurosis fugax is a time-critical sight-threatening emergency. Start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately and obtain urgent ophthalmology/vascular ultrasound assessment; imaging or biopsy must not delay treatment. Consider intravenous therapy for acute visual threat according to local protocols. Cranial ischaemic symptoms in suspected giant cell arteritis require immediate treatment; ultrasonography and biopsy support diagnosis but must not delay protection of vision.

stem: A 67-year-old patient has suspected giant cell arteritis but temporal artery ultrasound is negative after two weeks of glucocorticoids. She has limb claudication and unequal arm blood pressures. Which investigation best explores large-vessel involvement?

options.A: A routine bone density scan to assess osteoporosis risk
options.B: Repeating the rheumatoid factor test for diagnostic clarity
options.C: Cross-sectional vascular imaging such as PET-CT, CTA or MRA
options.D: An MRI of the heel alone to assess enthesitis
options.E: A plain cervical spine X-ray for vertebral disease

explanation: A negative temporal ultrasound does not exclude large-vessel GCA; choose vascular imaging based on context and availability. Temporal artery ultrasound loses sensitivity after treatment and can be negative in predominantly extracranial GCA. CTA, MRA or FDG-PET/CT can assess aortic branches and large-vessel inflammation depending on availability and steroid exposure. Clinical probability remains central. A negative temporal artery study does not completely exclude giant cell arteritis, particularly after treatment; consider large-vessel imaging when suspicion persists.

stem: A 74-year-old patient with classic bilateral shoulder and hip stiffness has persistent CRP elevation, fever, anaemia and a limited response to glucocorticoids. What is the most important clinical action?

options.A: Escalate steroids indefinitely without reassessment
options.B: Attribute the fever and anaemia to coexisting osteoarthritis
options.C: Diagnose fibromyalgia automatically without further review
options.D: Exclude disease because rheumatoid factor is negative
options.E: Re-evaluate for mimics including infection or malignancy

explanation: Atypical symptoms and poor steroid response warrant reassessment rather than automatic PMR dose escalation. Atypical or refractory PMR warrants reassessment for occult infection, malignancy, inflammatory arthritis, myopathy and GCA rather than indefinite glucocorticoid escalation. The 2026 BSR PMR guidance reinforces structured reassessment and steroid-sparing options in selected patients. The polymyalgia rheumatica module flags striking constitutional symptoms, refractory inflammation or atypical patterns as reasons to revisit malignancy, infection and large-vessel vasculitis.

stem: A 34-year-old man has recurrent sinusitis, otitis, cavitating lung nodules, haematuria and positive PR3- ANCA. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Polyarteritis nodosa without ANCA positivity
options.B: Microscopic polyangiitis with renal-limited disease
options.C: Takayasu arteritis affecting large vessels
options.D: IgA vasculitis with isolated skin and gut involvement
options.E: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis

explanation: Upper airway disease, cavitating pulmonary nodules, renal involvement and PR3-ANCA favour GPA. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis often combines ENT destruction, pulmonary nodules/cavitation and pauci-immune glomerulonephritis. PR3-ANCA supports but does not prove the diagnosis; tissue biopsy should be obtained where safe without delaying organ-saving therapy. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis combines ENT, pulmonary and renal disease; tissue confirmation should be sought where feasible without delaying treatment of rapidly progressive organ damage.

stem: A 60-year-old patient presents with pulmonary haemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis attributed to ANCA-associated vasculitis. Which induction approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Hydroxychloroquine alone, without any immunosuppressive agent
options.B: Delaying treatment until ANCA titres normalise spontaneously
options.C: Colchicine monotherapy for the vasculitic process
options.D: An intra-articular steroid injection into one joint only
options.E: Glucocorticoids with rituximab or cyclophosphamide under urgent specialist care

explanation: Life-or organ-threatening ANCA vasculitis needs urgent remission induction with rituximab or cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoids. Life-or organ-threatening AAV is treated urgently with glucocorticoids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide. Steroid-sparing avacopan may be considered in selected GPA/MPA patients; plasma exchange is not routine for every pulmonary-renal presentation and depends on renal severity and clinical circumstances. Pulmonary-renal syndrome needs parallel investigation for ANCA-associated disease, anti-GBM antibodies and mimics; life-threatening haemorrhage and renal decline warrant urgent multidisciplinary management.

stem: A 52-year-old patient has adult-onset asthma, marked eosinophilia, mononeuritis multiplex, pulmonary infiltrates and sinus disease. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: IgG4-related pancreatitis presenting with eosinophilia
options.B: Polymyalgia rheumatica with incidental eosinophilia
options.C: Behcet syndrome with pulmonary involvement
options.D: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
options.E: Rheumatoid vasculitis with asthma

explanation: Asthma, eosinophilic inflammation and systemic vasculitic neuropathy suggest EGPA. EGPA commonly combines asthma, eosinophilia, sinus inflammation and vasculitic neuropathy. ANCA may be negative. Treatment is determined by severity: organ-threatening vasculitis warrants induction immunosuppression, whereas selected non-organ-threatening disease may benefit from anti-IL-5 approaches. In eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, asthma and eosinophilia may precede overt vasculitis; peripheral neuropathy and cardiac disease help define severity.

stem: A 42-year-old man has livedo racemosa, painful testicular swelling, hypertension, abdominal pain and multiple mononeuropathies. Urine sediment is bland and ANCA is negative. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: IgA nephropathy
options.B: Lupus nephritis
options.C: Microscopic polyangiitis
options.D: Anti-GBM disease
options.E: Polyarteritis nodosa

explanation: Medium-vessel PAN can cause mesenteric, testicular and neurologic ischaemia but typically spares glomeruli and lungs. Polyarteritis nodosa causes medium-vessel ischaemia and neuropathy without typical glomerulonephritis or pulmonary capillaritis. Assess hepatitis B status and look for visceral aneurysms on appropriate angiography. Disease severity and viral association govern treatment. Polyarteritis nodosa predominantly affects medium arteries and typically lacks glomerulonephritis or pulmonary capillaritis; vascular imaging may reveal microaneurysms.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has arm claudication, asymmetrical upper limb pulses and an audible subclavian bruit; PET imaging shows aortic branch inflammation. Which disease is most likely?

options.A: Takayasu arteritis
options.B: Giant cell arteritis
options.C: Kawasaki disease
options.D: Thromboangiitis obliterans
options.E: Polyarteritis nodosa

explanation: Large-vessel vasculitis in a young woman with pulse deficits is characteristic of Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis causing pulse discrepancy, limb claudication and bruits, often in younger patients. CTA/MRA or PET can document vessel involvement; exclude mimics and evaluate for stenosis-related hypertension and organ ischaemia. Large-vessel inflammation can cause pulse asymmetry, bruits and limb claudication before fixed stenoses become apparent; PET and angiographic techniques address different aspects of activity and anatomy.

stem: A 30-year-old man with recurrent aphthae, genital ulcers and retinal vasculitis develops painful haemoptysis; CTA demonstrates pulmonary artery aneurysms. What is the most important management consideration?

options.A: Urgent specialist immunosuppression; avoid uncritical anticoagulation
options.B: Observing without treatment for up to a year before reassessment
options.C: Offering diagnostic arthrocentesis of an unaffected joint
options.D: Treating this presentation as isolated oral candidiasis
options.E: Routine anticoagulation without any vascular specialist review

explanation: Pulmonary arterial aneurysms in Behcet disease are life-threatening; bleeding risk makes anticoagulation decisions complex. Pulmonary artery aneurysm in Behcet disease carries a major haemorrhage risk; anticoagulation can be hazardous and should not be instituted reflexively for presumed pulmonary embolism. Urgent multidisciplinary assessment and powerful immunosuppression are usually central, with intervention for selected vascular lesions. Behcet-associated pulmonary artery aneurysm can cause catastrophic haemorrhage; invasive vascular intervention requires coordination with systemic control of vessel-wall inflammation.

stem: A 46-year-old woman has steroid-responsive bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement, pancreatic swelling and retroperitoneal fibrosis; serum IgG4 is elevated. Which test best establishes the diagnosis while excluding mimics?

options.A: A routine bone density scan
options.B: Appropriate tissue biopsy showing characteristic histopathology
options.C: An isolated positive ANA result
options.D: Diagnostic joint aspiration
options.E: A serum IgG4 level alone, without tissue confirmation

explanation: IgG4-related disease requires clinicopathological assessment; serum IgG4 is neither sufficiently sensitive nor specific. Elevated serum IgG4 is not diagnostic by itself. Biopsy assesses dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis where applicable, while excluding lymphoma and malignancy. Organ context and the proportion of IgG4-positive plasma cells matter. IgG4-related disease can affect pancreas, lacrimal glands and retroperitoneum, but a serum IgG4 rise alone is insufficient; tissue pathology and malignancy exclusion are central.

stem: A 37-year-old woman with lupus has fever, cytopenias, ferritin 18,000 micrograms/L, hypofibrinogenaemia and rising liver enzymes. Which complication is most likely?

options.A: Fibromyalgia with incidental cytopenias
options.B: Isolated serositis from active lupus
options.C: Uncomplicated iron-deficiency anaemia
options.D: Osteoarthritis with reactive cytopenias
options.E: Macrophage activation syndrome / secondary HLH

explanation: Extreme ferritin elevation with cytopenias, coagulopathy and organ dysfunction suggests hyperinflammatory HLH/MAS. Macrophage activation syndrome/secondary HLH causes hyperinflammation with marked ferritin elevation, cytopenias, falling fibrinogen and hepatic injury. It is life-threatening and demands urgent investigation for infection and triggers plus prompt specialist immunomodulatory treatment. Macrophage activation syndrome may be recognised by paradoxically falling ESR as fibrinogen is consumed, together with cytopenias, liver injury and rapidly rising ferritin.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis has painful digital ulcers despite warming measures and a calcium channel blocker. No critical infection is present. Which therapy class can be considered for persistent ischaemic digital disease?

options.A: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor
options.B: A systemic beta blocker for vasospasm
options.C: Subcutaneous calcitonin for digital ischaemia
options.D: Allopurinol for presumed crystal deposition
options.E: A thiazide diuretic used alone

explanation: PDE5 inhibitors can improve refractory Raynaud symptoms and digital ulcers; severe ischaemia may require intravenous prostanoids. Persistent systemic-sclerosis digital ulcers can benefit from phosphodiesterase-5 inhibition and, for severe refractory disease, intravenous prostanoid therapy. Assess for critical ischaemia, infection and local wound care needs; endothelin-receptor antagonists may reduce new ulcers in selected patients. Scleroderma digital ulcers are associated with structural microvascular disease as well as vasospasm; assess infection, tissue ischaemia and the need for specialist vasodilator escalation.

stem: A 53-year-old man has recurrent auricular chondritis sparing the lobule, nasal bridge inflammation, episcleritis and progressive hoarseness. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Granuloma annulare affecting the ear
options.B: Rosacea with secondary nasal inflammation
options.C: Tophaceous gout of the ear cartilage
options.D: Relapsing polychondritis
options.E: Psoriatic arthritis with ear involvement

explanation: Inflammation of cartilage-rich structures with ocular and airway disease suggests relapsing polychondritis. Relapsing polychondritis affects cartilaginous structures; sparing of the soft ear lobule is characteristic. Airway involvement may cause dangerous stenosis or malacia, so hoarseness and respiratory symptoms warrant urgent airway assessment and appropriate imaging/bronchoscopy planning. Relapsing polychondritis affects cartilaginous structures of the ears, nose and airway; stridor, voice change or respiratory difficulty should trigger urgent airway assessment.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with recurrent lacrimal and salivary swelling, hypergammaglobulinaemia and suspected Sjogren syndrome is anti-Ro negative. Which investigation can provide objective histological support for Sjogren classification?

options.A: Serum urate
options.B: Labial minor salivary gland biopsy
options.C: Temporal artery biopsy
options.D: HLA-B27 testing
options.E: Bone scintigraphy

explanation: Minor salivary gland focal lymphocytic sialadenitis supports classification when serology is uninformative. Labial salivary gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis may help classify seronegative Sjogren disease when clinical suspicion remains strong. Correlate with objective tear/saliva testing and exclude alternative causes of sicca and gland enlargement. Recurrent gland swelling has a differential extending beyond Sjögren disease, including IgG4-related disease, sarcoidosis and lymphoproliferative pathology; biopsy may be decisive.

stem: A 52-year-old man has unexplained skin tightening of the fingers, Raynaud phenomenon, abnormal nailfold capillaries and new dysphagia. Which autoantibody is associated particularly with diffuse skin involvement and interstitial lung disease in systemic sclerosis?

options.A: Anti-mitochondrial M2
options.B: Anti-AChR
options.C: Anti-CCP
options.D: Anti-GBM
options.E: Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70)

explanation: Anti-topoisomerase I positivity is associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis and ILD risk, though assessment is clinical. Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) is associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and increased ILD risk, whereas anticentromere antibodies associate more often with limited cutaneous disease and pulmonary vascular complications. Antibodies support phenotyping but do not determine an individual prognosis. Raynaud phenomenon with abnormal nailfold capillaroscopy and disease-specific antibodies supports a systemic-sclerosis spectrum even before extensive skin thickening develops.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has glenohumeral pain and progressive restriction of both active and passive external rotation, with diabetes and a normal plain radiograph. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Isolated supraspinatus tendinopathy
options.B: Subacromial bursitis
options.C: Thoracic outlet syndrome
options.D: Adhesive capsulitis
options.E: Cervical radiculopathy

explanation: Global restriction of passive shoulder motion, particularly external rotation, favours adhesive capsulitis. Adhesive capsulitis produces global loss of passive and active glenohumeral motion, classically external rotation. Diabetes and thyroid disease increase risk. Management usually involves education, analgesia, range-of-motion therapy and selected corticosteroid injection. Restriction of passive external rotation is particularly useful for distinguishing true capsular stiffness from isolated rotator cuff pain, where passive range is generally preserved.

stem: A 63-year-old woman has lateral hip pain and cannot lie on the affected side. Hip internal rotation is preserved and there is focal greater-trochanter tenderness. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: L3 nerve root radiculopathy
options.B: Avascular necrosis
options.C: Septic arthritis
options.D: Osteoarthritis of the hip joint
options.E: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome

explanation: Local trochanteric tenderness and preserved hip range support gluteal tendinopathy/GTPS. Greater trochanteric pain syndrome usually relates to gluteal tendinopathy rather than isolated bursitis. Lateral tenderness and painful side-lying favour the diagnosis over intra-articular hip disease, where restricted internal rotation and groin pain are more typical. Gluteal tendinopathy is suggested by lateral trochanteric tenderness and pain with single-leg loading; evaluate hip osteoarthritis and lumbar referred pain when features are atypical.

stem: A 49-year-old woman has medial ankle pain, hindfoot valgus, loss of the medial arch and cannot perform a single-leg heel raise. Which structure is most likely dysfunctional?

options.A: Peroneus brevis
options.B: Tibialis posterior tendon
options.C: Extensor hallucis longus
options.D: Tibialis anterior tendon
options.E: Achilles tendon

explanation: Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction produces progressive collapsing flatfoot and impaired inversion on heel rise. Tibialis posterior dysfunction weakens hindfoot inversion and arch support, leading to progressive collapsing flatfoot. Examine single-leg heel rise and flexible versus fixed deformity; management includes support, strengthening and foot/ankle specialist referral when progressive. The lower-limb regional pain module links progressive arch collapse to failure of medial dynamic support; fixed deformity or loss of function warrants more urgent foot and ankle assessment.

stem: A 55-year-old woman after distal-radius fracture develops severe disproportionate hand pain, swelling, colour and temperature asymmetry and allodynia. Which syndrome is most likely?

options.A: Palindromic rheumatism
options.B: Septic arthritis
options.C: Carpal tunnel syndrome
options.D: Complex regional pain syndrome
options.E: Cervical myelopathy

explanation: Disproportionate continuing pain with sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor and motor/trophic changes suggests CRPS. Complex regional pain syndrome is diagnosed clinically using Budapest criteria, requiring disproportionate pain and appropriate symptom/sign domains. Exclude infection, vascular compromise and mechanical complications. Early functional rehabilitation, desensitisation and pain management are important. The widespread pain module emphasises that disproportionate persistent pain can reflect altered nociceptive processing; physical signs and exclusion of important structural or vascular pathology remain essential.

stem: A 61-year-old man has shoulder pain on abduction with preserved passive external rotation. Pain is reproduced by resisted abduction, without systemic features. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Rotator cuff-related shoulder pain
options.B: Septic glenohumeral arthritis
options.C: Adhesive capsulitis
options.D: Glenohumeral ankylosis
options.E: Cervical myelopathy

explanation: Painful resisted motion with relatively preserved passive range favours rotator cuff pathology over capsulitis. Rotator cuff-related shoulder pain causes painful resisted movement with relatively preserved passive range, unlike adhesive capsulitis. Assess for traumatic full-thickness tears and red flags; progressive graded exercise and analgesia are first-line for uncomplicated tendinopathy. A painful resisted abduction test is not specific for a rotator cuff tear; consider the combination of strength, passive movement, trauma history and function.

stem: A 68-year-old woman has symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, obesity and no inflammatory arthritis. She asks for the intervention most likely to offer durable functional improvement. Which intervention should be central to management?

options.A: Hydroxychloroquine as first-line disease control
options.B: A trial of empirical oral prednisolone for pain
options.C: Individualised therapeutic exercise with weight management
options.D: Long-term high-dose opioid analgesia as first-line treatment
options.E: Routine arthroscopic washout and debridement

explanation: Exercise and weight management are core osteoarthritis treatments; arthroscopy and DMARDs are not routine treatments. NICE NG226 prioritises therapeutic exercise and weight management as core OA care. In overweight patients, even modest loss helps, while around 10% weight reduction generally offers greater benefit than 5%. Pharmacological analgesia supports participation but does not replace rehabilitation. Osteoarthritis education should integrate strengthening, aerobic activity, weight management and supported self-management; radiographic severity alone should not dictate disability assessment.

stem: A 57-year-old office worker has nocturnal paraesthesia in the thumb, index and middle fingers, thenar weakness and preserved little-finger sensation. Which nerve is principally affected?

options.A: Ulnar nerve at Guyon canal
options.B: Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
options.C: Axillary nerve
options.D: Radial nerve
options.E: Musculocutaneous nerve

explanation: Median neuropathy at the wrist causes radial three-and-a-half digit symptoms and may cause thenar weakness. Median neuropathy at the carpal tunnel causes radial three-and-a-half digit symptoms and thenar weakness, while the little finger is spared. Severe weakness, persistent numbness or diagnostic uncertainty warrants nerve conduction assessment and possible decompression referral. Persistent thenar wasting or objective weakness suggests more advanced median nerve compromise and lowers the threshold for specialist assessment beyond night splinting alone.

stem: A 60-year-old woman treated with rituximab for vasculitis develops new fever and non-productive cough. CT reveals bilateral ground-glass infiltrates and oxygen saturations are falling. Which opportunistic infection must be considered?

options.A: Parvovirus arthropathy
options.B: Scabies
options.C: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
options.D: Clostridioides difficile colitis
options.E: Tetanus

explanation: Immunosuppressed patients with hypoxia and ground-glass opacities need urgent assessment for PJP among other infections. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is a key consideration in immunosuppressed patients with hypoxaemia and diffuse ground-glass change. Evaluate opportunistic and conventional infection urgently; bronchoalveolar sampling or PCR may assist, and timely treatment should not await all results in unstable patients. Opportunistic infection may present without marked inflammatory markers in immunosuppressed patients; consider treatment-associated antibody depletion and concurrent steroid exposure.

stem: A 67-year-old man has severe nocturnal back pain, weight loss, anaemia, elevated total protein and lytic vertebral lesions. Which diagnosis should be prioritised?

options.A: Multiple myeloma
options.B: Polymyalgia rheumatica
options.C: Fibromyalgia
options.D: Paget disease alone
options.E: Ankylosing spondylitis

explanation: Anaemia, paraprotein clues and lytic bone lesions raise immediate concern for plasma cell malignancy. Multiple myeloma can present with lytic lesions, anaemia, renal dysfunction and monoclonal proteins. Request serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation, serum free light chains and urine studies, with haematology assessment; infection and metastatic cancer remain differentials. Malignant bone disease may mimic mechanical and inflammatory spinal pain; persistent night pain, systemic symptoms and destructive imaging warrant urgent investigation.

stem: A 71-year-old man has fever, a new murmur, splinter haemorrhages and positive rheumatoid factor with low complement; he is referred for possible systemic vasculitis. What is the most important alternative diagnosis?

options.A: Infective endocarditis
options.B: Osteoporosis
options.C: Rheumatoid arthritis solely
options.D: Polymyalgia rheumatica
options.E: Gout

explanation: Endocarditis can mimic immune-complex vasculitis; obtain blood cultures and echocardiographic assessment. Infective endocarditis can cause circulating immune complexes, positive rheumatoid factor, hypocomplementaemia and vasculitis-like manifestations. Obtain multiple blood cultures and echocardiography before immunosuppression where feasible, as steroids without treating infection may be harmful. Infective endocarditis and immune-complex disease can produce positive RF, low complement and renal abnormalities, so immunological tests cannot substitute for cultures and echocardiography.

stem: A 52-year-old man with a prosthetic knee has acute joint pain, warmth, raised CRP and a draining sinus tract communicating with the joint. Which diagnosis should be assumed until appropriately managed?

options.A: Fibromyalgia
options.B: Palindromic rheumatism
options.C: Osteoarthritis flare alone
options.D: Prosthetic joint infection
options.E: Asymptomatic loosening

explanation: A sinus tract communicating with a prosthesis is highly concerning for prosthetic joint infection; urgent orthopaedic and microbiology input is warranted. A sinus tract communicating with a prosthesis strongly supports prosthetic joint infection. Urgent orthopaedic and microbiology input is required; obtain suitable deep specimens and avoid empiric antibiotics before sampling in a stable patient when this is safe. Prosthetic joint infection may be caused by biofilm-forming organisms and requires surgical planning as well as microbiology; a draining sinus is particularly important diagnostically.

stem: A 73-year-old woman receiving denosumab for severe osteoporosis is scheduled to stop treatment without alternative therapy. What is the key risk that should drive a transition plan?

options.A: Rapid improvement in bone density after cessation
options.B: Retinal toxicity
options.C: Addison crisis
options.D: Acute gout
options.E: Rebound vertebral fractures after denosumab cessation

explanation: Stopping denosumab without follow-on antiresorptive treatment can cause rebound bone turnover and multiple vertebral fractures. Stopping denosumab without effective antiresorptive follow-on therapy can cause rebound bone turnover and multiple vertebral fractures. Plan transition, commonly to a bisphosphonate, with specialist consideration of timing, prior duration and bone turnover monitoring. The osteoporosis modules emphasise rebound vertebral-fracture risk after denosumab cessation; the follow-on antiresorptive plan is part of safe prescribing from the outset.

stem: A 74-year-old patient taking oral bisphosphonate for eight years develops weeks of prodromal thigh pain; X- ray shows lateral cortical thickening of the femoral shaft. What complication should be suspected?

options.A: Osteogenesis imperfecta
options.B: Septic arthritis
options.C: Giant cell tumour
options.D: Atypical femoral fracture
options.E: Osteomalacia alone

explanation: Long-term antiresorptive treatment can be associated with atypical femoral fractures, often heralded by thigh pain. Atypical femoral fracture is associated with long-term antiresorptive exposure and often presents with prodromal thigh pain and lateral cortical thickening. Image the entire femur and contralateral side, review antiresorptive treatment and seek orthopaedic assessment. Prodromal thigh pain in long-term bisphosphonate use should prompt full-length femoral imaging; incomplete atypical fractures may precede a complete transverse fracture.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with inflammatory bowel disease presents with proximal weakness, bone pain, low phosphate and elevated alkaline phosphatase; vitamin D is profoundly low. Which bone disorder best explains this pattern?

options.A: Paget disease
options.B: Primary osteoarthritis
options.C: Osteomalacia
options.D: Osteopetrosis
options.E: Chondrocalcinosis

explanation: Hypophosphataemia, vitamin D deficiency, bone pain and muscle weakness support defective mineralisation. Vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia causes defective mineralisation, bone pain and proximal weakness with often high ALP and low phosphate. Investigate calcium, phosphate, PTH, vitamin D and malabsorption; replace deficiency while monitoring biochemical response. Osteomalacia reflects impaired mineralisation rather than simply reduced bone mass; low phosphate, secondary hyperparathyroidism and high alkaline phosphatase help distinguish it from osteoporosis.

stem: A 75-year-old man has pelvic bone pain, enlarged skull circumference, isolated high alkaline phosphatase and radiographs showing mixed lytic and sclerotic bone expansion. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Hypervitaminosis A
options.B: Paget disease of bone
options.C: Rheumatoid arthritis
options.D: Osteonecrosis
options.E: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia

explanation: Paget disease causes focal increased bone remodelling, expansion, cortical thickening and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Paget disease features focal accelerated bone remodelling, bone enlargement, pain and elevated bone-derived ALP. Assess disease extent with imaging; symptomatic active disease generally responds to potent bisphosphonates, especially intravenous zoledronic acid when appropriate. Paget disease may be identified by an isolated ALP rise, characteristic bone expansion and cortical thickening; determine whether biochemical activity corresponds to symptomatic sites.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with glucocorticoid-treated RA sustained a low-trauma vertebral fracture. Her DXA T- score is -1.8. What is the correct interpretation for fracture prevention?

options.A: Bisphosphonates are always contraindicated
options.B: Only repeat DXA after ten years
options.C: She is at high fracture risk despite a T-score above -2.5
options.D: Normal T-score excludes fracture risk
options.E: No intervention can reduce future fractures

explanation: A fragility vertebral fracture indicates high future risk; management is not based solely on a densitometric osteoporosis threshold. A low-trauma vertebral fracture establishes clinically important skeletal fragility despite a T-score in the osteopenic range. Incorporate glucocorticoid exposure, prior fracture and other risks into a management plan; anti-osteoporosis treatment is usually indicated. A fragility vertebral fracture strongly affects risk classification even when DXA shows osteopenia rather than osteoporosis; glucocorticoids further increase fracture probability.

stem: A 7-year-old girl has persistent knee synovitis for four months and a painless reduction in visual acuity is not reported. She has ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA. Which surveillance is essential even without ocular symptoms?

options.A: Serial serum urate monitoring only
options.B: Regular slit-lamp screening for anterior uveitis
options.C: Annual carotid Doppler ultrasound
options.D: Routine monthly CT brain imaging
options.E: Routine screening colonoscopy

explanation: Chronic JIA-associated anterior uveitis can be asymptomatic; risk-adapted slit-lamp surveillance is essential. JIA-associated anterior uveitis may be silent and threaten vision despite a quiet joint examination. ANA-positive young-onset oligoarticular disease is high risk; ophthalmology slit-lamp screening intervals depend on risk and should continue as advised. Children with oligoarticular JIA can develop asymptomatic chronic anterior uveitis; screening must continue even if joint symptoms improve and the child denies eye pain.

stem: An 11-year-old with systemic JIA develops persistent fever, bruising, hepatosplenomegaly, ferritin 25,000, falling platelets and fibrinogen, and rising transaminases. Which complication is most likely?

options.A: Macrophage activation syndrome
options.B: Simple iron overload
options.C: Isolated viral rhinitis
options.D: Osgood-Schlatter disease
options.E: Osteochondritis dissecans

explanation: Cytopenias, hypofibrinogenaemia and marked hyperferritinaemia in systemic JIA indicate MAS, a medical emergency. MAS in systemic JIA can present with falling platelets and fibrinogen despite active systemic inflammation, striking ferritin elevation, hepatitis and coagulopathy. Escalate immediately to paediatric rheumatology/critical care for trigger evaluation and targeted immunosuppressive treatment. Systemic JIA with persistent fever, falling platelets, reduced fibrinogen and hepatitis should prompt emergency evaluation for macrophage activation syndrome.

stem: A 13-year-old girl presents with a violaceous heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, proximal weakness and raised CK. Which feature requires active assessment due to potentially serious extra-muscular involvement?

options.A: Swallowing dysfunction and aspiration risk
options.B: Reduced serum urate
options.C: Hyperuricaemia alone
options.D: Isolated carpal tunnel symptoms
options.E: Increased foot arch

explanation: Juvenile dermatomyositis can cause bulbar weakness and dysphagia; evaluate swallowing and systemic complications. Bulbar weakness in juvenile dermatomyositis can impair swallowing and cause aspiration, while severe disease can affect respiratory muscles. Assess swallow safety urgently alongside strength, skin disease, cardiac and pulmonary manifestations; intensive multidisciplinary treatment may be required. Juvenile dermatomyositis can include vasculopathy, skin ulceration and swallowing dysfunction; swallowing safety and organ involvement should accompany routine strength measurement.

stem: A patient taking leflunomide develops severe drug-induced hepatitis and the medication is discontinued. Rapid removal of the active metabolite is indicated. Which intervention accelerates elimination?

options.A: Vitamin K alone
options.B: Cholestyramine washout
options.C: Oral iron
options.D: Probenecid
options.E: Naloxone

explanation: Leflunomide’s active metabolite undergoes enterohepatic recirculation; cholestyramine accelerates elimination. Leflunomide undergoes prolonged enterohepatic recycling, so simply stopping the tablets does not rapidly clear its active metabolite. Cholestyramine washout is used in serious toxicity or pregnancy planning, with follow-up drug-level testing where indicated. Leflunomide has a long effective elimination period because of enterohepatic recirculation; a formal washout regimen is needed for certain serious adverse events and conception planning.

stem: A 64-year-old woman starting tofacitinib for RA has previous myocardial infarction, continues to smoke and has several cardiovascular risk factors. Which safety issue is most important in shared treatment selection?

options.A: No additional cardiovascular evaluation is needed before starting
options.B: All JAK inhibitors reduce the risk of venous thrombosis
options.C: No baseline infection screening is necessary before starting
options.D: Increased risks of major cardiovascular events, malignancy and thrombosis with JAK inhibitors
options.E: Live vaccines are always considered safe during treatment

explanation: Regulatory warnings highlight MACE, malignancy, VTE and serious infection concerns with JAK inhibition, especially in higher-risk patients. JAK inhibitors carry warnings about serious infections, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events and thrombosis, especially in patients with relevant risk factors. Document individual risk-benefit discussion, assess alternative DMARD options and manage modifiable cardiovascular risks. The pharmacology modules emphasise infection screening, vaccination review and comorbidity assessment before targeted therapy; JAK-inhibitor risk assessment is particularly important with cardiovascular risk factors.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with seropositive RA has been treated with rituximab. Six months later, peripheral CD19-positive B cells are undetectable, but rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies remain detectable at similar titres. What is the best explanation?

options.A: Activated naive T lymphocytes continuously secrete rheumatoid factor
options.B: Memory B cells express no CD20 and therefore survive unchanged
options.C: Long-lived plasma cells do not express CD20 and continue to secrete antibody
options.D: Rituximab selectively eliminates all immunoglobulin-secreting plasma cells
options.E: CD20 is expressed only on neutrophils

explanation: Rituximab targets CD20, expressed from pre-B to memory B cells but not on most plasma cells. Pre-existing antibody (including protective vaccine immunity) therefore persists, whereas new humoral responses are impaired. IgG can fall with repeated courses. Other reasons autoantibodies persist after B-cell depletion: tissue-resident or splenic B cells escaping depletion; early B-cell repopulation (check CD19 count, often 6–9 months); human anti-chimeric antibodies reducing rituximab effect. Anti-Ro and anti-dsDNA titres may fall partially; vaccine antibody titres usually stay stable. CD20 is expressed from pre-B to memory B cells but not on pro-B cells, plasmablasts or most plasma cells. Clinical response in RA is best in seropositive patients, and poorer when synovium is B-cell-poor. Check immunoglobulins before each cycle. Retreat on clinical flare or at fixed intervals (usually ≥6 months). Give non-live vaccines ≥2 weeks before infusion. Options when the response is inadequate: switch mechanism (abatacept, IL-6R, JAKi); obinutuzumab (type II anti-CD20) in lupus nephritis. Memory B cells are CD20-positive and rapidly reactivated. Tissue-resident memory T cells may explain flares recurring at the same sites. Rituximab, high-dose GC, abatacept and methotrexate all reduce vaccine responses.

stem: A patient with RA is starting tocilizumab. Which molecular target does this drug block?

options.A: TNF-alpha
options.B: Interleukin-1 receptor
options.C: Interleukin-6 receptor
options.D: Interleukin-17A
options.E: CD20

explanation: Tocilizumab and sarilumab block the IL-6 receptor. Monitoring includes neutrophils, platelets, transaminases and lipids, and the drug suppresses CRP and fever, which can mask infection. Other causes of an unexpectedly low CRP in sepsis: tocilizumab or sarilumab, JAK inhibitors (JAK1 relays IL-6 signalling), severe liver failure and very early infection. SLE flare with a normal CRP is typical, so a high CRP in SLE suggests infection or serositis. Tocilizumab is IV monthly or SC weekly; sarilumab is SC fortnightly. Adverse effects: neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, raised ALT, raised LDL (monitor lipids), diverticular perforation, injection-site reactions. Uses: RA (good as monotherapy), GCA (tocilizumab with a 26-week GC taper), relapsing PMR (sarilumab), systemic JIA and AOSD, early SSc-ILD (tocilizumab), ICI-arthritis, cytokine release syndrome. Withhold for serious infection and image early, because fever and CRP will not alert you.

stem: What are Janus kinases (JAKs), and why does their inhibition have broad effects?

options.A: Secreted immunoglobulins that circulate and directly neutralise TNF
options.B: Nuclear transcription factors that directly bind DNA
options.C: Intracellular tyrosine kinases that transmit signals from type I and II cytokine receptors
options.D: Cell-surface integrins mediating leukocyte adhesion
options.E: Extracellular proteases primarily responsible for cartilage collagen breakdown

explanation: JAK1, JAK2, JAK3 and TYK2 relay signals from many cytokine receptors. This breadth explains the class effects of JAK inhibitors, including infection (notably herpes zoster), venous thromboembolism, lipid changes and cardiovascular signals in at-risk patients.
