JAK Main cytokines Clue JAK1 IL-6, type I/II IFN, γc upadacitinib, filgotinib (JAK1selective) cytokines JAK2 EPO, TPO, GM-CSF, anaemia, thrombocytopenia IL-12/23 JAK3 γc cytokines (IL-2, lymphocyte function; 4, 7, 15, 21) tofacitinib (JAK1/3) TYK2 type I IFN, IL-12, ILdeucravacitinib (psoriasis; 23 SLE trials) TNF and IL-1 signal through NF-κB and MAP kinases, not JAK– STAT. Before starting: recombinant zoster vaccine; lipids at 8–12 weeks; FBC (lymphopenia, neutropenia, anaemia); LFTs; CK (rises are common). ORAL Surveillance (tofacitinib vs TNFi in people ≥50 with ≥1 CV risk factor) showed more MACE, malignancy, VTE, serious infection and death. Use only if no suitable alternative in people ≥65, current or long-term past smokers, or those with CV or malignancy risk, and with caution where there are VTE risk factors. Licensed uses now span RA, PsA, axSpA, GCA (upadacitinib) and AOSD/JIA. Dermatomyositis has trial data (brepocitinib). Stop 3 days before elective surgery.

stem: The anti-inflammatory effect of low-dose weekly methotrexate is thought to be mediated mainly by which mechanism?

options.A: Direct and selective cyclo-oxygenase-2 enzyme inhibition
options.B: Depletion of circulating CD20-positive B cells
options.C: Inhibition of calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation
options.D: Increased extracellular adenosine through AICAR transformylase inhibition
options.E: Irreversible inhibition of hepatic xanthine oxidase activity

explanation: Methotrexate polyglutamates inhibit AICAR transformylase, raising extracellular adenosine, which is antiinflammatory. Folate supplementation reduces toxicity without abolishing efficacy, which supports a mechanism beyond simple antifolate activity. Other antifolate or adenosine-related points: caffeine (an adenosine-receptor antagonist) may modestly blunt methotrexate efficacy at high intake (inconsistent data). Cytotoxic high-dose methotrexate works through DHFR inhibition and is a different pharmacology. Polyglutamation traps methotrexate intracellularly, so full effect takes 6–12 weeks. Bioavailability of oral methotrexate plateaus above about 15 mg; subcutaneous dosing avoids this. Usual RA regimen: start 15 mg/week and rise to 20–25 mg/week (or about 0.3 mg/kg) over 4–8 weeks, with folic acid 5 mg weekly. Switch to SC for an inadequate response or GI intolerance before judging failure.

stem: Leflunomide reduces lymphocyte proliferation by inhibiting which enzyme?

options.A: Calcineurin
options.B: Janus kinase 1
options.C: Thiopurine methyltransferase
options.D: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
options.E: Phosphodiesterase-4

explanation: Leflunomide (via teriflunomide) inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase and de novo pyrimidine synthesis in activated lymphocytes. Its active metabolite undergoes enterohepatic recirculation and persists for up to 2 years, which is why cholestyramine washout is used before conception or after serious toxicity. Other causes of raised ALT or cytopenias on leflunomide: alcohol, NAFLD, co-prescribed methotrexate (additive hepatotoxicity), viral hepatitis. Other leflunomide adverse effects: hypertension, diarrhoea, weight loss, alopecia, peripheral neuropathy, rare ILD (higher risk in Japanese populations and pre-existing ILD). Dose 10–20 mg daily (loading doses are usually omitted because of GI upset). Monitor FBC, LFTs and BP. Washout with cholestyramine 8 g three times daily for 11 days (or activated charcoal), then confirm two plasma teriflunomide levels below 0.02 mg/L 14 days apart. Use washout for pregnancy plans, serious toxicity or switching to another hepatotoxic drug.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of abatacept?

options.A: TNF-alpha neutralisation by a monoclonal antibody
options.B: Direct blockade of the interleukin-6 receptor
options.C: Selective JAK1 and JAK3 catalytic inhibition
options.D: Targeted B-cell depletion through anti-CD20 binding
options.E: A CTLA-4-immunoglobulin fusion protein that blocks CD80/86–CD28 co-stimulation of T cells

explanation: CTLA-4-immunoglobulin fusion protein that blocks CD80/86–CD28 co-stimulation of T cells Abatacept binds CD80/CD86 on antigen-presenting cells and prevents CD28-mediated T-cell activation. It has a relatively favourable serious-infection profile among biologics. Abatacept can be given IV monthly or SC weekly and is less immunogenic. Infection signal is lower than TNFi in observational data. It is effective in seropositive RA (best in high-titre ACPA) and JIA, and is used for the joints in RA-ILD. It also treats CTLA-4/LRBA deficiency (immune dysregulation with immunodeficiency). Prevention trials: 12 months of abatacept in ACPA-positive arthralgia delayed RA (about 6% vs 29% at 1 year), but the effect waned after stopping. Abatacept is not standard prevention; offer trials. Avoid in COPD (more respiratory adverse events in trials).

stem: A 30-year-old man with axial spondyloarthritis is starting secukinumab. What does this drug neutralise?

options.A: Interleukin-23 p19
options.B: Interleukin-17A
options.C: Interleukin-6 receptor
options.D: Tumour necrosis factor-alpha
options.E: B-cell activating factor

explanation: Secukinumab and ixekizumab are IL-17A inhibitors (bimekizumab inhibits IL-17A and IL-17F). They are effective in axial and peripheral spondyloarthritis and psoriasis but can provoke or worsen inflammatory bowel disease. Other drugs that can provoke or unmask IBD: IL-17A and IL-17A/F inhibitors, etanercept (paradoxical IBD), isotretinoin (debated), NSAIDs (flare). Other IL-17i adverse effects: mucocutaneous Candida (oral thrush, more with bimekizumab), eczematous reactions, neutropenia. Secukinumab and ixekizumab neutralise IL-17A; bimekizumab neutralises IL-17A and IL-17F. Effective for axial and peripheral SpA, enthesitis, dactylitis, nails and skin. Less effective than mAb TNFi for uveitis. Ineffective (and harmful) in Crohn’s. Take a history for bowel symptoms before starting (consider faecal calprotectin if suggestive). Prefer IL-17i when there is extensive psoriasis. Prefer mAb TNFi when there is IBD or recurrent uveitis.

stem: A patient with psoriatic arthritis has active spinal inflammation despite adequate NSAID therapy. Which cytokine-targeted pathway has not shown reliable efficacy for isolated axial disease?

options.A: TNF-alpha inhibition
options.B: IL-17A inhibition
options.C: IL-23 pathway inhibition
options.D: JAK inhibition
options.E: IL-6 receptor inhibition

explanation: IL-23 inhibitors are useful for several peripheral and skin manifestations of psoriatic arthritis, but they have not demonstrated established efficacy for isolated axial spondyloarthritis. Ustekinumab targets the shared IL-12/23 p40 subunit; p19 inhibitors selectively target IL-23. They must not be regarded as equivalent to IL-17 or TNF inhibitors for established axial inflammation.

stem: Apremilast is used in psoriatic arthritis. What is its mechanism of action?

options.A: Sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulation
options.B: Non-selective Janus kinase inhibition
options.C: Phosphodiesterase-4 inhibition, increasing intracellular cAMP
options.D: Direct interleukin-6 receptor blockade
options.E: CD20-directed monoclonal B-cell depletion

explanation: Apremilast is an oral PDE4 inhibitor. Common adverse effects are diarrhoea, nausea and weight loss; mood should be monitored because of rare depression. Mood change on apremilast vs other causes: active disease burden, steroid withdrawal, isotretinoin, chronic pain. Weight loss vs GI side effects vs undiagnosed malignancy or IBD. Apremilast needs no routine blood monitoring and no TB screening. Dose-titrate over 5 days to 30 mg twice daily (once daily if eGFR <30). It has modest efficacy (below TNFi) for joints, skin and enthesitis. It reduced oral ulcers in Behçet’s (RELIEF trial). Places in therapy: mild oligoarticular PsA or skinpredominant disease after csDMARD failure, where a b/tsDMARD is not appropriate; refractory Behçet’s mucocutaneous ulcers. Strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin) reduce efficacy, so avoid co-prescription.

stem: Why is concomitant methotrexate advised when infliximab is used for rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: To prevent all methotrexate-associated cytopenias
options.B: To increase anti-infliximab antibody formation
options.C: To neutralise circulating TNF independently
options.D: To prevent infusion reactions through direct antihistamine action
options.E: It reduces formation of anti-drug antibodies, improving drug survival and efficacy

explanation: Chimeric and humanised monoclonal antibodies are immunogenic. Combining them with a csDMARD lowers antidrug antibody formation and improves outcomes. IL-6 receptor inhibitors and JAK inhibitors have the best evidence as monotherapy. Other causes of secondary loss of response to a TNF inhibitor: non-adherence; new non-inflammatory pain (OA, fibromyalgia); weight gain (volume of distribution); intercurrent infection; wrong diagnosis (e.g. PsA treated as RA, crystal disease). Immunogenicity order: infliximab (chimeric) > adalimumab > golimumab and certolizumab; etanercept forms nonneutralising antibodies. Low trough level with antibodies means switch within class. Adequate trough level without response means switch mechanism. If methotrexate is contraindicated, low-dose methotrexate (even 7.5–10 mg), leflunomide or azathioprine can still reduce immunogenicity, or choose IL-6R or JAK monotherapy. Therapeutic drug monitoring is reactive, not routine, in most UK practice.

stem: A patient is starting weekly methotrexate. What is the main purpose of co-prescribing folic acid?

options.A: To increase efficacy through inhibition of urate synthesis
options.B: To prevent every infection during methotrexate therapy
options.C: To reduce gastrointestinal, mucocutaneous and hepatic adverse effects
options.D: To eliminate the need for blood monitoring
options.E: To enhance CD20-mediated B-cell depletion

explanation: Folic acid (commonly 5 mg once weekly on a different day from methotrexate, or per local regimen) reduces nausea, stomatitis and transaminase rises without meaningfully reducing efficacy. Methotrexate toxicities not prevented by folic acid: pneumonitis (idiosyncratic), teratogenicity, infection risk, accelerated nodulosis, and, largely, severe myelosuppression from overdose or interaction (which needs folinic acid, not folic acid). GI intolerance and “methotrexate fog” (malaise after dosing) are the commonest reasons for stopping. Alopecia and mouth ulcers respond to folate. Nausea also improves with SC dosing, taking it in the evening or an antiemetic. Folic acid 5 mg once weekly is usual. Increase to 5 mg up to 6 days/week (not on the methotrexate day) for persistent mucositis or LFT rises. Alcohol within national limits (≤14 units/week) is generally acceptable but individualised; heavy use is not.

stem: A 58-year-old woman taking methotrexate 20 mg weekly is prescribed trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection. Ten days later she presents with mouth ulcers, bruising and a neutrophil count of 0.4 x 10I/L. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: A drug interaction causing additive antifolate marrow toxicity
options.B: Stop methotrexate, admit for urgent assessment and give folinic acid rescue
options.C: Additive antifolate toxicity with methotrexate
options.D: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.E: At least 1 month before conception, continuing folic acid

explanation: drug interaction causing additive antifolate marrow toxicity Trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole add antifolate effects and reduce methotrexate clearance, causing potentially fatal myelosuppression. Both drugs should be stopped, FBC monitored and folinic acid rescue considered with urgent specialist advice. Other drugs that interact dangerously with methotrexate: co-trimoxazole and trimethoprim (antifolate), penicillins and probenecid (reduced renal clearance), PPIs (mainly highdose methotrexate), NSAIDs (small effect at low dose; take care in CKD), leflunomide (hepatotoxicity), and nitrous oxide anaesthesia (folate inactivation). Other causes of acute neutropenia: viral infection, sepsis, Felty’s, LGL leukaemia, other drugs (sulfasalazine, clozapine, carbimazole). Patterns of toxicity: mucositis first, then cytopenias with a nadir about 7–10 days later. Severity is worse with renal impairment, hypoalbuminaemia, dehydration, older age and dosing errors. Stop both drugs. Check FBC, U&E and LFTs. Give folinic acid (calcium folinate), commonly 15 mg every 6 hours, adjusted to counts and renal function. Admit if febrile or neutrophils are below 1.0. Use G-CSF for profound neutropenia and treat neutropenic sepsis empirically. Use nitrofurantoin or another non-antifolate for UTI in patients on methotrexate.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with a recent diagnosis of RA attends with mouth ulcers, conjunctival irritation and pancytopenia. On review, she has been taking her methotrexate 10 mg tablet every morning. What is the most important immediate step?

options.A: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.B: A drug interaction causing additive antifolate marrow toxicity
options.C: Stop methotrexate, admit for urgent assessment and give folinic acid rescue
options.D: Do not stop without follow-on therapy; plan a bisphosphonate (often zoledronate) about 6 months after the last dose
options.E: At least 1 month before conception, continuing folic acid

explanation: Inadvertent daily dosing is a well-recognised and potentially fatal error. Management is urgent: stop methotrexate, give folinic acid (calcium folinate), support counts and assess for sepsis. Clear written once-weekly instructions on a named day help prevent this. Differential of pancytopenia in RA: methotrexate toxicity (dose error, interaction, AKI), Felty’s syndrome, T-LGL leukaemia, MAS, B12 or folate deficiency, myelodysplasia, sulfasalazine or azathioprine toxicity, hypersplenism, parvovirus, lymphoma. Mucositis (mouth ulcers, sore eyes or skin) with cytopenias in a new methotrexate user strongly suggests daily dosing. Ask to see the pill packet. AKI precipitates toxicity even at correct doses. Stop methotrexate. Give folinic acid rescue early (it is most effective within 24 hours of the last dose). Hydration; G-CSF and transfusion as needed; barrier nursing; broadspectrum antibiotics if febrile. Glucarpidase is used for high-dose methotrexate with renal failure (oncology). Prevention: a single strength (2.5 mg) tablet, a named day on the prescription, patient education and pharmacy checks.

stem: Six weeks after starting methotrexate, a 63-year-old woman develops fever, a dry cough and breathlessness. SpO2 is 89% on air and CT shows bilateral ground-glass change. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: High-dose glucocorticoids including IV methylprednisolone pulses, with IVIG
options.B: High-dose glucocorticoids (including pulses) with cyclophosphamide
options.C: Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, which is the infection to suspect
options.D: Stop methotrexate, exclude infection including Pneumocystis, and start high-dose glucocorticoids
options.E: Urgent assessment for GCA, with high-dose glucocorticoids if it is suspected

explanation: Acute methotrexate pneumonitis is an idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction, usually within the first year. The drug is withdrawn, infection (including opportunistic organisms) excluded and corticosteroids given. Rechallenge after confirmed pneumonitis is not advised. Fever, cough and ground-glass change on methotrexate: methotrexate pneumonitis vs PJP (lymphopenic, high-dose GC), viral pneumonia (including COVID-19, CMV), atypical bacterial infection, RA-ILD acute exacerbation, druginduced ILD from other agents (leflunomide, TNFi, rituximab), pulmonary oedema, alveolar haemorrhage. Risk factors: older age, diabetes, hypoalbuminaemia, preexisting lung disease, prior DMARD lung toxicity. BAL often shows lymphocytosis with a high CD4:CD8 ratio. Eosinophilia occurs in about a third. Pneumonitis is rare (<1%). Methotrexate does not cause chronic RA-ILD and may delay its onset. Stop methotrexate. Do BAL and induced sputum for PJP PCR, viral PCR and cultures. Cover with empirical cotrimoxazole and antibiotics until infection is excluded. Prednisolone about 1 mg/kg, or IV methylprednisolone if hypoxic. Do not rechallenge. Stable pre-existing ILD is not an absolute contraindication to methotrexate (manage with the respiratory team). The EULAR course states that methotrexate can be continued in most patients with stable RA-ILD.

stem: A patient on methotrexate 20 mg weekly has routine bloods showing ALT 118 U/L (previously 35 U/L) with normal bilirubin and albumin. She feels well. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Add an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor
options.B: Withhold methotrexate, discuss with the rheumatology team and repeat the tests promptly
options.C: Switch to subcutaneous methotrexate
options.D: Reduce or withhold ciclosporin, manage blood pressure and discuss with the specialist team
options.E: Withhold further rituximab, consider an alternative DMARD and discuss immunoglobulin replacement with immunology if infections persist

explanation: ALT more than about three times the upper limit is a reason to withhold methotrexate and discuss with the rheumatology team while repeating tests promptly. The 2025 BSR csDMARD guideline moves away from fixed cutoffs: decisions weigh the trend and the absolute value, many isolated abnormalities are transient or unrelated, and alcohol, other hepatotoxins and fatty liver should be considered. Adults with liver-disease risk factors should have FIB-4 scoring (with elastography if indicated) when starting methotrexate. Causes of raised ALT on methotrexate other than drug hepatotoxicity: alcohol, NAFLD or metabolic syndrome (the commonest), statins, leflunomide, NSAIDs, isoniazid (latent TB treatment), viral hepatitis (HBV reactivation), autoimmune hepatitis (overlap with SLE or Sjögren’s), PBC (anti-mitochondrial antibody, especially in SSc or Sjögren’s), congestive hepatopathy, haemochromatosis. For a confirmed ALT above about 3 × ULN: withhold, repeat in 1–2 weeks and restart at a lower dose once settled. For persistent smaller rises: reduce the dose, increase folate, address alcohol and weight, and do a liver screen plus FIB-4 (with elastography if FIB-4 ≥1.3). Refer to hepatology if fibrosis risk is high. Liver biopsy is now rarely needed.

stem: Which monitoring schedule is most appropriate for a patient starting methotrexate?

options.A: Check renal function and FBC once at baseline only, with no further blood tests during treatment
options.B: FBC, LFTs and renal function at week 2, then about monthly for the first 3-6 months, then every 3 months, with the interval individualised to toxicity risk
options.C: Measure FBC and liver function tests every six months regardless of dose, duration or early toxicity signs
options.D: Monitor only visual acuity annually, since methotrexate toxicity mainly affects the eyes and vision
options.E: Perform a chest X-ray and spirometry monthly, with no routine blood count or liver monitoring needed

explanation: The 2025 BSR csDMARD guideline replaced the fixed 2-weekly schedule with risk-adapted monitoring: bloods at week 2, then roughly monthly for the first 3-6 months, then 3-monthly in stable patients without risk factors. The interval can be extended after an individual risk assessment, or shortened when there are toxicity risk factors. Extra tests are needed after dose increases, and risk is reassessed annually. Toxicity risk factors that justify closer monitoring: age >65, eGFR <60, alcohol excess, obesity or NAFLD, diabetes, coprescribed hepatotoxins or antifolates, recent dose escalation, combination csDMARDs. Note the different schedules. The EULAR course text quotes an older fixed schedule (2-weekly until stable for 6 weeks, then monthly for 3 months, then 3-monthly). For UK exams, the 2025 BSR risk-adapted schedule in the answer applies. Recheck about 2 weeks after any dose increase. Baseline: FBC, U&E, LFTs, CRP, HBV/HCV/HIV, chest radiograph (or recent imaging), and lung function if there is lung disease.

stem: Which DMARD can cause agranulocytosis, usually within the first 3 months, and therefore needs blood monitoring?

options.A: NSAIDs
options.B: TNF inhibitors
options.C: Sulfasalazine
options.D: Chikungunya virus
options.E: Infective endocarditis

explanation: Sulfasalazine can cause neutropenia or agranulocytosis, hepatitis and hypersensitivity, so FBC and LFTs are monitored. It can also cause reversible oligospermia. Other sulfasalazine adverse effects: rash and DRESS, hepatitis, megaloblastic anaemia (folate), haemolysis (G6PD deficiency), orange urine and tears (stains contact lenses), reversible oligospermia, drug-induced lupus (rare). Sulfonamide allergy is a contraindication. Agranulocytosis is idiosyncratic and usually occurs within the first 3 months. Sudden sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers need an urgent FBC. Titrate 500 mg/day up to 2–3 g/day over 4 weeks. Monitoring is often reduced to 3-monthly after the first year if stable. Compatible with pregnancy (give with folic acid 5 mg) and breastfeeding (care in premature, jaundiced or G6PD-deficient infants). Best-evidenced csDMARD for peripheral SpA arthritis; not effective for axial disease.

stem: A patient with severe RA is to start azathioprine. Which pre-treatment test is essential?

options.A: HLA-B*58:01 genotyping
options.B: Therapeutic exercise with weight loss and education
options.C: Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity or genotype
options.D: Treat-to-target escalation to achieve remission or low disease activity
options.E: Urgent management for suspected septic arthritis while cultures are pending

explanation: Low or absent TPMT activity causes accumulation of thioguanine nucleotides and severe myelotoxicity. Azathioprine is avoided with absent activity and dose-reduced with intermediate activity. NUDT15 variants are also relevant in some populations. Routine FBC monitoring is still required. Other causes of severe myelotoxicity on azathioprine: NUDT15 deficiency (East Asian and Hispanic populations), xanthine oxidase inhibitor co-prescription, ACE inhibitors (modest effect), co-trimoxazole, viral infection, hypersensitivity syndrome (fever, rash, hepatitis or pancreatitis, usually within the first weeks). Normal TPMT does not exclude toxicity. Absent TPMT activity: avoid azathioprine. Intermediate activity: about 50% dose. Normal: target about 2–2.5 mg/kg/day. Monitor FBC and LFTs. Azathioprine causes macrocytosis (MCV rise is expected). Long-term risks: non-melanoma skin cancer (sun protection) and lymphoma. Compatible with pregnancy and breastfeeding.

stem: A patient with severe psoriatic arthritis on ciclosporin has a sustained creatinine rise of 35% above baseline on two tests a week apart, with BP 152/94 mmHg. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Withhold further rituximab, consider an alternative DMARD and discuss immunoglobulin replacement with immunology if infections persist
options.B: Reduce or withhold ciclosporin, manage blood pressure and discuss with the specialist team
options.C: Urgent management for suspected septic arthritis while cultures are pending
options.D: Stop the TNF inhibitor and seek neurological evaluation
options.E: Withhold methotrexate, discuss with the rheumatology team and repeat the tests promptly

explanation: Ciclosporin causes dose-related nephrotoxicity and hypertension. A sustained creatinine rise above 30% from baseline warrants dose reduction or withholding. NSAIDs and many drug interactions increase nephrotoxicity. Other causes of rising creatinine on ciclosporin: NSAIDs, dehydration, interacting drugs (CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels: clarithromycin, azoles, diltiazem, grapefruit; inducers lower them), ACE inhibitors or ARBs, active nephritis in SLE, TMA. Other ciclosporin adverse effects: hypertrichosis, gingival hyperplasia, tremor, hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperuricaemia (gout), raised lipids, PRES. Measure BP and creatinine twice at baseline. Withhold if creatinine rises >30% on two occasions, then restart at a lower dose once it is back within about 15% of baseline. Treat hypertension with a dihydropyridine CCB (amlodipine; avoid diltiazem and verapamil, which raise levels). Tacrolimus and voclosporin have the same class effects; voclosporin needs no level monitoring.

stem: Which group of adverse effects is the main concern with intravenous cyclophosphamide, and which pretreatment discussion is particularly important in a patient who may want children?

options.A: Peripheral neuropathy as the principal concern, requiring baseline and serial nerve-conduction studies
options.B: Irreversible retinal toxicity as the principal concern, requiring baseline and annual ophthalmology review
options.C: Gonadal failure, haemorrhagic cystitis, marrow suppression and later malignancy; gonadotoxicity and fertility preservation must be discussed before treatment
options.D: Reversible alopecia and nausea only, with no long-term fertility or malignancy risk to discuss
options.E: Injection-site reactions and a small increase in diverticular perforation risk, requiring bowel symptom review

explanation: Cyclophosphamide can cause ovarian and testicular failure, related to age and cumulative dose. Fertility preservation and GnRH analogue protection should be discussed without delaying life-saving therapy. Hydration, mesna where indicated, urinalysis, FBC monitoring and Pneumocystis prophylaxis are part of safe use. Cumulative dose relates to bladder and haematological cancer risk. Other causes of haematuria in a patient on cyclophosphamide: active glomerulonephritis (dysmorphic red cells, casts), UTI, bladder carcinoma (late, doserelated; lifelong surveillance), anticoagulation. Other cyclophosphamide toxicities: nausea, alopecia, hyponatraemia (SIADH), infection (PJP, zoster), teratogenicity, pulmonary fibrosis (rare). Ovarian failure risk rises steeply after about age 30 and with cumulative dose above about 10 g. Euro-Lupus (3 g total) carries a much lower risk than NIH high-dose regimens. The leucocyte nadir is at about 10–14 days after an IV pulse. Prefer IV pulses (lower cumulative dose) over oral daily dosing. Check FBC before each pulse and at 10–14 days, reducing the dose for low nadirs, older age or renal impairment. Use mesna with high doses. Give PJP prophylaxis. Offer oocyte or embryo cryopreservation (or sperm banking) where time allows; GnRH agonists (e.g. goserelin) offer partial ovarian protection. Rituximab is preferred when fertility matters (AAV).

stem: A 66-year-old woman with RA takes hydroxychloroquine. She is prescribed azithromycin and citalopram. Which risk is of greatest concern?

options.A: Hepatotoxicity, requiring urgent liver function tests
options.B: Hereditary haemochromatosis
options.C: Increased bleeding risk, requiring INR monitoring
options.D: QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmia
options.E: Acute pancreatitis, requiring serum amylase or lipase

explanation: Hydroxychloroquine prolongs the QT interval, and combination with macrolides and some SSRIs increases the risk of torsades de pointes. An ECG and review of interacting drugs is advisable. Long-term use is also rarely associated with cardiomyopathy. Other QT-prolonging drugs often co-prescribed in rheumatology: macrolides, fluoroquinolones, SSRIs (citalopram, escitalopram), ondansetron, domperidone, tricyclics, methadone, azole antifungals, amiodarone. Electrolyte drivers: low K, Mg or Ca. Other causes of syncope in SLE or RA: congenital heart block (adult), myocarditis, PE. Hydroxychloroquine cardiomyopathy is rare, appears after long exposure, and shows restrictive or hypertrophic physiology and conduction disease (curvilinear bodies on biopsy). Other hydroxychloroquine toxicities: retinopathy, hypoglycaemia, psoriasis flare, skin pigmentation, myopathy or neuromyopathy, and haemolysis (G6PD deficiency, rare). ECG at baseline when interacting drugs or cardiac risk are present. Choose doxycycline or amoxicillin over azithromycin where possible, and sertraline over citalopram. Keep the hydroxychloroquine dose ≤5 mg/kg/day actual body weight.

stem: A patient with RA on tocilizumab has 3 days of left iliac fossa pain and feels unwell. Temperature is 37.4 °C and CRP is 4 mg/L. What is the most important consideration?

options.A: Reactivation of latent tuberculosis presenting as mesenteric lymphadenopathy
options.B: Hepatitis B reactivation presenting with jaundice and deranged liver enzymes
options.C: Methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity presenting with right iliac fossa pain, requiring immediate cessation
options.D: A flare of the underlying rheumatoid arthritis requiring urgent DMARD escalation and specialist review
options.E: IL-6 blockade suppresses CRP and fever, so diverticulitis or bowel perforation must be actively excluded with imaging

explanation: IL-6 inhibitors blunt the acute-phase response and fever, masking infection. Tocilizumab is associated with lower gastrointestinal perforation, especially with diverticular disease or concomitant glucocorticoids or NSAIDs. A low threshold for CT is needed. Acute abdomen on tocilizumab: diverticulitis or perforation (the main concern), appendicitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, mesenteric ischaemia (vasculitis), steroid-associated peptic perforation, opportunistic colitis (CMV). JAK inhibitors also carry a GI perforation signal (smaller). Risk factors: history of diverticulitis, concomitant glucocorticoids or NSAIDs, older age. Peritonism may be absent and fever, CRP and neutrophilia blunted; ESR may also be falsely low. Do an early CT abdomen and pelvis, involve surgeons early and withhold tocilizumab. Avoid IL-6R inhibitors in patients with prior diverticulitis or perforation.

stem: A patient on azathioprine is to start a xanthine oxidase inhibitor (allopurinol or febuxostat) for gout. What is the main concern, and how would toxicity present?

options.A: Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome, presenting with fever, rash, eosinophilia and organ dysfunction within weeks
options.B: Reduced azathioprine efficacy from induction of hepatic drug-metabolising enzymes, requiring a dose increase
options.C: An enhanced urate-lowering effect of allopurinol when combined with azathioprine, requiring a lower starting dose
options.D: Additive nephrotoxicity from combined azathioprine and allopurinol use, requiring closer renal monitoring
options.E: Xanthine oxidase inhibition raises 6-mercaptopurine levels, risking severe myelosuppression with fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers

explanation: Xanthine oxidase metabolises 6-mercaptopurine. Allopurinol or febuxostat with azathioprine causes toxic accumulation and potentially fatal marrow suppression; without major azathioprine dose reduction, profound neutropenia and sepsis can develop within weeks. If a patient presents this way, check the FBC urgently, stop azathioprine and treat neutropenic sepsis as an emergency. If the combination is unavoidable, azathioprine is reduced to about a quarter of the dose with close monitoring, or switched to a non-thiopurine agent. Alternatives that avoid the interaction: switch azathioprine to mycophenolate or methotrexate, or use a uricosuric (benzbromarone; probenecid if eGFR is adequate). Mercaptopurine has the same interaction. Other interactions of azathioprine: warfarin (reduced INR effect) and co-trimoxazole (additive marrow toxicity). The 6-thioguanine nucleotide pathway is TPMT-dependent; xanthine oxidase provides the alternative inactivation route. Blocking it shunts metabolism into active thioguanines. In gastroenterology, the combination is sometimes used deliberately (allopurinol 100 mg with azathioprine at 25– 33% dose) under metabolite monitoring. In rheumatology, avoid it unless specialist-supervised with weekly FBC initially.

stem: A patient on a biologic DMARD develops sepsis requiring IV antibiotics. What is the most appropriate immediate DMARD plan?

options.A: Continue the biologic unchanged, since sepsis does not alter infection risk on immunosuppression
options.B: Switch immediately to a biologic with a different mechanism of action while the sepsis is treated
options.C: Increase the biologic dose to compensate for reduced efficacy during the systemic infection
options.D: Stop all treatment permanently, including hydroxychloroquine and glucocorticoids, regardless of disease activity
options.E: Withhold the biologic and other non-essential immunosuppression until the infection is treated and the patient has recovered

explanation: Serious infection requires temporary withholding of biologic or targeted therapy, coordinated with the treating team. The 2025 BSR csDMARD guideline also advises pausing csDMARDs during severe infection needing admission or IV antibiotics. Long-term glucocorticoids must not be stopped abruptly because of adrenal suppression; sick-day dose increases may be needed. Deciding which drugs to pause in severe infection: biologics, JAK inhibitors and csDMARDs (2025 BSR) are paused. Hydroxychloroquine can usually continue. Glucocorticoids continue, with stress dosing. Restart once antibiotics are complete and the patient is clinically recovered (often about 1–2 weeks after resolution). Restart sooner for organ-threatening disease, with specialist discussion. Infection risk is highest in the first 6–12 months of a new advanced therapy and with concomitant GC above about 7.5–10 mg/day. Fever, CRP and neutrophilia may be blunted by IL-6 or JAK inhibition and by GC. Septic patients on long-term GC (≥5 mg for ≥4 weeks): hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours IV or 200 mg/24 h by infusion. Review vaccination and prophylaxis after recovery.

stem: A patient taking prednisolone 10 mg daily for 18 months stops it abruptly and presents with vomiting, hypotension and weakness. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Opioid withdrawal syndrome
options.B: Myxoedema (hypothyroid) crisis
options.C: Adrenal crisis due to hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression
options.D: Acute pancreatitis secondary to glucocorticoid-induced hypertriglyceridaemia
options.E: Addisonian crisis from autoimmune primary adrenal failure, unrelated to the steroid course

explanation: Prolonged glucocorticoid use suppresses the HPA axis. Adrenal crisis requires immediate parenteral hydrocortisone and fluids. Patients on long-term steroids need a steroid card, sick-day rules and gradual tapering. Differential of vomiting, hypotension and weakness in a patient who has stopped steroids: adrenal crisis; sepsis (which may precipitate crisis); disease flare (e.g. PMR or GCA relapse); GC withdrawal syndrome (arthralgia, myalgia, fatigue, mood change with normal markers and BP); hypercalcaemia; hyponatraemia from other causes; primary adrenal failure (Addison’s, which features hyperkalaemia and pigmentation). In GC-induced (secondary or tertiary) adrenal insufficiency the mineralocorticoid axis is preserved, so hyperkalaemia is unusual. Hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia occur. Any route can suppress the HPA axis (oral, IA, inhaled, topical, nasal), and the risk is highest with ≥5 mg prednisolone for ≥4 weeks, evening dosing, dexamethasone and CYP3A4 inhibitors. Crisis: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM immediately, then 200 mg/24 h (infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours), IV saline and glucose. Do not wait for cortisol results; take a sample before treatment only if it causes no delay. Then give a steroid emergency card, sick-day rules and an IM hydrocortisone kit. Testing HPA recovery: a 9 am cortisol ≥24 hours after the last prednisolone dose, once on 4–5 mg/day. >300 nmol/L: stop. 150–300: continue and recheck. <150: likely adrenal insufficiency; endocrine referral. Use a short Synacthen test for indeterminate results. Recovery can take 6– 12 months, and sick-day rules apply for up to a year after stopping.

stem: What are the key principles of long-term glucocorticoid use in inflammatory rheumatic disease?

options.A: Discontinue permanently after 3 months regardless of disease activity, to avoid cumulative toxicity
options.B: Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time and taper gradually after prolonged use
options.C: Use the maximum tolerated dose until remission, then stop abruptly without tapering
options.D: Only influenza vaccination is relevant during glucocorticoid therapy
options.E: Switch all patients to alternate-day dosing from the outset to reduce adrenal suppression

explanation: Glucocorticoids carry dose-and duration-dependent harms including infection, diabetes, hypertension, cataract, osteoporosis and adrenal suppression. Exposure should be minimised and tapered carefully. GC toxicity by system: bone (osteoporosis, osteonecrosis), muscle (steroid myopathy with normal CK and type II fibre atrophy), metabolic (diabetes peaking in the afternoon, weight gain, dyslipidaemia), CV (hypertension, MI, AF, HF), eye (posterior subcapsular cataract, glaucoma, central serous chorioretinopathy), skin (thinning, purpura, striae, poor healing), neuropsychiatric (insomnia, mania, psychosis, often at >40 mg), infection (zoster, PJP, TB, Strongyloides hyperinfection), GI (ulcer with NSAIDs, diverticular perforation), growth suppression in children. “Low dose is not no risk”: even ≤5 mg/day long term modestly raises the risk of infection, fracture, cataract and CV events. In myositis, falling strength with a normal CK suggests steroid myopathy, while rising strength with a normal CK suggests disease control. Plan the taper at the start. Rough taper: reduce by 5–10 mg every 1–2 weeks above 20 mg, by 2.5 mg every 2–4 weeks from 20 to 10 mg, and by 1 mg every 4 weeks below 10 mg; slow down near the physiological dose (about 5 mg). Give as a single morning dose. Bone protection, BP and glucose checks (pre-evening-meal capillary glucose), an annual eye check, vaccination and a steroid card. Use GC-sparing agents early. Before long-term GC: weight, BP, HbA1c, lipids, bone profile, FRAX ± DXA, eye and mental-health history, HBV, HCV, HIV and IGRA where relevant, and Strongyloides serology (or empirical ivermectin) if from an endemic area. Calcium about 1000–1200 mg/day total intake (not routine 1–2 g supplements) and vitamin D 800–1000 IU/day. A PPI is needed only if combined with NSAIDs, antiplatelets or anticoagulants, or at high GI risk.

stem: A patient with severe vasculitis is starting high-dose prednisolone with cyclophosphamide. Which prophylaxis is most appropriate, and which infection should you suspect if a patient on this regimen without prophylaxis develops breathlessness, exertional hypoxia and diffuse ground-glass change?

options.A: Low-dose colchicine prophylaxis against crystal arthritis flares
options.B: Daily low-dose aspirin for cardiovascular protection during treatment
options.C: Antifungal prophylaxis against invasive aspergillosis as the main concern
options.D: Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, which is the infection to suspect
options.E: Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics alone, without specific Pneumocystis prophylaxis

explanation: Pneumocystis prophylaxis should be considered when prednisolone above about 15–30 mg/day is given for more than 2–4 weeks, particularly with cyclophosphamide or rituximab. Co-trimoxazole is first-line; check for G6PD deficiency and monitor counts, renal function and potassium. PJP typically causes subacute dyspnoea, desaturation on exertion and diffuse ground-glass change in immunosuppressed patients. It needs bronchoscopic or inducedsputum sampling and prompt high-dose co-trimoxazole, with adjunctive steroids if hypoxic. Diffuse ground-glass change in an immunosuppressed patient: PJP; CMV pneumonitis; COVID-19 or influenza; methotrexate or other drug pneumonitis; alveolar haemorrhage (falling Hb, rising DLCO, haemoptysis may be absent); pulmonary oedema; acute exacerbation of ILD; MDA5-associated rapidly progressive ILD. PJP clues: lymphopenia (CD4 <200), raised LDH, raised serum β-D-glucan, normal or near-normal chest radiograph early, marked exertional desaturation, pneumothorax. Non-HIV PJP is more fulminant and carries higher mortality than HIV-associated PJP. Prophylaxis: co-trimoxazole 480 mg daily or 960 mg three times weekly. Alternatives are atovaquone, dapsone (after a G6PD check) or nebulised pentamidine. Treatment: cotrimoxazole 15–20 mg/kg/day of the trimethoprim component in divided doses for 21 days, plus prednisolone if PaO2 <9.3 kPa. Never combine co-trimoxazole prophylaxis with methotrexate without considering the interaction. Many centres use atovaquone in patients on methotrexate.

stem: A patient with RA has had four courses of rituximab over 3 years and now has recurrent chest infections. Serum IgG is 3.1 g/L. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Withhold methotrexate, discuss with the rheumatology team and repeat the tests promptly
options.B: Reduce or withhold ciclosporin, manage blood pressure and discuss with the specialist team
options.C: Switch to a biologic with a different mechanism immediately, without checking immunoglobulin levels first
options.D: Withhold further rituximab, consider an alternative DMARD and discuss immunoglobulin replacement with immunology if infections persist
options.E: Withhold the biologic and other non-essential immunosuppression until the infection is treated and the patient has recovered

explanation: Secondary hypogammaglobulinaemia is a recognised complication of repeated rituximab and increases serious infection risk. Immunoglobulins should be checked before each cycle. Other causes of low IgG in a rheumatology patient: prior cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate or high-dose GC; nephrotic syndrome or protein-losing enteropathy (IgG loss); CVID unmasked; CLL, lymphoma or myeloma (check paraprotein and free light chains); Good’s syndrome (thymoma). Risk factors for rituximab hypogammaglobulinaemia: low baseline IgG, multiple courses, high cumulative dose, prior cyclophosphamide, concomitant GC, older age. Low IgM is common and less important than low IgG. Late-onset neutropenia occurs in about 5–10% at 1–6 months. Check IgG, IgA and IgM before each cycle. If IgG is low with recurrent or severe infections: stop or space rituximab, test specific antibody responses (pneumococcal or tetanus), give prophylactic antibiotics, and give immunoglobulin replacement (IVIG or SCIG) via immunology if infections persist. Switch to a non-B-cell drug.

stem: Before starting rituximab, screening shows HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs negative and undetectable HBV DNA. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Take part in cervical screening, with consideration of more frequent screening and HPV vaccination because of increased risk
options.B: Anti-histone
options.C: Start antiviral prophylaxis (such as entecavir or tenofovir) with hepatology input, then proceed
options.D: Hepatitis B and C serology, HIV testing, latent TB screening, and baseline FBC, renal and liver function
options.E: Cross-sectional vascular imaging such as PET-CT, CTA or MRA

explanation: Resolved (occult) HBV carries a meaningful reactivation risk with B-cell depletion, which can cause fulminant hepatitis. Antiviral prophylaxis is advised with rituximab; with most other DMARDs, HBV DNA monitoring is usually sufficient. HBsAg-positive patients need antiviral therapy with almost all immunosuppression. HBV serology interpretation: | HBsAg | anti-HBc | anti-HBs | Meaning | Action before rituximab | |—|—|—|—|—| | + | + |-| Chronic infection | Antiviral therapy (hepatology) for almost all immunosuppression | |-| + |-or + | Resolved / occult | Prophylaxis (entecavir or tenofovir) with rituximab or high-risk regimens; HBV DNA monitoring for most others | |-|-| + | Vaccinated | Nothing further | |-|-|-| Susceptible | Vaccinate | Reactivation can occur up to 12 months or more after the last rituximab dose. Presentation is a hepatitis flare and can be fulminant (fatal liver failure). HBV DNA rises weeks before ALT. Prophylaxis is usually continued for at least 12–18 months after the last rituximab dose. Screen everyone before biologics, JAK inhibitors, rituximab or high-dose GC. HBsAg-positive patients on ≥20 mg/day prednisolone for >4 weeks also need prophylaxis.

stem: Before starting a TNF inhibitor, a 40-year-old woman has a positive interferon-gamma release assay. Chest radiograph is normal and she has no symptoms. What is the most appropriate plan?

options.A: Start the TNF inhibitor immediately, since the chest radiograph is normal
options.B: Treat latent TB (for example 3 months of isoniazid with rifampicin), starting the TNF inhibitor after at least 1 month if urgent, or on completion
options.C: A duodenal biopsy with PAS staining and T. whipplei PCR, assuming Whipple disease rather than latent TB
options.D: Repeat the interferon-gamma release assay again in three months before making any decision
options.E: Withhold the TNF inhibitor permanently, since the positive IGRA is an absolute contraindication

explanation: Latent TB should be treated before TNF inhibition. When biologic therapy is urgent, it can usually start after at least a month of latent TB treatment. Etanercept carries a lower but not negligible reactivation risk and does not remove the need for treatment. TB screening pitfalls: false-negative IGRA on high-dose GC or with lymphopenia (indeterminate results); a positive IGRA from past treated TB; recent contact with a negative IGRA (repeat test). Active TB must be excluded first (symptoms, chest radiograph or CT, sputum) before treating latent infection. Reactivation risk ranks monoclonal TNFi (infliximab, adalimumab) above etanercept, which is above non-TNF biologics (abatacept, tocilizumab and rituximab carry low risk, but screening is still standard). Extrapulmonary and disseminated TB is common on TNFi. Latent TB regimens: 3 months of isoniazid plus rifampicin (with pyridoxine), or 6 months of isoniazid. Rifampicin interacts with GC (double the dose), tofacitinib and warfarin. Monitor LFTs, particularly with methotrexate.

stem: Which set of investigations is required before starting a biologic DMARD?

options.A: HbA1c, fasting lipid profile and 25-hydroxyvitamin D level only
options.B: Baseline echocardiography in every patient, regardless of cardiac history
options.C: Serum ACE level and a chest radiograph to screen for occult sarcoidosis in every patient
options.D: Serum free light chains and a bone marrow biopsy in every patient before starting
options.E: Hepatitis B and C serology, HIV testing, latent TB screening, and baseline FBC, renal and liver function

explanation: Pre-biologic assessment includes viral hepatitis and HIV serology, TB risk assessment with IGRA and chest imaging as indicated, baseline bloods (often including immunoglobulins), vaccination review and pregnancy considerations. Full pre-biologic checklist: TB (IGRA ± chest radiograph); HBsAg, anti-HBc and HCV antibodies; HIV; VZV IgG if no history; FBC, U&E, LFTs; immunoglobulins (rituximab); lipids (IL-6R, JAKi); pregnancy plans and contraception; cancer history (recent malignancy, skin checks); demyelination and NYHA III–IV heart failure (avoid TNFi); diverticulitis (caution with IL-6R and JAKi); VTE and CV risk (JAKi); vaccinations up to date (non-live ideally ≥2 weeks before; live vaccines ≥4 weeks before starting). VZV serology is advised if there is no history of chickenpox or shingles. Lipids are checked for IL-6R and JAK inhibitors; immunoglobulins before rituximab.

stem: A patient is about to start, or is already on, rituximab, and her vaccinations (including COVID-19) are not up to date. How should vaccination be timed?

options.A: Give non-live vaccines before starting rituximab if possible, or late in the dosing cycle once started, since antibody responses are reduced
options.B: Delay all vaccination until at least 12 months after stopping rituximab, regardless of clinical urgency
options.C: Give a live vaccine concurrently with the rituximab infusion to maximise early protection
options.D: Do not vaccinate at all, since antibody responses will be blunted regardless of timing
options.E: Vaccinate only once B-cell depletion has fully resolved, since no earlier vaccination option exists

explanation: B-cell depletion impairs humoral vaccine responses for at least 6 months. Vaccines should be given beforehand where feasible. COVID-19 vaccines are non-live and recommended; anti-CD20 therapy blunts humoral responses, so vaccination is best timed late in the dosing cycle, and T-cell responses are relatively preserved. Boosters follow national schedules. Non-live vaccines are safe during immunosuppression; live vaccines are generally avoided on significant immunosuppression. For patients on methotrexate, current BSR guidance suggests withholding it for up to 2 weeks after influenza or COVID-19 vaccination if disease activity allows. Response hierarchy: rituximab and abatacept impair responses most, then methotrexate (influenza) and highdose GC. TNFi, IL-6R and IL-17i have little effect. Some JAKi (e.g. tofacitinib) modestly reduce pneumococcal responses. Where possible, vaccinate at least 6 months after the last rituximab dose and at least 2–4 weeks before the next one. Consider checking B-cell (CD19) repopulation. Recommend vaccinating household members. Offer early antivirals (and, where available, monoclonal antibodies) for COVID-19 in Bcell-depleted patients.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with RA is starting upadacitinib. She has never had shingles vaccination. Which is most appropriate?

options.A: Live attenuated (Zostavax) zoster vaccine, given before starting upadacitinib
options.B: No vaccination is required, since JAK inhibitors do not increase zoster risk
options.C: Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine alone; zoster vaccination is not indicated
options.D: Recombinant adjuvanted (non-live) zoster vaccine, two doses
options.E: Defer all vaccination until upadacitinib is eventually stopped

explanation: JAK inhibitors increase herpes zoster risk. The non-live recombinant vaccine is safe in immunosuppressed patients; the live vaccine should be avoided once significant immunosuppression has started. Zoster risk factors in rheumatology: JAK inhibitors (highest; dose-dependent, especially in Asian populations), anifrolumab, high-dose GC, cyclophosphamide, SLE itself, age >50. Disseminated or multidermatomal zoster needs IV aciclovir and a pause in immunosuppression. Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix): two doses 2–6 months apart (0 and 1–2 months in the immunocompromised), ideally before starting a JAKi but safe during therapy. The live zoster vaccine (Zostavax) is contraindicated on significant immunosuppression and has now been withdrawn in the UK.

stem: In which patients are live attenuated vaccines generally contraindicated?

options.A: Prednisolone 20 mg/day or more for at least 2 weeks, biologic DMARDs or combination immunosuppression
options.B: Hydroxychloroquine monotherapy at a standard dose
options.C: Low-dose methotrexate below 10 mg weekly
options.D: Sulfasalazine monotherapy for peripheral arthritis
options.E: Short courses of NSAIDs for symptom control

explanation: Live vaccines (MMR, varicella, yellow fever, oral typhoid, live zoster) carry a risk of vaccine-derived infection under significant immunosuppression. They need specialist risk assessment and timing, ideally before immunosuppression starts. Non-live vaccines are safe. Live vaccines: MMR, varicella, live zoster, yellow fever, BCG, oral typhoid, oral polio, intranasal influenza (LAIV), rotavirus (infants). Give live vaccines ≥4 weeks before starting immunosuppression. After stopping, wait ≥1 month after high-dose GC (up to 3 months after pulses or combined immunosuppression), ≥3 months for most csDMARDs and biologics, and 6– 12 months after rituximab (per specialist guidance). Low-dose GC (<20 mg/day, or short courses <2 weeks), hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine alone are not usually a contraindication. Some guidelines allow live vaccines on low-dose methotrexate (≤0.4 mg/kg/week, ≤25 mg) and azathioprine (≤3 mg/kg/day) after specialist risk assessment. For yellow fever, travellers on significant immunosuppression need an exemption certificate and protective advice.

stem: Which vaccines are particularly important for adults with inflammatory rheumatic disease on immunosuppression?

options.A: Oral typhoid and yellow fever as routine vaccinations for every patient
options.B: BCG vaccination in adults with no prior tuberculosis exposure
options.C: Live attenuated intranasal influenza vaccine in preference to the inactivated vaccine
options.D: MMR booster vaccination regardless of immunosuppression status
options.E: Influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal, recombinant zoster where eligible, and hepatitis B where indicated

explanation: Vaccination status should be reviewed at least annually. Non-live vaccines are generally safe and ideally given during quiescent disease and before immunosuppression is escalated. HPV vaccination should be considered where eligible. Practical schedule: annual influenza (inactivated); pneumococcal conjugate per current national schedule (e.g. PCV20 single dose, or PCV then PPV23); COVID-19 boosters; recombinant zoster (eligible age or on JAKi); hepatitis B if at risk or before rituximab in susceptible people; HPV (up to 45 in many schedules for immunosuppressed SLE); RSV for eligible older adults; tetanus as indicated. Vaccinate in quiescent disease and before escalation, but do not delay vaccination for this. Non-live vaccines are safe at any GC dose; very high doses may blunt responses. Ideally vaccinate before starting GC or when the dose is lower, but never delay.

stem: The child of a patient receiving a biologic is due routine childhood vaccines, including live vaccines. What is the best advice?

options.A: Delay all of the child’s vaccines, including non-live vaccines, until the parent’s biologic is stopped
options.B: Household contacts should be fully vaccinated; with live vaccines, practical hygiene precautions apply
options.C: The child should avoid any contact with the patient after live vaccines, indefinitely
options.D: Household contacts should avoid vaccination entirely to minimise viral shedding near the patient
options.E: Only the child’s influenza vaccine needs to be timed around the parent’s biologic doses

explanation: (for example after rotavirus vaccine) Immunising household contacts protects the immunosuppressed patient. Live vaccines are not contraindicated for contacts, but precautions apply, such as careful hand hygiene and avoiding nappy changing for about 2 weeks after rotavirus vaccine. Contacts can receive MMR, varicella (if a vaccine rash develops, avoid close contact until the lesions crust) and rotavirus (careful hand hygiene; the immunosuppressed person should ideally avoid nappy changing for about 2 weeks). Live intranasal influenza is avoided only in contacts of very severely immunosuppressed people (e.g. isolated transplant recipients). Oral polio is no longer used in the UK because the vaccine virus can be shed and transmitted. Infants exposed in utero to TNFi (other than certolizumab) in the third trimester: defer live vaccines (rotavirus, BCG) until 6 months of age. Breastfeeding on biologics does not alter the infant schedule.

stem: Which immune cells are the principal source of rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies in rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: Neutrophils and mast cells
options.B: B lymphocytes and plasma cells
options.C: Dendritic cells and macrophages
options.D: CD8-positive cytotoxic T lymphocytes
options.E: Synovial fibroblasts

explanation: lymphocytes and plasma cells Autoantibodies are produced by autoreactive B cells and plasma cells, which provides the rationale for B-cell depletion with rituximab, particularly in seropositive disease. Synovial plasma cells make RF and ACPA locally, forming immune complexes that activate complement and macrophages. Ectopic lymphoid follicles are seen in the lympho-myeloid pathotype. ACPA can bind osteoclast precursors directly and drive bone loss before arthritis. Pathogenesis cascade: loss of tolerance to citrullinated proteins at mucosal sites (lung, gums, gut), then epitope spreading, then a cytokine surge (TNF, IL-6, GM-CSF), then synovitis. RANKL drives osteoclastic erosion and MMPs drive cartilage loss. Synovial fibroblasts (THY1+ sublining, PRG4+ lining) are not targeted by current drugs.

stem: What are the diagnostic and prognostic characteristics of anti-CCP (ACPA) antibodies, and which result best predicts progression to RA in a patient with inflammatory arthralgia but no synovitis?

options.A: ACPA sensitivity exceeds 95%, so a negative result reliably excludes RA
options.B: ACPA titre tracks current swollen-joint count and can substitute for clinical examination
options.C: ACPA is an activity marker that falls reliably with successful treat-to-target therapy
options.D: ACPA specificity exceeds 95% and positivity is associated with erosive disease; high-titre ACPA
options.E: ACPA and rheumatoid factor are interchangeable and provide no additional prognostic information

explanation: (especially with RF) best predicts progression from arthralgia to RA ACPA has specificity of about 95% and sensitivity of about 60–75%. It may precede clinical arthritis by years and, especially at high titre with RF, predicts more aggressive erosive disease. In people with arthralgia, high-titre ACPA with RF co-positivity predicts progression to RA, and such patients merit early specialist review. ACPA-positive without RA: other inflammatory disease (PsA in 5–10%, antisynthetase syndrome with deforming arthritis, SLE “rhupus”, Sjögren’s), active TB, chronic lung disease in smokers, and healthy relatives. RF-positive with ACPA-negative status widens the differential (CHRONIC list). “Clinically suspect arthralgia” predicts RA: onset <1 year, MCP symptoms, morning stiffness ≥60 minutes, worst in the early morning, first-degree relative with RA, inability to make a fist, positive squeeze test. MRI or ultrasound tenosynovitis adds risk. At-risk (ACPA+ arthralgia): explain the risk honestly, stop smoking, treat periodontal disease, monitor closely and start DMARDs as soon as arthritis appears. Preventive drugs are not standard; offer trials. Abatacept for 12 months delayed RA while given; one dose of rituximab delayed onset by about 12 months; methotrexate plus GC improved symptoms and MRI inflammation without preventing RA; hydroxychloroquine and atorvastatin had no effect. Low-positive means >ULN to ≤3× ULN (2 points); high-positive means >3× ULN (3 points). Anti-CarP and anti-acetylated protein antibodies may identify some seronegative RA but are research tools.

stem: A 62-year-old man with hand arthralgia has a positive rheumatoid factor, chronic hepatitis C and no synovitis on examination or ultrasound. How should the RF result be interpreted?

options.A: Hepatitis C should be treated with a methotrexate-based DMARD combination before considering antivirals
options.B: A positive RF here mandates urgent renal biopsy to exclude cryoglobulinaemic glomerulonephritis
options.C: Hydroxychloroquine should be started immediately to prevent progression to erosive arthritis
options.D: RF can occur in chronic infection, other autoimmune disease and older adults, and is not diagnostic without a compatible clinical picture
options.E: The RF titre should be rechecked only after stopping all antiviral therapy

explanation: RF lacks specificity. It occurs in hepatitis C, cryoglobulinaemia, Sjögren’s, chronic infections and up to 10-15% of healthy older people. Diagnosis requires clinical synovitis and exclusion of mimics. Causes of a positive RF: hepatitis C (with or without mixed cryoglobulinaemia), Sjögren’s (very common), SLE, SSc, MCTD, sarcoidosis, endocarditis, TB, syphilis, leprosy, HIV, PBC, chronic liver disease, lymphoma and other B-cell disorders, and healthy older people (up to 10–25%). In HCV, arthralgia is common; arthritis is less common and usually non-erosive. HCV-associated arthritis: intermittent, symmetrical smalljoint or monoarticular, non-erosive, ACPA-negative. Look for purpura, neuropathy and low C4 (cryoglobulinaemia). Do not start DMARDs for RF alone. Treat HCV with directacting antivirals. Hydroxychloroquine or low-dose GC can be used for symptoms if needed; avoid hepatotoxic DMARDs until the liver has been assessed.

stem: A 39-year-old woman has 8 weeks of symmetrical MCP and PIP joint swelling with prolonged morning stiffness. RF and anti-CCP are negative and CRP is normal. What is the best interpretation?

options.A: Repeat RF and anti-CCP in three months and treat only if either becomes positive
options.B: Diagnose fibromyalgia, since objective markers of inflammation are normal
options.C: Arrange nerve conduction studies as the priority investigation
options.D: Seronegative RA remains possible; diagnosis rests on clinical synovitis and exclusion of alternatives
options.E: Exclude RA entirely because CRP is normal

explanation: Serology and acute-phase reactants support probability and prognosis, but negative tests do not exclude RA. Persistent synovitis warrants early specialist assessment and DMARD treatment. Seronegative symmetrical polyarthritis: seronegative RA, PsA without skin disease (check scalp, umbilicus and natal cleft; ask about family history), viral arthritis (parvovirus B19, hepatitis B prodrome, rubella or vaccine, chikungunya), SLE or other CTD (ANA, ENA), polyarticular gout or CPPD (pseudo-RA), haemochromatosis (2nd and 3rd MCP), sarcoid, hypothyroid arthropathy, RS3PE, paraneoplastic arthritis, checkpoint-inhibitor arthritis, erosive hand OA, enteropathic arthritis. Seronegative patients reach 6/10 on the 2010 criteria only with >10 joints (at least one small) plus raised APR or ≥6 weeks of symptoms, so seronegative RA is under-classified early. Ultrasound or MRI synovitis and tenosynovitis support the diagnosis. Investigations: ANA and ENA, urate and crystal analysis where possible, parvovirus IgM, HBV, HCV and HIV, ferritin and transferrin saturation, TFTs, CK, ultrasound of hands and feet, radiographs of hands, feet and chest. Treat-totarget with methotrexate as in seropositive disease. Seronegative RA has slightly less radiographic progression but similar symptom burden.

stem: What is the role of the 2010 ACR/EULAR RA classification criteria in clinical practice, and how would you score a woman with 4 weeks of swelling of two MCP joints and one PIP joint, low-positive RF, negative anti- CCP and a raised CRP?

options.A: They are classification criteria and do not replace clinical diagnosis; she scores 5 points and does not yet meet the criteria
options.B: 6 points; she meets the classification criteria
options.C: 4 points; she does not meet the classification criteria
options.D: 7 points; she meets the classification criteria
options.E: They are diagnostic criteria that confirm RA once met, and she does not meet them

explanation: A score of 6/10 or more classifies RA in a patient with at least one joint with definite synovitis not better explained by another disease. Typical erosive disease can also be classified directly. Scoring here: 1–3 small joints = 2; lowpositive RF = 2; abnormal CRP = 1; symptoms under 6 weeks = 0, giving a total of 5. Classification criteria are designed for research cohorts; early treatment can still proceed on clinical grounds. Common misclassification risks: PsA, SLE, viral arthritis, polyarticular CPPD and gout, PMR with peripheral synovitis. Domain Category Points 1 large / 2–10 large / 1–3 small / 4– 0 / 1 / 2 / Joints 10 small / >10 (≥1 small) 3 / 5 negative / low-positive (≤3× ULN) / 0 / 2 / 3 Serology high-positive (>3× ULN) normal / abnormal CRP or ESR 0 / 1 APR <6 weeks / ≥6 weeks 0 / 1 Duration DIP, 1st MTP and 1st CMC joints are excluded (OA and gout sites). Direct classification applies with typical erosions in ≥3 separate joints, or in long-standing inactive disease that previously met the criteria.

stem: Which plain radiographic finding in a patient with inflammatory arthritis points away from RA and towards calcium pyrophosphate deposition?

options.A: Chondrocalcinosis
options.B: Periarticular osteopenia with uniform joint-space narrowing
options.C: Central ‘gull-wing’ erosions with osteophytes
options.D: Punched-out erosions with overhanging sclerotic edges
options.E: Marginal erosions with new bone formation and bony ankylosis

explanation: Chondrocalcinosis suggests calcium pyrophosphate deposition. RA causes periarticular osteopenia, symmetrical uniform joint space narrowing and marginal erosions. Radiographic patterns: | Feature | RA | OA | PsA | Gout | CPPD | |—|—|—|—|—|—| | Distribution | symmetrical MCP, PIP, wrist, MTP | DIP, PIP, 1st CMC | DIP, ray pattern, asymmetric | 1st MTP, asymmetric | wrist (TFCC), knee, 2nd/3rd MCP | | Erosions | marginal (“bare area”) | central (erosive OA: gull-wing) | marginal with new bone, pencil-incup | punched-out with overhanging edges | subchondral cysts | | Bone density | periarticular osteopenia | preserved | preserved | preserved | preserved | | Other | uniform joint space narrowing | osteophytes, sclerosis | periostitis, ankylosis, acro-osteolysis | tophi, preserved joint space until late | chondrocalcinosis, hook osteophytes (haemochromatosis) | Chondrocalcinosis sites: knee menisci, TFCC of the wrist, symphysis pubis, hip labrum. CPPD can coexist with RA, and RA erosions are less common in patients with chondrocalcinosis.

stem: What does a positive power Doppler signal on ultrasound of an MCP joint indicate?

options.A: Avascular tissue with no blood flow, consistent with chronic fibrosis
options.B: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals
options.C: Osteophyte formation at the joint margin
options.D: Tendon-sheath calcification consistent with calcific tendinitis
options.E: Active synovial inflammation with increased vascularity

explanation: Power Doppler detects increased synovial blood flow in active synovitis. It is more sensitive than clinical examination for subclinical synovitis, though operator-dependent. Doppler signal without inflammatory arthritis: OA with inflammatory flare, crystal arthritis, infection, post-injection or post-trauma, technical artefact (high gain, low PRF), normal nutrient vessels. Grey-scale synovial hypertrophy without Doppler signal can be inactive or fibrotic synovium. OMERACT semi-quantitative grading runs 0–3 for greyscale and Doppler. Doppler persisting in clinical remission predicts flare and radiographic progression. Ultrasound is several times more sensitive than X-ray for early erosions and detects tenosynovitis (an early RA marker; ECU tenosynovitis is common). Uses: confirming synovitis when examination is equivocal; distinguishing inflammatory from non-inflammatory pain (see entry on non-inflammatory pain); guiding injections. Routine ultrasound-guided treat-to-target has not improved outcomes over clinical T2T in trials (ARCTIC, TaSER).

stem: A 52-year-old woman has 10 weeks of symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis, strongly positive anti-CCP and DAS28-CRP 5.4. What is the most appropriate initial treatment, and why does timing matter (the “window of opportunity”)?

options.A: Methotrexate with short-term glucocorticoid bridging, started as soon as RA is diagnosed, ideally within
options.B: Methotrexate; oral glucocorticoids are not routine and, if needed, are used only at low dose for short periods
options.C: Methotrexate monotherapy, with biologic therapy prioritised ahead of any glucocorticoid bridging
options.D: Sulfasalazine alone, continued indefinitely regardless of response at 3 months
options.E: High-dose glucocorticoids including IV methylprednisolone pulses, with IVIG

explanation: 3 months of symptom onset A csDMARD should start as soon as RA is diagnosed, with methotrexate as the anchor drug, ideally with short-term glucocorticoids tapered and stopped as quickly as feasible. Biologics are not first-line in DMARD-naive patients. The window of opportunity is the first few months after symptom onset, when prompt DMARD treatment most improves the chance of remission and limits damage; early referral and DMARD initiation, ideally within 3 months, improve long-term outcomes. Very early RA (<12 weeks) achieves DAS28 remission in about 50%, versus about 15% in late-early RA. The biggest gain comes from starting any DMARD early rather than from the specific drug. Up to 75% of untreated patients develop erosions within 2 years. Bridging options: an oral prednisolone taper (e.g. 10–20 mg, then taper over 8–12 weeks), IM methylprednisolone 80–120 mg, intra-articular injections, or step-down regimens (COBRA 60 → 7.5 mg over 6 weeks; COBRA-light 30 mg). Stop within about 3 months. Low-dose GC reduces radiographic progression in early RA (COBRA, CAMERA-II, BeSt). Leflunomide or sulfasalazine if methotrexate is contraindicated. Methotrexate monotherapy is preferred over initial triple therapy. Use NSAIDs only for symptoms. NICE and EULAR targets: refer within 6 weeks of symptom onset (even with normal CRP and RF), early arthritis clinic within 3 weeks of referral. Avoid primary-care steroids before assessment because they mask synovitis.

stem: What is the primary treatment target in RA, how often should disease activity be assessed, and which DAS28 value defines remission?

options.A: DAS28 low disease activity only, reassessed annually, with escalation only after radiographic progression is confirmed
options.B: Sustained remission, or low disease activity if unrealistic, assessed every 1–3 months while active, with escalation if no improvement by 3 months or target not met by 6 months; DAS28 remission is below 2.6
options.C: Treat-to-target escalation to achieve remission or low disease activity, reassessed only once yearly
options.D: CDAI remission alone, assessed every 6 months, with escalation only if swollen joints exceed tender joints
options.E: ACR/EULAR Boolean remission alone, reassessed every 12 months regardless of reported symptoms

explanation: Treat-to-target aims for remission (by composite measures such as DAS28, CDAI, SDAI or Boolean definitions) or, if not achievable, low disease activity, with regular assessment and escalation. Tight control with frequent composite disease activity measurement and prompt escalation improves outcomes. DAS28: remission below 2.6; low activity 3.2 or less; moderate up to 5.1; high above 5.1. DAS28 remission can coexist with residual swollen joints, so SDAI, CDAI or Boolean definitions are stricter. Things that falsely raise DAS28: fibromyalgia and central sensitisation (high TJC and patient global), OA, depression, high ESR from age, anaemia or paraprotein. Things that falsely lower it: IL-6 or JAK blockade suppressing CRP and ESR (DAS28 overestimates remission on tocilizumab, so prefer CDAI). Score Remission Low Moderate High DAS28 <2.6 ≤3.2 ≤5.1 >5.1 ≤3.3 ≤11 ≤26 >26 SDAI ≤2.8 ≤10 ≤22 >22 CDAI Boolean remission: TJC, SJC, CRP (mg/dL) and patient global (0–10) each ≤1; patient global ≤2 is now accepted. SDAI = TJC28 + SJC28 + PtGA + PhGA + CRP (mg/dL); CDAI omits CRP, so it can be calculated at the bedside. DAS28 ignores the feet. Once the target is sustained, review every 3–6 months. Radiographs of hands and feet yearly in the first years. Function is measured with HAQ-DI (0–3).

stem: A woman with seropositive RA has taken methotrexate 10 mg weekly for 3 months (DAS28-CRP 4.8), or takes 20 mg weekly with persistent nausea and an inadequate response. What should happen before methotrexate is abandoned?

options.A: Add an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor now, without further optimising the methotrexate regimen first
options.B: Optimise it: increase to 20–25 mg weekly, switch to subcutaneous administration (better bioavailability and tolerability), optimise folic acid and reassess within 1–3 months
options.C: Escalate directly to a biologic DMARD without further optimising methotrexate
options.D: Switch to subcutaneous methotrexate at the same weekly dose, without any further dose titration
options.E: Switch to leflunomide monotherapy instead of further optimising methotrexate

explanation: Methotrexate should be titrated rapidly to an optimal dose (usually 20–25 mg weekly, or 0.3 mg/kg) before it can be judged to have failed. Subcutaneous administration improves bioavailability and often reduces gastrointestinal intolerance. Apparent failure that is not true failure: non-adherence (ask about “methotrexate day” omissions and intolerance), inadequate dose or duration (<3 months at target dose), non-inflammatory pain, wrong diagnosis (PsA, CPPD, PMR, CTD). Intolerance strategies: split oral dose 12 hours apart, evening dosing, antiemetic, higher folate, SC route. If still not at target after 3–6 months on optimised methotrexate, escalate to a b/tsDMARD (next entry). Combination csDMARD therapy (triple therapy) is an alternative strategy where access to biologics is limited (and in NICE pathways), but it adds toxicity.

stem: A patient with seropositive RA remains active (DAS28-CRP about 4.6) despite 6 months of optimised methotrexate off glucocorticoids. What is the next step, and how does the choice change in a 68-year-old current smoker with a previous MI?

options.A: Add a second csDMARD (triple therapy) rather than consider a biologic or JAK inhibitor at this stage
options.B: Add a biologic, or consider a JAK inhibitor after risk assessment; in older patients, smokers, or those with CV, malignancy or VTE risk, choose a biologic such as a TNF inhibitor
options.C: Choose a JAK inhibitor as the preferred first advanced therapy for everyone, regardless of cardiovascular risk profile
options.D: Continue methotrexate alone for a further 6 months before considering any advanced therapy at all
options.E: Choose rituximab first-line, irrespective of seropositivity status or infection risk

explanation: If the target is not reached with an optimised methotrexate strategy after 3–6 months, a bDMARD should be added; a JAK inhibitor may be considered after weighing cardiovascular, malignancy and thromboembolic risk. JAK inhibitors should be used only if no suitable alternative exists in patients aged 65 or over, current or long-term past smokers, or those with cardiovascular, malignancy or VTE risk factors. Access may also depend on local commissioning criteria. Choosing the next drug by comorbidity:-Heart failure (NYHA III–IV) or demyelination: avoid TNFi.-Prior diverticulitis or perforation: avoid IL-6R inhibitors; caution with JAKi.-Recent malignancy or lymphoma: rituximab is preferred.-Recurrent serious infection: abatacept or rituximab (check IgG).-Pregnancy plans: certolizumab or another TNFi.-Cannot take methotrexate: IL-6R inhibitor or JAKi as monotherapy.-ILD: abatacept or rituximab.-Seronegative disease: rituximab works less well.-Obesity: IV or weight-based dosing (tocilizumab IV, infliximab), or a non-TNF drug. The current EULAR position is that methotrexate failure is itself a poor prognostic factor, so there is no longer a separate step of trying a second csDMARD in patients without poor prognostic factors. NICE access criteria in England still specify DAS28 thresholds (>5.1 for severe disease, and 3.2–5.1 for moderate disease for some drugs). Biosimilars are the first choice where available. Combine with methotrexate where possible.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has been in sustained DAS28 remission for 18 months on methotrexate 15 mg weekly and adalimumab 40 mg fortnightly. Glucocorticoids were stopped 2 years ago. She asks about reducing medication. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Stop both methotrexate and adalimumab simultaneously now that remission is sustained
options.B: Taper methotrexate first while continuing adalimumab fortnightly unchanged
options.C: Stop methotrexate now, continuing adalimumab unchanged, rather than tapering the biologic
options.D: No tapering should be attempted; lifelong unchanged combination therapy is required
options.E: Consider tapering adalimumab by dose reduction or interval extension while continuing methotrexate

explanation: In sustained remission without glucocorticoids, b/tsDMARDs may be tapered, especially when combined with a csDMARD. Stopping all DMARDs commonly leads to flare. Tapering should be gradual with a plan to return to the previous dose if flare occurs. Flare risks during tapering: RF/ACPA positivity, Doppler activity on ultrasound, short remission duration, stopping rather than spacing, and stopping the csDMARD first. Sequence: GC off → b/tsDMARD interval extension or dose reduction (after ≥6 months of sustained remission) → csDMARD dose reduction last. Complete DMARD withdrawal is rarely successful (flare in about 50%), but most patients regain control after restarting. Ultrasoundguided tapering does not clearly beat clinical tapering.

stem: A patient with RA on adalimumab and methotrexate initially responded well but lost response after 18 months. Low trough levels and anti-drug antibodies are found. What is an appropriate next step?

options.A: TNF inhibitors
options.B: Switch to another TNF inhibitor or to a drug with a different mechanism
options.C: Increase the adalimumab dose or frequency beyond the licensed regimen
options.D: Add a second biologic with a different mechanism while continuing adalimumab unchanged
options.E: Repeat anti-drug antibody testing in 24 months before making any treatment change

explanation: After failure of a first bDMARD, any other bDMARD (from the same or another class) or a JAK inhibitor (after risk assessment) can be used. Immunogenicity-driven secondary failure is a good reason to try another TNF inhibitor. Combining biologics is not recommended. Primary non-response (no improvement by 3–6 months) suggests switching mechanism. Secondary loss of response with anti-drug antibodies can respond to a second TNFi (or adding methotrexate). Rituximab works best in seropositive disease. After two mechanisms fail, consider D2T assessment. Never combine two biologics (infection risk without added efficacy).

stem: A patient with RA has a history of multiple sclerosis and needs a biologic. Which drug class should generally be avoided?

options.A: IL-6 receptor inhibitors
options.B: Monoclonal-antibody TNF inhibitor
options.C: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor
options.D: Certolizumab pegol
options.E: TNF inhibitors

explanation: TNF inhibitors have been associated with new or worsening demyelinating disease and are avoided in established demyelination. Other TNFi neurological effects: optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, Guillain-Barré or CIDP-like neuropathy, PML (rare, more with rituximab). New neurology on a TNFi also needs exclusion of TB meningitis and Listeria. Safer choices with MS or demyelination: rituximab (also an MS therapy), abatacept, IL-6R inhibitors, JAKi (after risk assessment). If demyelination occurs on a TNFi, stop it permanently.

stem: A 71-year-old man with RA has NYHA class III heart failure and active disease despite methotrexate. Which treatment is usually avoided?

options.A: IL-17 inhibitor
options.B: Rituximab
options.C: A TNF inhibitor
options.D: An IL-6 receptor inhibitor
options.E: Abatacept
