explanation: TNF inhibitor TNF inhibitors can worsen moderate-to-severe (NYHA III-IV) heart failure. A non-TNF biologic is preferred. NYHA I–II: use TNFi cautiously, with echo and monitoring. NYHA III–IV: avoid (worse outcomes in heart-failure trials of infliximab and etanercept). Alternatives: abatacept, rituximab, tocilizumab or sarilumab. Note the lipid rise with IL-6R inhibition. JAKi are generally avoided with established CVD.

stem: A 66-year-old male ex-smoker with high-titre anti-CCP RA has bibasal crackles. HRCT shows basal reticulation, traction bronchiectasis and honeycombing. Which pattern is most likely?

options.A: High-resolution CT chest
options.B: Usual interstitial pneumonia
options.C: Interstitial lung disease
options.D: B lymphocytes and plasma cells
options.E: Apremilast

explanation: UIP is the commonest HRCT pattern in RA-ILD, unlike most other connective tissue disease-related ILDs where NSIP predominates. Risk factors include male sex, older age, smoking, high-titre RF/ACPA and the MUC5B promoter variant. Differential of RA-ILD: methotrexate pneumonitis (acute, rare), other drug lung toxicity (leflunomide, TNFi exacerbation, rituximab), infection (TB, PJP, NTM), heart failure, bronchiectasis and obliterative bronchiolitis (airways disease), Caplan’s nodules, lung cancer (higher in RA), smoking-related ILD (RB-ILD, DIP), and coexisting IPF (MUC5B). Clinically significant in about 10% (subclinical in up to 30%). UIP is the commonest pattern, then NSIP. UIP, extensive disease, low FVC or DLCO, older age, male sex and high-titre RF/ACPA predict progression and death. Screen at-risk patients with HRCT (PFTs alone miss cases), plus PFTs including DLCO and a 6-minute walk test. Monitor PFTs every 3–6 months for 1–2 years, then every 6–12 months; repeat HRCT at 1–2 years.

stem: A patient with RA-associated interstitial lung disease has active arthritis and needs treatment escalation. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Switch to a TNF inhibitor as first-line therapy, since it best controls both joint and lung disease
options.B: Add rituximab regardless of ILD pattern or severity, without respiratory input
options.C: Use long-term high-dose glucocorticoids as the primary ILD-modifying treatment
options.D: Individualised treatment with respiratory input, based on the lung pattern, its progression and the joint disease
options.E: Stop methotrexate in all cases of RA-associated ILD regardless of disease stability

explanation: RA-ILD needs multidisciplinary assessment. Options depend on ILD pattern, severity and progression; agents such as rituximab, abatacept or mycophenolate are used on a case-by-case basis, and antifibrotics may be considered for progressive fibrosis. Options:-Immunosuppression for ILD: mycophenolate, rituximab or azathioprine.-Joints: abatacept is often chosen (it may stabilise ILD); JAKi have observational data.-Antifibrotics: nintedanib for progressive pulmonary fibrosis (INBUILD); pirfenidone in UIP (TRAIL1).-Methotrexate can usually continue in stable ILD. Use TNFi cautiously because of reports of ILD exacerbation.-Supportive: stop smoking, vaccinate, pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen, early transplant referral.-Steroids: short-term only; avoid long-term high doses. Manage in an ILD MDT.

stem: A woman with long-standing seropositive RA has recurrent infections, splenomegaly and neutrophils of 0.6 x 10I/L, not drug-related. Which test best distinguishes Felty’s syndrome from T-cell large granular lymphocyte leukaemia?

options.A: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy alone
options.B: Peripheral blood flow cytometry with T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies
options.C: Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels alone
options.D: Troponin I
options.E: HLA-DR4 genotyping alone

explanation: Felty’s syndrome and T-LGL leukaemia overlap clinically and both associate with HLA-DR4. An expanded clonal CD3+CD8+CD57+ population supports T-LGL leukaemia. Neutropenia in RA: drugs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, leflunomide, tocilizumab, rituximab late-onset neutropenia, JAKi); Felty’s syndrome; T-LGL leukaemia; SLE overlap (“rhupus”); B12 or folate deficiency; viral infection; hypersplenism (cirrhosis); myelodysplasia. Felty’s triad: seropositive (often nodular, long-standing) RA, splenomegaly and neutropenia (<2.0), plus leg ulcers, recurrent infections, lymphadenopathy, vasculitis and nodular regenerative hyperplasia of the liver (with portal hypertension). It is strongly linked to HLA-DR4. Large granular lymphocytes may be seen on the blood film in both Felty’s and T-LGL leukaemia. Felty’s: control RA (methotrexate first-line; rituximab for refractory disease). Use G-CSF for severe infection (it can flare arthritis or vasculitis). Splenectomy is a last resort. T-LGL leukaemia: methotrexate, ciclosporin or cyclophosphamide, with haematology input.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with 25 years of erosive RA is listed for hip replacement under general anaesthesia. She reports occasional occipital headache. What is the most important pre-operative investigation?

options.A: Temporal artery ultrasound
options.B: DEXA bone densitometry
options.C: MRI of the cervical spine with urgent spinal assessment
options.D: Plain lateral cervical spine radiograph in a neutral position only, without flexion-extension views
options.E: Lateral cervical spine imaging in flexion and extension (or MRI)

explanation: Atlantoaxial subluxation is common in long-standing erosive RA and may be asymptomatic. An anterior atlanto-dental interval over 3 mm is abnormal. Detecting instability before intubation prevents cord injury. Occipital headache in RA: atlanto-axial disease vs cervical spondylosis, GCA (in older people), C2 neuralgia, medication-overuse headache. Cervical RA patterns: anterior atlanto-axial subluxation (commonest; anterior ADI >3 mm abnormal; posterior ADI <14 mm or anterior ADI >9–10 mm indicates high myelopathy risk); basilar invagination (cranial settling, with brainstem compression and risk of sudden death); subaxial “staircase” subluxation. Symptoms: occipital pain, Lhermitte’s sign, hand clumsiness, gait disturbance, bladder dysfunction. Flexion–extension radiographs (performed carefully), MRI for cord compression, CT for bone. Anaesthetic plan: inline stabilisation, fibreoptic intubation, soft collar. Surgery (C1–C2 fusion, occipito-cervical fixation) for myelopathy or severe instability.

stem: A patient with RA presents with a painful red eye with reduced vision. Ophthalmology confirms necrotising scleritis. What does this most strongly indicate?

options.A: Simple dry-eye disease, requiring only lubricant drops
options.B: Enthesitis-related arthritis
options.C: A benign, self-limiting form of episcleritis requiring no treatment
options.D: Hydroxychloroquine-related maculopathy rather than scleral inflammation
options.E: Systemic vasculitic disease activity requiring urgent systemic immunosuppression

explanation: Necrotising scleritis in RA reflects systemic vasculitis and carries significant morbidity and mortality without treatment. High-dose glucocorticoids plus a DMARD or biologic are used with urgent ophthalmology involvement. Red eye in RA: Episcleritis: mild discomfort, normal vision, blanches with phenylephrine, self-limiting.-Scleritis: severe boring pain, tender, violaceous, sightthreatening.-Necrotising scleritis or scleromalacia perforans: painless thinning.-Peripheral ulcerative keratitis (corneal melt): an emergency.-Keratoconjunctivitis sicca: secondary Sjögren’s.-Drug effects: GC cataract or glaucoma, hydroxychloroquine retinopathy.-Infectious keratitis or uveitis in immunosuppressed patients: HSV, VZV, CMV. Other features of rheumatoid vasculitis (long-standing seropositive nodular disease, smokers): nail-fold infarcts, purpura, leg ulcers, digital gangrene, mononeuritis multiplex, scleritis and PUK, mesenteric or renal involvement. Low complement and high-titre RF are typical. Incidence has fallen from about 5% to ≤1%. High-dose GC (including IV methylprednisolone) plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide for necrotising scleritis, PUK or systemic vasculitis. TNFi (adalimumab or infliximab) is also used for scleritis. Topical lubricants and ophthalmology-led local care.

stem: Which approach best fits cardiovascular risk management in a 55-year-old UK patient with RA?

options.A: Proactive assessment of cardiovascular and metabolic risk, obesity, mood and smoking
options.B: Treat hyperlipidaemia alone, with no additional formal cardiovascular risk calculation
options.C: Repeat cardiovascular risk assessment only once, at RA diagnosis, with no further reassessment
options.D: Use a national risk tool that includes RA (such as QRISK3), reassess regularly, and control disease activity and traditional risk factors
options.E: Avoid statins in RA because of the inflammation-related ‘lipid paradox’

explanation: RA confers excess cardiovascular risk. Assessment should be repeated at least every 5 years and after major treatment changes, with good disease control and judicious use of NSAIDs and glucocorticoids. RA roughly doubles CV risk (IHD 1.5–2×; heart failure about 2×; VTE 1.5–2×). The “lipid paradox”: active inflammation lowers cholesterol. ACPA is linked to CV death. QRISK3 includes RA, SLE, steroid use and severe mental illness. If the risk tool does not include RA, multiply the calculated risk by 1.5. Lipids should be measured when disease is stable. Statins have the same efficacy as in the general population (TRACE-RA showed a trend to benefit). Disease control (methotrexate, TNFi) is associated with fewer events. Minimise NSAIDs and GC. Check lipids 4–8 weeks after starting IL-6R or JAKi (the LDL rise with IL-6 blockade has not translated into excess events).

stem: When should annual hydroxychloroquine retinopathy screening begin, and how does this change with risk factors (for example 5.5 mg/kg/day and eGFR 52)?

options.A: Begin annual screening immediately, regardless of dose or treatment duration
options.B: No screening is required if the patient remains asymptomatic
options.C: After 5 years of treatment without risk factors; after 1 year if risk factors are present (dose above 5 mg/kg/day, eGFR below 60, or concomitant tamoxifen)
options.D: After 10 years of treatment in all patients, irrespective of dose or renal function
options.E: Annual screening from treatment initiation using fundus photography alone, without OCT

explanation: For patients without additional risk factors, annual screening starts after 5 years of therapy. If risk factors are present (dose above 5 mg/kg/day, eGFR below 60 or tamoxifen), annual monitoring starts after 1 year, and the dose should also be reduced to 5 mg/kg/day or less. Screening uses spectral-domain OCT with widefield fundus autofluorescence; routine baseline testing for new starters is no longer recommended in current UK guidance, although the EULAR course still advises baseline imaging within the first year. Other retinal or visual problems in rheumatology patients: GC cataract and central serous chorioretinopathy, uveitis, retinal vasculitis (Behçet’s, SLE), APS retinal vein occlusion, CMV retinitis (immunosuppression). Patients of Asian heritage often show extramacular (pericentral) toxicity, so widefield imaging is needed. Toxicity is irreversible and can progress after stopping. Early loss is parafoveal (bull’s-eye maculopathy is a late sign). Dose by actual body weight, ≤5 mg/kg/day (e.g. 60 kg gives 300 mg/day, which can be given as alternating 200/400 mg). If definite toxicity is found, stop the drug and discuss alternatives with the ophthalmologist.

stem: What is the usual perioperative approach to methotrexate and to a subcutaneous TNF inhibitor in a patient with RA having an elective joint replacement?

options.A: Stop methotrexate 2 weeks before surgery in all patients regardless of renal function or disease control
options.B: Continue the biologic unchanged through the perioperative period in all cases regardless of infection risk
options.C: Stop the biologic permanently rather than timing surgery within its normal dosing cycle
options.D: Stop glucocorticoids abruptly before surgery to reduce the risk of wound infection
options.E: Continue methotrexate in most patients unless renal function is unstable or infection is present; withhold the biologic so surgery falls at the end of its dosing interval, restarting once the wound is healing

explanation: Continuing methotrexate does not increase wound complications and reduces flare risk. Biologic timing depends on the drug’s dosing interval. Glucocorticoids should not be stopped abruptly perioperatively. Individual surgical and anaesthetic advice still applies. Surgery timing (ACR/AAHKS-based, as in the EULAR course): | Drug | Interval | Operate in | |—|—|—| | Etanercept | weekly | week 2 | | Adalimumab, sarilumab | 2weekly | week 3 | | Golimumab SC | monthly | week 5 | | Infliximab | 4, 6 or 8-weekly | week 5, 7 or 9 | | Tocilizumab | SC weekly / IV 4-weekly | week 2 / week 5 | | Abatacept | SC weekly / IV monthly | week 2 / week 5 | | Rituximab | 6monthly | month 7 | | Ustekinumab | 12-weekly | week 13 | | JAK inhibitors | daily | stop 3 days before; operate on day 4 | Continue csDMARDs (methotrexate, leflunomide, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine). Continue the usual GC dose; routine supraphysiological “stress dosing” is not needed for most patients on their usual dose, but anaesthetists may give hydrocortisone cover for major surgery in long-term users (see the GC entry). Restart about 14 days after surgery once healing is satisfactory. Assess the cervical spine before intubation. Do not delay emergency surgery; hold the biologic until healed. Continue all drugs for minor procedures (dental, skin, cataract).

stem: A patient with active inflammatory arthritis asks whether he should exercise during a flare. What is the best advice?

options.A: Complete rest and immobilisation of all joints until the flare fully resolves
options.B: High-impact aerobic exercise is preferred over isometric exercise during a flare
options.C: Avoid all exercise until disease activity scores reach remission
options.D: Exercise should be deferred until biologic therapy has been escalated
options.E: Adapt exercise to symptoms, maintaining movement and rehabilitation while avoiding overload of acutely inflamed joints

explanation: Tailored exercise improves function, cardiovascular health and fatigue in inflammatory arthritis. Core non-drug care: education and a written flare plan; aerobic plus strengthening exercise (safe even in active disease, with isometric work for hot joints); hand exercises (SARAH programme); splints; podiatry and orthoses; occupational therapy and joint protection; work support; CBT for pain, fatigue and mood; smoking cessation; healthy weight; Mediterranean-style diet. Fatigue is one of the most troublesome symptoms and often persists in remission. Treat anaemia, depression and sleep problems, and use graded exercise and CBT-based self-management.

stem: A patient with RA (or axial SpA) reports worsening pain with high patient-reported scores, but there are no swollen joints, CRP is normal and imaging shows no active inflammation. What should be considered before escalating immunosuppression?

options.A: Arrange only a CT scan of the sacroiliac joints to confirm ongoing inflammatory activity before any other step
options.B: Start opioid analgesia as the first-line treatment for the reported pain, without further reassessment
options.C: Management principles are the same; biologics require objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP or MRI inflammation)
options.D: Increase the current DMARD dose further without any additional clinical or laboratory reassessment
options.E: Consider non-inflammatory pain (fibromyalgia, central sensitisation, mechanical OA), mood and sleep disturbance, and comorbidity; reassess the diagnosis before switching treatment

explanation: Treatment should match demonstrable inflammatory activity. Disease activity scores (DAS28, BASDAI) can be inflated by non-inflammatory pain, fibromyalgia, mechanical pain and mood. Before switching, confirm the diagnosis, adherence, objective inflammatory activity (swollen joints, CRP, ultrasound or MRI) and the reason for failure. Pain mechanisms in RA: nociceptive (synovitis, damage, secondary OA); neuropathic (carpal tunnel syndrome, cervical myelopathy, vasculitic neuropathy); nociplastic (fibromyalgia in about 20%). Other drivers: depression and anxiety (1 in 3–4), obesity, hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, statin myalgia, GC withdrawal, osteonecrosis or insufficiency fracture. Separate pain plan: exercise, CBT and pain management programmes, sleep hygiene, judicious analgesia (avoid long-term opioids and gabapentinoids), duloxetine or amitriptyline for selected patients, and treatment of entrapment neuropathy. Use CDAI or ultrasound to judge inflammation. In axSpA, ASDAS (which includes CRP) is less affected by pain than BASDAI.

stem: A patient with RA has recurrent serious infections and active disease. What should be reviewed before choosing the next treatment?

options.A: Serum urate and 24-hour urinary urate excretion
options.B: DAS28 and CRP trend over the preceding 3 months alone
options.C: HLA-B27 status and family history of spondyloarthritis
options.D: Prior infection history, glucocorticoid exposure, vaccination status, comorbidities and the infection profile of each option
options.E: Serum immunoglobulin levels only, with no other infection-risk assessment

explanation: Glucocorticoid dose is a major modifiable infection risk. Abatacept and IL-6 or TNF inhibitors differ in serious infection profiles. Serious infection risk is highest in the first 6–12 months of therapy; TNFi raises it roughly 1.5–2×. GC dose is the strongest modifiable factor. Abatacept probably has the lowest serious-infection risk; rituximab adds the risk of hypogammaglobulinaemia; JAKi add zoster risk. Taper GC to ≤5 mg or stop. Vaccinate (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, recombinant zoster). Treat bronchiectasis (sputum clearance, consider prophylactic azithromycin, though note the QT interaction with hydroxychloroquine). Check IgG. Prefer abatacept or rituximab (if IgG is normal). Treat skin and foot portals of entry.

stem: A 29-year-old man has 7 months of inflammatory back pain, MRI sacroiliitis, negative HLA-B27 and a good response to naproxen. Does he meet the ASAS axial SpA classification criteria, and through which arm?

options.A: He meets the clinical arm: HLA-B27 plus two or more SpA features
options.B: He does not meet either arm, because MRI sacroiliitis alone is never sufficient
options.C: He meets the clinical arm only if CRP is also elevated
options.D: He meets the imaging arm: sacroiliitis plus at least one SpA feature
options.E: He meets the criteria only if radiographic (not MRI) sacroiliitis is also present

explanation: The criteria apply to back pain of 3 months or more starting before age 45. The imaging arm requires sacroiliitis (active MRI inflammation or definite radiographic change) plus at least one SpA feature; inflammatory back pain and good NSAID response each count. The clinical arm requires HLA-B27 plus at least two features. Mimics of axSpA: mechanical or degenerative back pain; fibromyalgia (a common misdiagnosis in women); osteitis condensans ilii; DISH; sacral insufficiency fracture; septic sacroiliitis (unilateral; S. aureus, TB, Brucella); post-partum or athletic BME; SAPHO; hyperparathyroidism (subchondral resorption at the SIJ); fluorosis; X-linked hypophosphataemia (enthesopathy); ochronosis; Paget’s; metastases; hypermobility. ASAS features: IBP, arthritis, heel enthesitis, uveitis, dactylitis, psoriasis, Crohn’s or colitis, good NSAID response, family history, HLA-B27, raised CRP. Peripheral SpA criteria require arthritis, enthesitis or dactylitis plus ≥1 of (uveitis, psoriasis, IBD, preceding infection, B27, sacroiliitis) or ≥2 of (arthritis, enthesitis, Rheumatology SCE — 5-option SBA 26 dactylitis, IBP history, family history). Referral strategy: chronic back pain (≥3 months) starting before 45 plus at least one of IBP, B27, imaging sacroiliitis, peripheral SpA features, uveitis, psoriasis, IBD, family history, NSAID response or raised CRP. Screen patients presenting to ophthalmology, dermatology and gastroenterology. The original ASAS criteria performed below target in the inception cohort (sensitivity 82%, specificity 77%), and misuse as diagnostic criteria led to over-labelling. Classification is not diagnosis.

stem: Which MRI finding defines active sacroiliitis in axial SpA, and how should a small area of sacroiliac bone marrow oedema be interpreted in a postpartum woman with mechanical back pain and a normal CRP?

options.A: Fat metaplasia and ankylosis alone define chronic structural damage, without any role for bone marrow oedema
options.B: NSAID response alone confirms active sacroiliitis, regardless of any MRI findings
options.C: Any degree of bone marrow oedema, in any location, always confirms active sacroiliitis requiring biologic therapy
options.D: Periarticular bone marrow oedema on STIR or fat-suppressed T2 in a typical location defines active sacroiliitis; it is non-specific and occurs in healthy people, so clinical context is essential
options.E: Synovitis or capsulitis alone, without bone marrow oedema, is sufficient to define active sacroiliitis and start a biologic

explanation: Bone marrow oedema clearly present and typically located is required. Structural lesions such as erosions and fat metaplasia support the diagnosis but do not alone define active sacroiliitis. Sacroiliac bone marrow oedema is not specific: its distribution, extent, accompanying structural lesions and the clinical picture determine significance, and overdiagnosis is a recognised problem. Non-SpA causes of SIJ BME: post-partum (up to about 60% shortly after delivery), runners and military recruits, mechanical back pain (up to about 20% of healthy people), osteitis condensans ilii (iliac-sided triangular sclerosis in multiparous women; sacrum normal, no erosions), insufficiency fracture (H-shaped sacral pattern), septic sacroiliitis (unilateral, effusion, soft-tissue oedema), degenerative change in older people, gout or CPPD of the SIJ (rare). Mechanical BME typically sits in the anterior iliac side of the lower joint, is small and has no erosions. Erosions and fat metaplasia (backfill, ankylosis) add specificity. Synovitis, capsulitis or enthesitis alone do not qualify. Sequences: STIR or T2 fat-suppressed for activity, T1 for structural lesions. Contrast is rarely needed. Do not request SIJ MRI as a screening test when pre-test probability is low. In post-partum women, consider repeating MRI after 6–12 months if the clinical picture is unclear.

stem: Which modified New York grading of sacroiliitis is required for radiographic axial SpA (ankylosing spondylitis)?

options.A: Bilateral grade 1, or unilateral grade 2
options.B: Bilateral grade 2 or more, or unilateral grade 3-4
options.C: Unilateral grade 2 alone is sufficient
options.D: Bilateral grade 1 or more, regardless of unilateral grade
options.E: Any grade 1 change, bilateral or unilateral

explanation: Modified New York criteria require radiographic sacroiliitis (bilateral grade 2 or more, or unilateral grade 3-4) plus at least one clinical criterion: inflammatory back pain for over 3 months, limited lumbar motion, or reduced chest expansion. Radiographic SIJ sclerosis without SpA: OCI, DISH (bridging of the upper ligamentous part only), degenerative change, hyperparathyroidism, Paget’s, renal osteodystrophy. Grade Appearance 0 normal 1 suspicious 2 minimal: small erosions or sclerosis, no change in width 3 unequivocal: erosions, sclerosis, widening, narrowing, partial ankylosis 4 complete ankylosis Inter-reader agreement on plain films is poor. Low-dose CT resolves equivocal X-rays (erosions, sclerosis, ankylosis) but shows no inflammation.

stem: A 26-year-old man with mechanical low back pain has a positive HLA-B27 result ordered by his GP. What does this result mean?

options.A: A positive result alone confirms axial spondyloarthritis without further assessment
options.B: HLA-B27 is found in over 50% of the general white UK population
options.C: Enthesitis-related arthritis
options.D: About 8% of the white UK population carries HLA-B27 and most never develop spondyloarthritis
options.E: A negative HLA-B27 result excludes axial spondyloarthritis

explanation: HLA-B27 is found in roughly 85-95% of white patients with AS but also about 8% of the general population, so its predictive value in unselected back pain is low. It is useful only with clinical and imaging findings. HLA-B27 in context: present in about 85–95% of white AS patients but only about 50% in African and Middle Eastern populations. Prevalence in Europe is 6–9% (higher in Scandinavians, about 14–16%; very high in Haida and other indigenous groups). Only 1–5% of carriers develop axSpA (10–30% if a first-degree relative is affected). Request it only with a clinical suspicion of SpA (≥1 SpA feature). A positive result in non-specific mechanical back pain adds little; a negative result lowers but does not exclude probability.

stem: Which ASDAS-CRP values define disease activity states, and how should a fall from 3.6 to 2.4 twelve weeks after starting a TNF inhibitor be interpreted?

options.A: ASDAS below 1.3 is inactive disease; a fall of 1.1 or more is a clinically important improvement, so a fall of 1.2 supports continuing treatment
options.B: ASDAS below 2.1 is inactive disease, and any fall at all is a major improvement
options.C: ASDAS has no validated improvement threshold; only the absolute value is informative
options.D: A fall of less than 0.5 units still qualifies as a major improvement
options.E: ASDAS cannot be calculated without first obtaining a formal BASDAI score

explanation: ASDAS: below 1.3 inactive; 1.3 to below 2.1 low; 2.1 to 3.5 high; above 3.5 very high disease activity. A fall of 1.1 or more is clinically important improvement and 2.0 or more is major improvement. Continuation is supported by an ASDAS improvement of at least 1.1 units after 12–16 weeks. ASDAS-CRP combines back pain, morning stiffness duration, patient global, peripheral pain or swelling, and CRP. BASDAI (6 patient questions; ≥4 means active) is the traditional NICE threshold, with a response defined as a ≥2point (or 50%) fall. ASDAS is preferred because it includes CRP and has validated cut-offs. Treat-to-target: ASDAS <2.1, ideally <1.3. Review every 3–6 months while active. Repeat imaging is not routine; spinal X-ray progression is assessed no more often than every 2 years.

stem: What is first-line treatment for active axial SpA, when is a biologic indicated (for example persistent ASDAS 3.3 after naproxen then etoricoxib at full dose for 6 weeks), and which non-drug measures remain important after starting it?

options.A: A biologic should be started immediately after diagnosis, without any trial of NSAID therapy first
options.B: Exercise and physiotherapy alone, without any pharmacological therapy, remain first-line regardless of activity
options.C: A biologic is indicated only after conventional synthetic DMARD failure, exactly as in peripheral RA
options.D: Methotrexate as the first disease-modifying treatment, escalating to a biologic only after methotrexate failure
options.E: A full-dose NSAID with exercise first; after two NSAIDs over 4 weeks with ASDAS still 2.1 or more, start a TNF or IL-17 inhibitor, or a JAK inhibitor after risk assessment

explanation: full-dose NSAID with exercise and education first; after at least two NSAIDs over 4 weeks with ASDAS still 2.1 or more, start a TNF or IL-17 inhibitor (or a JAK inhibitor after risk assessment); exercise, physiotherapy, education and smoking cessation remain core throughout NSAIDs are first-line, used continuously if needed for symptom control, after considering gastrointestinal, renal and cardiovascular risk. b/tsDMARDs are indicated when ASDAS is 2.1 or more despite at least two NSAIDs over a total of 4 weeks; a TNF inhibitor or IL-17 inhibitor is the usual first choice. Exercise and physiotherapy remain core treatment regardless of drug therapy, and smoking worsens disease activity and structural progression. 60–80% respond to NSAIDs within 48–72 hours, and a good response supports the diagnosis. All b/tsDMARDs achieve ASAS40 in about 40–50% (vs 15–25% with placebo). Response is best in younger patients with short disease duration, raised CRP and MRI inflammation. Longterm TNFi (>4 years) is associated with slower syndesmophyte formation. NSAID safety: coxib or NSAID plus PPI for GI risk; naproxen has the most neutral CV profile; monitor eGFR and BP; avoid after 20 weeks of pregnancy. Choosing the first b/tsDMARD: recurrent uveitis or IBD → mAb TNFi (or upadacitinib); significant psoriasis → IL-17i (or TNFi); pregnancy plans → certolizumab; age ≥65, smoking, CV or VTE risk → avoid JAKi; otherwise a biosimilar TNFi on cost. Licensing: bimekizumab and upadacitinib are licensed for both r-and nr-axSpA; tofacitinib for r-axSpA. Non-drug: supervised exercise (land or water, group) beats home exercise; passive modalities have little evidence; stop smoking; manage weight. Surgery: THR for structural hip disease regardless of age; corrective osteotomy at specialist centres. After first b/tsDMARD failure: check the diagnosis, adherence and non-inflammatory pain (fibromyalgia, mechanical pain, fracture, hip OA). After primary TNFi non-response, change mechanism (IL-17i or JAKi); after loss of response or intolerance, a second TNFi is reasonable. Response rates fall with each switch.

stem: What is the role of conventional synthetic DMARDs and of long-term oral glucocorticoids in axial SpA?

options.A: Hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine and azathioprine
options.B: Long-term oral glucocorticoids are recommended to suppress axial inflammation when NSAIDs fail
options.C: Neither treats axial disease; sulfasalazine may be considered for peripheral arthritis, and local glucocorticoid injection may help peripheral arthritis or enthesitis
options.D: Methotrexate is effective for axial disease but not peripheral arthritis
options.E: Sulfasalazine is preferred over NSAIDs for first-line axial symptom control

explanation: csDMARDs do not meaningfully treat axial inflammation; sulfasalazine is the best-evidenced csDMARD for peripheral SpA arthritis. Systemic glucocorticoids have little evidence of benefit in axial disease and cause cumulative harm. Do not delay biologics to try csDMARDs in purely axial disease. Image-guided SIJ steroid injection can help selected patients. A short oral GC course may bridge a peripheral flare. Use paracetamol or tramadol only for residual pain; avoid long-term strong opioids.

stem: What is the typical presentation of SpA-associated uveitis, how is an acute attack managed, and which biologic is preferred when a patient with axial SpA has three attacks a year?

options.A: Chronic, bilateral, granulomatous panuveitis typically managed with long-term oral glucocorticoids and routine ophthalmology review
options.B: Chronic, bilateral, insidious anterior uveitis more typical of ANA-positive JIA, managed with long-term oral glucocorticoids alone
options.C: Posterior uveitis with retinal vasculitis more typical of Behçet or SLE, managed primarily with intravitreal antibiotics
options.D: Acute, unilateral, recurrent anterior uveitis with a painful red eye and blurred vision; same-day ophthalmology for topical steroid and a cycloplegic; a monoclonal anti-TNF antibody is preferred for recurrent attacks
options.E: Etanercept as the preferred biologic for preventing recurrent attacks, since it penetrates ocular tissue well

explanation: HLA-B27-associated uveitis presents with a painful red eye, photophobia and blurred vision. It needs same-day slitlamp assessment, topical corticosteroids and a cycloplegic, with review of systemic therapy if recurrent. Monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies reduce uveitis recurrence. Etanercept is less effective at preventing uveitis (and may trigger it), and IL-17 inhibitors have a weaker evidence base. Uveitis patterns by disease: | Pattern | Disease | |—|—| | Acute, unilateral, alternating anterior, painful | HLA-B27 (axSpA, ReA, IBD), Behçet’s (anterior with hypopyon) | | Chronic, bilateral, silent anterior | ANA+ oligoarticular JIA, IBD (sometimes), PsA (more often bilateral and chronic than B27-AAU) | | Granulomatous (mutton-fat KPs), panuveitis | sarcoidosis, Blau, TB, syphilis, VKH | | Posterior with retinal vasculitis or occlusive vasculitis | Behçet’s, SLE, APS, susceptibility to CMV or toxoplasma | | Tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis | TINU (adolescents) | Other red eyes: conjunctivitis (ReA), episcleritis or scleritis (RA, AAV, RP, IBD), keratitis (HSV, PUK), acute angleclosure glaucoma. Complications of recurrent AAU: posterior synechiae (irregular pupil), cataract, glaucoma (including steroidinduced), cystoid macular oedema. A hypopyon in a white eye suggests Behçet’s. Severe attacks may need periocular or systemic GC. For prevention: adalimumab (licensed for non-infectious uveitis) or infliximab, certolizumab or golimumab; sulfasalazine modestly reduces attacks if a biologic is not indicated. Teach patients to seek same-day care for a painful red eye.

stem: A patient with axial SpA, RA or psoriatic arthritis also has active Crohn’s disease and needs a biologic. Which agents treat both, and which should be avoided?

options.A: Monoclonal TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) treat both; avoid etanercept (ineffective in IBD) and IL-17 inhibitors, which can provoke or worsen IBD
options.B: IL-23 inhibitors are preferred, since they treat both axial and bowel disease effectively
options.C: Etanercept is preferred because it avoids anti-drug antibody formation
options.D: IL-17 inhibitors are preferred for their additional benefit on bowel inflammation
options.E: Avoid all biologics and manage with sulfasalazine and mesalazine alone

explanation: Monoclonal TNF inhibitors treat both the joint disease and inflammatory bowel disease, whereas the soluble receptor etanercept is ineffective in IBD and IL-17 inhibitors can exacerbate it. In PsA, IL-12/23 or IL-23 inhibitors and some JAK inhibitors also treat both peripheral joints and IBD, but IL-23 pathway drugs do not treat axial disease. Gut-and-joint drug map: | Drug | Gut | Axial | Peripheral | |-–|—|—|—| | Infliximab, adalimumab | Crohn’s + UC | I | I | | Certolizumab | Crohn’s (some regions) | I | I | | Golimumab | UC | I | I | | Upadacitinib | Crohn’s + UC | I | I | | Ustekinumab, risankizumab, guselkumab | Crohn’s + UC | I | I (PsA) | | Vedolizumab | gut-selective | I (may unmask arthritis) | I | | Etanercept | I | I | I | | IL-17i | worsens | I | I | Use NSAIDs cautiously (short courses or coxibs) in IBD. Sulfasalazine and mesalazine treat mild colitis and peripheral arthritis. Thiopurines and methotrexate help IBD maintenance but not axial disease. Co-manage with gastroenterology.

stem: A 41-year-old woman with axial SpA has extensive plaque psoriasis (about 15% body surface area) and active spinal disease despite NSAIDs. Which agent is generally preferred?

options.A: Triamcinolone hexacetonide
options.B: IL-17 pathway inhibition
options.C: Warfarin anticoagulation
options.D: Monoclonal-antibody TNF inhibitor
options.E: An IL-17 inhibitor

explanation: For axial SpA with extensive or high-impact psoriasis, the 2025 BSR guideline prefers an IL-17 inhibitor or a monoclonal TNF inhibitor, ideally with dermatology input. IL-23 inhibitors treat psoriasis but did not show efficacy in axial SpA trials, and etanercept is less effective for skin. The 2025 BSR axSpA guideline prefers an IL-17i or a monoclonal TNFi when psoriasis is extensive or highimpact. IL-17A/F (bimekizumab) gives very high skin clearance (PASI 90 to 100) but more oral candidiasis. Etanercept is less effective for skin, and IL-23 inhibitors do not treat axial disease. Co-manage with dermatology. Consider nail and scalp disease, and genital and flexural sites, as high-impact. Paradoxical psoriasis on a TNFi points towards switching to an IL-17 or IL-23 pathway drug.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with axial SpA has been in sustained remission on a TNF inhibitor for 2 years and asks to reduce treatment. Which is most appropriate?

options.A: Stop the TNF inhibitor abruptly, since sustained remission predicts continued control off treatment
options.B: Switch to a different TNF inhibitor before considering any dose reduction
options.C: Monoclonal-antibody TNF inhibitor
options.D: Certolizumab pegol
options.E: Consider gradual tapering of the TNF inhibitor rather than stopping it

explanation: In sustained remission, tapering a biologic can be considered as a shared decision. The 2025 BSR axial SpA guideline does not recommend withdrawing targeted therapy in sustained remission, because discontinuation is associated with a high flare rate. In sustained remission (ASDAS <1.3 for ≥6 months), reduce the dose or extend the interval as a shared decision. Complete withdrawal leads to flare in most patients within months, although most regain response on restarting.

stem: A man with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis falls from standing height and has new neck pain, with no fracture on plain radiographs. What is the next step, and how should his bone health be managed?

options.A: Reassurance and early mobilisation are appropriate, since plain radiographs have already excluded a fracture
options.B: Urgent CT or MRI of the whole spine, since fractures follow minor trauma and are missed on plain films; assess fracture risk alongside exercise, smoking cessation and falls prevention
options.C: Routine physiotherapy manipulation of the neck to formally assess range of movement after the fall
options.D: Spinal DXA as the primary tool for fracture-risk assessment immediately after this kind of trauma
options.E: Treat for presumed chlamydial infection and manage the neck pain with NSAIDs alone

explanation: The ankylosed spine is rigid and osteoporotic. Fractures follow minor trauma, are often missed on plain films, are frequently unstable and may be non-contiguous, so cross-sectional imaging of the whole spine is required. Axial SpA increases vertebral fracture risk, which should be assessed and treated in addition to controlling inflammation. New spinal pain in AS: unstable three-column fracture (cervicothoracic or thoracolumbar junction), Andersson lesion (spondylodiscitis or pseudarthrosis), infective discitis, cauda equina syndrome from dural ectasia with arachnoid diverticula (in long-standing disease), atlantoaxial subluxation, epidural haematoma. Immobilise in the patient’s usual posture and never force the neck straight. Spine DXA is falsely normal or high because of syndesmophytes, so use hip DXA (or lateral spine or QCT). CT of the whole spine, plus MRI if there are neurological signs. Urgent spinal surgical opinion. Long term: bisphosphonate where indicated, vitamin D, falls prevention and control of inflammation. DISH carries the same fracture risk.

stem: A 62-year-old man with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis has an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a PR interval of 240 ms. Which pathology best explains both findings?

options.A: Aortitis with aortic root dilatation and fibrosis extending into the conduction system
options.B: Mitral valve prolapse with a mid-systolic click
options.C: Rheumatic mitral stenosis from childhood streptococcal infection
options.D: Hereditary haemochromatosis
options.E: Osteomalacia

explanation: AS-associated aortitis causes aortic regurgitation, and subaortic fibrosis can extend to the AV node, causing conduction defects from first-degree to complete heart block. Aortic regurgitation with conduction disease: AS or HLA-B27 aortitis, ReA, Takayasu, GCA, syphilitic aortitis, Marfan or Loeys-Dietz (root dilatation without conduction disease), relapsing polychondritis, Cogan’s syndrome, IgG4-related aortitis, Behçet’s. Carditis in HLA-B27 disease features aortic root thickening, AR, subaortic fibrous “bump”, and AV conduction block (first-degree to complete). Conduction disease can occur without other SpA features (“B27 lone heart block”). CV risk is increased overall (inflammation, NSAIDs, smoking). ECG, echo and cardiology review. Pacing for high-grade block. Valve or root surgery as indicated. Control inflammation and CV risk factors.

stem: What does a “bamboo spine” on radiography represent?

options.A: Osteophyte formation from degenerative disc disease
options.B: Flowing anterior ossification sparing the sacroiliac joints (DISH)
options.C: An IL-17 inhibitor
options.D: Bridging syndesmophytes with vertebral fusion in advanced axial SpA
options.E: Disc-space calcification from ochronosis

explanation: Bamboo spine reflects syndesmophytes bridging disc spaces in late radiographic axial SpA. Spinal new bone: syndesmophytes (thin, vertical, marginal; axSpA); non-marginal “chunky” syndesmophytes and paravertebral ossification, asymmetric (PsA, ReA); flowing anterior ossification (DISH); osteophytes (horizontal then vertical, degenerative); fluorosis; ochronosis (disc calcification); hypoparathyroidism (ligament calcification); X-linked hypophosphataemia (enthesopathy).

stem: How does the management of non-radiographic axial SpA compare with that of radiographic axial SpA?

options.A: Biologics are not licensed for non-radiographic disease under any circumstances
options.B: csDMARDs are preferred over biologics in non-radiographic disease
options.C: Management principles are the same; biologics require objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP or MRI inflammation)
options.D: Non-radiographic disease requires a lower ASDAS threshold for biologic eligibility than radiographic disease
options.E: Non-radiographic disease is a distinct condition with an entirely different treatment pathway

explanation: Both forms are managed similarly. Biologic eligibility in non-radiographic disease requires objective inflammation. nr-axSpA and r-axSpA have a similar symptom burden and similar treatment response. Women are more often nonradiographic. NICE eligibility for biologics in nr-axSpA requires a raised CRP or MRI inflammation.

stem: A 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has thoracic spinal stiffness. Radiographs show flowing anterior ossification along four contiguous thoracic vertebrae with preserved disc heights and normal sacroiliac joints. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Ochronosis (alkaptonuria)
options.B: Spinal tuberculosis (Pott’s disease)
options.C: Ankylosing spondylitis
options.D: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH)
options.E: SAPHO syndrome

explanation: DISH shows flowing anterolateral ossification over at least four contiguous vertebrae with preserved disc height and no sacroiliac erosion or fusion. It is associated with diabetes, obesity and metabolic syndrome. DISH: older (>50), obese, diabetic men; mechanical stiffness with little pain; right-sided thoracic flowing ossification over ≥4 contiguous levels; preserved discs; normal SIJ (bridging may occur at the upper ligamentous portion); peripheral enthesophytes; dysphagia or airway problems from cervical osteophytes; normal CRP; B27 not increased. Analgesia, physiotherapy, management of metabolic risk, and surgery for dysphagia or myelopathy. Treat it like AS regarding fracture risk after trauma (whole-spine CT). Heterotopic ossification after hip replacement is more common.

stem: A 24-year-old man develops a hot swollen knee and heel pain 3 weeks after urethritis. Urine NAAT is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. Synovial fluid culture is negative and crystals are absent. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics for 6 months to eradicate the arthritis
options.B: No treatment is needed, since reactive arthritis always resolves within days
options.C: Start a biologic immediately without treating the underlying infection
options.D: Treat the chlamydial infection (for example doxycycline for 7 days), arrange partner notification, and treat the arthritis with NSAIDs or joint injection
options.E: Staphylococcus aureus; aspirate the joint and take blood cultures, then start IV flucloxacillin

explanation: Reactive arthritis requires treatment of the triggering genitourinary infection and contact tracing, but prolonged antibiotics do not alter the arthritis. NSAIDs and intra-articular glucocorticoid are first-line; sulfasalazine is used for chronic disease. Monoarthritis after urethritis: reactive arthritis vs disseminated gonococcal infection (tenosynovitis, pustules, migratory pattern), septic arthritis, gout, HIVassociated arthritis, early PsA or IBD arthritis. Enteric ReA triggers: Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, C. difficile. Post-streptococcal ReA follows S. pyogenes. Onset 1–4 weeks after infection. Asymmetric lower-limb oligoarthritis, enthesitis, dactylitis, conjunctivitis or AAU, circinate balanitis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum, oral ulcers, sterile urethritis. B27 is positive in 60–80%. Most cases resolve in 6–12 months; 15–30% become chronic or recurrent. NSAIDs and IA steroid; a short oral GC course for severe polyarthritis. Treat active chlamydia (and partners) and test for other STIs including HIV. Antibiotics do not help postenteric ReA. Sulfasalazine or methotrexate for chronic disease; TNFi for refractory disease.

stem: A 33-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis develops an asymmetrical oligoarthritis of a knee and ankle during a colitis flare. What is the expected course of this arthritis?

options.A: Independent of bowel disease activity and often becomes chronic (a Type 2 pattern)
options.B: A small-joint polyarthritis unrelated to the colitis, requiring methotrexate
options.C: Enthesitis-related arthritis
options.D: This pattern usually parallels bowel activity and is self-limiting
options.E: Progressive and erosive, requiring early biologic therapy regardless of bowel activity

explanation: Type 1 enteropathic arthritis affects fewer than five large joints and parallels IBD activity. Type 2 is a small-joint polyarthritis independent of gut activity. NSAIDs can worsen IBD and are used cautiously. Type Joints Course Links Type 1 <5 parallels IBD erythema (pauciarticular) activity, selfnodosum, large limiting (<10 joints uveitis weeks) Type 2 ≥5 independent of uveitis (polyarticular) IBD, persistent small joints HLA-B27 Axial SIJ and independent of (50–70%) spine IBD Control the bowel disease (type 1 improves with it). Use NSAIDs cautiously (short courses or coxibs). Sulfasalazine for peripheral arthritis; IA steroid; mAb TNFi or upadacitinib for both. Vedolizumab can unmask arthritis. Look for other IBD-associated features: erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, AAU, episcleritis, PSC.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has palmoplantar pustulosis and painful swelling over the sternoclavicular joints. Imaging shows osteitis and hyperostosis of the anterior chest wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: SAPHO syndrome
options.B: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH)
options.C: Osseous sarcoidosis
options.D: Polyarteritis nodosa
options.E: Takayasu arteritis

explanation: SAPHO (synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, osteitis) characteristically affects the anterior chest wall. Treatment includes NSAIDs, bisphosphonates and, in refractory cases, TNF inhibitors. Anterior chest wall pain and swelling: SAPHO; CRMO or CNO (paediatric equivalent); SpA (sternoclavicular, manubriosternal); septic sternoclavicular arthritis (IV drug use, diabetes); Tietze syndrome or costochondritis; condensing osteitis of the clavicle; Friedrich’s disease (avascular necrosis of the medial clavicle); malignancy (lymphoma, metastasis); fibrous dysplasia. Bone scan shows the “bull’s head” sign at the sternocostoclavicular region. Skin disease (palmoplantar pustulosis, severe acne, hidradenitis) may precede or follow osteitis by years. Cultures may grow Cutibacterium acnes (debated significance). NSAIDs first. Bisphosphonates (IV pamidronate or zoledronate) for osteitis. TNFi for refractory disease. Also methotrexate or sulfasalazine, IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitors (skin), and JAKi (case series). Short courses of doxycycline or azithromycin have mixed results. Paradoxical PPP can occur on TNFi.

stem: A 45-year-old man has inflammatory arthritis of a knee and two DIP joints. He has no current or past psoriasis, but his mother has psoriasis. He has nail pitting and RF is negative. How does he score on the CASPAR criteria?

options.A: 3 points; he meets the criteria
options.B: 5 points; he meets the criteria
options.C: 2 points; he does not meet the criteria
options.D: 1 point; he does not meet the criteria
options.E: 4 points; he meets the criteria, driven by current psoriasis alone

explanation: points; he meets the criteria CASPAR requires inflammatory articular disease plus 3 or more points: current psoriasis 2 (or personal history 1, or family history 1 if no personal history), typical nail dystrophy 1, negative RF 1, dactylitis 1 and juxta-articular new bone formation 1. Here: family history 1 + nails 1 + RF negative 1 = 3. DIP-predominant arthritis: PsA vs nodal or erosive OA (bony nodes, older women, mechanical), gout (tophi, crystals), multicentric reticulohistiocytosis (coral-bead papules), reactive arthritis, and RA (DIPs usually spared). Nail disease mimics: onychomycosis (send clippings), trauma, lichen planus. CASPAR: inflammatory articular disease (joint, spine or entheseal) plus ≥3 points from:-current psoriasis 2, or personal history 1, or family history 1 (if no personal history)-typical nail dystrophy (pitting, onycholysis, hyperkeratosis) 1-negative RF 1 dactylitis (current or recorded) 1-juxta-articular new bone on hand or foot Xray 1 Specificity about 99%, sensitivity about 91%. Look for occult psoriasis: scalp, ears, umbilicus, natal cleft, perianal skin and nails. Consider a dermatology opinion. Screen for comorbidities at diagnosis.

stem: A patient with psoriasis has a diffusely swollen second toe, nail pitting and DIP synovitis. What is the diagnosis, and what is dactylitis?

options.A: Gout, with tophaceous deposition within the digit
options.B: Reactive arthritis, with dactylitis as the sole diagnostic feature
options.C: Psoriatic arthritis with dactylitis: diffuse swelling of a whole digit from flexor tenosynovitis, joint synovitis and soft-tissue inflammation
options.D: Septic flexor tenosynovitis requiring emergency surgical drainage
options.E: 3 points; he meets the criteria

explanation: Dactylitis, nail dystrophy and DIP involvement are characteristic of PsA. Dactylitis is a hallmark of PsA and other SpA, and persistent dactylitis is a target for treatment escalation. Causes of a sausage digit: PsA, ReA, other SpA; gout or tophaceous disease; sarcoid dactylitis (lytic phalangeal lesions, lupus pernio); TB dactylitis (spina ventosa, children); sickle cell dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome, infants); syphilis; septic tenosynovitis (Kanavel signs: fusiform swelling, flexed posture, pain on passive extension, sheath tenderness); trauma; thyroid acropachy; secondary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy. “Hot” (tender, acute) dactylitis predicts erosion more than “cold” (non-tender) dactylitis. Feet are more often affected than hands. Ultrasound shows flexor tenosynovitis with soft-tissue oedema. NSAIDs and local steroid injection to the tendon sheath. csDMARDs have limited efficacy. Persistent dactylitis warrants a bDMARD (TNFi, IL-17i or IL-23i).

stem: Hand radiographs in a patient with long-standing psoriatic arthritis show a pencil-in-cup deformity. What causes this appearance?

options.A: Subchondral cyst formation without bone resorption
options.B: Periarticular osteopenia with marginal erosions
options.C: Bone resorption at the distal end with proliferative new bone at the base of the adjacent phalanx
options.D: Central erosion with surrounding osteophyte formation (a ‘gull-wing’ deformity)
options.E: Punched-out erosions with overhanging sclerotic margins

explanation: Osteolysis with adjacent new bone formation is typical of PsA. Other features include periostitis, ivory phalanx, ankylosis and relative preservation of bone density. Arthritis mutilans (telescoping “opera-glass” digits) in PsA vs RA, multicentric reticulohistiocytosis, neuropathic arthropathy, hyperparathyroidism or renal osteodystrophy, leprosy, and erosive OA (gull-wing deformity, which is central and not pencil-in-cup). Other PsA radiographic features: fluffy periostitis, enthesophytes, acro-osteolysis, DIP ankylosis, “ivory phalanx” (sclerosis of the distal phalanx), absence of periarticular osteopenia, ray pattern, asymmetric SIJ disease, chunky paramarginal syndesmophytes.

stem: What are the seven criteria for minimal disease activity (MDA) in psoriatic arthritis, and how many must be met?

options.A: 4 of 7 domains met, with rheumatoid factor negativity mandatory for minimal disease activity
options.B: Tender and swollen joints each 1 or less, PASI 1 or less, pain and patient-global VAS low, HAQ 0.5 or less, and tender entheseal points 1 or less; 5 of these 7 domains are required
options.C: A DAPSA score of 4 or less alone defines minimal disease activity, regardless of the seven MDA domains
options.D: 6 of 7 domains met, excluding the tender entheseal point count from the assessment
options.E: PASI of 1 or less alone defines minimal disease activity, without reference to the other six domains

explanation: MDA criteria: tender joints 1 or less, swollen joints 1 or less, PASI 1 or less (or BSA 3% or less), patient pain VAS 15 or less, patient global VAS 20 or less, HAQ 0.5 or less and tender entheseal points 1 or less. RF status forms part of classification, not disease activity. MDA (≥5 of 7): TJC ≤1, SJC ≤1, PASI ≤1 or BSA ≤3%, pain VAS ≤15, PtGA VAS ≤20, HAQ ≤0.5, tender entheses ≤1. VLDA requires all 7 and is the closest to complete remission. MDA captures skin and enthesitis, whereas DAPSA does not. Treat-to-target: assess every 3 months while active; adjust if there is no improvement by 3 months or the target is not met by 6 months (TICOPA showed better outcomes with tight control).

stem: Which components make up the DAPSA score in psoriatic arthritis?

options.A: Tender joints 1 or less, swollen joints 1 or less and PASI 1 or less only (the MDA domains)
options.B: 66 swollen and 68 tender joint counts, CRP, patient global assessment and patient pain
options.C: HAQ score and tender entheseal point count only
options.D: 68 tender and 66 swollen joint counts plus ESR, without any patient-reported measure
options.E: PASI and body-surface area only, without joint counts

explanation: DAPSA sums 66 swollen and 68 tender joints, CRP (mg/dL), patient global and pain scores. Remission is 4 or less, low activity above 4 to 14, moderate above 14 to 28 and high above 28. DAPSA remission ≤4, low ≤14, moderate ≤28, high >28; cDAPSA omits CRP (useful on IL-6 or JAK blockade or with a normal CRP). DAPSA ignores skin, enthesitis and axial disease, so pair it with domain measures.

stem: A woman with newly diagnosed PsA has 7 swollen joints and moderate plaque psoriasis. What is the most appropriate first DMARD, and what is the role of oral glucocorticoids?

options.A: Leflunomide; oral glucocorticoids are first-line and used long-term at moderate dose
options.B: Methotrexate; oral glucocorticoids are not routine and, if needed, are used only at low dose for short periods
options.C: Sulfasalazine; oral glucocorticoids should be avoided even for short-term bridging
options.D: A biologic as first-line therapy, bypassing methotrexate
options.E: Add an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor

explanation: A csDMARD should be started promptly for polyarthritis, with methotrexate preferred when skin involvement is relevant. Hydroxychloroquine is ineffective in PsA. Systemic glucocorticoids have limited benefit, can provoke pustular or erythrodermic psoriasis on withdrawal and cause cumulative harm; intra-articular injection is useful for oligoarticular flares. Other csDMARDs: leflunomide (good evidence, TOPAS) and sulfasalazine (peripheral arthritis only, little skin effect). Ciclosporin is rarely used (nephrotoxicity, hypertension). Hydroxychloroquine is ineffective and may flare psoriasis. Poor-prognosis features that justify early escalation: polyarticular disease, raised CRP, dactylitis, erosions, high HAQ, nail disease. Methotrexate 15–25 mg weekly with folate. Consider FIB-4 or elastography if NAFLD or alcohol excess is suspected (common in PsA). If methotrexate is unsuitable (liver disease, pregnancy plans), use leflunomide or sulfasalazine, or proceed directly to a biologic. Enthesitis and axial disease bypass csDMARDs.

stem: A patient with PsA has active polyarthritis despite methotrexate 20 mg weekly for 4 months and extensive plaque psoriasis (PASI 14). What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: A TNF inhibitor
options.B: Add an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor
options.C: Switch to leflunomide monotherapy and reassess again in 12 months
options.D: Switch to subcutaneous methotrexate
options.E: IL-17 inhibitor

explanation: After csDMARD failure in peripheral PsA a bDMARD is started. With relevant skin disease, IL-17A, IL-17A/F, IL-23 or IL12/23 inhibitors may be preferred because of their greater skin efficacy than TNF inhibitors. Biologic choice by domain: | Situation | Preferred | |—|—| | Significant psoriasis | IL-17A (secukinumab, ixekizumab), IL-17A/F (bimekizumab) or IL-23 (guselkumab, risankizumab) | | Axial | TNFi or IL-17i (JAKi) | | Uveitis | mAb TNFi | | IBD | mAb TNFi, IL-23i or ustekinumab, upadacitinib; avoid IL-17i | | Nails | IL-17, IL-23 or TNFi | | Enthesitis or dactylitis | any bDMARD (TNF, IL-17, IL-23) | | Pregnancy plans | certolizumab | Step 3 (bDMARD failure): switch bDMARD, or JAKi (tofacitinib, upadacitinib) after CV, VTE and cancer risk assessment. Abatacept is an option but has little skin effect. Weight loss improves response. Rheumatology SCE — 5-option SBA 36

stem: A 66-year-old woman with PsA has mild oligoarthritis despite methotrexate and declines injections. A biologic or JAK inhibitor is not considered appropriate. Which oral drug is most suitable?

options.A: Apremilast
options.B: Plasma exchange
options.C: Usual interstitial pneumonia
options.D: An IL-17 inhibitor
options.E: Sulfasalazine, switched from methotrexate

explanation: In mild disease with inadequate response to at least one csDMARD where a biologic or JAK inhibitor is not appropriate, a PDE4 inhibitor may be considered. Intra-articular glucocorticoid also helps oligoarticular flares. Apremilast: modest efficacy, no laboratory monitoring, oral; GI upset and weight loss; mood monitoring. Suited to mild oligoarticular disease without poor prognostic factors, or skin-predominant disease, when a b/tsDMARD is unsuitable. Deucravacitinib (TYK2) is licensed for psoriasis, with PsA trials ongoing. Image-guided or landmark IA steroid for single joints. Consider subcutaneous options if the patient will accept them later, and offer self-injection support.

stem: A patient with PsA has persistent Achilles enthesitis confirmed on ultrasound despite two NSAIDs and a local programme of physiotherapy. Peripheral joints are quiet. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: A second NSAID trial for a further 3 months before considering any escalation of treatment
options.B: Image-guided glucocorticoid injection directly into the body of the Achilles tendon itself
options.C: Start a biologic DMARD such as a TNF or IL-17 inhibitor; csDMARDs have little effect on enthesitis, and steroid injection around the Achilles should be avoided
options.D: Methotrexate or leflunomide, since conventional synthetic DMARDs are effective for enthesitis
options.E: Add an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor without first confirming that NSAIDs and physiotherapy have failed

explanation: Heel pain: SpA enthesitis (Achilles insertion, plantar fascia) vs mechanical Achilles tendinopathy (mid-portion, athletic), plantar fasciopathy, retrocalcaneal bursitis, Haglund deformity, calcaneal stress fracture, fluoroquinolone tendinopathy, gout or xanthoma (familial hypercholesterolaemia, with nodular thickened tendons), DISH or enthesophytes, X-linked hypophosphataemia. Ultrasound signs of enthesitis: hypoechogenicity, thickening, Doppler signal at the insertion, erosions and enthesophytes. Fibromyalgia tender points can mimic enthesitis on examination. csDMARDs do not help enthesitis. Use NSAIDs, physiotherapy, heel raises and orthoses, then a bDMARD (TNFi, IL-17i, IL-23i or JAKi). Never inject steroid into the Achilles tendon. Plantar fascia injection, if used, should be given from the medial side, not through the heel pad.

stem: A patient with mild-looking psoriasis has distressing genital and scalp lesions and active arthritis. How should the skin disease be weighed when choosing treatment?

options.A: Only total body surface area, regardless of site or psychological impact
options.B: As clinically relevant, because impact and sensitive sites matter as well as body surface area
options.C: Dermatology referral is unnecessary since the arthritis is the dominant problem
options.D: Mild disease by body-surface-area alone, so standard rather than high-skin-efficacy therapy is appropriate
options.E: PASI alone, without considering site-specific impact such as genital or scalp disease

explanation: Psoriasis is clinically relevant when it is extensive or has substantial impact, including scalp, nail, genital and flexural disease. This influences drug choice and joint care with dermatology. Define clinically relevant psoriasis as BSA >10%, PASI >10, DLQI >10, or involvement of special sites (scalp, nails, genital, palmoplantar, flexural, face). Choose agents with high skin efficacy (IL-17 or IL-23). Topicals and phototherapy for mild skin disease. Deucravacitinib, methotrexate, ciclosporin or acitretin are dermatological options; acitretin is teratogenic for 3 years after stopping.

stem: Paradoxical psoriasiform eruptions, including palmoplantar pustulosis, are a recognised class effect of which drugs?

options.A: IL-17 inhibitors, via an effect on mucosal immunity
options.B: Certolizumab pegol
options.C: Rituximab, via depletion of skin-resident B cells
options.D: TNF inhibitors
options.E: Monoclonal-antibody TNF inhibitor

explanation: Paradoxical psoriasis is a recognised class effect of TNF inhibitors. Management includes topical therapy, switching TNF inhibitor or changing to an IL-17 or IL-23 pathway agent. Paradoxical reactions to TNFi: psoriasis (palmoplantar pustulosis, scalp, plaques), hidradenitis, IBD (etanercept), uveitis (etanercept), sarcoid-like granulomas, drug-induced lupus (anti-dsDNA, anti-histone), vasculitis, demyelination, alopecia areata. Main differential: true psoriasis flare, or eczema and fungal infection of the feet. Paradoxical psoriasis is driven by unopposed plasmacytoid dendritic cell type I IFN. It occurs with any TNFi and in any indication (including in patients without prior psoriasis, e.g. Crohn’s or RA). It is more common in women and smokers. Mild: topical steroids or vitamin D analogues, continuing the TNFi. Moderate to severe: switch to an IL-17 or IL-23 pathway drug (or ustekinumab, which treats both if IBD is present). Switching TNFi helps in some patients but recurrence is common.

stem: Alongside inflammatory disease control, which comorbidity strategy is particularly important in psoriatic arthritis?

options.A: Annual chest radiograph screening for malignancy as the main comorbidity priority
options.B: Routine screening for interstitial lung disease in every patient
options.C: Proactive assessment of cardiovascular and metabolic risk, obesity, mood and smoking
options.D: Screening for osteoporosis as the principal comorbidity concern
options.E: Routine screening for hepatitis B and C as the principal comorbidity concern

explanation: PsA is associated with obesity, diabetes, hypertension, fatty liver and depression. Obesity also reduces response to some biologics. At diagnosis and regularly: BP, lipids, HbA1c, BMI and waist circumference, LFTs and FIB-4 (fatty liver), urate, depression screening (PHQ), smoking and alcohol. Multiply CV risk by about 1.5 where not captured. Weight loss of ≥5% improves response. GLP-1 receptor agonists help weight and may reduce disease activity (emerging data).

stem: A man has acute pain, redness and swelling of the first MTP joint. Which test confirms gout most specifically, and how should a serum urate of 330 micromol/L measured during the flare be interpreted?

options.A: A plain radiograph showing a punched-out erosion with overhanging edge, interpreted as diagnostic without aspiration
options.B: A normal serum urate measured during the flare, which reliably excludes gout
options.C: Synovial fluid showing needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent MSU crystals; urate often falls during a flare, so repeat it at least 2 weeks after the flare settles
options.D: Ultrasound double-contour sign alone, without synovial fluid analysis, interpreted as fully diagnostic
options.E: Dual-energy CT alone, repeated weekly until urate normalises

explanation: Crystal identification is the reference standard. Ultrasound and dual-energy CT support the diagnosis, but serum urate can be normal during a flare (in about 10–40%) and hyperuricaemia alone does not prove gout. Repeat measurement 2 or more weeks after the flare, and crystal analysis, help when the diagnosis is uncertain. Acute podagra: gout vs septic arthritis, cellulitis, CPP arthritis (rarely at the 1st MTP), BCP periarthritis of the 1st MTP (“hydroxyapatite pseudopodagra” in young women), PsA or ReA dactylitis, bunion bursitis, trauma or sesamoiditis, stress fracture, Charcot foot, Löfgren’s (ankles). Typical flare: maximal within 6–24 hours, often nocturnal, with desquamation; resolves within 1–2 weeks. 1st MTP is the first site in about half of patients. Atypical presentations: polyarticular low-grade gout in older women on diuretics and transplant recipients; tophi on Heberden’s nodes; “puffy hand”; spinal gout (mimics discitis). Aspirate whenever feasible (including asymptomatic previously affected joints between flares). Clinical diagnosis is acceptable in typical recurrent podagra. Always send Gram stain and culture when infection is possible.

stem: Synovial fluid from an acutely swollen knee shows rhomboid crystals with weak positive birefringence under compensated polarised light. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Gram stain and bacterial culture
options.B: Basic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite)
options.C: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals
options.D: Septic arthritis is a major concern; send cultures and treat urgently if clinical suspicion is high
options.E: Chondrocalcinosis

explanation: CPP crystals are rhomboid or rod-shaped with weak positive birefringence. Basic calcium phosphate crystals are not birefringent. Crystals do not exclude coexisting infection, so culture is still required. Acute monoarthritis of the knee in an older person: CPP arthritis, gout, septic arthritis (can coexist), haemarthrosis (anticoagulants, trauma), OA flare, ruptured Baker’s cyst, insufficiency fracture or SONK (spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee), Lyme disease (in endemic areas). Feature MSU CPP needle, 1–30 µm rhomboid or rod, Shape polymorphic, smaller Birefringence strong weak or absent (many invisible) negative (yellow when positive (blue Sign when parallel) parallel to the compensator) intra-and extracellular Location often intracellular Mnemonic: CPP is Positive with Parallel = blue (“ABC”: Alignment, Blue, Calcium).

stem: A febrile older patient with a history of gout has a hot swollen knee; synovial fluid shows MSU crystals but a WCC of 85,000/mm³ with 95% neutrophils and he has rigors. What must be excluded, and what is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Diagnose gout confidently because MSU crystals were found, and treat with colchicine alone
options.B: Inject intra-articular glucocorticoid immediately for symptom relief, pending culture results
options.C: Treat as reactive arthritis, given the crystal-positive but systemic presentation
options.D: Septic arthritis: send Gram stain and culture and start empirical antibiotics pending results; do not inject steroid or label it gout until infection has been assessed
options.E: Reassure the patient that finding MSU crystals excludes septic arthritis by definition

explanation: Crystal arthritis and infection can coexist. Very high synovial WCC, rigors or systemic upset mean infection must be excluded with Gram stain and culture, and empirical antibiotics are justified while results are awaited. A hot joint should not be injected or labelled gout until infection has been assessed. Synovial fluid guide (WCC/mm³): normal <200; noninflammatory 200–2,000 (OA, trauma, AVN); inflammatory 2,000– 50,000 (RA, SpA, crystals, viral); septic usually >50,000 with >90% neutrophils (but crystal arthritis can exceed 50,000, and septic arthritis can be lower in immunosuppressed patients, prostheses, gonococcal or TB infection). Synovial glucose is low and lactate high in sepsis. Large-joint or polyarticular gout flares can cause fever, high CRP and leucocytosis. Risks for coexisting infection: prostheses, tophaceous skin breakdown, immunosuppression, diabetes, IV drug use. Blood cultures; empirical IV flucloxacillin (or local protocol); orthopaedic review. Treat the flare with colchicine or NSAID only alongside antibiotics until culture is negative at 48 hours.

stem: When should urate-lowering therapy be discussed and started, for example in a 35-year-old man with his first flare and a urate of 540 micromol/L?

options.A: Only after a second flare within 12 months, regardless of urate level or any comorbidity present
options.B: Only once tophi have already become clinically visible on examination
options.C: ULT should not be started before the age of 40, regardless of urate level or flare frequency
options.D: Discuss and offer ULT to everyone with gout; it treats recurrent flares, tophi, urate arthropathy and stones, and is advised early under age 40 or with high urate or comorbidity
options.E: Only after renal stones have already formed as a complication of hyperuricaemia

explanation: The BSR gout guideline advises that ULT is discussed and offered to everyone with gout. A single first flare without risk factors does not mandate it. It is clearly indicated for recurrent flares, tophi, urate arthropathy and renal stones, and EULAR advises starting close to diagnosis in young patients (under 40), those with very high urate (above 480 micromol/L) or comorbidities such as renal impairment, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease or heart failure. Education about the chronic nature of gout and the treatment target is central. The 2020 ACR guideline strongly recommends ULT for ≥1 tophus, radiographic damage or ≥2 flares per year. It conditionally recommends ULT after a first flare with CKD stage ≥3, urate >540 µmol/L (9 mg/dL) or urolithiasis. Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia is not treated. Start once the flare has settled (or during it, with antiinflammatory cover). Nurse-led treat-to-target with education achieved target urate in >90% in a UK trial (Doherty, Nottingham) and reduced flares and tophi.

stem: What is the target serum urate on ULT, and how does it differ in tophaceous gout with frequent flares?

options.A: Below 420 micromol/L for all patients, with no lower target for tophaceous disease
options.B: Below 600 micromol/L, since gout rarely needs stricter control
options.C: The same target applies regardless of tophi or flare frequency
options.D: Titrate urate-lowering treatment towards a target with monitoring
options.E: Below 360 micromol/L for most; below 300 micromol/L for severe or tophaceous gout until tophi resolve

explanation: EULAR and NICE recommend a target below 360 micromol/L (6 mg/dL) for most patients, with a lower target (below 300 micromol/L, 5 mg/dL) for tophi, chronic arthropathy or frequent flares, which accelerates crystal dissolution. The current BSR gout guideline (2017) is stricter and recommends 300 micromol/L or lower for everyone, so UK practice may use the lower target. Once crystal burden has resolved, the usual target can be resumed. Long-term levels below 180 micromol/L are avoided. Check urate monthly during titration, then at least yearly. Tophi shrink at a rate proportional to how far urate is below target. Explain that early flares on ULT signal crystal dissolution, not failure.

stem: How should allopurinol be started in a man with gout and normal renal function, how are flares prevented in the early months, and what should happen to allopurinol if a flare occurs once he is established on it?

options.A: Start at the maximum dose of 900 mg immediately to reach target faster
options.B: Stop allopurinol immediately until the flare fully resolves, then restart at the same dose
options.C: Start 100 mg daily and increase by 100 mg every 2–4 weeks to target urate; give low-dose colchicine
options.D: No flare prophylaxis is required when starting allopurinol
options.E: Start at 300 mg daily with no titration, provided renal function is normal

explanation: (0.5–1 mg daily) for about 6 months; continue allopurinol unchanged during any flare Starting low and titrating gradually reduces flares and hypersensitivity risk; in CKD a lower starting dose is used (50 so prophylaxis is given for about 6 months (longer with tophi or continued flares), adjusted for renal function; a lowdose NSAID (with PPI) or low-dose prednisolone are alternatives if colchicine is unsuitable. Stopping or changing the dose during a flare causes urate fluctuation and can prolong attacks, so established ULT should be continued. Causes of failure to reach target on allopurinol: nonadherence (the commonest), under-dosing (the maximum is 900 mg), ongoing diuretic use, high alcohol or fructose intake, CKD, very high crystal burden, overproduction states, interacting drugs. Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS, SJS/TEN; mortality up to 25%) is rare. Risk is highest in the first 8 weeks, with a high starting dose, CKD, diuretics and HLA-B*58:01. Other interactions: azathioprine and mercaptopurine (reduce to 25% or avoid), warfarin, amoxicillin rash. In ALL-HEART, allopurinol did not reduce CV events in IHD. Give a “pill in the pocket” supply for early self-treatment of flares. Allopurinol doses above creatinine-clearance-based limits can be reached gradually in CKD with monitoring (titrate by 50 mg steps).

stem: A 54-year-old man presents 6 hours into an acute gout flare of the first MTP joint. eGFR is 85 and he takes no interacting drugs. Which colchicine regimen is preferred?

options.A: 2 mg three times daily for 5 days, then stopped abruptly
options.B: 1 mg, followed 1 hour later by 0.5 mg on day 1, then low dose until the flare settles
options.C: High-dose colchicine, 1 mg every 2 hours until diarrhoea occurs, as in historical regimens
options.D: Intravenous colchicine, preferred for rapid relief
options.E: 500 micrograms twice daily for 2 weeks regardless of response

explanation: mg, followed 1 hour later by 0.5 mg on day 1, then low dose until the flare settles Low-dose colchicine is as effective as older high-dose regimens with far fewer adverse effects, and works best when started within 12-24 hours. NSAIDs, a short oral glucocorticoid course or joint aspiration and injection are alternatives. Options by comorbidity:-Colchicine low-dose regimen; reduce in CKD and older age; avoid with CYP3A4 or P-gp inhibitors.-NSAID at full dose with a PPI (e.g. naproxen 500 mg twice daily); avoid if eGFR <30, heart failure, peptic ulcer or anticoagulation. Prednisolone 30–35 mg for 3–5 days (non-inferior to NSAIDs).-IA steroid for 1–2 accessible joints, after excluding infection.-IM or IV GC or ACTH if the oral route is not possible.-IL-1 blockade (see the next entries).-Combination therapy (e.g. colchicine plus steroid) for severe polyarticular flares. Plus ice, rest and elevation.

stem: A 75-year-old man with gout and CKD stage 3b is taking clarithromycin for pneumonia and develops a gout flare. What is the most appropriate flare treatment?

options.A: High-dose NSAID with a proton pump inhibitor
options.B: Standard-dose colchicine, since eGFR is only mildly reduced
options.C: Double the clarithromycin dose and add colchicine regardless of the interaction risk
options.D: A short course of oral prednisolone
options.E: HLA-B*58:01 genotyping

explanation: short course of oral prednisolone Colchicine must be avoided with strong CYP3A4 or P-glycoprotein inhibitors (clarithromycin, ciclosporin, some azoles) because of life-threatening toxicity, especially in CKD. NSAIDs are inadvisable in CKD 3b. Strong CYP3A4 or P-gp inhibitors that make colchicine dangerous: clarithromycin, erythromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir and cobicistat, ciclosporin, verapamil, diltiazem, grapefruit. Statins add myopathy risk. Signs of colchicine toxicity: diarrhoea, vomiting, then multiorgan failure, myoneuropathy, marrow failure. In CKD 3b with an interacting antibiotic: oral prednisolone (or IA steroid if a single accessible joint). Anakinra is useful in hospitalised patients with CKD.

stem: A patient with recurrent gout flares has contraindications to colchicine, NSAIDs and glucocorticoids. What can be considered for flare treatment?

options.A: An IL-1 inhibitor such as canakinumab or anakinra
options.B: A short course of oral prednisolone
options.C: A trial of high-dose vitamin C supplementation
options.D: Topical NSAID gel alone for a large-joint flare
options.E: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid injection

explanation: IL-1 beta, released via the NLRP3 inflammasome, drives gouty inflammation. IL-1 blockade is an option when standard flare treatments are contraindicated, after excluding infection. Canakinumab (anti-IL-1β, single SC dose) is approved for frequent flares when NSAIDs, colchicine and steroids are contraindicated or ineffective. Anakinra (IL-1Ra) is off-label but used for 3–5-day courses in hospital and CKD. Exclude infection first.

stem: A 48-year-old man of Han Chinese ancestry with recurrent gout and CKD stage 3 is due to start allopurinol. Which pre-treatment test is most appropriate?

options.A: Joint aspiration and intra-articular glucocorticoid injection
options.B: Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity or genotype
options.C: An IL-1 inhibitor such as canakinumab or anakinra
options.D: A short course of oral prednisolone
options.E: HLA-B*58:01 genotyping

explanation: HLA-B58:01 is strongly associated with severe allopurinol hypersensitivity (SJS/TEN, DRESS). It is common in Han Chinese, Korean and Thai populations, and testing is advised where available, particularly with CKD. HLA-B57:01 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity. HLA-B58:01 carriage is common in Han Chinese, Korean and Thai populations (and in people of African ancestry in US guidance). HLA-B57:01 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity; HLA-B*15:02 predicts carbamazepine SJS/TEN in South-East Asian populations. If positive, avoid allopurinol and use febuxostat (if there is no major CVD) or a uricosuric. Educate about rash and fever and the need to stop at once.
