stem: A man with tophaceous gout and CKD (eGFR 48) has not reached target despite allopurinol titrated to 900 mg with good adherence. What are the options, and how does a previous MI change them?

options.A: Colchicine 1 mg, followed 1 hour later by 0.5 mg on day 1, then a low maintenance dose until the flare settles
options.B: Switch to azathioprine (with or without tacrolimus), stopping mycophenolate at least 6 weeks before conception, and confirm stable disease before conceiving
options.C: Rising anti-dsDNA with falling C3 and C4 predicts flare; isolated serological activity warrants closer monitoring (including urinalysis), not treatment escalation
options.D: Switch to febuxostat titrated to target with flare prophylaxis, or add a uricosuric; febuxostat should be avoided in major cardiovascular disease, so a uricosuric is preferred after a previous MI
options.E: Below 360 micromol/L for most; below 300 micromol/L for severe or tophaceous gout until tophi resolve

explanation: When target urate is not reached on an appropriate allopurinol dose, options include switching to febuxostat (another xanthine oxidase inhibitor, if there is no major cardiovascular disease) or adding a uricosuric. A cardiovascular mortality signal in the CARES trial led to advice to avoid febuxostat in pre-existing major cardiovascular disease unless no alternative is suitable. Uricosurics such as benzbromarone (available on a named-patient basis in the UK) can be added or substituted. Probenecid is ineffective with reduced renal function. Pegloticase is reserved for refractory tophaceous disease in specialist settings and is not widely available. CARES (US, high dropout) found higher CV and all-cause death than with allopurinol. FAST (Europe) found no excess CV risk. Regulators still advise caution. Febuxostat: Rheumatology SCE — 5-option SBA 42 80 mg daily, rising to 120 mg; no dose change in mild to moderate CKD; contraindicated with azathioprine or mercaptopurine. Benzbromarone works in moderate CKD but carries rare severe hepatotoxicity. Lesinurad has been withdrawn. Uricosurics need high fluid intake (with or without urine alkalinisation) and are avoided with urate stones. Pegloticase (IV every 2 weeks) plus methotrexate more than doubles sustained response (MIRROR); screen for G6PD deficiency and stop if pre-infusion urate rises above 360 µmol/L (predicts infusion reactions). Emerging options: SEL-212, URAT1 inhibitors (pozdeutinurad, dotinurad), tigulixostat.

stem: A 59-year-old man with gout takes bendroflumethiazide for hypertension. What is the most appropriate antihypertensive change?

options.A: Switch to losartan or a calcium-channel blocker
options.B: Continue allopurinol while treating the flare
options.C: Switch to a loop diuretic such as furosemide instead of the thiazide
options.D: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor
options.E: A short course of oral prednisolone

explanation: Thiazide and loop diuretics raise serum urate. Losartan has a modest uricosuric effect. Low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention should not be stopped. Drugs with useful uricosuric effects: losartan (hypertension), fenofibrate (lipids), SGLT2 inhibitors (diabetes, HF, CKD; also lower gout incidence), amlodipine (modest). Continue low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention. Thiazide-like and loop diuretics raise urate; avoid them where possible in gout (but not at the expense of heart failure control).

stem: Which lifestyle advice is most appropriate for a patient with chronic gout?

options.A: FBC, LFTs and renal function at week 2, then about monthly for the first 3-6 months, then every 3 months, with the interval individualised to toxicity risk
options.B: Weight management, moderation of alcohol and sugar-sweetened drinks, and management of cardiovascular and renal risk, recognising that lifestyle alone rarely controls established gout
options.C: Use a national risk tool that includes RA (such as QRISK3), reassess regularly, and control disease activity and traditional risk factors
options.D: PPI therapy with reflux measures, assessment of dysmotility and aspiration risk, and prokinetics or dilatation where indicated
options.E: Glucocorticoids with an immunosuppressant (preferably a monoclonal anti-TNF antibody, or azathioprine); anticoagulation may be added only if bleeding risk is low

explanation: Gout is associated with hypertension, CKD, metabolic syndrome, obesity and cardiovascular disease. Lifestyle change is an adjunct to urate-lowering therapy. Diet alone lowers urate by only about 60 µmol/L at most, so most patients still need ULT. Avoid blaming patients; genetics outweigh diet. Vitamin C supplements do not help meaningfully. Cherries and low-fat dairy have only observational support. Gradual weight loss (crash diets and fasting trigger flares); limit beer and spirits and avoid binges; reduce sugarsweetened drinks, fructose, offal and shellfish; DASH or Mediterranean diet; hydration; exercise. Screen BP, lipids, HbA1c and renal function. Low-dose colchicine (0.5 mg) is licensed in some countries for CV risk reduction in coronary disease.

stem: A 78-year-old woman has fever, severe neck pain and stiffness, a raised CRP and calcification around the odontoid peg on CT. How does this finding relate to the CPPD classification criteria?

options.A: ANA at a titre of 1:80 or higher on HEp-2 cells (or an equivalent test) at any time, then 10 or more weighted points with at least one clinical criterion
options.B: He meets the imaging arm: sacroiliitis plus at least one SpA feature
options.C: They are classification criteria and do not replace clinical diagnosis; she scores 5 points and does not yet meet the criteria
options.D: It is crowned dens syndrome, which on its own is a sufficient criterion for CPPD classification
options.E: In moderate/high-risk populations monoarthritis counts as a major criterion and fever ≥38 °C and ESR

explanation: After the entry criterion (joint pain, swelling or tenderness), crowned dens syndrome or CPP crystals in synovial fluid are sufficient. Meningitis and GCA are important differentials. Fever with neck pain and stiffness in an older person: crowned dens syndrome vs bacterial meningitis (lumbar puncture if any doubt), GCA or PMR, cervical discitis or epidural abscess, retropharyngeal abscess, acute calcific longus colli tendinitis (C1–C2 prevertebral calcification, painful swallowing), cervical spondylosis flare, atlanto-axial disease (RA). CT shows halo or crown calcification of the transverse ligament or cruciform ligament around the dens. CRP is often very high. It responds dramatically to NSAIDs, colchicine or short-course GC.

stem: A man aged 44–52 (or a woman aged 41–42) has early-onset or polyarticular CPPD, sometimes with firm 2nd/3rd MCP swelling, hook-like osteophytes, chondrocalcinosis, diabetes and raised liver enzymes. Which investigations are most appropriate to find an underlying cause?

options.A: Serum ACE and a chest radiograph alone, to screen specifically for sarcoidosis
options.B: Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies alone, assuming an inflammatory arthritis
options.C: Serum urate and 24-hour urinary urate excretion alone, assuming underlying gout
options.D: Calcium, PTH, magnesium, phosphate, ALP, ferritin and transferrin saturation (then HFE genotyping), and TSH; hook osteophytes at the 2nd/3rd MCPs suggest haemochromatosis
options.E: ANA and complement levels alone, assuming an underlying connective tissue disease

explanation: Early-onset (before about 55–60 years) or florid polyarticular CPPD warrants screening for metabolic causes: hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis, hypomagnesaemia (including Gitelman syndrome) and hypophosphatasia (low ALP). Familial CPPD (ANKH variants) is another cause. Hereditary haemochromatosis classically causes a 2nd/3rd MCP arthropathy with hook osteophytes and CPPD; raised transferrin saturation and ferritin with HFE C282Y homozygosity confirm it. Venesection prevents organ damage but often does not improve established arthropathy. Other causes of 2nd/3rd MCP arthropathy with osteophytes: idiopathic CPPD (“pseudo-OA”), manual labour OA (jackhammer), acromegaly (widened joint spaces), Wilson’s disease (young, with neurological or hepatic features and chondrocalcinosis), ochronosis. Other causes of hypomagnesaemia: PPIs, diuretics, short bowel, alcohol, Bartter syndrome. Haemochromatosis arthropathy also affects wrists, hips (rapid OA), ankles and the 4th–5th MCPs. Look for diabetes, cirrhosis, skin bronzing, hypogonadism and cardiomyopathy. Transferrin saturation >45% is the best screen; ferritin is also an acute-phase reactant. Treat the metabolic cause: magnesium replacement (may reduce attacks), parathyroidectomy (which can trigger a flare), venesection to ferritin about 50–100 µg/L. Consider ANKH genetic testing in familial or early-onset disease without a metabolic cause. Pathophysiology: excess extracellular pyrophosphate (ePPi) from chondrocyte ATP via ENPP1 and the ANKH transporter combines with calcium. ALP degrades PPi, with magnesium as a cofactor, which explains the links with hypophosphatasia and hypomagnesaemia. Serum PPi is normal except in hypophosphatasia.

stem: An 82-year-old woman has acute CPP crystal arthritis of one knee. She has CKD stage 4 and heart failure. Septic arthritis has been excluded. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: High-dose oral NSAID with gastroprotection as first-line, since renal impairment is only a relative concern
options.B: Joint aspiration and intra-articular glucocorticoid injection
options.C: A short course of oral prednisolone
options.D: Urate-lowering therapy started immediately to dissolve the crystals
options.E: HLA-B*58:01 genotyping

explanation: Aspiration plus intra-articular glucocorticoid is optimal for acute CPP arthritis in a large joint, particularly when NSAIDs or colchicine are hazardous. There is no treatment that dissolves CPP crystals, and urate-lowering drugs have no role. Acute CPP arthritis: ice, rest, aspiration plus IA GC (firstline in a single large joint). Alternatives: oral or IM GC; lowdose colchicine; NSAID with gastroprotection (caution in older people); ACTH. Anakinra for severe, polyarticular or refractory attacks in hospitalised older patients; IL-6 blockade in case reports. No drug dissolves CPP crystals.

stem: A patient has frequent recurrent attacks of CPP crystal arthritis. What can reduce recurrence?

options.A: Allopurinol, titrated to a target serum urate below 360 micromol/L
options.B: High-dose NSAID continued indefinitely regardless of renal function
options.C: Low-dose colchicine prophylaxis, if tolerated and renal function allows
options.D: Intra-articular glucocorticoid injection given prophylactically between attacks
options.E: Methotrexate as first-line prophylaxis, given its proven efficacy in a large randomised trial

explanation: Low-dose colchicine or a low-dose NSAID may reduce recurrent attacks. Methotrexate or hydroxychloroquine are occasionally used for chronic inflammatory CPPD. Chronic or recurrent CPP arthritis: low-dose colchicine (0.5–1 mg/day) or low-dose NSAID; low-dose GC; hydroxychloroquine. Methotrexate was no better than placebo in a small RCT, so its use is limited. Anakinra or tocilizumab for refractory disease (observational). OA with CPPD is managed as OA, and joint replacement outcomes are similar.

stem: A 56-year-old man has 9 months of activity-related knee pain and 10 minutes of morning stiffness. Examination shows crepitus without effusion. How should osteoarthritis be diagnosed?

options.A: Clinically, without imaging
options.B: Only after MRI confirms cartilage loss
options.C: Only if synovial fluid analysis excludes inflammatory arthritis
options.D: BRAF V600E mutation analysis
options.E: Only in patients under 45 years of age

explanation: OA can be diagnosed clinically in people aged 45 or over with activity-related joint pain and either no morning stiffness or stiffness lasting 30 minutes or less. Imaging is reserved for atypical features or suspected alternative diagnoses. Red flags that need imaging or bloods: age <45; stiffness >30 minutes or a warm effusion (inflammatory arthritis, crystals); rapid progression or severe night or rest pain (AVN, SONK or insufficiency fracture, tumour, infection, rapidly destructive OA); constitutional symptoms; locking (mechanical meniscal tear or loose body); hip or spine referred pain to the knee (always examine the hip, especially in children with SUFE). X-ray features: focal joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, sclerosis, cysts. Kellgren–Lawrence grade ≥2 is definite OA. Request weight-bearing knee films with a skyline view. Degenerative meniscal tears on MRI are usually incidental. OA synovial fluid is non-inflammatory (WCC <2,000/µL). Use WOMAC, KOOS/HOOS or the Oxford hip and knee scores to track outcome.

stem: A 63-year-old woman with BMI 34 has knee OA with activity-related pain. Which intervention has the strongest evidence as core treatment?

options.A: Graded aerobic and strengthening exercise
options.B: Bariatric surgery as first-line treatment, regardless of BMI or a trial of conservative care
options.C: Therapeutic exercise with weight loss and education
options.D: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid injection
options.E: Clinically, without imaging

explanation: Strengthening and aerobic exercise, weight loss where appropriate and education are core for everyone with OA, and improve pain and function regardless of radiographic severity. Exercise has an effect size similar to NSAIDs and lasts while the exercise continues. Weight loss of ≥5–10% gives clinically meaningful benefit, with more loss giving more benefit. In STEP 9, semaglutide reduced knee OA pain alongside weight loss. Education: OA is not inevitably progressive, exercise does not “wear out” the joint, and pacing helps. Structured programmes include GLA:D and ESCAPEpain. Exercise: quadriceps and hip abductor strengthening plus aerobic fitness; tai chi and aquatic exercise also help. Aids: a walking stick in the opposite hand, footwear and insoles, unloader braces for unicompartmental disease, OT aids. Adjuncts: manual therapy only alongside exercise. TENS, therapeutic ultrasound and laser are not recommended. Severe obesity: bariatric surgery.

stem: What is the first-line pharmacological option for knee OA and for symptomatic hand OA?

options.A: Oral paracetamol taken regularly, as first-line
options.B: Oral strong opioids, for short-term flare control
options.C: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid injection, as first-line
options.D: Oral glucosamine sulphate, as first-line
options.E: A topical NSAID

explanation: topical NSAID Topical NSAIDs are first-line for knee and hand OA because of their safety and minimal systemic exposure. Oral NSAIDs are used at the lowest dose for the shortest time with gastroprotection, and oral analgesics generally for limited periods. Paracetamol alone and weak opioids are not routinely recommended for OA. Intra-articular steroids may be considered for painful interphalangeal joints. NSAID choice: naproxen or ibuprofen ≤1.2 g/day carry lower CV risk; celecoxib carries lower GI risk (PRECISION). Avoid NSAIDs in CKD stage 4–5, heart failure and with anticoagulants. Adjuncts: topical capsaicin (knee and hand); duloxetine (widespread pain, depression or central sensitisation); paracetamol only short-term if NSAIDs are contraindicated (minimal benefit). Avoid strong and weak opioids. For hand OA: hand exercises, joint protection and OT, thumb-base splints, IA steroid for inflamed IP or CMC1 joints. Pharmaceutical-grade chondroitin has some support for hand OA pain in some guidance.

stem: What is the role of intra-articular glucocorticoid injection in knee OA?

options.A: No benefit over placebo in any trial
options.B: A permanent disease-modifying effect with repeated injections
options.C: Routinely recommended every 4 weeks for maintenance thertherapy
options.D: It gives short-term relief, particularly for a flare with effusion, once infection is excluded
options.E: Triamcinolone hexacetonide

explanation: Intra-articular steroids give relief for weeks as an adjunct to core treatment. Frequent repeated injections are discouraged. Relief usually lasts 2–6 weeks (sometimes longer). Ultrasound guidance is needed for the hip. Repeated 3monthly triamcinolone was associated with greater cartilage loss on MRI (McAlindon). Rapidly progressive OA after injection has been reported. Avoid injection within about 3 months before arthroplasty (infection risk). Limit to 3–4 injections per joint per year. Extended-release triamcinolone (microspheres) prolongs knee relief with less glucose rise. Hyaluronic acid is not recommended by most guidelines (benefit close to placebo). PRP and stem cells are not recommended outside trials.

stem: What is the role of arthroscopic lavage and debridement in knee OA?

options.A: A topical NSAID
options.B: Clearly superior to physiotherapy for degenerative meniscal tears (contradicted by FIDELITY and ESCAPE)
options.C: It is not used for OA pain because it is no better than sham surgery
options.D: Recommended first-line for all patients with mechanical symptoms
options.E: Effective for diffuse OA pain without mechanical locking

explanation: Trials show arthroscopic lavage or debridement does not help OA pain. Arthroscopy is reserved for true mechanical locking. True mechanical symptoms (locking from a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear or loose body) are the exception where arthroscopy may help. Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy for degenerative tears offers no benefit over physiotherapy (FIDELITY, ESCAPE trials). Emerging options for refractory knee pain in patients unfit for surgery: genicular nerve radiofrequency ablation and genicular artery embolisation. Unicompartmental replacement and high tibial osteotomy suit younger, active patients with single-compartment disease. Cartilage repair is for focal defects in young patients, not established OA.

stem: What is the role of strong opioids in osteoarthritis?

options.A: First-line for moderate OA pain, given proven long-term efficacy
options.B: Preferred over NSAIDs because of a better long-term safety profile
options.C: Recommended for widespread OA pain with central sensitisation
options.D: They are not used routinely, because harms outweigh limited long-term benefit
options.E: Safe for long-term use provided renal function is monitored

explanation: Long-term opioids have little benefit for OA pain and substantial harms. Duloxetine may help selected patients with chronic pain and central sensitisation. Use opioids only in exceptional circumstances and shortterm (risks: falls, fractures, dependence, constipation, hypogonadism). Duloxetine, exercise, weight loss, CBT and pain management programmes are preferred for chronic OA pain with sensitisation features.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has painful thumb-base OA limiting her work. Which non-pharmacological measure is particularly recommended?

options.A: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid injection
options.B: Oral NSAIDs as first-line, before considering any splint
options.C: A thumb-base orthosis for long-term symptom relief, with hand exercises
options.D: Surgical trapeziectomy as the first-line intervention
options.E: A topical NSAID

explanation: thumb-base orthosis for long-term symptom relief, with hand exercises Orthoses for thumb-base OA, education, ergonomic advice and exercise improve function. Surgery is considered when symptoms persist despite conservative care. Radial-sided thumb pain: CMC1 OA (grind test, shoulder sign) vs de Quervain’s (Finkelstein), scaphoid fracture or non-union, scaphotrapeziotrapezoid (STT) OA, radial sensory neuritis (Wartenberg), intersection syndrome, gout, and CPPD (wrist). Splints (prefabricated or custom) and education; IA steroid (US-guided) for flares. Surgery is trapeziectomy (with or without ligament reconstruction), with arthrodesis or arthroplasty as alternatives.

stem: A 61-year-old woman has erosive hand OA with central erosions and gull-wing deformities. She asks about disease-modifying drugs. What is the correct advice?

options.A: Conventional and biologic DMARDs are not effective and are not used for hand OA
options.B: Methotrexate is first-line and reliably halts erosive progression
options.C: Hydroxychloroquine reliably reduces pain and erosive progression (the HERO trial)
options.D: TNF inhibitors are effective and licensed for erosive hand OA
options.E: A topical NSAID

explanation: Trials of hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate and TNF inhibitors in hand OA, including erosive disease, were negative. PsA (DIP, marginal “mouse-ear” erosions, periostitis, nails), multicentric reticulohistiocytosis (coral-bead papules, mutilans), gout (tophi on Heberden’s nodes), RA (spares DIPs, marginal erosions). Erosive hand OA presents abruptly, often perimenopausally, with inflamed IP joints. CRP is normal, RF and ACPA are negative, and it can progress to ankylosis. It carries a higher pain and disability burden than nodal OA. HOPE trial: prednisolone 10 mg for 6 weeks reduced pain in inflammatory hand OA. A recent RCT found methotrexate reduced pain in hand OA with synovitis. Hydroxychloroquine (HERO) and TNF blockade were ineffective. Denosumab reduced erosive progression in phase 2 (not licensed for this). Otherwise manage as for nodal hand OA.

stem: A 71-year-old man has severe hip pain and disability from radiographic OA despite exercise, weight management, analgesia and a walking aid. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Referral for consideration of joint replacement after shared decision-making
options.B: Continue conservative management indefinitely, since age and comorbidity preclude surgery
options.C: Defer referral until radiographic severity reaches Kellgren-Lawrence grade 4
options.D: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid injection as an alternative to surgery
options.E: Bariatric surgery as a prerequisite before any orthopaedic referral

explanation: Joint replacement is considered when symptoms substantially affect quality of life despite non-surgical management. Age, BMI and comorbidity alone should not be barriers to referral. Refer before prolonged deterioration. Do not exclude patients on age, BMI, smoking or radiographic severity alone; optimise these factors instead. Before referral, exclude a hip source in knee pain (and vice versa) and lumbar spine referral. Optimise weight, diabetes, anaemia and dental health. Avoid IA steroid in the 3 months before surgery. Prehabilitation improves recovery.

stem: A patient with knee OA asks whether glucosamine will slow progression. What is the best advice?

options.A: Strongly recommended, with clear evidence of slowed radiographic progression
options.B: Evidence is inconsistent and it is not recommended as a treatment for OA
options.C: Effective for rapid symptom relief within days
options.D: Proven to reduce the need for future joint replacement
options.E: A topical NSAID

explanation: Core treatment remains exercise, weight management and education, with topical NSAIDs as first-line medication. Independent trials (GAIT) show no clinically meaningful benefit from glucosamine or chondroitin for knee or hip OA; industry-sponsored crystalline glucosamine sulphate trials are more positive. Vitamin D supplements did not slow knee OA. Bisphosphonates, hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate and TNF or IL-1 blockers are not recommended routinely.

stem: A 42-year-old woman is diagnosed with fibromyalgia. Which treatment has the strongest evidence?

options.A: Strong opioids, titrated to effect for persistent pain
options.B: Long-term glucocorticoids for widespread pain control
options.C: Clinically, without imaging
options.D: Growth hormone replacement for associated fatigue
options.E: Graded aerobic and strengthening exercise

explanation: Exercise has the strongest evidence. Low-dose amitriptyline, duloxetine and pregabalin have weaker evidence for selected patients; strong opioids, glucocorticoids and growth hormone are not recommended. Exercise is the only strong recommendation in EULAR guidance: graded aerobic and strengthening exercise, started low and progressed slowly, continued long term. CBT and ACT help mood, catastrophising and coping. Meditative movement, mindfulness, hydrotherapy and acupuncture have weak to moderate benefit. Drug Target Notes Amitriptyline 10–50 sleep, pain first choice; mg at night anticholinergic effects Duloxetine 60 mg, pain with nausea at the start milnacipran depression or fatigue Pregabalin pain with poor controlled drug in the UK; sleep or anxiety dependence risk sleep, pain US-licensed Cyclobenzaprine (sublingual, TNX-102 (2025) SL) Tramadol rescue serotonin syndrome risk with SNRIs or TCAs Not recommended: strong opioids (opioid-induced hyperalgesia), NSAIDs alone, benzodiazepines, glucocorticoids, sodium oxybate. NICE (chronic primary pain) advises antidepressants only, plus exercise, CBT or ACT, or acupuncture.

stem: A woman has a year of widespread pain, fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive symptoms, with no synovitis and normal inflammatory markers, CK and thyroid function. What is the diagnosis, and which findings fulfil the 2016 revised fibromyalgia criteria?

options.A: Rheumatoid arthritis, since widespread pain and fatigue are typical early presenting features of RA
options.B: Polymyalgia rheumatica, given the age range and overall symptom pattern described here
options.C: Chronic fatigue syndrome, diagnosed once thyroid function and inflammatory markers are normal
options.D: Myositis, given the degree of fatigue and widespread pain, even with a persistently normal CK
options.E: Fibromyalgia, a positive clinical diagnosis: WPI 7 or more with SSS 5 or more (or WPI 4–6 with SSS 9 or more), generalised pain in at least 4 of 5 regions, for at least 3 months

explanation: Fibromyalgia is a positive clinical diagnosis. Example: widespread pain index 8, symptom severity score 6, and generalised pain in 4 of 5 regions for 4 months. Required: WPI 7 or more with SSS 5 or more (or WPI 4– 6 with SSS 9 or more), generalised pain in at least 4 of 5 regions, and symptoms for at least 3 months. A fibromyalgia diagnosis does not exclude other conditions; coexisting disease should be considered, but symptom severity should not be equated with inflammation. Inflammatory: PMR (>50, raised CRP), RA, axSpA (especially in women), SLE, Sjögren’s, myositis (weakness, raised CK). Endocrine and metabolic: hypothyroidism, osteomalacia or low vitamin D, hyperparathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, diabetes. Neurological: small-fibre neuropathy, MS, Parkinson’s disease, myopathy. Drugs: statins, aromatase inhibitors, opioid-induced hyperalgesia, bisphosphonates, steroid withdrawal. Musculoskeletal: hypermobility spectrum disorder, generalised OA. Other: myeloma or metastases, sleep apnoea, depression, anaemia, HCV, HIV, coeliac disease, ME/CFS (post-exertional malaise). Fatigue is present in >75%, non-restorative sleep, “fibro fog”, and mood disorder in 30–50% (common but not causal). Overlapping syndromes: IBS, migraine, TMD, bladder pain, vulvodynia, POTS. In the 2016 criteria, jaw, chest and abdomen do not count toward generalisation. A Fibromyalgia Severity score (WPI + SSS) ≥12 is consistent with FM. Screening tool: FiRST. The ACR 1990 criteria (≥11/18 tender points) are obsolete. Tests: FBC, CRP or ESR, U&E, LFTs, bone profile, CK, TSH, vitamin D, ferritin, HbA1c, coeliac serology if GI symptoms. Avoid untargeted ANA and RF (low-titre ANA in about 10% of healthy people). Red flags for another diagnosis: fever, weight loss, abnormal bloods, objective weakness, synovitis, rash, neurological signs. Poor prognosis is predicted by catastrophising, depression, opioid use, litigation and delayed diagnosis.

stem: A woman can place her palms flat on the floor, hyperextend both elbows beyond 10 degrees and oppose both thumbs to the forearm (Beighton score 5–6), with widespread joint pain and fatigue but no skin fragility, family history or features of a heritable connective tissue disorder. Does she meet the adult hypermobility threshold, and how should she be managed?

options.A: No; the Beighton threshold for adults up to the age of 50 is 6 or more, not 5
options.B: No; a Beighton score of 5 only counts as positive before puberty begins
options.C: Yes, and she meets full diagnostic criteria for classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
options.D: No, because skin fragility must also be present before any hypermobility points can be scored
options.E: Yes (5 or more for adults up to 50); she has hypermobility spectrum disorder if hEDS criteria are not met, managed with explanation and physiotherapy

explanation: Scoring: palms flat 1, elbows 2 (one per side), thumbs 2 = 5. Thresholds are 6 or more before puberty, 5 or more from puberty to 50, and 4 or more over 50. A diagnosis of hypermobile EDS also requires systemic features and exclusion of alternatives. Symptomatic hypermobility that does not meet the 2017 hEDS criteria is classified as a hypermobility spectrum disorder. Management is de-medicalising reassurance, graded exercise, joint stabilisation and painmanagement strategies. Unlike vascular EDS or Marfan syndrome, there is no routine need for vascular surveillance. Other heritable hypermobility conditions: vascular EDS (thin translucent skin, arterial, bowel or uterine rupture), classical EDS (hyperextensible skin, atrophic scars), Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, Stickler, OI, kyphoscoliotic EDS. Acquired increases in range of movement: training (dancers), hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism. Beighton (9 points): little-finger MCP extension >90° (1 per side), thumb to forearm (1 per side), elbow hyperextension >10° (1 per side), knee hyperextension >10° (1 per side), palms flat with knees straight (1). Associations of symptomatic hypermobility: chronic widespread pain, fatigue, POTS and dysautonomia, functional GI disorders, anxiety, recurrent subluxation, early OA. Graded strengthening, proprioception and core stability; pacing; CBT and pain management; avoid long-term opioids; treat POTS (fluids, salt, compression). Use orthoses and splints sparingly.

stem: A 59-year-old woman has lateral hip pain, worse lying on that side and climbing stairs, with tenderness over the greater trochanter. What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.A: Corticosteroid injection alone, without any exercise programme, as first-line
options.B: Referral for hip arthroscopy to debride the trochanteric bursa
options.C: Strict rest and avoidance of all weight-bearing activity for 6 weeks
options.D: Education with a progressive gluteal tendon loading exercise programme
options.E: Shockwave therapy as the first-line intervention, before any exercise trial

explanation: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome is usually gluteal tendinopathy. Education plus exercise outperformed corticosteroid injection at one year, while injection gives short-term relief with more recurrence. Lateral hip pain: gluteal tendinopathy or trochanteric bursitis vs hip OA (groin pain, reduced internal rotation), L4–5 radiculopathy, meralgia paraesthetica, ITB syndrome, femoral neck stress fracture, AVN, atypical femoral fracture (on bisphosphonates), SpA enthesitis. Pain lying on the affected side, pain on single-leg stance for 30 seconds, crossing the legs and stairs. It mostly affects women aged 40–60. LEAP trial: education plus exercise beat steroid injection at 52 weeks. Injection gives short-term relief with more recurrence. Shockwave therapy for refractory cases; gluteal tendon repair for full-thickness tears.

stem: How do you distinguish frozen shoulder from subacromial pain (for example a woman with diabetes and 4 months of global restriction of active and passive movement, versus a decorator with a painful arc and preserved passive external rotation), and how do treatment options compare?

options.A: Frozen shoulder preserves passive range while subacromial pain restricts it equally in all directions
options.B: Frozen shoulder causes global loss of active and passive movement, worst for external rotation, with a normal radiograph; subacromial pain preserves passive range. Treatments give broadly similar 12-month outcomes
options.C: Manipulation under anaesthesia clearly outperforms both physiotherapy and arthroscopic capsular release at 12 months
options.D: Subacromial pain causes global restriction of passive movement in all directions, unlike frozen shoulder
options.E: Both conditions require arthroscopic intervention as first-line treatment before any trial of physiotherapy

explanation: Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) causes painful loss of passive movement, especially external rotation, with a normal radiograph; diabetes and thyroid disease are risk factors. In subacromial (rotator cuff-related) pain, passive range is preserved and active elevation is painful. Rotator cuff tears also preserve passive range. Night pain and pain on reaching behind the back occur in both. In the UK FROST trial, none of the three approaches gave a clinically important advantage at 12 months; manipulation was the most cost-effective option, while capsular release carried more serious adverse events. Choice depends on patient preference and local resources. Loss of passive external rotation: frozen shoulder, glenohumeral OA (crepitus; X-ray changes), posterior dislocation (missed after seizure or electric shock), locked fracture-dislocation, inflammatory arthritis, septic arthritis, Milwaukee shoulder, AVN of the humeral head. Painful arc: subacromial pain syndrome, calcific tendinitis, partial cuff tear, ACJ arthritis (high arc 160–180°). Referred: C5 radiculopathy, Pancoast tumour, diaphragmatic pain, cardiac pain, PMR (bilateral, raised CRP). Frozen shoulder runs through freezing, frozen and thawing phases over 1–3 years. Associations: diabetes (up to 20%, often bilateral), thyroid disease, Dupuytren’s, prolonged immobilisation, stroke, and checkpoint inhibitors. Early IA steroid injection plus physiotherapy (most effective early); hydrodilatation; MUA or arthroscopic capsular release if refractory. For subacromial pain: exercise-based physiotherapy first, subacromial steroid for short-term relief.

stem: A 54-year-old woman has nocturnal paraesthesia in the thumb, index and middle fingers with thenar wasting. Nerve conduction studies confirm severe median nerve compression at the wrist. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Switch to subcutaneous methotrexate
options.B: Repeat nerve conduction studies in 6 months before considering any intervention
options.C: A further trial of night splinting for 3 more months
options.D: Referral for surgical carpal tunnel decompression
options.E: A short oral corticosteroid course as an alternative to surgical referral

explanation: Thenar wasting or severe conduction changes indicate axonal loss and warrant decompression. Splinting or injection suits mild to moderate disease. Secondary causes include hypothyroidism, acromegaly, RA, pregnancy and amyloidosis. CTS mimics: C6–C7 radiculopathy (neck pain, reflex change, sensory loss beyond the hand), pronator syndrome (thenar eminence sensation affected, no nocturnal symptoms), AIN syndrome (purely motor; cannot make the “OK” sign), thoracic outlet syndrome, polyneuropathy, MND (wasting without sensory loss), syringomyelia. Thenar eminence sensation is spared in CTS because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the retinaculum. Associations: pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, RA (flexor tenosynovitis), acromegaly, amyloid (ATTR, AL, dialysis β2-microglobulin), obesity, gout, wrist fracture. Phalen’s, Tinel’s and Durkan’s tests; relief from flicking the hand. Mild to moderate disease: night splint and steroid injection (effective short to medium term). Thenar wasting, axonal loss on NCS or failure of conservative care: surgical release. Treat the underlying cause. In bilateral CTS in older men, consider screening for ATTR (echo, cardiac biomarkers, IIITc-DPD scintigraphy if suspected).

stem: A 40-year-old man has 6 months of low back pain. Inflammatory markers and examination are normal, there are no red flags, and he has marked fear-avoidance and deconditioning. What is most appropriate?

options.A: Explain the pain mechanism, support graded activity and rehabilitation, and address psychosocial factors while remaining alert to red flags
options.B: Urgent MRI of the lumbar spine to exclude structural pathology
options.C: Strict bed rest until symptoms fully resolve
options.D: Long-term opioid therapy titrated to pain scores
options.E: Urgent referral for epidural steroid injection as first-line treatment

explanation: Chronic non-specific back pain is best managed with education, graded activity and psychological approaches. Imaging without red flags rarely helps and can reinforce fear. STarT Back risk stratification. Explain the pain mechanism (pain does not equal damage); keep active and return to work; group exercise or graded activity; CBT-informed combined physical and psychological programmes for high-risk patients; NSAIDs short-term. Avoid opioids, gabapentinoids and benzodiazepines for chronic low back pain. No imaging without red flags.

stem: A woman 6–8 weeks after a wrist or distal radius fracture has burning pain out of proportion to the injury, allodynia, swelling, colour and sweating asymmetry and reduced finger movement; radiographs show only the healing fracture. What is the diagnosis and approach?

options.A: Reflex sympathetic dystrophy from nerve entrapment at the fracture site, treated with surgical decompression
options.B: A somatic symptom disorder, best managed with prolonged immobilisation to prevent further injury
options.C: Complex regional pain syndrome (type 1), diagnosed clinically using the Budapest criteria; manage with early explanation and graded rehabilitation (physiotherapy or OT, desensitisation, graded motor imagery) with pain
options.D: Osteomyelitis, requiring urgent surgical debridement and IV antibiotics
options.E: Explain the pain mechanism, support graded activity and rehabilitation, and address psychosocial factors while remaining alert to red flags

explanation: management and psychological support CRPS is a clinical diagnosis. Type 1 has no definable nerve injury. Outcomes are best with early, graded rehabilitation, desensitisation, mirror or graded motor imagery, and psychological support, in a multidisciplinary approach. Prolonged immobilisation worsens it. Infection (cellulitis, osteomyelitis), DVT, fracture non-union, inflammatory arthritis, gout, peripheral nerve injury or entrapment, Raynaud’s or vascular insufficiency, factitious disorder (tight tourniquet), disuse. Budapest criteria: continuing disproportionate pain; symptoms in ≥3 of 4 categories and signs in ≥2 of 4 categories (sensory: allodynia, hyperalgesia; vasomotor: temperature asymmetry >1 °C, colour; sudomotor or oedema; motor or trophic: reduced ROM, weakness, tremor, dystonia, hair, nail and skin changes); and no better explanation. CRPS I accounts for about 90% (CRPS II involves a major nerve injury). F:M is 3–4:1, peaking at 50– 70 years. It follows 2–5% of distal radius fractures. “Warm” CRPS is early and inflammatory; “cold” CRPS carries a worse prognosis and often includes dystonia. The threestage model is no longer valid. About 70–80% improve within a year. Drugs: neuropathic agents; bisphosphonates (IV neridronate, pamidronate, zoledronate) in early CRPS with bone changes; short oral GC for early warm CRPS; topical lidocaine or capsaicin; IV ketamine in specialist centres. Avoid long-term opioids. NSAIDs are of limited value. Interventional: sympathetic blocks (limited evidence); spinal cord or dorsal root ganglion stimulation for refractory cases. Amputation is exceptional. Prevention: avoid tight casts, mobilise early. Vitamin C 500 mg for 50 days after distal radius fracture has mixed evidence. Supportive findings: spotty osteopenia on X-ray; periarticular uptake in the delayed phase of a bone scan.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has 9 months of subacromial pain with an intact rotator cuff, only partly helped by 3 months of exercise and one steroid injection. She asks about arthroscopic subacromial decompression. What is the most accurate advice?

options.A: Early arthroscopic decompression gives a clear, lasting benefit over rehabilitation
options.B: Repeated steroid injections, continued indefinitely, are the mainstay of treatment
options.C: An MRI arthrogram is required before any further conservative treatment
options.D: Decompression has not outperformed placebo arthroscopy; continue progressive rehabilitation
options.E: Surgery should be offered now, since conservative treatment has already been tried for long enough

explanation: Placebo-controlled surgical trials found that arthroscopic subacromial decompression was no better than investigational arthroscopy alone, and neither gave a clinically important benefit over no treatment. Older practice of routine decompression for impingement has largely been abandoned. A progressive loading programme remains the mainstay. CSAW and FIMPACT trials showed arthroscopic subacromial decompression was no better than placebo or diagnostic arthroscopy. Progressive loading programme (scapular and cuff strengthening) for 12 weeks or more, with or without subacromial steroid or US-guided barbotage if calcific deposits are present. Refer to surgery for full-thickness tears, calcific deposits refractory to barbotage, or ACJ OA.

stem: Two weeks after a fall, a 56-year-old man cannot actively elevate the arm above 60 degrees and has weak external rotation, with near-full passive range. Ultrasound shows a full-thickness cuff tear with minimal retraction. What is the best management?

options.A: Physiotherapy alone for at least 6 months before any imaging
options.B: Reassurance, since near-full passive range excludes a significant tear
options.C: Subacromial steroid injection, deferring any surgical opinion
options.D: Prompt shoulder surgical referral for consideration of early repair
options.E: Observation for 3 months to allow the tear to heal spontaneously

explanation: An acute traumatic full-thickness cuff tear with loss of active elevation in a fit patient should be referred early. Repair outcomes are better before tendon retraction and muscle atrophy develop. Delaying with injection or prolonged conservative care risks an irreparable tear. Weak active elevation with full passive range: cuff tear, suprascapular nerve palsy (spinoglenoid ganglion, traction), axillary nerve injury after dislocation (regimental badge sensory loss), neuralgic amyotrophy, C5 radiculopathy, pain inhibition (calcific tendinitis), deltoid avulsion. Drop-arm sign and external rotation lag sign. Acute tears often occur in people >40 after dislocation or a fall. Chronic degenerative tears in people >60 are often asymptomatic. Acute traumatic tear in a fit patient: ultrasound or MRI and surgical repair ideally within 3–6 weeks. Degenerative tears: physiotherapy first. Massive irreparable tears: reverse shoulder arthroplasty or tendon transfer.

stem: An 82-year-old woman has a swollen, destroyed shoulder with a large blood-stained, non-inflammatory effusion and superior migration of the humeral head. Which crystals are most likely responsible?

options.A: Monosodium urate crystals
options.B: No crystals; this is a purely degenerative process
options.C: Basic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite)
options.D: Gram stain and bacterial culture
options.E: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals

explanation: Milwaukee shoulder is a destructive arthropathy of elderly women with rotator cuff loss and large, often bloodstained effusions with low cell counts. Basic calcium phosphate crystals are implicated. They are not seen on routine polarised microscopy, although alizarin red staining can help. Destructive shoulder arthropathy in older people: Milwaukee shoulder (BCP), rapidly progressive OA, septic arthritis (low threshold to aspirate), neuropathic (Charcot) shoulder from syringomyelia (with loss of pain and temperature sensation in a cape distribution), AVN, CPPD destructive arthropathy, RA, amyloid (“shoulder pad” sign), haemophilic or anticoagulant haemarthrosis, metastasis. Analgesia, physiotherapy, repeated aspiration with steroid injection, tidal irrigation, reverse total shoulder arthroplasty for severe cases. Always send fluid for culture.

stem: A carpenter has 6 weeks of lateral elbow pain on gripping, with pain on resisted wrist extension. He requests a steroid injection to return to work quickly. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Immediate steroid injection, since this gives the best long-term outcome
options.B: Surgical release of the common extensor origin as first-line treatment
options.C: Education and progressive loading; injection helps briefly but worsens 1-year outcome
options.D: Complete rest from gripping activities for 6 months, avoiding any loading exercise
options.E: Education with a progressive gluteal tendon loading exercise programme

explanation: Lateral elbow tendinopathy is usually self-limiting. Randomised data show that corticosteroid injection improves pain at 4 to 6 weeks but leads to poorer recovery and higher recurrence at 1 year than placebo. Older texts recommended early injection; current practice favours education and progressive loading. Bilateral or multisite enthesitis should prompt consideration of spondyloarthritis. Lateral elbow pain: tendinopathy vs radial tunnel syndrome (pain 3–5 cm distal to the epicondyle, middle finger test, no weakness; coexists in about 5%), PIN syndrome (finger drop without sensory loss), radiocapitellar OA, plica, posterolateral instability, C6 radiculopathy, SpA enthesitis. Load management, forearm strap, isometric then eccentric loading. Most resolve within 1–2 years. Shockwave therapy has mixed evidence. Surgery is rarely needed. PRP evidence is mixed.

stem: A 45-year-old plumber has a hot, red, tender swelling over the olecranon, with surrounding cellulitis and a temperature of 38.2°C. A small abrasion is present over the bursa. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Intra-articular (not bursal) aspiration with empirical IV antibiotics
options.B: Oral NSAIDs alone, without aspiration, since the abrasion is unlikely to be significant
options.C: Immediate corticosteroid injection into the bursa for rapid symptom relief
options.D: Oral antibiotics without aspiration, reserving aspiration for cases that fail to improve
options.E: Aspirate for Gram stain, culture and crystals; start antistaphylococcal antibiotic

explanation: Septic olecranon bursitis is common after skin breaches in manual workers and is usually due to Staphylococcus aureus. Fluid should be sent for culture and polarised microscopy, since gout is the main alternative. Corticosteroid must not be injected when infection is possible. Olecranon swelling: septic bursitis (S. aureus; also streptococci), gout (tophi, crystals), RA nodules or bursitis, traumatic or haemorrhagic bursitis, CPPD, TB or atypical mycobacteria (chronic), uraemic bursitis (dialysis). Fluid WCC in septic bursitis is often lower than in septic arthritis (>2,000–5,000/µL is suspicious). Gram stain sensitivity is moderate. Aspirate (avoiding a direct track through cellulitic skin), then oral antibiotics if mild and IV if systemically unwell or immunosuppressed. Repeat aspiration as needed. Surgical bursectomy for refractory or recurrent septic bursitis. Nonseptic, non-crystal bursitis: compression and NSAIDs; consider steroid only once infection is excluded.

stem: A 40-year-old cyclist has paraesthesia of the little finger and the ulnar half of the ring finger, with weakness of finger abduction. Which clinical finding best localises the ulnar nerve lesion to the elbow rather than to Guyon’s canal at the wrist?

options.A: The A1 pulley at the metacarpal head
options.B: Weakness of thumb opposition and abductor pollicis brevis
options.C: Preserved sensation over the dorsal ulnar hand, regardless of lesion site
options.D: Sensory loss over the dorsal ulnar aspect of the hand
options.E: Median nerve at the carpal tunnel

explanation: The dorsal ulnar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the wrist and does not pass through Guyon’s canal. Loss of dorsal ulnar hand sensation therefore indicates a lesion proximal to the wrist, most often cubital tunnel syndrome. Intrinsic weakness, Froment’s sign and palmar sensory loss occur with lesions at either site. C8–T1 radiculopathy (medial forearm sensory loss via the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve), thoracic outlet syndrome, Pancoast tumour (Horner’s syndrome), MND, HNPP. Cubital tunnel (the second commonest entrapment): symptoms worse with elbow flexion; intrinsic wasting, Froment’s and Wartenberg’s signs, clawing (often less with a proximal lesion because FDP to the ring and little fingers is also weak, the “ulnar paradox”). Guyon’s canal causes: cycling (“handlebar palsy”), ganglion, hook of hamate fracture, ulnar artery thrombosis (“hypothenar hammer”). Guyon’s canal lesions spare the dorsal ulnar hand. Avoid prolonged elbow flexion (night extension splint, elbow pad). Surgery (in situ decompression or transposition) for weakness or refractory symptoms.

stem: A 32-year-old woman, 3 months after the birth of her first child, has radial wrist pain when lifting the baby. Ulnar deviation of the wrist with the thumb flexed into the palm reproduces the pain. Which tendons are affected?

options.A: Flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus
options.B: Warfarin anticoagulation
options.C: Flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus
options.D: Extensor carpi ulnaris and extensor digiti minimi
options.E: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis

explanation: De Quervain’s tenosynovitis affects the first extensor compartment (APL and EPB). It is common in new parents and is reproduced by Finkelstein-type manoeuvres. First-line treatment is activity modification, a thumb spica splint and corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath. Radial wrist pain in a new parent: de Quervain’s vs CMC1 OA (grind test), scaphoid fracture, intersection syndrome (pain 4–6 cm proximal to the wrist with crepitus, involving the 2nd compartment where APL and EPB cross ECRL and ECRB), Wartenberg’s syndrome (superficial radial nerve; dorsoradial paraesthesia, Tinel’s sign), inflammatory tenosynovitis (RA), post-partum CTS. Thumb spica splint and steroid injection (very effective, often first-line). Surgical release of the first compartment if refractory (look for a separate EPB subsheath).

stem: A 58-year-old man with diabetes has painful clicking and intermittent locking of the ring finger in flexion. A tender nodule is palpable at the base of the finger in the palm. At which structure does the tendon catch?

options.A: The flexor digitorum superficialis at the PIP joint
options.B: Diabetic cheiroarthropathy (limited joint mobility)
options.C: The extensor tendon at the MCP joint
options.D: The A1 pulley at the metacarpal head
options.E: Development of MALT lymphoma

explanation: Trigger finger is stenosing tenosynovitis of the flexor tendon at the A1 pulley. Steroid injection into the tendon sheath is effective first-line treatment, although response is lower in diabetes. Percutaneous or open A1 pulley release is used if injection fails. Associations: diabetes (often multiple digits, poorer injection response), RA (flexor tenosynovitis), hypothyroidism, amyloid, gout, Dupuytren’s. Paediatric trigger thumb is a different entity (Notta’s node). Steroid injection (about 60–90% success, lower in diabetes); repeat once if needed. Percutaneous or open A1 pulley release. In RA, avoid A1 release because it worsens ulnar drift; synovectomy is preferred.

stem: A 66-year-old man has Dupuytren’s disease of both palms. He has a 35-degree fixed flexion deformity at the right ring finger MCP joint and cannot lay the right palm flat on a table. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Serial splinting in extension to gradually correct the contracture
options.B: Intralesional collagenase injection, now first-line in the UK
options.C: Refer to a hand surgeon to discuss needle fasciotomy or limited fasciectomy
options.D: Observation only, since Dupuytren’s contracture rarely progresses
options.E: Low-dose radiotherapy as the first-line treatment for this degree of contracture

explanation: A positive tabletop test, an MCP contracture of about 30 degrees or any PIP contracture with functional impairment are usual triggers for referral. Options include percutaneous needle fasciotomy and limited fasciectomy, with dermofasciectomy for recurrent disease. Splinting alone does not correct established contracture. Palmar thickening and contracture: diabetic cheiroarthropathy (prayer sign, waxy skin), palmar fasciitis and polyarthritis (paraneoplastic, rapid onset, ovarian cancer), SSc sclerodactyly, trigger finger, camptodactyly, flexor tendon adhesion, ulnar nerve claw hand. Risk factors: men of northern European ancestry, family history (autosomal dominant with variable penetrance), diabetes, alcohol, smoking, epilepsy drugs (phenobarbital), manual work. Dupuytren’s diathesis (Garrod’s knuckle pads, Ledderhose plantar fibromatosis, Peyronie’s disease) predicts aggressive, recurrent disease. Ring and little fingers are most affected. Observe while function is preserved. Intervene with a positive tabletop test, MCP contracture of about 30° or any functionally limiting PIP contracture. Options: needle fasciotomy (quicker recovery, higher recurrence), limited fasciectomy, dermofasciectomy for recurrence. Collagenase is no longer available in Europe. Low-dose radiotherapy can be used for early progressive disease (NICE IPG).

stem: An obese man has burning pain and numbness over the anterolateral thigh, worse with a tight belt. Power, knee reflex and straight leg raise are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: L3 radiculopathy
options.B: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve entrapment
options.C: Femoral neuropathy
options.D: Femoroacetabular impingement (cam type)
options.E: Small-fibre neuropathy

explanation: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2-L3) is purely sensory and can be compressed near the anterior superior iliac spine. Risk factors include obesity, pregnancy, tight belts and diabetes. Normal motor findings and reflexes distinguish it from L3 radiculopathy and femoral neuropathy. L2–L3 radiculopathy (weak hip flexion and adduction), femoral neuropathy (weak quadriceps, absent knee jerk; consider retroperitoneal haematoma on anticoagulation, needing urgent CT), diabetic amyotrophy (proximal pain then weakness and weight loss), hip disease, pelvic tumour. Meralgia paraesthetica (LFCN, L2–L3) is purely sensory: anterolateral thigh burning, worse standing or walking. Causes: obesity, tight belts or trousers, pregnancy, diabetes, prone surgery, iliac crest bone graft, seat-belt trauma. It is often self-limiting. Reassurance, weight loss, loose clothing, neuropathic agents, US-guided nerve block (diagnostic and therapeutic), and rarely surgical decompression or neurectomy.

stem: A 50-year-old woman who wears narrow high-heeled shoes has burning forefoot pain radiating into the third and fourth toes. Squeezing the forefoot while pressing the third web space produces a painful click. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Interdigital (Morton’s) neuroma
options.B: Tarsal tunnel syndrome
options.C: SAPHO syndrome
options.D: Small-fibre neuropathy
options.E: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome

explanation: Morton’s neuroma is perineural fibrosis of the common digital nerve, usually in the third web space. Mulder’s click is characteristic. Management includes wider footwear, a metatarsal pad, steroid injection and, if refractory, excision. Forefoot pain: Morton’s neuroma vs MTP synovitis (RA, often early and with a positive squeeze test), intermetatarsal bursitis, metatarsal stress fracture, Freiberg’s infraction (AVN of the 2nd metatarsal head; adolescent girls), plantar plate tear (2nd toe deviation), metatarsalgia from fat pad atrophy or claw toes, tarsal tunnel syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, gout. Wide toe box, metatarsal pad and US-guided steroid injection. Alcohol sclerosis or radiofrequency ablation has variable evidence. Neurectomy if refractory (risk of stump neuroma). Ultrasound shows a hypoechoic mass.

stem: A 44-year-old runner has burning paraesthesia over the sole of the foot, worse after prolonged standing. Tapping behind and below the medial malleolus reproduces the symptoms. Which nerve is most likely compressed?

options.A: Posterior tibial nerve under the flexor retinaculum
options.B: Tibialis posterior tendon
options.C: Sural nerve at the lateral ankle
options.D: Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
options.E: Superficial peroneal nerve

explanation: Tarsal tunnel syndrome is compression of the posterior tibial nerve or its plantar branches beneath the flexor retinaculum. Causes include ganglia, tenosynovitis and varicosities. Nerve conduction studies and MRI or ultrasound help confirm the cause. Burning sole pain: tarsal tunnel syndrome vs plantar fasciopathy, S1 radiculopathy, length-dependent polyneuropathy (bilateral; check glucose, B12, alcohol, paraprotein, thyroid), small-fibre neuropathy (Sjögren’s, sarcoid, amyloid), Baxter’s nerve entrapment (first branch of the lateral plantar nerve; medial heel pain), calcaneal stress fracture, erythromelalgia. Arch-support orthoses; treat tenosynovitis (RA, SpA); NSAIDs and neuropathic agents; injection; ultrasound or MRI for a mass; surgical release (variable results).

stem: A 46-year-old teacher has 4 months of plantar heel pain that is worst with the first steps in the morning. She is tender at the medial calcaneal tubercle. There are no features of spondyloarthritis. What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.A: Immediate corticosteroid injection through the plantar skin as first-line treatment
options.B: Urgent MRI to exclude a calcaneal stress fracture before any treatment
options.C: Complete non-weight-bearing rest in a cast for 6 weeks
options.D: Referral for surgical fasciotomy as first-line treatment
options.E: Plantar fascia and calf stretching, supportive footwear and load modification

explanation: Most plantar heel pain settles within a year with conservative measures. Steroid injection gives short-term benefit but risks fat-pad atrophy and fascial rupture, and should never be given through the plantar skin. Imaging is reserved for atypical or refractory cases. Plantar heel pain: plantar fasciopathy vs SpA enthesitis (bilateral, enthesitis elsewhere, raised CRP), calcaneal stress fracture (squeeze test positive), fat pad atrophy (central heel, older people), Baxter’s nerve entrapment, tarsal tunnel syndrome, S1 radiculopathy, calcaneal tumour or infection, Sever’s disease in children (calcaneal apophysitis). Plantar fascia-specific and calf stretching, heel cups or insoles, night splints, weight loss, load modification. Shockwave therapy for refractory cases. Steroid injection gives short-term benefit (risks fat pad atrophy and rupture; give it via a medial approach). Most cases resolve within 12 months. Surgery is rarely needed.

stem: A 68-year-old man taking prednisolone 10 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica is prescribed levofloxacin for pneumonia. Which complication is particularly increased by this combination?

options.A: Atypical femoral fracture
options.B: Peptic ulceration with gastrointestinal bleeding
options.C: Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily)
options.D: Achilles tendinopathy and tendon rupture
options.E: QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmia

explanation: Fluoroquinolones increase the risk of tendinopathy and tendon rupture, especially of the Achilles tendon, and the risk is greatest in older people and with concomitant corticosteroids. Their use is restricted, and patients should be told to stop the drug at the first sign of tendon pain. Other drug causes of tendinopathy: statins (rare), aromatase inhibitors (tenosynovitis, trigger finger), local steroid injection, anabolic steroids, isotretinoin. Patient factors: age >60, renal failure, transplant recipients, RA, diabetes, gout. Avoid fluoroquinolones unless there is no alternative, particularly with concomitant GC (MHRA advice). If tendon pain develops: stop the drug, rest the tendon and get ultrasound. A ruptured Achilles needs orthopaedic review (Simmonds’ test).

stem: A 64-year-old woman with knee osteoarthritis develops sudden pain and swelling of the right calf after gardening. A crescent of bruising appears below the medial malleolus. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: Compression ultrasound of the leg
options.B: High-resolution CT chest
options.C: CT of the chest
options.D: MRI of the lumbar spine
options.E: D-dimer alone, without imaging

explanation: A ruptured popliteal (Baker’s) cyst mimics DVT, and the two can coexist. Ultrasound distinguishes them. The ‘crescent sign’ of bruising around the malleolus suggests cyst rupture, but DVT must still be excluded before treatment. Acute calf pain: DVT, ruptured Baker’s cyst (“pseudothrombophlebitis”), gastrocnemius (medial head) tear (“tennis leg”), plantaris rupture, compartment syndrome, cellulitis, superficial thrombophlebitis, haematoma on anticoagulation, popliteal artery aneurysm thrombosis (pulses), myositis. Compression ultrasound. Treat the underlying knee synovitis (aspiration and IA steroid). Analgesia and elevation for cyst rupture. Anticoagulate if DVT is confirmed (both can coexist).

stem: A 24-year-old footballer has 6 months of deep groin pain on sitting and during kicking. Pain is reproduced by passive hip flexion, adduction and internal rotation. Radiographs show a non-spherical femoral head-neck junction. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Transient osteoporosis of the hip
options.B: Rotator cuff-related shoulder pain
options.C: Adhesive capsulitis
options.D: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome
options.E: Femoroacetabular impingement (cam type)

explanation: A positive FADIR test with a cam deformity indicates femoroacetabular impingement, which can cause labral and chondral damage. Management starts with activity modification and physiotherapy; arthroscopic surgery is considered for persistent symptoms. SUFE presents in younger adolescents. Young adult hip or groin pain: FAI (cam or pincer) with labral tear vs adductor-related groin pain, inguinal-related pain (sportsman’s hernia), osteitis pubis, femoral neck stress fracture (urgent MRI; tension-side fractures need surgery), AVN, SUFE (adolescents), DDH, iliopsoas tendinopathy or bursitis (“snapping hip”), axSpA, sacroiliitis, referred lumbar pain. FADIR (flexion, adduction, internal rotation) is sensitive but not specific. X-ray shows a cam deformity (non-spherical head–neck junction, raised alpha angle) or pincer deformity (crossover sign, acetabular over-coverage). MR arthrogram assesses the labrum and cartilage. Activity modification and physiotherapy (core and hip strengthening). Intra-articular injection can be diagnostic. Hip arthroscopy (FASHIoN and UK FAIT trials showed modest benefit over physiotherapy) for persistent symptoms without significant OA.

stem: A patient with low back pain develops bilateral sciatica and new perineal or saddle sensory loss, with or without urinary retention. What is the most appropriate action, and which other back pain features are red flags?

options.A: Emergency lumbar MRI immediately, at any time of day, with same-day spinal surgical referral for suspected cauda equina syndrome
options.B: Outpatient MRI within 2 weeks, with routine rather than emergency neurosurgical referral
options.C: Reassurance is appropriate if a bladder scan alone shows no urinary retention
options.D: Urgent lumbar X-ray as the first and most informative investigation of choice
options.E: Observation overnight on the ward with a repeat neurological examination in the morning

explanation: Suspected cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency, and delay worsens bladder, bowel and sexual outcomes. Outcomes are best when decompression occurs before retention (incomplete CES, CES-I); established retention (CES-R) carries a worse prognosis. Emergency MRI is indicated regardless of time of day, and a normal bladder scan does not exclude the diagnosis. CES mimics and causes: central disc herniation (the commonest cause, at L4/5 or L5/S1), spinal stenosis with acute decompensation, epidural abscess or haematoma (anticoagulation, post-procedure), metastatic cord or cauda equina compression, AS with dural ectasia (arachnoid diverticula), conus medullaris lesion, GBS, transverse myelitis (SLE, Sjögren’s, NMOSD), functional neurological disorder. Non-spinal back pain: AAA, renal colic or pyelonephritis, pancreatitis, gynaecological disease or endometriosis, hip OA, herpes zoster. CES features: bilateral leg symptoms, saddle or perineal anaesthesia, new bladder dysfunction (reduced sensation, poor stream, retention), bowel incontinence, sexual dysfunction, reduced anal tone. A history of cancer is the most specific red flag; others have low specificity individually. The national pathway (GIRFT) aims for MRI within about 4 hours. Do a post-void bladder scan, but do not wait for retention. Red-flag bloods: FBC, CRP or ESR, protein electrophoresis and free light chains, calcium, ALP, PSA. Spondylodiscitis: blood cultures and biopsy before antibiotics if stable, and treat for at least 6 weeks. Metastatic spinal cord compression: dexamethasone and urgent oncology.

stem: A 74-year-old man has bilateral buttock and thigh aching after walking 200 m. It is relieved by sitting or leaning forward on a shopping trolley but not by standing still. Foot pulses are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Peripheral arterial disease (vascular claudication)
options.B: Bilateral hip osteoarthritis
options.C: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve entrapment
options.D: Osteoporotic insufficiency fracture of the sacrum
options.E: Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)

explanation: Neurogenic claudication is relieved by lumbar flexion (sitting, stooping) rather than by simply stopping, and pulses are preserved. Vascular claudication eases on standing still. MRI confirms canal stenosis; decompression is considered for disabling or progressive symptoms. Hip OA (groin pain, reduced internal rotation), trochanteric pain syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, venous claudication, spinal AVM, ATTR amyloid (lumbar stenosis is an early “red flag” feature). Feature Neurogenic Vascular Relief sitting or flexion standing still (minutes) (seconds to minutes) Posture worse with irrelevant extension or standing Cycling, uphill tolerated provokes walking symptoms Pulses and normal reduced ABPI Sensory common uncommon symptoms Flexion-based physiotherapy, walking or cycling programme, weight loss, analgesia. Epidural steroids give little benefit in stenosis. Decompression (laminectomy) beats continued conservative care for severe, refractory symptoms. Adding fusion is usually unnecessary without instability (Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study).

stem: A 29-year-old man has 3 weeks of L5 sciatica with no neurological deficit or red flags. His GP started pregabalin and diazepam. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Continue both and add amitriptyline for neuropathic pain
options.B: Increase the pregabalin dose and add a short course of oral corticosteroids
options.C: Continue diazepam long-term for muscle spasm, in addition to pregabalin
options.D: Explain the pain mechanism, support graded activity and rehabilitation, and address psychosocial factors while remaining alert to red flags
options.E: Stop both; use an NSAID if needed, keep active, consider epidural steroid if severe

explanation: Gabapentinoids, other antiepileptics, oral corticosteroids and benzodiazepines are not recommended for sciatica because of lack of benefit and harms. Older texts suggested diazepam for spasm; this is no longer advised. Most disc-related sciatica improves within 3 months. Sciatica has a lifetime incidence of 13–40% and peaks at 45–64. Most cases improve over 6–12 weeks; large sequestered fragments often regress. 10– 20% still have symptoms at 1 year. SLR at 30–70° has about 90% sensitivity; crossed SLR has about 90% specificity for disc herniation. The femoral stretch test assesses L2–L4. Stay active and do physiotherapy. Short-course NSAIDs. Image-guided epidural steroid for acute severe sciatica (short-term relief only; does not reduce surgery). Pregabalin was no better than placebo (PRECISE). Use amitriptyline or duloxetine only selectively, with stopping rules. Microdiscectomy for CES, progressive motor deficit, or disabling pain beyond 6–12 weeks with matching MRI: it gives faster relief, but 1–2-year outcomes are similar.

stem: A man has back pain radiating to the dorsum of the foot, weak great toe extension and ankle dorsiflexion, dorsal foot sensory loss and normal reflexes. Which nerve root is affected?

options.A: S1
options.B: L4
options.C: L5
options.D: Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
options.E: Tibialis posterior tendon

explanation: L5 radiculopathy, usually from an L4/5 disc, causes weakness of EHL, ankle dorsiflexion and hip abduction, with dorsal foot and great toe sensory loss; the major reflexes are usually preserved. A reduced ankle reflex with weak plantarflexion and lateral foot sensory loss indicates S1. Foot drop: L5 radiculopathy (inversion and hip abduction weak, back pain) vs common peroneal neuropathy (inversion spared), sciatic neuropathy (piriformis or deep gluteal syndrome), lumbosacral plexopathy (tumour, haematoma, diabetic amyotrophy), mononeuritis multiplex (vasculitis), MND, HNPP, parasagittal cortical lesion (UMN signs). Root Weakness Sensory Reflex L3 knee extension, hip anterior thigh knee adduction to medial knee L4 knee extension, ankle medial shin knee dorsiflexion and inversion L5 EHL, ankle (medial dorsum of dorsiflexion, hip foot, great hamstring) abduction, inversion toe S1 plantarflexion, lateral foot, ankle eversion, hip sole extension

stem: A 15-year-old fast bowler has 2 months of low back pain that is worse on extension and on standing on one leg while extending the spine. Neurology is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Disc herniation (flexion-related pain)
options.B: Scheuermann’s disease
options.C: Spondylolysis (pars interarticularis stress fracture)
options.D: Facet joint syndrome
options.E: Osteoid osteoma

explanation: Pars stress fractures, usually at L5, occur in adolescents who repeatedly hyperextend, such as fast bowlers and gymnasts. MRI (or SPECT/CT) detects early stress reaction. Management is activity modification and rehabilitation; bracing is sometimes used. Adolescent extension-related pain: spondylolysis vs facet irritation, Scheuermann’s, disc herniation (flexion-related), osteoid osteoma (night pain relieved by NSAIDs), ERA or juvenile SpA, discitis (young children who refuse to walk), tumour (Ewing’s, leukaemia, ABC). Pars stress fractures (usually L5) occur in extension sports, with prevalence about 6%. Progression risk is higher in girls, dysplastic slips, high-grade slips and during the growth spurt. Meyerding grades I–V. The “one-legged hyperextension (stork) test” is positive. Rest from sport for 6–12 weeks; core and hamstring physiotherapy; a brace for early (acute) lysis to promote healing; fusion for high-grade (III–IV), progressive or neurologically symptomatic slips.

stem: A 16-year-old boy has a rigid thoracic kyphosis that does not correct on extension. Radiographs show wedging of three adjacent vertebrae with Schmorl’s nodes. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Enthesitis-related arthritis
options.B: Hyperparathyroidism
options.C: Scheuermann’s disease
options.D: Congenital kyphosis
options.E: Postural kyphosis

explanation: Scheuermann’s kyphosis is a structural adolescent kyphosis defined by wedging in at least three adjacent vertebrae. Postural kyphosis corrects on extension. Most cases are managed with extension-focused physiotherapy; bracing or surgery is reserved for severe deformity. Postural kyphosis (corrects on extension), congenital kyphosis, AS (older, sacroiliitis), osteoporotic wedge fractures, infection (TB gibbus), neuromuscular disease. Scheuermann’s: wedging ≥5° of ≥3 adjacent vertebrae, endplate irregularity, Schmorl’s nodes, rigid thoracic kyphosis >45°. Extension-focused physiotherapy; a brace while still growing; surgery for severe deformity (>70–75°) or intractable pain.

stem: A 61-year-old woman has chronic low back pain without sciatica. Non-surgical treatment has failed, and clinical assessment suggests facet joint origin. Her pain is moderate to severe. Which intervention is appropriate to consider?

options.A: Lumbar fusion surgery as first-line treatment
options.B: Spinal cord stimulation, without a prior diagnostic block
options.C: Discography to confirm the diagnosis before any intervention
options.D: Facet joint steroid injection alone, repeated routinely every 3 months
options.E: Radiofrequency denervation after a positive medial branch block

explanation: Radiofrequency denervation can be considered for chronic low back pain thought to arise from the facet joints, but only after a positive diagnostic medial branch block. Facet steroid injections have not shown benefit over placebo, and spinal injections are not recommended for non-specific low back pain. Facet RF denervation (NICE NG59) is used only after a positive diagnostic medial branch block and failed nonsurgical care; benefit in RCTs is mixed (MINT). Other interventions: epidural steroid for acute severe sciatica only; basivertebral nerve ablation for Modic-related chronic LBP (emerging); spinal cord stimulation for persistent spinal pain after surgery with neuropathic leg pain. Do not offer facet steroid injections, discography, fusion or disc replacement for non-specific LBP outside research.

stem: A 44-year-old woman has 18 months of chronic primary pain without an identifiable underlying condition. She is taking codeine, pregabalin and naproxen with little benefit. Which management is most appropriate?

options.A: Increase the opioid dose and add a benzodiazepine for sleep
options.B: Exercise and psychological therapy, considering an antidepressant, and tapering analgesics
options.C: Continue all three drugs unchanged while adding gabapentin
options.D: Start a biologic DMARD, since conventional analgesics have failed
options.E: Refer for spinal fusion surgery given the chronicity of symptoms

explanation: For chronic primary pain, current guidance supports exercise programmes, psychological therapies and acupuncture, and allows consideration of selected antidepressants. Opioids, gabapentinoids, NSAIDs, paracetamol and benzodiazepines should not be started, and existing ones should be reviewed and tapered through shared decisionmaking. NICE NG193 chronic primary pain options: supervised group exercise, CBT or ACT, acupuncture (within a course), and antidepressants (amitriptyline, citalopram, duloxetine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline). Do not start gabapentinoids, opioids, NSAIDs, paracetamol, benzodiazepines, local anaesthetic or steroid injections, or ketamine. Taper existing opioids and gabapentinoids gradually (about 10% every 2–4 weeks) with shared goals; watch for withdrawal and mood change. Consider a pain management programme. Screen for depression and suicide risk.

stem: A 72-year-old woman has a painful acute L1 osteoporotic compression fracture. What does early management involve, and when is vertebral augmentation appropriate?

options.A: Analgesia and mobilisation; augmentation only for severe persistent pain at a recent fracture
options.B: Long-term daily calcitonin for pain control
options.C: Immediate vertebroplasty for all acute compression fractures regardless of severity
options.D: Strict bed rest for 6 weeks to allow fracture healing
options.E: High-dose oral glucocorticoids to reduce inflammation at the fracture site

explanation: Older texts recommended calcitonin for fracture pain, but long-term calcitonin is no longer used because of an increased malignancy risk. Vertebral augmentation is limited to severe persistent pain at a recent fracture confirmed on MRI. Osteoporosis treatment and falls assessment should follow. Acute vertebral fracture: osteoporosis vs metastasis or myeloma (posterior element involvement, convex posterior border and soft-tissue mass on MRI, pedicle destruction, above T5), infection, trauma. Low-energy fracture in a younger patient or a man warrants a secondary osteoporosis screen. Many vertebral fractures are silent (height loss >4 cm, kyphosis). Vertebral fracture assessment on DXA or a lateral spine film detects them. Analgesia (paracetamol, short NSAIDs or opioids with laxatives), early mobilisation, physiotherapy, a short spinal brace in selected patients. NICE TA279: augmentation (vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty) only for severe ongoing pain after a recent fracture confirmed on MRI despite optimal analgesia; sham-controlled trials were mixed. Start osteoporosis treatment (often an anabolic agent if there are multiple vertebral fractures) and a falls assessment.

stem: What DXA T-score defines osteoporosis in a postmenopausal woman?

options.A: -2.5 or lower
options.B: Avacopan
options.C: Enthesitis-related arthritis
options.E: 3 points; he meets the criteria

explanation: A T-score of-2.5 or lower at the lumbar spine, femoral neck or total hip defines osteoporosis;-1.0 to-2.5 is osteopenia. T-scores apply to postmenopausal women and men aged 50 or over. Low BMD is not always osteoporosis: osteomalacia (raised ALP, low phosphate or calcium, Looser zones), myeloma, hyperparathyroidism, renal osteodystrophy, OI, hypophosphatasia, mastocytosis, Gaucher’s. Severe or established osteoporosis means T ≤-2.5 plus a fragility fracture. A hip or vertebral fragility fracture establishes osteoporosis clinically regardless of BMD. Fractures of the skull, face, fingers and toes are not fragility sites. Core secondary screen: FBC, ESR or CRP, adjusted calcium, phosphate, ALP, albumin, eGFR, LFTs, 25(OH)D, PTH, TSH, SPEP and FLC, coeliac serology (tTG); testosterone, SHBG, LH and FSH in men. Targeted tests: 24-hour urine calcium, cortisol, tryptase, PSA, HbA1c.

stem: What does FRAX estimate?

options.A: The lifetime risk of any fracture
options.B: The 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture and of hip fracture
options.C: The current T-score adjusted for age alone
options.D: The probability of fracture within 5 years only
options.E: BMD alone, without clinical risk factors

explanation: FRAX combines age, sex, BMI, prior fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, glucocorticoids, RA, secondary osteoporosis and alcohol, with or without femoral neck BMD. Standard FRAX underestimates risk with high-dose glucocorticoids and multiple fractures. FRAX inputs: age, sex, BMI, prior fracture, parental hip fracture, current smoking, GC (≥5 mg for ≥3 months), RA, secondary osteoporosis, alcohol ≥3 units/day, ± femoral neck BMD. It underestimates risk with high-dose GC, recent, multiple or vertebral fractures, falls, diabetes and spine–hip discordance. UK practice (NOGG) uses age-dependent FRAX thresholds with high and very high risk categories. The US uses fixed thresholds (MOF ≥20% or hip ≥3%).
