QFracture is an alternative UK tool that includes falls and more comorbidities.

stem: A woman on prednisolone has, or is about to start, long-term glucocorticoids: for example a 68-year-old on 7.5 mg daily with a wrist fragility fracture and femoral neck T-score -1.8, or a 74-year-old starting 40 mg daily for GCA. How should bone protection be decided?

options.A: Only the 74-year-old needs bone protection; the 68-year-old can simply wait for a DXA result first
options.B: Both need bone protection now: prior fragility fracture, age 70 or over, or 7.5 mg/day or more for 3 months confer high fracture risk despite an osteopenic T-score
options.C: Neither patient needs bone protection until an actual fragility fracture has already occurred
options.D: A DXA scan must always be obtained before any bone-protective treatment can be started
options.E: Only the 68-year-old needs treatment, since her T-score is already clearly abnormal

explanation: with calcium and vitamin D) should start with the glucocorticoid without waiting for DXA Glucocorticoids increase fracture risk at higher BMD than in postmenopausal osteoporosis, and fracture risk rises within weeks of starting them. Fracture risk depends on the whole clinical picture. People aged 70 or over, those with a prior fragility fracture, or those on 7.5 mg/day or more for 3 months or more should start bone protection without waiting for DXA. GIOP is the commonest secondary cause. The main mechanism is osteoblast and osteocyte apoptosis (reduced formation), with an early resorption rise, reduced calcium absorption, hypogonadism, and myopathy with falls. Risk rises within 3–6 months even at 2.5–7.5 mg/day. 30–50% of long-term users fracture. Assess within 6 months of starting ≥2.5 mg/day for ≥3 months in adults ≥40 (FRAX + BMD); in under-40s only with a prior fracture or other risks. Adjust FRAX for >7.5 mg/day: MOF ×1.15, hip ×1.2. Moderate risk: oral bisphosphonate first-line; zoledronate if oral is unsuitable. High or very high risk: teriparatide is superior to alendronate for vertebral fractures in GIOP. Denosumab is effective but needs a bisphosphonate follow-on. Ongoing: reassess every 12–18 months; consider stopping bone therapy once GC stops and risk falls. Women of childbearing potential: use bisphosphonates cautiously (long skeletal retention); prefer teriparatide, calcium and vitamin D where possible.

stem: What is first-line pharmacological treatment for most postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, and which counselling point is essential for oral alendronate?

options.A: Raloxifene, with no particular administration instructions needed before or after the dose
options.B: Denosumab by subcutaneous injection every 6 months, with no fasting requirement beforehand
options.C: Teriparatide by daily subcutaneous injection, continued indefinitely without a defined treatment limit
options.D: An oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate) with calcium and vitamin D; take once weekly on an empty stomach with water, stay upright for 30 minutes and delay food
options.E: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation alone, without any prescription anti-resorptive drug

explanation: Oral bisphosphonates are first-line unless contraindicated or not tolerated, with IV zoledronate as an alternative. Correct administration avoids poor absorption and oesophagitis, and calcium and other medicines should be separated from the dose. Dental review is important. Contraindications to oral bisphosphonates: eGFR <30–35, oesophageal stricture or achalasia, inability to stay upright for 30 minutes, hypocalcaemia, pregnancy. Alternatives: IV zoledronate (needs eGFR ≥35 and hydration) or denosumab (no renal clearance). Fracture reduction: alendronate and risedronate reduce vertebral fractures by about 40– 70% and hip fractures by about 40%. Zoledronate (5 mg IV yearly) reduces vertebral fractures by about 70%, reduced mortality after hip fracture, and causes an acute-phase reaction (mainly with the first dose). Denosumab reduces vertebral fractures by about 68% and hip by about 40%. Raloxifene reduces vertebral fractures only, carries VTE risk and reduces breast cancer. HRT is first-line for women <60 or within 10 years of menopause with symptoms. Non-drug measures: progressive resistance and impact exercise, balance training (tai chi, Otago), falls prevention (home hazards, vision, sedative review, hip protectors in care homes), stop smoking, protein 1–1.2 g/kg/day.

stem: A 72-year-old with two recent vertebral fractures and a spine T-score of -3.6 needs treatment. What is the best initial approach, and what are the key contraindications of romosozumab and teriparatide?

options.A: An antiresorptive alone is preferred, since anabolic agents are reserved only for bisphosphonate treatment failure
options.B: Romosozumab is safe regardless of cardiovascular history, including a recent myocardial infarction or stroke
options.C: Teriparatide is contraindicated in all patients over the age of 70, regardless of fracture risk
options.D: An antiresorptive first, followed later by an anabolic agent, gives an equivalent fracture-reduction response
options.E: An anabolic agent first (teriparatide, or romosozumab without prior MI or stroke), then antiresorptive therapy; romosozumab is avoided post-MI or stroke, teriparatide in Paget’s disease or bone malignancy

explanation: Very high fracture risk (recent or multiple vertebral fractures, very low T-score) favours anabolic therapy first, followed by an antiresorptive to consolidate gains. An imbalance in serious cardiovascular events was seen in a pivotal trial of romosozumab, which is given monthly for 12 months only and must be followed by antiresorptive therapy. Because of an osteosarcoma signal in rats, teriparatide is contraindicated in the situations above; treatment is limited to 24 months, and it is effective in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis. The EULAR course notes the rat osteosarcoma signal has not been borne out in human surveillance, but the label contraindications still apply. Very high risk includes recent fracture (within 12–24 months, especially vertebral or hip), multiple fractures, fracture on treatment, T ≤-3.0 (≤-3.5 in some guidance), very high FRAX and high-dose GC. VERO: teriparatide beat risedronate for vertebral fractures. ARCH: romosozumab followed by alendronate beat alendronate alone. Abaloparatide (PTHrP analogue, 80 µg) is an alternative. Sequencing: anabolic then antiresorptive is best. Bisphosphonate then anabolic is acceptable but gives a blunted response. Going from denosumab to teriparatide causes transient hip bone loss, so avoid it or overlap the two. Always follow an anabolic immediately with an antiresorptive.

stem: A 70-year-old woman has received denosumab 60 mg every 6 months for 5 years. She wants to stop because of planned dental work. What is the most important advice?

options.A: Stop immediately with no follow-on treatment, since denosumab has no rebound effect
options.B: Do not stop without follow-on therapy; plan a bisphosphonate (often zoledronate) about 6 months after the last dose
options.C: Switch directly to teriparatide, with no bisphosphonate follow-on
options.D: Continue denosumab unchanged through the dental procedure, with no other action needed
options.E: Delay the next dose indefinitely until dental work is fully complete

explanation: Stopping or delaying denosumab causes rapid rebound bone turnover and a risk of multiple vertebral fractures. A bisphosphonate is given as follow-on, with turnover markers guiding further dosing. Rebound after stopping denosumab: turnover overshoots above baseline 3–18 months after the last dose, with a risk of multiple vertebral fractures, especially after longer use and in people with prior vertebral fractures. Denosumab has no drug holiday. Give zoledronate about 6 months after the last denosumab dose, monitoring CTX at 3 and 6 months and repeating zoledronate if CTX rises. Or continue denosumab long term (studied to 10 years). Dental work: routine dentistry is fine. For extractions, there is no need to stop; coordinate timing (dental work about 3–4 months after a dose, next dose after healing) and use good oral hygiene. Biosimilars are now available.

stem: A woman on alendronate for 8 years has 2 months of dull thigh pain. Which rare complications are linked to long-term antiresorptives, and what should be done?

options.A: Statin-induced myopathy; check creatine kinase levels and stop the statin immediately
options.B: Reassurance only, since thigh pain is a common and expected benign effect of bisphosphonates
options.C: Metastatic bone disease; arrange an urgent oncology referral for further staging
options.D: Atypical femoral fracture and osteonecrosis of the jaw; get full-length femoral radiographs and stop the bisphosphonate if an AFF or stress reaction is found
options.E: Continue alendronate unchanged and simply review again at the 12-month follow-up

explanation: Prodromal thigh or groin pain in long-term bisphosphonate users may precede an atypical femoral fracture, which is often bilateral. Osteonecrosis of the jaw and AFF are rare complications of long-term antiresorptive therapy with bisphosphonates or denosumab. Good dental hygiene and dental review before treatment reduce ONJ risk, and drug holidays can be considered in lower-risk long-term bisphosphonate users. Thigh pain on bisphosphonates: AFF or stress reaction vs hip OA, trochanteric pain, L3 radiculopathy, osteomalacia (Looser zone on the medial femoral neck), hypophosphatasia (bisphosphonates worsen it), metastasis, Paget’s. AFF: a transverse subtrochanteric or shaft fracture from low energy, with lateral cortical “beaking”. Risk rises after 3–5 years and in Asian patients and those on GC. ONJ: exposed necrotic jaw bone for >8 weeks without prior radiation; about 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 100,000 patient-years in osteoporosis, far higher at oncology doses. Risk factors: extraction or implants, poor hygiene, GC, smoking, diabetes, long duration, anti-angiogenic drugs. Other bisphosphonate effects: hypocalcaemia, AF (zoledronate; inconsistent), uveitis or scleritis, oesophagitis. Stop the antiresorptive, give teriparatide, and arrange orthopaedic review (prophylactic intramedullary nailing for incomplete fractures with pain). Image the contralateral femur. Check vitamin D and ALP. Overall, fractures prevented far outnumber AFFs.

stem: A woman has taken alendronate for 5 years. When should treatment continue (for example after a prior hip fracture with a hip T-score of -2.6), and when is a drug holiday appropriate (no fractures, no steroids, femoral neck T-score -2.1)?

options.A: Stop permanently in everyone after 5 years of treatment, regardless of fracture history or risk
options.B: Switch to denosumab in everyone reaching 5 years of treatment, regardless of ongoing fracture risk
options.C: Continue only if a DXA scan shows further bone loss occurring during a planned holiday
options.D: A drug holiday is never appropriate once bisphosphonate treatment has been started at all
options.E: Continue (oral up to 10 years) with a prior hip or vertebral fracture, age 70 or over, fracture on treatment, or prednisolone 7.5 mg/day or more; otherwise take an 18-month to 3-year holiday

explanation: After 5 years of oral bisphosphonate (3 years of zoledronic acid), treatment should be reviewed. Continuation is generally advised for people aged 70 or over, those with a previous hip or vertebral fracture, those who fractured on treatment, or those on at least 7.5 mg prednisolone daily. Otherwise, a holiday with reassessment is reasonable. The EULAR course criteria differ slightly: continue at age ≥75 or a hip T-score ≤-2.5 (up to 10 years oral or 6 years IV). FLEX and HORIZON extension trials showed fewer vertebral fractures with continuation in high-risk patients. Reassess BMD and FRAX after about 2 years of holiday, and earlier after a new fracture. Denosumab has no holiday.

stem: Before IV zoledronic acid in a housebound 79-year-old with 25(OH)D 18 nmol/L, or before denosumab in an 81-year-old with eGFR 22, what is most important?

options.A: Check renal function only, with no attention paid to vitamin D or calcium status
options.B: Proceed directly to treatment, since both drugs are safe regardless of baseline vitamin D or calcium
options.C: Give denosumab first in both cases, regardless of baseline renal function
options.D: Replete vitamin D and correct calcium first, then give the drug and recheck calcium afterwards; consider CKD-mineral bone disorder in advanced CKD
options.E: No specific precautions are needed here beyond standard treatment consent

explanation: Vitamin D deficiency increases the risk of symptomatic hypocalcaemia after IV bisphosphonates or denosumab, so deficiency should be corrected with a loading regimen first; oral bisphosphonates can start alongside replacement. Denosumab can cause severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia, particularly with eGFR below 30 or on dialysis, so hypocalcaemia and vitamin D deficiency should be corrected first and calcium monitored after dosing. In advanced CKD, CKD-mineral bone disorder (including adynamic bone) should also be considered. Loading dose: cholecalciferol about 300,000 IU over 6–10 weeks (e.g. 50,000 IU weekly for 6 weeks), then 800–2000 IU daily. Recheck calcium at 1 month (this can unmask primary hyperparathyroidism). In CKD 4–5: check PTH and ALP; a bone biopsy helps if turnover is uncertain. Antiresorptives suit high-turnover disease; teriparatide suits adynamic bone. Avoid or reduce bisphosphonates when eGFR is <30–35.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with coeliac disease has proximal weakness and diffuse bone pain. Calcium is lownormal, phosphate low, alkaline phosphatase and PTH raised. Radiographs show Looser zones in the pubic rami. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT
options.B: 3 points; he meets the criteria
options.C: Paget disease of bone
options.D: Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency
options.E: Primary hyperparathyroidism

explanation: Vitamin D deficiency reduces calcium absorption, causing secondary hyperparathyroidism, phosphaturia and defective mineralisation. Looser zones are characteristic. Treatment is vitamin D loading with calcium and management of malabsorption. DIFFERENTIALS & OTHER CAUSES Pattern Ca Causes of osteomalacia:-low/N Vitamin D Calcium-limited: nutritional deficiency deficiency, malabsorption (coeliac, gastric bypass, FGF23-mediated N pancreatic disease), liver (XLH, TIO) disease, CKD, enzymeinducing antiepileptics, vitamin Fanconi N D-dependent rickets (1A, 1B, N/high Hypophosphatasia 2).-Phosphate-limited, FGF23-mediated: XLH, ADHR, Clinical features: bone pain and tenderness (ribs, pelvis, tibiae), proximal myopathy with TIO, fibrous dysplasia, IV ferric a waddling gait (normal CK), and pseudofractures. Looser zones appear at the pubic carboxymaltose.-Phosphaterami, medial femoral neck, ribs and axillary border of the scapula. A bone scan shows limited, renal tubular: Fanconi symmetrical hot spots that mimic metastases. It is often mistaken for fibromyalgia, PMR syndrome (tenofovir, adefovir, or myositis. myeloma light chains, ifosfamide, Wilson’s disease); hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets with hypercalciuria; phosphate binders and antacids.-Mineralisation inhibitors: aluminium, fluoride, etidronate.-Low ALP: hypophosphatasia. PO4 ALP PTH 25(OH)D 1,25(OH)2D FGF23 low/N high high low variable N N/mild low high N low or high high inappropriately N N/high low/N low high N N N/high low/N low N N N Vitamin D loading, calcium if intake is low, treat malabsorption (higher doses; activated vitamin D in liver or kidney disease). ALP rises transiently, then normalises over months.

stem: A 24-year-old man with short stature, lifelong bowed legs and an affected mother has low phosphate with renal phosphate wasting, normal calcium and raised FGF23. What is the diagnosis and targeted therapy?

options.A: Autosomal recessive hypophosphataemic rickets; calcitriol alone
options.B: X-linked hypophosphataemia; burosumab
options.C: Tumour-induced osteomalacia; tumour resection
options.D: A short course of oral prednisolone
options.E: IL-1 blockade (canakinumab or anakinra)

explanation: PHEX mutations cause excess FGF23, renal phosphate wasting and low or inappropriately normal calcitriol. Burosumab neutralises FGF23; conventional therapy is oral phosphate with active vitamin D. XLH is the commonest heritable rickets (X-linked dominant PHEX). Children have bowed legs, short stature and dental abscesses. Adults have pseudofractures, enthesopathy (mimicking SpA or DISH), early OA, hearing loss and spinal stenosis. Burosumab (anti-FGF23) is licensed for children and symptomatic adults and is superior to conventional therapy for healing rickets. Conventional therapy is oral phosphate plus calcitriol; monitor for nephrocalcinosis (renal ultrasound), hyperparathyroidism and urine calcium.

stem: A woman in her late 40s or early 50s has recurrent metatarsal stress fractures, early loss of adult teeth (and sometimes chondrocalcinosis) and has been referred for alendronate. ALP is persistently low. What is the diagnosis, which drug should be avoided, and what is the next step?

options.A: Osteomalacia; replace vitamin D before considering any other treatment
options.B: Osteoporosis; start alendronate as planned
options.C: Paget’s disease; start zoledronic acid
options.D: Hypophosphatasia; avoid bisphosphonates; check pyridoxal-5’-phosphate and ALPL genetics
options.E: Osteogenesis imperfecta; refer for genetic counselling only

explanation: A persistently low ALP with stress fractures and premature tooth loss suggests hypophosphatasia (ALPL mutations). A raised pyridoxal-5’-phosphate supports the diagnosis. Bisphosphonates resemble pyrophosphate, an ALP substrate; they and other antiresorptives can worsen the mineralisation defect and have been linked to atypical femoral fractures in this condition. Enzyme replacement (asfotase alfa) is used in severe disease. Other causes of low ALP: zinc or magnesium deficiency, hypothyroidism, Wilson’s disease, pernicious anaemia, coeliac disease, milk-alkali syndrome, massive transfusion, cardiac surgery or bypass, recent bisphosphonate or denosumab therapy, glucocorticoids, cachexia, clofibrate. Always confirm low values on repeat testing. Raised urinary phosphoethanolamine. Associations: chondrocalcinosis and CPPD (pyrophosphate accumulation), calcific periarthritis, AFF-like fractures, muscle weakness, pain. Avoid antiresorptives. Teriparatide has been used off-label. Physiotherapy, orthopaedic and dental care.

stem: How is Paget’s disease monitored and treated: for example a 74-year-old with femoral pain and bowing, ALP 310 U/L and increased uptake throughout the femur, versus a 71-year-old with incidental asymptomatic pelvic disease and mildly raised ALP?

options.A: ALP should be normalised in all patients regardless of symptoms, using repeated zoledronic acid
options.B: Calcium levels are the primary marker of disease activity, not ALP
options.C: Raised ALP with normal calcium and phosphate is the activity marker; a single zoledronic acid infusion treats pagetic bone pain, but asymptomatic disease is only monitored
options.D: Osteosarcoma arising within pagetic bone, requiring urgent oncological referral
options.E: Both patients require treatment, since any ALP elevation mandates zoledronic acid

explanation: ALP reflects increased bone turnover; hypercalcaemia is unusual unless the patient is immobilised. In Paget’s disease, a bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid preferred) treats bone pain. Intensive treatment aimed at normalising ALP does not prevent complications better than symptom-directed treatment, so it is not supported in asymptomatic patients. Treatment is still considered before elective surgery on pagetic bone. Teriparatide is contraindicated because of osteosarcoma risk. Sclerotic metastases (prostate, breast), lymphoma, fibrous dysplasia, hyperparathyroidism (brown tumours), mastocytosis, osteopetrosis, hyperostosis frontalis interna, fluorosis. Other causes of raised ALP: liver disease (check GGT), osteomalacia, fracture healing, hyperparathyroidism, metastases, adolescence, pregnancy. 70–90% are asymptomatic. It affects older people of British or northern European ancestry (Lancashire), M:F 3:2, and incidence is falling. Genetics: SQSTM1 (p62) in 20–50% of familial cases, RANK, OPTN, VCP (multisystem proteinopathy). Sites: pelvis, spine, femur, skull, tibia. X-ray signs: “blade of grass” lytic front, osteoporosis circumscripta, cotton-wool skull, picture-frame and ivory vertebrae, thickened iliopectineal line. Complications: fractures (banana-type), secondary OA (the commonest cause of pain), deafness (30–50% with skull disease), basilar invagination, spinal stenosis, high-output cardiac failure, hypercalcaemia on immobilisation, osteosarcoma (<0.5%). Zoledronate 5 mg IV once (most durable effect). Alternatives: risedronate 30 mg daily for 2 months, alendronate 40 mg daily for 6 months, pamidronate. Replete vitamin D first and give calcium and vitamin D for about 10 days afterwards. Monitor ALP (or P1NP) at 3–6 months, then yearly. Retreat for recurrent pain with a rising ALP. Calcitonin is no longer recommended. Supportive care: analgesia, heel raises, hearing aids, arthroplasty (more blood loss). Prophylactic zoledronate in SQSTM1 carriers reduced new lesions (ZiPP) but is not routine.

stem: A 48-year-old man has bone pain, proximal weakness and rib fractures. Phosphate is low with renal phosphate wasting, calcium normal and FGF23 raised; there is no family history. Which investigation is most likely to find the cause?

options.A: Thyroid function tests
options.B: MRI of both hips
options.C: Anti-Jo-1
options.D: Anti-SRP
options.E: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT

explanation: Adult-onset FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemia suggests tumour-induced osteomalacia. These small mesenchymal tumours express somatostatin receptors, so 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT is the most sensitive localisation test, followed by anatomical imaging. Complete resection is curative. TIO tumours are small benign phosphaturic mesenchymal tumours (in bone, soft tissue, sinuses or skin) that secrete FGF23, causing a low TmP/GFR and low or inappropriately normal 1,25(OH)2D. It is often misdiagnosed as fibromyalgia or SpA. Localise with Ga-68 DOTATATE PET/CT, then MRI, with venous sampling for FGF23 if needed. Before surgery, or if the tumour is unresectable, give oral phosphate plus calcitriol or burosumab. Other acquired causes: IV ferric carboxymaltose (recheck phosphate), fibrous dysplasia, epidermal naevus syndrome.

stem: A 78-year-old man with long-standing Paget’s disease of the femur develops increasing, constant pain with a tender soft-tissue swelling over the femur. ALP is rising despite recent zoledronic acid. What must be excluded first?

options.A: A simple insufficiency fracture through pagetic bone
options.B: Osteosarcoma arising in pagetic bone
options.C: A further Paget’s flare requiring repeat zoledronic acid alone
options.D: The A1 pulley at the metacarpal head
options.E: Complex regional pain syndrome

explanation: Sarcomatous change occurs in under 1% of patients with Paget’s disease but carries a poor prognosis. New severe pain, swelling or a pathological fracture with rising ALP after treatment needs urgent MRI and biopsy. New severe constant pain, swelling, a lytic lesion or a pathological fracture in pagetic bone, with ALP rising despite treatment: urgent MRI, CT staging and biopsy at a sarcoma centre. Giant cell tumour is a rarer complication (skull and facial bones; may respond to dexamethasone).

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with two thoracic vertebral fragility fractures. DXA shows a lumbar spine Z- score of -2.9. Which set of investigations is most important to identify secondary causes?

options.A: Testosterone, myeloma screen, coeliac serology, calcium/PTH and vitamin D
options.B: Full pre-biologic screening (hepatitis B/C, HIV, latent TB) alone
options.C: Thyroid function tests and a fasting glucose alone
options.D: Genetic testing for osteogenesis imperfecta alone
options.E: A repeat DXA scan in 2 years before any further investigation

explanation: Up to half of men with osteoporosis have a secondary cause, including hypogonadism, myeloma, glucocorticoids, alcohol, coeliac disease and hyperparathyroidism. Myeloma must be excluded in any patient with vertebral fractures and a low Z-score. Treatment should not wait for a further DXA. Secondary causes in men (about 50% have one): hypogonadism (including ADT), alcohol, GC, myeloma or MGUS, coeliac disease, hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, Cushing’s, mastocytosis (urticaria pigmentosa, raised tryptase), hypercalciuria, HIV, anticonvulsants, COPD, homocystinuria, haemochromatosis, OI (blue sclerae). Bisphosphonates, denosumab and teriparatide or abaloparatide are effective in men. Treat hypogonadism (testosterone if indicated). Men have higher post-fracture mortality.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has asymptomatic hypercalcaemia (adjusted calcium 2.75 mmol/L) with a PTH in the upper part of the reference range. Her 25(OH)D is replete. The calcium:creatinine clearance ratio is 0.006. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Takayasu arteritis
options.B: Primary hyperparathyroidism
options.C: Tertiary hyperparathyroidism due to chronic kidney disease
options.D: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
options.E: Antisynthetase syndrome

explanation: A calcium:creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01 strongly suggests FHH (usually a CASR variant), and parathyroidectomy does not help. Values above 0.02 favour primary hyperparathyroidism, and intermediate values warrant genetic testing. Vitamin D should be replete before the test is interpreted. Hypercalcaemia with non-suppressed PTH: primary hyperparathyroidism, FHH (CASR, GNA11, AP2S1), lithium, thiazides (unmasking), tertiary hyperparathyroidism (CKD), MEN1 or 2A. Hypercalcaemia with suppressed PTH: malignancy (PTHrP, lytic metastases, myeloma), granulomatous disease (raised 1,25D; sarcoid, TB, lymphoma), vitamin D toxicity, milk-alkali syndrome, thyrotoxicosis, immobilisation (Paget’s), Addison’s, vitamin A, theophylline. Calcium:creatinine clearance ratio = (urine Ca × serum Cr) / (serum Ca × urine Cr). Below 0.01 suggests FHH; above 0.02 suggests PHPT. FHH: reassurance, no surgery; family screening; genetic confirmation. PHPT surgical criteria: calcium >0.25 mmol/L above ULN, osteoporosis or fragility fracture, eGFR <60, stones or hypercalciuria, age <50.

stem: A woman in the third trimester of pregnancy develops progressive hip pain. MRI shows diffuse marrow oedema of the femoral head and neck without a subchondral fracture line. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Transient osteoporosis of the hip
options.B: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome
options.C: Osteonecrosis of the femoral head
options.D: Spinal tuberculosis (Pott’s disease)
options.E: Femoroacetabular impingement (cam type)

explanation: Transient osteoporosis of the hip affects women in late pregnancy and middle-aged men. Diffuse marrow oedema without the focal subchondral line of osteonecrosis is typical. It is self-limiting over months; management is analgesia and protected weight-bearing to prevent fracture. Diffuse marrow oedema of the hip: transient osteoporosis or bone marrow oedema syndrome (reversible) vs osteonecrosis (focal, double-line sign), subchondral insufficiency fracture, stress fracture, septic arthritis or osteomyelitis, early inflammatory arthritis, pigmented villonodular synovitis, tumour. Pregnancy-and lactationassociated osteoporosis presents with vertebral fractures post-partum. Analgesia and protected weight-bearing (crutches) until resolution (6–12 months). Bisphosphonates (or iloprost) may hasten recovery outside pregnancy. Avoid bisphosphonates in pregnancy. Early MRI to exclude fracture.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with SLE who received high-dose prednisolone last year has 6 weeks of groin pain on weight-bearing. Hip radiographs are normal. What is the most sensitive investigation for the likely diagnosis?

options.A: Plain radiographs of both hips
options.B: Kidney biopsy
options.C: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT
options.D: High-resolution CT chest
options.E: MRI of both hips

explanation: Glucocorticoid-associated osteonecrosis of the femoral head is often bilateral and is common in SLE. MRI detects it before radiographic change, when joint-preserving measures such as core decompression are most likely to help. Both hips should be imaged. Groin pain in SLE: AVN vs septic arthritis (immunosuppressed), insufficiency fracture (GIOP), lupus arthritis, iliopsoas haematoma or abscess, hernia, referred lumbar pain. Risk in SLE is about 5–10%, linked to GC dose (especially >20 mg/day early, and pulses), aPL, Cushingoid habitus, vasculitis and Raynaud’s. Femoral head disease is bilateral in about 50%. Other sites: femoral condyles, humeral head, talus. ARCO staging (I–IV). Before collapse: protected weightbearing, reduce GC, core decompression with or without graft or cells. Bisphosphonates and anticoagulation (if thrombophilic) have mixed evidence. After collapse or with secondary OA: arthroplasty. Large weight-bearing lesions usually collapse within 2–3 years.

stem: A 7-year-old girl has precocious puberty, large irregular café-au-lait patches and expansile ‘ground-glass’ lesions in several long bones. What is the genetic basis, and which metabolic complication can occur?

options.A: An autosomal dominant NF1 mutation; lesions may cause scoliosis
options.B: A postzygotic activating GNAS mutation; lesions may secrete FGF23
options.C: A PHEX mutation; lesions may cause renal phosphate wasting
options.D: A RANK mutation; lesions may cause osteopetrosis
options.E: An ALPL mutation; lesions may cause fractures with a low ALP

explanation: postzygotic activating GNAS mutation; lesions may secrete FGF23 McCune-Albright syndrome combines polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, ‘coast of Maine’ café-au-lait macules and endocrine hyperfunction. The GNAS mutation is somatic and mosaic, and a germline mutation would be lethal. Growth hormone excess worsens craniofacial fibrous dysplasia, and phosphate wasting should be checked. FD/MAS is caused by a post-zygotic GNAS activating mutation (mosaic). Fibrous dysplasia is monostotic in about 70%, at craniofacial sites, the proximal femur (“shepherd’s crook”), ribs and tibia, with “ground-glass” lesions. Caféau-lait macules have “coast of Maine” borders and often respect the midline. Endocrine features: peripheral precocious puberty (commonest), hyperthyroidism, GH excess, neonatal Cushing’s, FGF23 phosphate wasting. Analgesia; IV bisphosphonates for pain (they do not heal lesions; oral forms are ineffective); denosumab is investigational (rebound hypercalcaemia). Treat endocrinopathies, especially GH excess. Correct phosphate and vitamin D. Intramedullary rodding for deformity. Malignant transformation is <1% (risk rises with GH excess or radiation). Compare neurofibromatosis type 1, where café-au-lait macules have smooth “coast of California” borders.

stem: A 52-year-old man with pulmonary sarcoidosis has an adjusted calcium of 3.0 mmol/L, suppressed PTH, a low-normal 25(OH)D and a raised 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. What is the mechanism and the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase upregulation from PTH excess; parathyroidectomy
options.B: IL-17 pathway inhibition
options.C: Osteoclast-mediated bone resorption from PTHrP; bisphosphonates
options.D: Macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase; glucocorticoids, fluids, stop vitamin D
options.E: Direct vitamin D receptor activation; stop glucocorticoids

explanation: Granuloma macrophages convert 25(OH)D to calcitriol without feedback control. Hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria respond to glucocorticoids; hydroxychloroquine is an alternative. Vitamin D and calcium supplements should be avoided, and renal function and nephrocalcinosis monitored. 1,25(OH)2D-mediated hypercalcaemia: sarcoidosis, TB, fungal infection, lymphoma, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, berylliosis, silicone or paraffin granulomas, Crohn’s disease, CYP24A1 mutations (loss of 24hydroxylase; idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia, stones). Hydration, stop calcium and vitamin D supplements, sun avoidance, prednisolone 20–40 mg (calcium normalises within days to weeks). Hydroxychloroquine or ketoconazole are steroid-sparing options. Monitor renal function, urine calcium and nephrocalcinosis.

stem: What are the entry criterion and minimum score for the 2019 EULAR/ACR SLE classification criteria?

options.A: A malar rash plus photosensitivity alone, with no minimum point threshold required
options.B: Any single positive autoantibody, with no formal entry criterion required at all
options.C: Four of eleven clinical and immunological criteria being met, with no weighting applied
options.D: ANA at a titre of 1:80 or higher on HEp-2 cells (or an equivalent test) at any time, then 10 or more weighted points with at least one clinical criterion
options.E: A SLEDAI score of 4 or more, with no serological requirement at all specified

explanation: Criteria count only if not better explained by another condition, need not occur simultaneously, and only the highestweighted item in each domain counts. Renal and neuropsychiatric domains carry high weights; biopsy-proven class III or IV lupus nephritis alone scores 10. Classification criteria do not replace clinical diagnosis. Domain Items (points) fever >38.3 °C (2) Constitutional leucopenia <4 (3); thrombocytopenia Haematological <100 (4); AIHA (4) delirium (2); psychosis (3); seizure (5) Neuropsychiatric non-scarring alopecia (2); oral ulcers Mucocutaneous (2); SCLE or DLE (4); ACLE (6) effusion (5); acute pericarditis (6) Serosal joint involvement (6) Musculoskeletal proteinuria >0.5 g/24 h (4); class II or V Renal (8); class III or IV (10) any (2) aPL low C3 or C4 (3); both low (4) Complement SLE-specific Ab anti-dsDNA or anti-Sm (6) Sensitivity about 96%, specificity about 93%. SLICC criteria (≥4 with ≥1 clinical and ≥1 immunological, or biopsy nephritis plus ANA or dsDNA) remain valid. About 10–20% of patients with clinician-diagnosed early lupus do not meet the criteria. Treat them anyway (HCQ).

stem: A 32-year-old woman with arthralgia has an ANA of 1:160 but no other clinical features of connective tissue disease. What is the best interpretation?

options.A: A titre of 1:160 confirms SLE even without other clinical features
options.B: ANA should be repeated monthly to monitor for evolving disease
options.C: A negative ANA would be expected in early SLE, making this diagnosis more likely
options.D: The titre alone determines whether immunosuppression should start
options.E: ANA positivity alone does not establish SLE or another connective tissue disease

explanation: ANA is sensitive but non-specific and occurs in healthy people and other conditions. A negative ANA makes SLE much less likely. ANA positivity without SLE: healthy people (about 13% at 1:80, 3–5% at ≥1:160), older age, relatives, autoimmune thyroid or liver disease, other CTDs, infection (EBV, HCV, HIV, TB, endocarditis), malignancy, drugs. A DFS70 (dense fine speckled) pattern alone argues against systemic autoimmune disease. ANA sensitivity is 95–98% on HEp-2 IIF. Rare ANA-negative SLE occurs with anti-Ro on substrates lacking Ro60 or heavy proteinuria; if suspicion is high, test anti-Ro or ENA directly. Do not repeat ANA to monitor activity. Do not order ANA without clinical suspicion. Investigate further (ENA, dsDNA, complement, urinalysis, FBC) only with compatible features.

stem: Which antibody is most specific for SLE?

options.A: Anti-Jo-1
options.B: Anti-Sm
options.C: MRI of both hips
options.D: Anti-histone
options.E: Anti-NXP2

explanation: Anti-Sm is highly specific but insensitive (about 10-30%). Anti-dsDNA is also highly specific and tracks activity, particularly nephritis. Antibody Frequency Associations 60–70% nephritis; tracks activity; dsDNA Crithidia or Farr assays most specific 10–30% about 99% specific; does Sm not track activity U1-RNP 25– 40% Raynaud’s, myositis, MCTD; possibly less nephritis Ro (Ro60, 30–40% SCLE, photosensitivity, Ro52) Sjögren’s, neonatal lupus and CHB, cytopenias 10–15% with Ro; neonatal lupus La 10–20% psychosis, depression, Ribosomal P lupus hepatitis 50–70% non-specific Histone (>95% in DIL) C1q 30–60% active proliferative LN; negative result has high NPV 60–80% nephritis; may be positive Nucleosome when dsDNA is negative 30–40% thrombosis, obstetric aPL events, livedo, low platelets, valves

stem: Which serological pattern predicts an impending renal flare in quiescent SLE, and how should a modest isolated rise in anti-dsDNA without clinical change be managed?

options.A: Rising anti-dsDNA alone, without any complement change, is more predictive than the combined pattern
options.B: Rising anti-dsDNA with falling C3 and C4 predicts flare; isolated serological activity warrants closer monitoring (including urinalysis), not treatment escalation
options.C: Any isolated serological rise should prompt immediate treatment escalation
options.D: Falling complement alone, without any change in anti-dsDNA, is the more specific predictor
options.E: Serological activity should be ignored entirely unless accompanied by a rise in CRP

explanation: Rising anti-dsDNA with falling complement reflects immune-complex activity, particularly nephritis. Serological activity supports closer monitoring, but treatment escalation should follow clinical or organ activity rather than isolated serology. A markedly raised CRP in SLE should prompt a search for infection or serositis. About 10–15% of patients are serologically active but clinically quiescent; continue HCQ. Persistently low C4 with normal C3 may reflect inherited partial C4 deficiency (low copy number). A CH50 near zero suggests congenital early classical-pathway deficiency. Cell-bound C4d panels may help diagnose ANA-positive patients with an uncertain picture. Shorten the review interval (urinalysis, UPCR, FBC, C3/C4, dsDNA every 4–8 weeks). Check HCQ adherence (wholeblood levels <200 ng/mL suggest non-adherence).

stem: Who should take hydroxychloroquine in SLE, and what is the correct dose for a 60 kg woman?

options.A: Only patients with renal impairment should take hydroxychloroquine
options.B: Only patients with confirmed nephritis should take hydroxychloroquine
options.C: At a fixed dose of 400 mg daily, regardless of body weight
options.D: All patients unless contraindicated, at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day, so 300 mg daily for 60 kg
options.E: Only during pregnancy; it can be stopped once the baby is born

explanation: Hydroxychloroquine reduces flares, damage accrual and thrombosis and improves survival. It is continued in pregnancy and breastfeeding. At 5 mg/kg actual body weight, 60 kg gives 300 mg/day, which can be achieved with alternating doses; 400 mg daily would be about 6.7 mg/kg/day and increase retinal toxicity risk. If HCQ is not tolerated: chloroquine (more retinotoxic) or mepacrine (skin; yellow skin discoloration; no retinal toxicity). Rare HCQ toxicities: cardiomyopathy and conduction disease, QT prolongation, neuromyopathy (curvilinear bodies), hypoglycaemia, pigmentation, psoriasis flare. HCQ benefits: flares fall by about 50%; it reduces nephritis progression, thrombosis, seizures, CV events, CHB recurrence and pre-eclampsia, and improves lipids and glucose. Retinal toxicity is about 1% at 5 years and 10–20% at 20 years. Reduce the dose if eGFR is <30. Whole-blood levels >750–1150 ng/mL are linked to fewer flares, but do not exceed 5 mg/kg.

stem: What is the target for maintenance glucocorticoid dosing in SLE?

options.A: 5 mg/day prednisolone equivalent or less, withdrawn when possible
options.B: 20 mg/day or less, reduced slowly over several years
options.C: 10 mg/day or less, maintained indefinitely once remission is reached
options.D: 7.5 mg/day or less, which carries no excess long-term risk
options.E: 15 mg/day or less, only tapered after 5 years of stability

explanation: mg/day prednisolone equivalent or less, withdrawn when possible Glucocorticoids are useful for rapid control, including IV methylprednisolone pulses in organ-threatening disease, but maintenance should be minimised. Early addition of immunosuppressants or biologics facilitates tapering. GC strategy: IV methylprednisolone 250–1000 mg for 1–3 days allows a lower oral start (≤0.5 mg/kg/day, maximum about 40 mg) and a faster taper. Reach ≤5 mg/day within about 6 months, then try to withdraw. Damage accrues even at 5–7.5 mg/day and rises sharply above 7.5 mg/day. Start a steroid-sparing agent early rather than waiting for steroid dependence.

stem: A patient with SLE has persistent arthritis, rash or cutaneous lupus (without major organ involvement) despite hydroxychloroquine, with or without azathioprine, and cannot reduce prednisolone below 10 mg daily. What are the steroid-sparing options?

options.A: High-dose glucocorticoids alone, continued indefinitely at the current unchanged dose
options.B: Switching hydroxychloroquine for chloroquine, with no other treatment change made
options.C: Cyclophosphamide as the preferred next steroid-sparing agent of first choice
options.D: Stopping hydroxychloroquine entirely and relying on prednisolone alone long-term
options.E: Methotrexate (or azathioprine or mycophenolate) first; add belimumab or anifrolumab if disease remains active or steroids cannot be tapered to 5 mg/day

explanation: For non-organ-threatening disease not controlled by hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate are options, chosen by organ phenotype, toxicity and pregnancy plans. Belimumab or anifrolumab are added when there is inadequate response or glucocorticoids cannot be tapered to 5 mg/day or less. The 2026 BSR guideline suggests anifrolumab may be more appropriate than belimumab in non-renal SLE, and names it the preferred first-line biologic for refractory cutaneous lupus; belimumab requires autoantibody positivity with high activity. Rituximab is an option when other choices are less suitable, particularly in organ-threatening disease. Smoking cessation and photoprotection are essential, and smoking reduces hydroxychloroquine efficacy. Things that look like refractory lupus but are not: fibromyalgia (in 20– 30%), OA, damage (Jaccoud’s), steroid myopathy, hypothyroidism, non-adherence, drug rash, rosacea or seborrhoeic dermatitis (malar rash mimics), dermatomyositis (knuckle involvement, heliotrope, raised CK), tinea or psoriasis (SCLE mimics). Severity Treatment Mild (skin, HCQ, topicals, NSAIDs, short low-dose GC; joints, methotrexate if persistent mucosa) HCQ + methotrexate, azathioprine or MMF Moderate with a GC bridge; add belimumab or anifrolumab pulse GC + MMF or cyclophosphamide (± Severe a third agent in LN); rituximab if refractory; IVIG or PLEX as rescue Erosive rhupus: treat like RA (methotrexate, abatacept, rituximab). Ultrasound helps separate true synovitis from fibromyalgia.

stem: What are the mechanisms of anifrolumab and belimumab, and which adverse effect is increased with anifrolumab?

options.A: Anifrolumab depletes CD20-positive B cells; belimumab blocks IL-6
options.B: Anifrolumab inhibits TNF-alpha; belimumab inhibits IL-17
options.C: Anifrolumab and belimumab both block the same BLyS/BAFF pathway
options.D: Anifrolumab blocks IL-6 receptor signalling; belimumab blocks type I interferon
options.E: Anifrolumab blocks the type I interferon receptor (IFNAR1) and increases herpes zoster; belimumab inhibits soluble BLyS/BAFF

explanation: Anifrolumab reduced disease activity and glucocorticoid use in moderate-to-severe non-renal SLE. Belimumab reduces B-cell survival; it reduces flares and glucocorticoid use in autoantibody-positive SLE and improves renal outcomes when added to standard lupus nephritis treatment. Anifrolumab: 300 mg IV every 4 weeks (a weekly SC autoinjector is licensed in the US after TULIP-SC). In TULIP-2, BICLA response was 48% vs 32%. It works especially for skin and joints and is effective regardless of IFN signature (more so if IFN-high). Zoster is 6–7% vs 1–2%; there are also more URTIs and bronchitis. Not established in severe LN (IRIS ongoing) or NPSLE. Belimumab: IV 10 mg/kg (weeks 0, 2, 4, then every 4 weeks) or SC 200 mg weekly; licensed from age 5 (IV). Works best in serologically active disease. Watch for a depression and suicidality signal. In BEAT-LUPUS, belimumab after rituximab reduced severe flares (it counters the postrituximab BAFF rebound). Give recombinant zoster vaccine before anifrolumab. Ask about mood on belimumab. Neither has been studied in severe active NPSLE.

stem: What is the role of rituximab in SLE?

options.A: It is first-line therapy for all new lupus nephritis, ahead of mycophenolate
options.B: It is used off-label for refractory organ-threatening disease, such as haematological, neuropsychiatric or renal involvement
options.C: It is only used for mild, non-organ-threatening skin and joint disease
options.D: It is contraindicated in SLE because of the EXPLORER and LUNAR trial results
options.E: It is reserved for pregnancy, as the only immunosuppressant considered safe

explanation: Randomised trials missed their primary endpoints, but real-world evidence supports rituximab in refractory disease. Immunoglobulins and HBV status should be checked beforehand. EXPLORER (non-renal) and LUNAR (LN) missed their primary endpoints, but observational data and NHS commissioning support use. Typical dose: 1 g × 2, two weeks apart, with methylprednisolone, often with cyclophosphamide or MMF. Serum sickness is more common in SLE. Indications: refractory LN, AIHA, ITP, TTP, NPSLE or myelitis, rhupus, CAPS. Before treatment: HBV, immunoglobulins, vaccines ≥2 weeks earlier. Obinutuzumab (type II anti-CD20) is licensed for LN.

stem: When is a kidney biopsy indicated in SLE: for example new proteinuria, haematuria and rising creatinine, or a UPCR of 65 mg/mmol on two occasions with a bland sediment and normal creatinine in a patient who feels well?

options.A: Biopsy only once the serum creatinine has already doubled in value
options.B: Biopsy only if proteinuria exceeds 3 g/day; otherwise manage entirely empirically
options.C: Biopsy is never required if the patient feels subjectively clinically well
options.D: Biopsy (if safe) for persistent proteinuria of 0.5 g/day or more, an active glomerular sediment or an unexplained fall in eGFR, so both patients need a biopsy
options.E: Biopsy only in the first patient; the second needs none since creatinine is normal

explanation: Biopsy defines the histological class, activity and chronicity and guides treatment, subject to bleeding risk. It is advised for persistent proteinuria of 0.5 g/day or more, especially with glomerular haematuria or casts. Clinically silent nephritis is well recognised, so regular urinalysis, protein quantification, renal function and blood pressure checks are essential. LN mimics: hypertensive or diabetic nephropathy; drug toxicity (NSAIDs, PPI interstitial nephritis, CNI); aPL nephropathy or TMA, TTP, aHUS; pre-eclampsia; renal vein thrombosis; post-infectious, IgA or ANCA GN; anti-GBM; MGRS; lupus podocytopathy (MCD or FSGS-like, nephrotic with class I/II). LN affects 40–50% of adults and 50–70% of children, usually within 5 years. Risk is higher with Black, Hispanic or Asian ancestry, male sex, young age, anti-dsDNA, low complement and anti-C1q. 10–30% of proliferative LN progresses to kidney failure within 10–15 years. Screen: urinalysis, UPCR, BP and eGFR every 6–12 months if stable, and every 3 months if high-risk or active. Spot UPCR is preferred to 24-hour collection. Consider repeat biopsy for refractory disease, suspected class change, or before stopping maintenance (residual activity predicts relapse).

stem: Renal biopsy in lupus nephritis shows endocapillary proliferation with subendothelial deposits involving at least 50% of glomeruli. What is the ISN/RPS class?

options.A: Mycophenolate mofetil
options.B: Class III
options.C: Class IV
options.D: TNF inhibitors
options.E: Anti-SRP

explanation: Class III is focal (under 50% of glomeruli) and class IV diffuse (50% or more) proliferative nephritis. Class V is membranous; class VI is advanced sclerosis (90% or more of glomeruli). Class Histology Usual approach I minimal mesangial treat extrarenal disease only usually none; if proteinuria >3 II mesangial g, consider podocytopathy proliferative (GC ± CNI) focal (<50% of III induction then maintenance glomeruli), subendothelial deposits diffuse (≥50%) as III; most aggressive IV V membranous immunosuppress if nephrotic (subepithelial) or >1 g/day despite RAAS blockade; III/IV + V is treated as III/IV ≥90% globally VI no immunosuppression for the kidney; prepare for RRT sclerosed and transplant The 2018 revision dropped the A/C and S/G sub-labels in favour of a modified NIH activity index (0–24) and chronicity index (0–12). A chronicity index ≥4 predicts poor renal survival. Always report podocytopathy and TMA.

stem: What is the initial therapy for class IV lupus nephritis (proteinuria 3.2 g/day, creatinine 98 µmol/L), and what is the low-dose (Euro-Lupus) cyclophosphamide regimen?

options.A: Oral prednisolone alone, with no steroid-sparing agent, continued at a fixed low dose indefinitely
options.B: IV methylprednisolone then an oral taper, with hydroxychloroquine and mycophenolate plus belimumab, a calcineurin inhibitor or obinutuzumab (Euro-Lupus: 500 mg IV every 2 weeks for 6 doses)
options.C: Rituximab monotherapy, without any concomitant immunosuppressant or glucocorticoid taper
options.D: Mycophenolate alone, started at the lowest possible dose from the very outset
options.E: High-dose glucocorticoids alone, continued long-term without any steroid-sparing agent

explanation: Current EULAR (2025) and BSR (2026) recommendations favour combination therapy for class III/IV nephritis: mycophenolate plus belimumab, plus a calcineurin inhibitor (voclosporin or tacrolimus) or plus obinutuzumab, on a background of hydroxychloroquine and glucocorticoids (IV pulses then a taper to 5 mg/day or less by about 4–6 months). Mycophenolate alone or Euro-Lupus cyclophosphamide (with or without belimumab) are alternatives with lower efficacy. The low-dose regimen has similar efficacy to high-dose cyclophosphamide with less gonadal and infection toxicity, and is followed by maintenance with azathioprine or mycophenolate. Targets are a 25% fall in uPCR by 3 months, 50% by 6 months and uPCR below 70 mg/mmol by 12 months. Add-on Trial Best for BLISS-LN proteinuria <3 g, Belimumab (43% vs frequent extrarenal 32%) flares; less effective with cyclophosphamide AURORA (CR heavy proteinuria, mixed Voclosporin or 41% vs 23%) class V; avoid if eGFR tacrolimus ≤45 fewer flares, steroid Obinutuzumab REGENCY (CR about sparing; watch IgG 46% vs 33% at week 76) MMF 2–3 g/day (preferred in Black and Hispanic patients and women of childbearing age). High-dose NIH cyclophosphamide is reserved for crescentic or rapidly progressive GN. The EULAR course defines complete response as UPCR <50 mg/mmol with stable eGFR on ≤5 mg/day prednisolone by 12 months. Proteinuria may take 18–24 months to settle. Not on track: check adherence (MPA and HCQ levels), switch induction agent, add a third agent or anti-CD20, consider re-biopsy. Pure class V: RAAS blockade; if nephrotic or >1 g/day, MMF plus CNI. Consider anticoagulation in nephrotic class V with albumin <20–25 g/L.

stem: After successful induction for lupus nephritis, what is the recommended maintenance strategy?

options.A: Stop all immunosuppression entirely once clinical remission is reached at 6 months
options.B: Switch to cyclophosphamide pulses every 3 months as long-term maintenance therapy
options.C: Continue induction-dose glucocorticoids completely unchanged for the full 3-year period
options.D: Continue mycophenolate-based therapy (with belimumab, a calcineurin inhibitor or obinutuzumab) for at least 3 years, with glucocorticoid and antimalarial withdrawal
options.E: Mycophenolate mofetil monotherapy, stopped abruptly at 6 months regardless of response

explanation: Maintenance should continue for at least 3 years. The 2026 BSR guideline prefers continuing the induction combination (mycophenolate with obinutuzumab, belimumab or a calcineurin inhibitor), using mycophenolate alone if combinations are unsuitable, and azathioprine if mycophenolate is not tolerated or pregnancy is planned. Full glucocorticoid withdrawal should be attempted. Renal function, proteinuria, sediment, complement and anti-dsDNA are monitored. Use mycophenolate at the lowest effective dose (about 1–2 g/day), and continue belimumab, voclosporin or obinutuzumab if used in induction. Continue for ≥3–5 years after response, then withdraw slowly. Switch to azathioprine for pregnancy. Continue HCQ indefinitely. Monitor every 2–4 weeks during induction and every 3 months once stable (BP, eGFR, UPCR, sediment, FBC, albumin, C3/C4, dsDNA, IgG on anti-CD20). Persistent proteinuria >0.7–0.8 g/day at 12 months predicts poor renal outcome.

stem: Which measures complement immunosuppression in lupus nephritis?

options.A: High-dose NSAIDs for symptomatic relief of arthralgia
options.B: Long-term prophylactic anticoagulation in all patients, regardless of APS status
options.C: Avoiding all antihypertensives until proteinuria resolves
options.D: Permissive hypertension, since blood pressure control does not affect renal outcomes
options.E: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria, lipid management, and an SGLT2 inhibitor where appropriate

explanation: Renoprotection reduces proteinuria and progression but does not replace treatment of active proliferative nephritis. EULAR 2025 suggests adding an SGLT2 inhibitor if proteinuria persists after 12 months of treatment. Potassium and renal function need monitoring. Renoprotection checklist: HCQ (reduce if eGFR <30); ACE inhibitor or ARB with BP <130/80 (systolic <120 if tolerated); SGLT2 inhibitor once stable with eGFR ≥20 (evidence from CKD trials, not LN-specific); statin; avoid NSAIDs; sodium restriction; PJP prophylaxis with high-dose GC; bone protection; vaccination; fertility preservation if using cyclophosphamide. In kidney failure, transplantation is preferred (recurrence <5–10%), with anticoagulation if APS is present.

stem: A woman with SLE has isolated severe thrombocytopenia (12 x 10I/L) with mucosal bleeding. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.A: Platelet transfusion alone, without any immunosuppression
options.B: High-dose glucocorticoids including IV methylprednisolone pulses, with IVIG
options.C: Oral prednisolone alone at a low dose, reassessed in 2 weeks
options.D: Watchful waiting, since ITP in SLE is usually self-limiting
options.E: Anticoagulation first, given the risk of associated antiphospholipid syndrome

explanation: Acute severe immune thrombocytopenia is treated with high-dose glucocorticoids and IVIG when bleeding or a rapid rise is needed. Maintenance agents include MMF, azathioprine or ciclosporin; rituximab, thrombopoietin receptor agonists or splenectomy are later options. Thrombocytopenia in SLE: immune (ITP-like), TTP or TMA (schistocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin, ADAMTS13 <10%), aPL-associated or catastrophic APS, HLH or MAS, drugs (azathioprine, MMF, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, co-trimoxazole), hypersplenism, marrow infiltration, Evans syndrome, pseudothrombocytopenia (EDTA clumping). Maintenance options: MMF, azathioprine, ciclosporin, rituximab, TPO receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim), splenectomy. Aspirin can still be used in aPL thrombocytopenia once platelets are >50.

stem: A patient with active generalised SLE develops seizures and psychosis. Infection, metabolic causes and drugs have been excluded. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Oral prednisolone alone, without any steroid-sparing agent
options.B: Antipsychotic medication alone, without immunosuppression
options.C: High-dose glucocorticoids (including pulses) with cyclophosphamide
options.D: Plasma exchange alone, without glucocorticoids or cyclophosphamide
options.E: Anticoagulation alone, regardless of antiphospholipid antibody status

explanation: Inflammatory neuropsychiatric lupus is treated with high-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide (or rituximab if refractory), plus symptomatic therapy. Thrombotic events related to aPL are managed with anticoagulation. NP events in SLE are attributable to SLE in only about a third. Mimics: infection (LP, cultures; PML on rituximab), steroid psychosis (first 1–2 weeks at >40 mg/day), metabolic disturbance (uraemia, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia), PRES (hypertension, CNIs), TTP, aPL thrombosis, drugs, primary psychiatric disease, NMOSD (AQP4-IgG), MOG antibody disease, MS. The ACR nomenclature lists 19 syndromes (12 CNS, 7 PNS). Attribution weighs timing (within 6 months of diagnosis), event type, confounders and supportive features (activity, MRI, CSF, anti-ribosomal P, aPL). Mechanisms: thrombotic or ischaemic (focal) vs inflammatory or antibody-mediated (diffuse: anti-NMDA NR2, anti-ribosomal P). Investigations: MRI with contrast, DWI, FLAIR and SWI; CSF (mainly to exclude infection); aPL, anti-ribosomal P, AQP4 and MOG; EEG; NCS; neuropsychological tests. Transverse myelitis is an emergency: pulse GC and cyclophosphamide within hours, plus PLEX if poor response; treat as NMOSD if AQP4-positive. Seizures: antiepileptics; long-term treatment may be unnecessary after a single provoked seizure with normal MRI and EEG. Cognition: treat vascular risk, mood and sleep; do not escalate immunosuppression. Chorea: usually aPL-related; antithrombotics. Maintenance: MMF or azathioprine. Refractory disease: rituximab, IVIG, PLEX.

stem: A patient with SLE on immunosuppression develops fever and pleuritic chest pain. What must be considered before attributing this to a lupus flare?

options.A: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
options.B: Infection (including opportunistic infection) and pulmonary embolism
options.C: A simple viral upper respiratory tract infection, requiring no further work-up
options.D: Malignancy alone, without considering infection or thromboembolism
options.E: A flare of serositis alone, once a chest radiograph is normal

explanation: Infection is a leading cause of death in SLE and can mimic or coexist with a flare. Thromboembolism must also be considered, especially with aPL. Feature Infection Flare rigors, high low-grade Fever neutrophilia, leucopenia, lymphopenia WCC left shift >50 mg/L CRP normal or mild rise (except serositis or arthritis) >0.5 Procalcitonin normal rising dsDNA, falling Serology unchanged C3/C4 If in doubt, treat both: cultures and antibiotics, with senior review of lupus therapy. Consider opportunistic organisms (PJP, CMV, TB, fungi, Nocardia, Listeria, zoster). Do a CTPA for pleuritic pain with aPL. Risk factors for serious infection: activity, GC (even 5–10 mg), cyclophosphamide or B-cell depletion, lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinaemia, LN, low albumin, hyposplenism. HCQ is protective.

stem: A patient with SLE on mycophenolate and prednisolone develops fever with a neutrophil count of 0.3 x 10I/L. What should happen?

options.A: Oral antibiotics only, since she is not currently febrile with chills
options.B: Increase mycophenolate to treat presumed disease activity
options.C: Urgent assessment and treatment for neutropenic sepsis, with review of drug toxicity
options.D: Observation with a repeat FBC in 48 hours, since she is not acutely unwell
options.E: Stop prednisolone only, continuing mycophenolate unchanged

explanation: Urgent assessment and treatment for neutropenic sepsis, with review of drug toxicity Fever with neutropenia is a medical emergency requiring prompt cultures and empirical antibiotics. Neutropenic sepsis pathway: cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, withhold myelotoxic drugs (MMF, azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, co-trimoxazole), and consider G-CSF. Isolated asymptomatic lupus leucopenia or lymphopenia does not need immunosuppression. Check TPMT and NUDT15 before azathioprine.

stem: A patient with SLE develops fever, confusion, thrombocytopenia and worsening renal function. What is the key immediate principle?

options.A: Treat only for the single most likely diagnosis, to avoid unnecessary immunosuppression
options.B: Assume a lupus flare alone, since fever is common in active SLE
options.C: Wait for ADAMTS13 results before starting any treatment
options.D: Treat only for catastrophic APS, since thrombocytopenia is the dominant feature
options.E: Assess urgently and in parallel for infection, thrombotic microangiopathy, catastrophic APS macrophage activation syndrome and severe lupus activity

explanation: Fever, confusion, thrombocytopenia and renal decline in SLE can reflect several life-threatening processes at once. A blood film for schistocytes, ADAMTS13, ferritin, fibrinogen, cultures and aPL testing help distinguish infection, thrombotic microangiopathy, catastrophic APS, MAS and severe lupus activity. Process Key tests schistocytes, ADAMTS13 <10%, high LDH, TTP low haptoglobin ≥3 organs within a week, microthrombi, Catastrophic aPL (often LA, triple-positive) APS ferritin >5,000–10,000, falling ESR, HLH or MAS fibrinogen and platelets, raised triglycerides, sCD25, haemophagocytosis on marrow cultures, procalcitonin, prolonged PT and Sepsis or DIC APTT, low fibrinogen dsDNA, C3/C4, active sediment Lupus flare Treat in parallel: plasma exchange for TTP (with caplacizumab where indicated); anticoagulation plus GC plus PLEX and/or IVIG for CAPS; GC plus anakinra or ciclosporin for MAS; antibiotics.

stem: A patient with SLE reports severe fatigue. Disease activity indices are low. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Repeat disease activity indices weekly until a cause is found
options.B: Increase immunosuppression empirically, since fatigue likely reflects subclinical activity
options.C: Refer for a sleep study as the first and only step
options.D: Assess and address sleep, mood, anaemia, thyroid disease, vitamin D, pain and deconditioning, as well as disease activity
options.E: Reassure that fatigue in SLE always resolves once serology normalises

explanation: Fatigue in SLE is multifactorial. Exercise, sleep and psychological approaches are useful. Fatigue occurs in 80–90% and correlates poorly with activity. Screen and treat depression and anxiety (25–40%), sleep disorders, fibromyalgia, anaemia, hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency and deconditioning. Graded aerobic exercise and psychological interventions are most effective. Anifrolumab and belimumab modestly improve fatigue.

stem: Which preventive measures are recommended in SLE, what cutaneous advice suits photosensitive patients, and how should the excess cardiovascular risk be managed?

options.A: Apply sunscreen only when symptoms flare, rather than using it year-round regardless of activity
options.B: Vitamin D supplementation alone is sufficient, with no formal vascular risk review required
options.C: Standard cardiovascular risk calculators alone are adequate, without any adjustment for SLE-specific risk
options.D: The SAV3E framework: sunscreen, antimalarial use, vitamin D, vaccination, and vascular risk management; cardiovascular risk is roughly 2-3 times increased, so risk factors need regular review
options.E: No specific vaccination advice is needed beyond the standard general population immunisation schedule

explanation: SLE confers excess cardiovascular and infection risk; annual cardiovascular risk review and vaccination are part of routine care. Ultraviolet light can trigger cutaneous and systemic flares, so regular broad-spectrum sunscreen and avoidance of excessive UV exposure are advised throughout the year. Myocardial infarction and stroke risk is roughly two-to three-fold increased; management combines disease control, glucocorticoid minimisation, attention to aPL and treatment of traditional risk factors. CV drivers: traditional risk factors plus activity, LN and CKD, aPL, GC, IFN-driven endothelial damage and proinflammatory HDL. Standard calculators underestimate risk; multiply by about 2 or use carotid plaque imaging. UVA passes through window glass and some fluorescent or LED lighting. Sun: SPF ≥50 broad-spectrum sunscreen and UVprotective clothing; replace vitamin D. BP: <130/80, with ACE inhibitor or ARB if proteinuric. Lipids: statins by upgraded risk category; LN, CKD or APS often place patients at high or very high risk. Other: aspirin for high-risk aPL profiles; minimise GC; continue HCQ; stop smoking; exercise. Vaccines: influenza, pneumococcal (PCV20 or PCV15 + PPSV23), COVID-19, HPV (to 45), recombinant zoster (before anifrolumab or JAKi), hepatitis B. Annual checks: lipids, HbA1c, CV risk, SDI, bone health, cervical screening.

stem: A 62-year-old man taking hydralazine develops arthralgia, serositis and a positive ANA. Anti-dsDNA is negative and complement is normal. Which antibody is most typical?

options.A: Anti-MDA5
options.B: Anti-histone
options.C: Anti-Sm
options.D: Anti-NXP2
options.E: Anti-Jo-1

explanation: Drug-induced lupus (hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline) typically has anti-histone antibodies, rarely involves the kidney or CNS, and resolves after withdrawal. TNF inhibitor-induced lupus more often features antidsDNA. Type Drugs Serology Features procainamide, anti-histone arthralgia, Classic >95%; myalgia, fever, DIL hydralazine (slow serositis; dsDNA and acetylators), low kidney and isoniazid, complement CNS rare minocycline (prare ANCA, hepatitis), quinidine, methyldopa, chlorpromazine, sulfasalazine, terbinafine Antiinfliximab, rash, arthritis, dsDNA TNFetanercept, about 90%, serositis induced adalimumab low (ATIL) complement about 50% Drug-PPIs, thiazides, anti-Ro annular CCBs, ACE induced photosensitive inhibitors, SCLE rash terbinafine, taxanes, TNFi, ICIs IFN-α, ICIs, JAK Other variable can unmask and other true SLE targeted agents Stop the drug; symptoms settle within weeks, though ANA can persist for months to years. Use NSAIDs, short lowdose GC or HCQ if symptoms persist. If features persist beyond about 6 months, reconsider true SLE. Do not rechallenge. Hydralazine can also cause ANCA vasculitis (MPO, often with anti-histone and anti-elastase).

stem: A 49-year-old woman develops annular, polycyclic, photosensitive plaques on her upper back and arms 6 weeks after starting terbinafine. Anti-Ro is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Tinea corporis, confirmed by fungal scraping
options.B: Levamisole-adulterated cocaine
options.C: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
options.D: Drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus
options.E: Polymorphic light eruption

explanation: SCLE causes non-scarring annular or papulosquamous lesions and is strongly associated with anti-Ro. Triggers include terbinafine, PPIs, thiazides, calcium-channel blockers and checkpoint inhibitors. Annular photosensitive lesions: SCLE vs tinea corporis (scrape for fungus), granuloma annulare, erythema annulare centrifugum, psoriasis, polymorphic light eruption, dermatomyositis, Sjögren’s annular erythema (Asian patients), neonatal lupus. Stop the trigger (lesions resolve over weeks to months), photoprotection, topical steroids, HCQ. Look for systemic SLE (about 50% of SCLE meets criteria, usually mild). In women of childbearing age, anti-Ro has implications for future pregnancy (CHB).

stem: Which set of conditions defines remission in SLE according to the DORIS definition?

options.A: SLEDAI of 4 or less, with prednisolone 7.5 mg/day or less
options.B: Complete normalisation of complement and anti-dsDNA, regardless of clinical findings
options.C: Clinical SLEDAI 0 with glucocorticoids stopped entirely, since any dose excludes remission
options.D: Clinical SLEDAI 0, physician global assessment below 0.5, prednisolone 5 mg/day or less, with stable antimalarials, immunosuppressants and biologics allowed
options.E: Physician global assessment below 0.5 alone, without reference to glucocorticoid dose

explanation: Serology is ignored in clinical SLEDAI. Lupus low disease activity state (SLEDAI 4 or less, prednisolone 7.5 mg/day or less) is an alternative target. LLDAS: SLEDAI-2K ≤4 with no major-organ activity, no haemolysis or GI activity, no new features, PGA ≤1, prednisolone ≤7.5 mg/day, with standard immunosuppressants and biologics tolerated. Spending ≥50% of follow-up in LLDAS halves damage, flares and mortality. Reaching a target on high-dose GC does not count. Treat-to-target: assess activity at every visit and damage yearly. Aim for remission or LLDAS within 6–12 months with prednisolone ≤5 mg. Escalate if the target is not met by 3– 6 months, after checking adherence (up to 50% are nonadherent) and excluding non-lupus causes. Flare predictors: young onset, prior LN, CNS disease or vasculitis, persistently active serology, stopping HCQ, rapid GC withdrawal, pregnancy, UV, infection.

stem: Which laboratory tests form the antiphospholipid antibody criteria, and why must positive results be repeated?

options.A: Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm antibodies, repeated at least 12 weeks apart for confirmation
options.B: ANA and complement levels, repeated at least 6 weeks apart for confirmation
options.C: Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies, with no need for any repeat testing
options.D: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies, repeated at least 12 weeks apart, because transient antibodies are common
options.E: A single lupus anticoagulant test only, with no repetition considered necessary

explanation: Positivity must be persistent on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart, with moderate to high titres for solid-phase assays. Transient aPL occur with infection, drugs and other conditions, and low-titre results have little clinical significance. Triple positivity identifies the highest-risk profile. Causes of transient or non-pathogenic aPL: infections (syphilis, HIV, HCV, EBV, parvovirus, COVID-19, leprosy), drugs (chlorpromazine, procainamide, hydralazine, phenytoin, quinidine), malignancy (lymphoma), older age, other autoimmune diseases. Other prothrombotic states to consider: factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C, protein S or antithrombin deficiency, PNH (flow cytometry), myeloproliferative neoplasm (JAK2), HIT, malignancy, nephrotic syndrome, Behçet’s. LA is the strongest single predictor of thrombosis. Testing is unreliable during acute thrombosis and on anticoagulants (see next entry). Do a dRVVT plus an LA-sensitive APTT (two tests).

stem: A patient with a recent pulmonary embolism started apixaban before antiphospholipid testing. Lupus anticoagulant is reported as positive. How should this be interpreted?

options.A: A true positive result, confirming APS regardless of anticoagulation
options.B: DOACs can cause false-positive lupus anticoagulant results; repeat off anticoagulation or with DOACremoval techniques, and confirm persistence
options.C: A result that cannot be interpreted and should simply be ignored
options.D: An indication to switch immediately to warfarin without retesting
options.E: Confirmation of high-risk APS, requiring lifelong warfarin without further testing

explanation: DOACs, heparin and VKAs interfere with clotting-based LA assays, whereas solid-phase assays for anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I are unaffected. Options: retest LA ≥2 days after stopping a DOAC (if clinically safe); use DOAC-removal agents (DOAC-Stop) before LA testing; switch to LMWH (with anti-Xaneutralising reagents); rely on solid-phase assays and antiβ2GPI, which are unaffected; or use the Taipan or Ecarin ratio (insensitive to VKAs). Confirm persistence at 12 weeks. Pre-test counselling matters, because finding highrisk APS changes the choice of anticoagulant (a DOAC is not appropriate).

stem: Which obstetric complications meet the clinical criteria for APS?

options.A: Two unexplained miscarriages before 10 weeks, with no further criteria needed
options.B: Any history of infertility or a single miscarriage at any gestation
options.C: A single episode of pre-eclampsia at any gestation, regardless of severity
options.D: Delivery before 37 weeks’ gestation for any obstetric indication at all
options.E: Three or more unexplained miscarriages before 10 weeks, unexplained fetal death beyond 10 weeks, or delivery before 34 weeks for severe pre-eclampsia or placental insufficiency

explanation: These are the revised Sapporo (Sydney) clinical criteria. Maternal anatomical and hormonal causes and parental chromosomal abnormalities should be excluded for recurrent early loss. The 2023 ACR/EULAR APS classification criteria weight obstetric items differently: recurrent early losses score lowest, while severe pre-eclampsia or placental insufficiency before 34 weeks score highest. Recurrent miscarriage work-up: parental karyotype (balanced translocation), uterine anomalies (3D ultrasound), thyroid disease, diabetes, PCOS, hyperprolactinaemia, inherited thrombophilia (limited relevance), cervical insufficiency (second-trimester loss), infection, maternal age. Sydney clinical obstetric criteria:-≥3 unexplained consecutive miscarriages before 10 weeks-≥1 unexplained fetal death at or beyond 10 weeks-≥1 delivery before 34 weeks for severe pre-eclampsia, eclampsia or placental insufficiency The 2023 criteria give the most weight to severe early preeclampsia or placental insufficiency before 34 weeks.

stem: A 30-year-old woman has triple-positive antiphospholipid antibodies but no history of thrombosis or pregnancy complications. What is the recommended prophylaxis?

options.A: Full-dose therapeutic anticoagulation with warfarin
options.B: No prophylaxis is needed in asymptomatic carriers
options.C: Prophylactic-dose LMWH indefinitely, without aspirin
options.D: Clopidogrel, in preference to aspirin
options.E: Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily)

explanation: Asymptomatic carriers with a high-risk aPL profile are offered low-dose aspirin, along with management of other thrombotic risk factors. Hydroxychloroquine is added in SLE. Low-dose aspirin for a high-risk aPL profile (and consider it for low-risk profiles in SLE), plus HCQ in SLE. Manage CV risk factors. Avoid oestrogen-containing contraception and HRT. Use thromboprophylaxis (LMWH) in high-risk situations such as surgery, immobilisation, the post-partum period and long-haul travel.

stem: A woman with persistent antiphospholipid antibodies has a first unprovoked DVT. What is the recommended long-term anticoagulation, and which anticoagulant should be avoided if she is triple-positive?

options.A: Warfarin anticoagulation
options.B: Switch to a DOAC after an initial period of warfarin, once stable
options.C: No long-term anticoagulation is needed after a first provoked event
options.D: Long-term warfarin with target INR 2–3; avoid DOACs such as rivaroxaban
options.E: Antiplatelet therapy alone, without any anticoagulant

explanation: A first unprovoked venous event in APS warrants long-term vitamin K antagonist therapy with INR 2–3. Rivaroxaban was associated with more thrombotic events than warfarin in triple-positive APS (TRAPS trial), so DOACs are avoided in high-risk APS. They may be considered only in selected lower-risk (single-or double-positive) venous APS when a VKA is not feasible or a stable INR cannot be achieved. Other trials: ASTRO-APS (apixaban, more strokes) and Ordi-Rimola (rivaroxaban, more arterial events). Point-ofcare INR may be inaccurate when LA is strongly positive; check against laboratory INR. Recurrence despite INR 2–3: check adherence and time in therapeutic range, then increase the target to 3–4, add lowdose aspirin, or switch to therapeutic LMWH. Add HCQ (and possibly a statin) as adjuncts. Provoked VTE with a low-risk profile can be considered for 3–6 months of treatment only after specialist review.

stem: A young adult (with or without SLE) has an ischaemic stroke with persistently positive lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies. What is the most appropriate long-term treatment?

options.A: Low-dose aspirin alone, without anticoagulation
options.B: A DOAC such as rivaroxaban, given its ease of use
options.C: Prophylactic-dose LMWH alone, continued indefinitely
options.D: Long-term warfarin; DOACs are avoided after arterial events in APS
options.E: No long-term anticoagulation, since this was a single isolated event

explanation: Arterial thrombosis with persistent aPL is managed with a vitamin K antagonist: INR 2–3 or 3–4 (balancing bleeding and recurrence), or INR 2–3 plus low-dose aspirin. This applies whether lupus activity is high or low. Young stroke differential: cardioembolism (PFO with paradoxical embolism, AF, Libman–Sacks or infective endocarditis), arterial dissection, vasculitis (primary CNS, Takayasu, Behçet’s, SLE), RCVS, CADASIL, Fabry disease, sickle cell disease, moyamoya, DADA2 (lacunar strokes, livedo), drugs (cocaine, amphetamines), inherited thrombophilia (venous events more than arterial), Sneddon’s syndrome, homocystinuria. Investigate with MRI and MRA, echo (TOE for vegetations), Holter and a thrombophilia screen. Manage BP, lipids and smoking. Continue HCQ in SLE.

stem: A woman with known APS develops renal failure, livedo, confusion and thrombocytopenia over 5 days, with microthrombi on skin biopsy. What is the first-line treatment?

options.A: Anticoagulation plus high-dose glucocorticoids plus plasma exchange and/or IVIG
options.B: Anticoagulation alone, without any immunosuppression
options.C: High-dose glucocorticoids alone, without anticoagulation
options.D: Plasma exchange alone, without anticoagulation or glucocorticoids
options.E: IV methylprednisolone and IVIG alone, without anticoagulation

explanation: Catastrophic APS (multi-organ small-vessel thrombosis within a week) has high mortality. Triple therapy is first-line and triggers such as infection are treated; rituximab or eculizumab are used for refractory disease. TTP (ADAMTS13 <10%), aHUS (complement), HIT (heparin exposure; PF4 antibodies), DIC (sepsis), HELLP, malignant hypertension, scleroderma renal crisis, sepsis. CAPS: thrombosis in ≥3 organs within a week, histological small-vessel occlusion, and aPL. Mortality is about 30– 50%. Common organs: kidney, lung (ARDS, DAH), brain, heart, skin, adrenals (haemorrhage), liver. About half have a trigger: infection, surgery, stopping anticoagulation, SLE flare, pregnancy or the puerperium. Triple therapy: therapeutic heparin, high-dose GC (pulses) and PLEX and/or IVIG. Treat the trigger. For refractory disease: rituximab or eculizumab (complement C5 inhibition). Intensive care.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with three consecutive unexplained miscarriages before 10 weeks has persistent medium-high titre anticardiolipin antibodies. She is newly pregnant. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: No treatment, since she has not had a prior thrombosis
options.B: Switch to therapeutic-dose LMWH with low-dose aspirin before 6 weeks’ gestation, continuing through pregnancy and postpartum
options.C: High-dose aspirin alone, without any heparin
options.D: Low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic-dose LMWH
options.E: Warfarin throughout pregnancy, switching to LMWH only near delivery
