explanation: Obstetric APS without prior thrombosis is treated with low-dose aspirin and prophylactic LMWH, continuing LMWH for 6 weeks postpartum. Live birth rates in treated obstetric APS are about 70–80%. HCQ added to standard therapy is under study (HYPATIA) and is often used for refractory cases. Start aspirin before conception (or from a positive test) and LMWH from a positive pregnancy test or the fetal heart. Monitor with uterine artery Doppler at 20–24 weeks and serial growth scans. Refractory obstetric APS: add HCQ, consider increasing LMWH to intermediate or therapeutic dose, add low-dose prednisolone in the first trimester, or IVIG (expert centre). Women with aPL-positivity but no events: aspirin, plus postpartum LMWH for 6 weeks if highrisk or other risk factors.

stem: How should thrombotic APS be managed in pregnancy, including in a woman on warfarin who finds she is 5 weeks pregnant?

options.A: Low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic-dose LMWH
options.B: Stop anticoagulation entirely for the first trimester to avoid teratogenicity
options.C: Continue warfarin unchanged throughout pregnancy
options.D: Switch to therapeutic-dose LMWH with low-dose aspirin before 6 weeks’ gestation, continuing through pregnancy and postpartum
options.E: Switch to a DOAC for the remainder of pregnancy

explanation: Thrombotic APS needs therapeutic anticoagulation throughout pregnancy and postpartum. Warfarin is teratogenic (embryopathy risk is greatest between 6 and 12 weeks) and DOACs are not used in pregnancy. Warfarin is compatible with breastfeeding postpartum. Warfarin embryopathy: nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses (chondrodysplasia punctata). Later exposure carries fetal intracranial haemorrhage risk. Peri-delivery: plan neuraxial anaesthesia timing (stop prophylactic LMWH 12 hours before, therapeutic 24 hours before). Restart LMWH after delivery and bridge back to warfarin. Use a monitored anti-Xa level in extremes of weight or renal impairment. Women on warfarin should be counselled before conception and do early pregnancy tests.

stem: What is the role of hydroxychloroquine in thrombosis in SLE?

options.A: It fully replaces anticoagulation in confirmed thrombotic APS
options.B: It has no effect on thrombotic risk and is used only for skin and joint disease
options.C: It is used only once thrombosis has already occurred, not as background therapy
options.D: It may reduce thrombotic risk as background therapy but does not replace anticoagulation in confirmed thrombotic APS
options.E: It should be stopped once a patient starts anticoagulation

explanation: Hydroxychloroquine is part of background SLE therapy and may add benefit in aPL-positive patients. HCQ reduces thrombosis in aPL-positive SLE (observational data). Mechanisms include reduced aPL binding to phospholipid bilayers, reduced platelet activation and improved lipids. Continue HCQ in all SLE patients. It is adjunctive only: confirmed thrombotic APS still needs a VKA. HCQ is also used in refractory obstetric APS. Statins are an adjunct in recurrent thrombosis.

stem: A patient meets the systemic sclerosis classification criteria. What is the minimum total score required?

options.C: Right-heart catheterisation
options.D: 3 points; he meets the criteria

explanation: Skin thickening of the fingers of both hands extending proximal to the MCP joints scores 9 and is sufficient alone. Otherwise weighted items (puffy fingers, sclerodactyly, fingertip lesions, telangiectasia, abnormal nailfold capillaries, PAH or ILD, Raynaud’s, SSc-specific antibodies) are summed. Item Points 9 Bilateral finger skin thickening proximal to (sufficient) the MCPs Puffy fingers / sclerodactyly distal to the 2 / 4 MCPs Digital ulcers / pitting scars 2 / 3 2 Telangiectasia 2 Abnormal nailfold capillaries PAH and/or ILD 2 Raynaud’s 3 ACA, Scl-70 or RNA pol III 3 Sensitivity about 91%, specificity about 92%. The criteria do not apply if skin thickening spares the fingers or a mimic explains the features better.

stem: A woman has a year of Raynaud’s and puffy fingers, a centromere-pattern ANA and giant capillaries with haemorrhages on nailfold capillaroscopy. How should this be interpreted, and how does the scleroderma capillaroscopy pattern evolve?

options.A: Primary Raynaud’s phenomenon requiring only reassurance, since the capillaroscopy pattern is normal
options.B: Established diffuse systemic sclerosis requiring immediate systemic immunosuppression without delay
options.C: Very early systemic sclerosis (VEDOSS) needing monitoring for organ involvement; the capillaroscopy pattern evolves from early through active to late with capillary loss
options.D: Mixed connective tissue disease, defined specifically by this capillaroscopy pattern alone
options.E: A normal finding in healthy young women, requiring no further follow-up or monitoring

explanation: Raynaud’s with puffy fingers, SSc-specific antibodies and a scleroderma capillaroscopy pattern indicates very early SSc, so baseline and serial screening for ILD, PAH and other organ involvement is needed. Primary Raynaud’s has normal capillaroscopy and negative autoantibodies. The capillaroscopic stage correlates with digital ulcer risk. Secondary Raynaud’s: SSc, SLE, MCTD, Sjögren’s, myositis (especially antisynthetase), UCTD; vibration white finger (hand-arm vibration syndrome); hypothenar hammer syndrome; thoracic outlet syndrome (unilateral); atherosclerosis or Buerger’s disease (smokers); cryoglobulinaemia, cold agglutinins, paraprotein; drugs (βblockers, ergots, sympathomimetics, chemotherapy such as bleomycin and cisplatin, interferon); hypothyroidism. Feature Primary Secondary (SSc) Raynaud’s teens to 20s usually after 30 Onset mild, severe, painful, may Severity symmetrical be asymmetric Ulcers, pitting, no yes gangrene Capillaroscopy normal scleroderma pattern positive, SSc-ANA negative or low titre specific Abnormal capillaroscopy plus an SSc antibody gives a >60–80% chance of progression to SSc. Refer anyone with Raynaud’s plus puffy fingers, a positive ANA or abnormal capillaroscopy. A handheld dermatoscope works for clinic capillaroscopy.

stem: What does the modified Rodnan skin score measure?

options.A: Digital ulcer count and severity, scored 0 to 3
options.B: Internal organ involvement, scored across 12 domains
options.C: Nailfold capillary density, scored at 8 sites
options.D: Pulmonary function decline, scored over 17 body sites
options.E: Skin thickness at 17 body sites scored 0-3 (maximum 51)

explanation: The mRSS is the main skin outcome in diffuse SSc trials and correlates with disease severity and mortality. The mRSS scores 17 sites from 0 to 3 (total 0–51). Skin progresses over the first 1–3 years in dcSSc, then often softens. Early rapid progression predicts organ involvement and mortality.

stem: Which clinical phenotypes are associated with anti-centromere, anti-Scl-70 and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies?

options.A: Anti-centromere: limited disease and late PAH. Anti-Scl-70: diffuse disease and ILD. Anti-RNA polymerase III: rapid skin progression, renal crisis and cancer near onset
options.B: Anti-centromere: diffuse disease with early renal crisis. Anti-Scl-70: limited disease with late PAH
options.C: Anti-RNA polymerase III is associated with limited cutaneous disease and a low overall cancer risk
options.D: All three of these antibodies carry an equally high risk of scleroderma renal crisis
options.E: These antibodies are non-specific and carry no prognostic value in systemic sclerosis

explanation: Anti-PM/Scl is associated with myositis overlap. Patients with anti-RNA polymerase III need close blood pressure and renal monitoring, and age-appropriate cancer screening. Antibody Frequency Subset Associations 20–40% late PAH, calcinosis, ACA limited digital ischaemia; ILD uncommon; better survival Scl-70 15–40% early ILD, digital ulcers, diffuse > limited cardiac disease; worse survival 5–25% rapid skin progression, RNA pol diffuse renal crisis, cancer ±2– III 3 years from onset, GAVE, contractures U3-RNP 4– 10% PAH, cardiac and diffuse muscle disease, GI; poor prognosis Th/To 2–5% ILD, PAH limited PM/Scl 2–3% myositis, ILD, overlap calcinosis, mechanic’s hands; good prognosis U1-RNP 5–10% arthritis, myositis, PAH MCTD 2–4% myositis, arthritis Ku overlap Antibodies are present in 90–95% and are largely mutually exclusive. With anti-RNA pol III: home BP monitoring, and extra cancer vigilance (breast and lung) within 2– 3 years of onset.

stem: A 44-year-old woman with limited cutaneous SSc has frequent painful Raynaud’s attacks despite keeping warm. What is the first-line drug?

options.A: A dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker such as nifedipine
options.B: A beta-blocker such as propranolol
options.C: Gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE)
options.D: An ACE inhibitor such as ramipril
options.E: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor such as fluoxetine

explanation: dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker such as nifedipine CCBs are first-line, with PDE5 inhibitors as an alternative or addition. IV iloprost is used for severe attacks. Betablockers may worsen vasospasm. General: whole-body warmth, stop smoking, avoid vasoconstrictors (β-blockers, sympathomimetics, decongestants, triptans). First line: a dihydropyridine CCB (nifedipine MR, amlodipine) and/or a PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil, tadalafil). Alternatives: losartan, fluoxetine, topical nitrates. Severe or refractory: IV iloprost. Refractory: botulinum toxin to the palm, digital sympathectomy, fat grafting.

stem: A patient with SSc has a painful digital ulcer despite nifedipine; another has five new ulcers this year despite nifedipine and sildenafil, which heal with iloprost. What is used for healing, and what reduces new ulcers?

options.A: Wound care, infection assessment, and a PDE5 inhibitor and/or IV iloprost for healing; bosentan reduces new digital ulcers but does not speed healing
options.B: Topical nitrates applied directly onto the open ulcer bed itself
options.C: Oral antibiotics alone, without any vascular treatment, for all ulcers
options.D: Observation only, since digital ulcers in SSc typically heal spontaneously
options.E: Surgical debridement used as first-line treatment, before any medical therapy trial

explanation: PDE5 inhibitors and IV prostanoids help ulcer healing. Infected ulcers need antibiotics, and critical ischaemia needs urgent vascular assessment. Bosentan requires monthly LFTs and effective contraception. Digital ulcer types and mimics: ischaemic fingertip ulcers vs ulcers over calcinosis or extensor surfaces (traction, mechanical), infection or osteomyelitis (probe to bone; Xray or MRI), macrovascular occlusion (ulnar artery occlusion is common in SSc; also emboli, thoracic outlet syndrome), vasculitis, cholesterol emboli, cryoglobulinaemia, Buerger’s disease. Critical ischaemia: admit for IV iloprost, analgesia and consider 24–72 hours of anticoagulation plus aspirin. Arrange urgent vascular and hand surgery review. Do duplex or angiography for macrovascular disease.

stem: Which patients are at greatest risk of scleroderma renal crisis, how is renal crisis treated (for example BP 186/104, rising creatinine and microangiopathic haemolysis in early diffuse SSc on glucocorticoids), and what is the role of prophylactic ACE inhibition?

options.A: Highest risk: longstanding limited cutaneous disease with anti-centromere antibody; avoid ACE inhibitors, which worsen outcomes
options.B: ACE inhibitors are given prophylactically to all anti-RNA polymerase III-positive patients
options.C: Highest risk: early (under 4 years) rapidly progressive diffuse disease, anti-RNA polymerase III and tendon friction rubs. Treat with an ACE inhibitor such as captopril, continued even on dialysis
options.D: Treat with an ARB rather than an ACE inhibitor, since ARBs act more quickly in this context
options.E: Stop the ACE inhibitor immediately if the creatinine rises at all after starting it

explanation: ACE inhibitors are not given prophylactically. ACE inhibitors are the mainstay of renal crisis and are continued even if dialysis is needed, as recovery can occur over months. CCBs can be added for blood pressure control. Prophylactic ACE inhibition has not prevented renal crisis and may be associated with worse outcomes. Creatinine may rise initially during treatment, which should not prompt withdrawal. AKI in SSc: renal crisis vs ANCA (MPO) GN (consider Dpenicillamine history), drug nephrotoxicity (NSAIDs, CNIs), TTP, aHUS, hypovolaemia (GI loss), pre-eclampsia, obstructive uropathy. Renal crisis is a TMA emergency: new accelerated hypertension (often >150/85, or a systolic rise ≥30 mmHg) with AKI, schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, headache, visual disturbance, seizures, heart failure and pericardial effusion. Normotensive SRC occurs in about 10% and carries a worse prognosis. Incidence is 2–5% overall and 10– 15% in early diffuse disease. Ciclosporin also raises risk. Captopril 6.25–12.5 mg, increased every 4–8 hours, aiming for a fall of 10–20 mmHg per day without hypotension. Then add a CCB, then an α-blocker, then IV prostacyclin. 20–50% need dialysis; recovery can continue for up to 2 years, so delay transplant listing. Eculizumab for refractory TMA. One-year mortality is 10–20%. Prevention: home BP monitoring, avoid high-dose GC, and keep prednisolone ≤10–15 mg with BP checks.

stem: A woman with newly diagnosed anti-Scl-70-positive diffuse SSc needs baseline assessment; another patient has ILD involving 25% of the lungs with FVC 68% and declining. What is the key baseline investigation, and what is first-line treatment?

options.A: Echocardiography alone, without any pulmonary function testing
options.B: Cyclophosphamide as first-line, ahead of mycophenolate, for all SSc-ILD
options.C: High-resolution CT only once symptoms are already present
options.D: HRCT chest with full PFTs (FVC and DLCO) in every patient at baseline; mycophenolate is first-line for significant or progressive SSc-ILD
options.E: An annual chest radiograph alone, without HRCT or PFTs

explanation: HRCT is advised at baseline in all patients with SSc, with PFTs including FVC and DLCO and regular follow-up PFTs, especially in early disease. MMF, cyclophosphamide or rituximab are used for SSc-ILD, with MMF commonly first. Nintedanib is added for progressive fibrosis, and tocilizumab may be considered in early ILD with raised acute-phase reactants. High-dose glucocorticoids risk renal crisis. Breathlessness in SSc: ILD, PAH, cardiac disease (diastolic dysfunction, myocarditis), aspiration from reflux, anaemia (GAVE), chest wall restriction from truncal skin, myositis (respiratory muscles), drug pneumonitis (methotrexate, cyclophosphamide), infection, lung cancer (higher in SSc-ILD). ILD is present on HRCT in 50–65%, and 25– 30% develop clinically progressive disease. It is the leading cause of death (30–35%). The usual pattern is NSIP. Risk factors: dcSSc, Scl-70, Th/To, U3-RNP, Ro52, male sex, African ancestry, early disease, raised CRP. Extent >20% on HRCT (Goh staging) predicts progression. Significant progression means FVC falls ≥10%, or 5–9% with DLCO ≥15%. Trial evidence: SLS-II (MMF ≈ cyclophosphamide, better tolerated); SLS-I (cyclophosphamide); RECITAL and DESIRES (rituximab); focuSSced (tocilizumab preserved FVC); SENSCIS (nintedanib slowed FVC decline by 40– 45%, including on MMF). Selected rapid progressors: AHSCT. End stage: oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation, lung transplant (needs reflux control). Monitoring: PFTs every 3–6 months in early disease, at least yearly otherwise; treat reflux.

stem: A 40-year-old man has early diffuse cutaneous SSc with rapidly progressive skin thickening (mRSS 28) and no significant organ involvement. Which treatment is most appropriate for the skin disease?

options.A: High-dose glucocorticoids alone, continued long-term
options.B: Cyclophosphamide alone, reserved specifically for skin disease
options.C: Rituximab as first-line, ahead of methotrexate or mycophenolate
options.D: Mycophenolate mofetil (or methotrexate or rituximab)
options.E: An ACE inhibitor, since it also helps skin fibrosis

explanation: Methotrexate, MMF or rituximab are used for skin fibrosis. Autologous stem cell transplantation is considered in selected rapidly progressive patients at experienced centres. Early dcSSc skin: methotrexate or MMF (preferred if ILD is present), or rituximab. Tocilizumab when CRP is raised (benefit mainly in lung preservation). GC only at ≤10–15 mg. Symptomatic care: emollients and antihistamines for itch, laser for telangiectasia, surgical removal of calcinosis (drug evidence for sodium thiosulfate, diltiazem or bisphosphonates is weak), physiotherapy for contractures, mouth exercises for microstomia. Emerging: CAR-T, anifrolumab.

stem: What is the role of autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in systemic sclerosis?

options.A: It is now first-line therapy for all diffuse SSc, regardless of organ risk
options.B: It carries no excess mortality compared with conventional immunosuppression
options.C: It is avoided in any patient with lung involvement
options.D: It is considered for selected patients with rapidly progressive diffuse disease at risk of organ failure, at experienced centres
options.E: It is used routinely for limited cutaneous disease with mild skin involvement

explanation: Trials show survival benefit in selected patients, balanced against substantial treatment-related mortality. Careful cardiopulmonary screening is required. ASTIS, SCOT and ASSIST trials showed event-free and overall survival benefit despite 5–10% treatment-related mortality. It suits selected patients under 65 with rapidly progressive dcSSc and without severe cardiac disease or advanced organ failure (cardiac MRI and right heart catheterisation screening).

stem: A woman with limited SSc has progressive breathlessness with FVC 92%, DLCO 41% (FVC/DLCO 2.2) and a raised tricuspid regurgitant velocity. How is PAH screened for and confirmed?

options.A: Spirometry alone, repeated only every 5 years regardless of symptoms
options.B: Serum troponin alone, checked only if the patient becomes symptomatic
options.C: Observation only, since FVC is well preserved at 92% predicted
options.D: Screen at least annually (PAH is often asymptomatic early; a normal echo doesn’t exclude it) using DLCO, NT-proBNP and echocardiography; confirm by right heart catheterisation
options.E: Right-heart catheterisation performed routinely in every patient annually

explanation: such as DETECT; confirm by right heart catheterisation Isolated low DLCO with a high FVC/DLCO ratio suggests PAH. Diagnosis needs right heart catheterisation: mean PAP above 20 mmHg, PAWP 15 mmHg or less, and PVR above 2 Wood units. PH groups in SSc (often coexisting): 1, PAH including pulmonary veno-occlusive disease (PVOD worsens on vasodilators: suspect it with septal lines, ground glass, lymphadenopathy or a very low DLCO); 2, left heart disease (diastolic dysfunction); 3, ILD with hypoxia; 4, CTEPH (V/Q scan). PAH affects 8–12% of patients. Risk factors: limited cutaneous disease, ACA, U3-RNP, Th/To, long duration, many telangiectasias, FVC/DLCO >1.6, raised NT-proBNP. DETECT applies to disease >3 years with DLCO <60%. Screening detects milder disease and improves survival. Echo, PFTs and NT-proBNP yearly; RHC if suspected; refer to a PH centre.

stem: A patient with SSc has newly diagnosed PAH (WHO functional class III) on right heart catheterisation, with low to intermediate risk. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: A single PDE5 inhibitor alone, reserving combination therapy for later escalation
options.B: High-dose glucocorticoids as the primary treatment
options.C: A TNF inhibitor
options.D: Observation with a repeat right heart catheterisation in 6 months before starting treatment
options.E: Initial combination therapy with a PDE5 inhibitor and an endothelin receptor antagonist

explanation: Initial combination therapy is standard. IV prostacyclin is added for high-risk patients. Vasoreactivity-guided CCB therapy does not apply to connective tissue disease-associated PAH. Initial dual therapy: an ERA (ambrisentan, macitentan) plus a PDE5 inhibitor (tadalafil, sildenafil), or riociguat in place of the PDE5 inhibitor. High risk: add parenteral prostacyclin (epoprostenol, treprostinil) or selexipag. Sotatercept (activin signalling inhibitor) is licensed as add-on therapy. Supportive care: diuretics, oxygen, rehabilitation, transplant referral. Anticoagulation is not routine (GAVE bleeding risk). Pregnancy is strongly advised against (ERAs are teratogenic). Three-year survival is 50–60% in older series and is improving.

stem: A woman with SSc has diarrhoea, bloating and weight loss. A glucose hydrogen breath test is positive. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: A single continuous course of broad-spectrum antibiotics for life
options.B: Total parenteral nutrition as first-line, before any antibiotic trial
options.C: Pancreatic enzyme replacement alone, without antibiotics
options.D: Oral vancomycin as first-line for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth
options.E: Rotating or intermittent courses of antibiotics for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

explanation: Small bowel dysmotility predisposes to bacterial overgrowth and malabsorption. Prokinetics help dysmotility, and nutritional screening with dietetic input is important. Rotate antibiotics (rifaximin, doxycycline, metronidazole, co-amoxiclav). Prokinetics (prucalopride, low-dose erythromycin, domperidone). Octreotide for pseudoobstruction. Correct B12 (often low from SIBO), vitamin D, iron and fat-soluble vitamins. Screen nutrition with MUST, BMI and albumin; parenteral nutrition for intestinal failure. Malnutrition predicts mortality. Pneumatosis intestinalis is often benign but needs surgical assessment if there is peritonism.

stem: A patient with SSc has severe reflux and dysphagia. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: PPI therapy with reflux measures, assessment of dysmotility and aspiration risk, and prokinetics or dilatation where indicated
options.B: Immediate oesophageal dilatation without a trial of medical therapy
options.C: Observation only, since dysphagia in SSc rarely needs active management
options.D: High-dose immunosuppression, since dysmotility reflects active inflammation
options.E: A PDE5 inhibitor, since it also improves oesophageal motility

explanation: Oesophageal dysmotility with reflux is near-universal in SSc. Aspiration can contribute to lung disease. High-dose PPI (often twice daily) with H2 blocker add-on at night; raise the head of the bed; small meals; prokinetics. Endoscopy for dysphagia, alarm features or Barrett’s surveillance; dilatation for strictures. Treat reflux aggressively in ILD (aspiration) and before lung transplant. GI involvement occurs in about 90% (mouth to anus).

stem: A 63-year-old woman with limited cutaneous SSc for 18 years has anaemia and melaena. Endoscopy shows linear red stripes in the gastric antrum. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE)
options.B: Multiple myeloma
options.C: Oesophageal variceal bleeding from portal hypertension
options.D: Peptic ulcer disease from chronic NSAID use
options.E: Right-heart catheterisation

explanation: GAVE (“watermelon stomach”) causes chronic GI bleeding in SSc and is treated endoscopically (argon plasma coagulation) with iron replacement. Iron-deficiency anaemia in SSc: GAVE, oesophagitis, telangiectasia bleeding anywhere in the GI tract, malabsorption (SIBO, coeliac overlap), NSAIDs, anticoagulants. Other causes of anaemia: renal crisis (MAHA), anaemia of chronic disease, B12 deficiency. Iron (often IV), endoscopic argon plasma coagulation (repeated) or band ligation. Transfusion if severe. GAVE is associated with anti-RNA pol III and early diffuse disease.

stem: What is the leading cause of death in systemic sclerosis?

options.A: Scleroderma renal crisis, now that it is uncommon with ACE inhibitor prophylaxis
options.B: Pulmonary complications: interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension
options.C: Right-heart catheterisation
options.D: Gastrointestinal bleeding from GAVE
options.E: Cardiac arrhythmia from myocardial fibrosis alone

explanation: Since ACE inhibitors transformed renal crisis outcomes, ILD and PAH are the main causes of SSc-related death. SSc-related deaths are about 55% of the total. Causes: ILD (commonest), PAH, cardiac disease; renal crisis is now uncommon. Non-SSc deaths: cancer, infection, atherosclerotic CVD. Poor prognostic factors: older onset, male sex, diffuse disease with high or rapidly rising mRSS, friction rubs, FVC <70%, PAH, cardiac involvement, renal crisis, raised CRP, anaemia.

stem: Which measures help hand function in systemic sclerosis?

options.A: Intra-articular steroid injection into every affected joint monthly
options.B: Hand physiotherapy and occupational therapy, stretching, skin care and joint protection
options.C: Systemic immunosuppression alone, without any rehabilitation input
options.D: Surgical release of contractures as the first-line measure
options.E: Botulinum toxin injection as the first-line measure for hand stiffness

explanation: Rehabilitation helps maintain range of movement and function. Hand OT and physiotherapy, splints, paraffin wax baths, stretching, skin care (emollients), and protecting the digits from cold and trauma. Mouth-stretching exercises and dental hygiene for microstomia. Treat calcinosis and contractures surgically where needed. Psychological support (body image, depression).

stem: What are the cardinal features of Sjögren’s disease?

options.A: Dry eyes and dry mouth due to lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands
options.B: Symmetrical peripheral synovitis with morning stiffness
options.C: Progressive proximal muscle weakness with a raised CK
options.D: Raynaud’s phenomenon with digital ulceration
options.E: Recurrent oral and genital ulceration

explanation: Sjögren’s can also affect joints, skin, lungs, kidneys, nerves and blood, and carries an increased lymphoma risk. Sicca causes:-Drugs (the commonest cause): anticholinergics, TCAs, SSRIs, antihistamines, diuretics, βblockers, opioids, antipsychotics, ICIs.-Age and lifestyle: ageing, menopause, mouth breathing, smoking, anxiety, dehydration.-Infection: HCV, HIV (DILS), HTLV-1, EBV.-Infiltrative: IgG4-RD, sarcoid, amyloid, lymphoma, haemochromatosis.-Other: head and neck radiation, GVHD, diabetes, fibromyalgia, blepharitis or meibomian gland dysfunction, contact lenses, prior LASIK. Oral: red, fissured, depapillated tongue; “cracker sign”; cervical (gum-line) caries; candidiasis and angular cheilitis. Eyes: grittiness, mucus strands, punctate erosions, filamentary keratitis. Also nasal crusting, dry cough (xerotrachea), xerosis, vaginal dryness. Fatigue (70–80%) is the most disabling symptom.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has dry eyes and mouth. Anti-Ro/SSA is positive and Schirmer’s test is 4 mm in 5 minutes in both eyes. Lip biopsy has not been performed. How does she score on the 2016 Sjögren’s classification criteria?

options.A: 3; she does not meet the classification criteria
options.B: 5; she meets the classification criteria on serology alone
options.C: 6; she meets the classification criteria even without any positive test
options.D: 4; she is classified as having Sjögren’s
options.E: 3 points; he meets the criteria

explanation: Weighted items: labial gland focus score 1 or more (3), anti-Ro/SSA (3), ocular staining score 5 or more (1), Schirmer 5 mm/5 min or less (1), unstimulated salivary flow 0.1 mL/min or less (1). A score of 4 or more classifies, provided inclusion criteria are met and exclusions are absent. Anti-La alone does not score. Entry requires ocular or oral dryness symptoms, or suspected SjD from an ESSDAI domain. Exclusions: head and neck radiation, active HCV (PCR-positive), AIDS, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, GVHD, IgG4-RD. Either a positive biopsy or anti-Ro is needed, because the minor items total only 3. Stop anticholinergic drugs before testing. Investigations: Schirmer I, ocular staining score, tear breakup time, unstimulated sialometry, salivary ultrasound, labial biopsy if seronegative. Also anti-Ro and anti-La, RF, immunoglobulins, C3/C4, cryoglobulins, SPEP and FLC, FBC, urinalysis, U&E and bicarbonate.

stem: What does the ESSDAI measure in Sjögren’s disease?

options.A: Systemic disease activity across 12 organ domains
options.B: Patient-reported dryness, fatigue and pain alone
options.C: Glandular involvement only, without other organ domains
options.D: Response to rituximab specifically, as a treatment-response index
options.E: Diagnostic classification, not disease activity

explanation: The ESSDAI guides systemic treatment. The patient-reported ESSPRI captures dryness, fatigue and pain. ESSDAI domains: constitutional, lymphadenopathy, glandular, articular, cutaneous, pulmonary, renal, muscular, PNS, CNS, haematological and biological. It is the primary outcome in trials.

stem: Which medication class commonly worsens dryness in Sjögren’s disease?

options.A: ACE inhibitors and ARBs
options.B: Topical beta-blockers for glaucoma
options.C: Anticholinergic drugs, sedating antihistamines and tricyclic antidepressants
options.D: TNF inhibitors
options.E: SGLT2 inhibitors for diabetes

explanation: Medication review is an important part of managing sicca symptoms. Review and switch drying drugs: anticholinergic bladder drugs (try mirabegron), sedating antihistamines (use nonsedating), TCAs (alternative analgesics), diuretics, opioids, antipsychotics. Also avoid caffeine, alcohol and smoking.

stem: What is the stepwise management of dry eyes in Sjögren’s disease, including severe dry eye with corneal damage despite frequent tears?

options.A: Oral pilocarpine alone, without any topical treatment
options.B: Preservative-free artificial tears and gels with lid hygiene first; for refractory disease, topical ciclosporin
options.C: Systemic immunosuppression as first-line, before any topical treatment
options.D: Punctal plugs as the first step, before any lubricant trial
options.E: Rituximab as first-line for routine dry eye without corneal damage

explanation: (or lifitegrast) with ophthalmology input, plus autologous serum drops, punctal plugs or short topical steroid courses Ocular lubricants are foundational; use preservative-free drops if more than 4 times daily, and gels or ointments at night. Refractory disease is managed under ophthalmology care with topical immunomodulatory drops, autologous serum drops or punctal plugs. Short courses of topical steroid may be used with care. Avoid dry environments and screen glare, and use wraparound glasses. Scleral lenses for severe disease. Oral pilocarpine also helps the eyes. Watch for corneal ulceration or melt.

stem: How is xerostomia managed according to residual gland function, and which dental complication is particularly important?

options.A: Pilocarpine prescribed for all patients, regardless of residual salivary gland function
options.B: Tailor to gland function: stimulation for mild dysfunction, pilocarpine or cevimeline if function remains, saliva substitutes if none; rapid dental caries is the key complication
options.C: Dental extraction as the first-line response to any caries risk identified
options.D: Saliva substitutes used first-line, even with substantial residual gland function remaining
options.E: No specific dental surveillance is needed beyond routine general population screening

explanation: Muscarinic agonists stimulate residual function; sweating and urinary frequency are common adverse effects. Immunosuppressants do not improve dryness. Regular dental review, fluoride and treatment of oral candidiasis are essential. General measures: frequent sips of water, sugar-free gum or xylitol lozenges, a humidifier. Dental: high-fluoride toothpaste (5000 ppm), fluoride varnish, review every 3–6 months, treat candida. Substitutes: gels, sprays, oxygenated glycerol triester. Pilocarpine 5 mg 3–4 times daily (contraindicated in asthma, narrow-angle glaucoma and uncontrolled cardiac disease).

stem: What is the role of systemic treatment in Sjögren’s disease with fatigue and arthralgia but no organ involvement, and with mild inflammatory arthritis?

options.A: Immunosuppression started empirically for fatigue alone, without assessing reversible causes
options.B: High-dose glucocorticoids as first-line treatment for even mild inflammatory arthritis
options.C: Fatigue alone does not warrant immunosuppression; assess reversible causes first. For arthritis: hydroxychloroquine with short-term glucocorticoids if needed, and methotrexate for persistent disease
options.D: Biologic therapy started as first-line for arthralgia without any synovitis present
options.E: Methotrexate started immediately for fatigue, before any other assessment

explanation: Fatigue, pain and dryness respond poorly to immunosuppression; exercise, sleep and treatment of comorbidity are central. The BSR guideline allows a 6–12 month trial of hydroxychloroquine for significant fatigue and systemic symptoms, but not routine immunosuppressants. Hydroxychloroquine is used for musculoskeletal and cutaneous features. Fatigue contributors: hypothyroidism (15–30% have autoimmune thyroiditis), anaemia, coeliac disease, depression, poor sleep (nocturia, dry mouth), fibromyalgia, PBC, RTA with hypokalaemia. Arthritis in SjD is symmetrical, non-erosive and intermittent (Jaccoud-type is possible). Erosions or anti-CCP suggest RA overlap.

stem: A woman with Sjögren’s has severe refractory systemic disease, such as cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis with palpable purpura, neuropathy and glomerulonephritis (HCV-negative, type II cryoglobulins). What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: B-cell targeted therapy with rituximab plus glucocorticoids, adding plasma exchange for lifethreatening disease
options.B: Watchful waiting, since cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis in Sjögren’s is usually self-limiting
options.C: Topical treatment alone, since systemic involvement is not present
options.D: Oral prednisolone alone, without rituximab or plasma exchange
options.E: Anticoagulation as the primary treatment, given the vasculitic presentation

explanation: Rituximab is used for severe refractory systemic disease, particularly cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis, which is a severe fatigue (TEARS and TRACTISS trials). By manifestation: | Manifestation | Treatment | |—|—| | Cutaneous vasculitis or purpura | GC; rituximab if cryoglobulinaemic | | ILD | GC + MMF or azathioprine; rituximab; nintedanib if progressive | | Cryoglobulinaemic GN, vasculitic neuropathy | pulse GC + rituximab or cyclophosphamide; PLEX | | Sensory ganglionopathy | often refractory: IVIG, rituximab | | Small-fibre neuropathy | neuropathic agents; IVIG in selected cases | | Cytopenias | GC, rituximab, IVIG | | CNS or myelitis | pulse GC + cyclophosphamide or rituximab | Belimumab is used off-label in some cases.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with Sjögren’s has persistent unilateral parotid enlargement for 6 months, palpable purpura, low C4 and mixed cryoglobulins. What is the most important concern?

options.A: Risk-stratified malignancy screening
options.B: The A1 pulley at the metacarpal head
options.C: B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma
options.D: Sarcoidosis with Heerfordt syndrome
options.E: Development of MALT lymphoma

explanation: Lymphoma risk (about 5-10% lifetime, mostly MALT) is higher with persistent gland enlargement, purpura, low C4, cryoglobulinaemia, monoclonal gammopathy and lymphopenia. Ultrasound and biopsy of the gland are warranted. Parotid enlargement:-Bilateral: SjD, IgG4-RD (Mikulicz), sarcoid (Heerfordt’s: parotitis, uveitis, facial palsy, fever), HIV (DILS, lymphoepithelial cysts), HCV, diabetes, alcohol, bulimia, malnutrition, amyloid, mumps, drugs (iodine).-Unilateral or firm: MALT lymphoma, pleomorphic adenoma, Warthin’s tumour, parotid carcinoma, bacterial parotitis or stones. Lymphoma predictors: persistent parotid enlargement, palpable purpura, low C4 (and C3), cryoglobulins, monoclonal component, raised β2-microglobulin and FLC, CD4 lymphopenia, neutropenia, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, high ESSDAI, young onset, male sex, focus score ≥3, germinal centres. High-risk patients: review every 3–6 months with parotid ultrasound, and biopsy any persistent mass (core or open). MALT lymphoma: rituximab-based regimens (± chemotherapy) with haematology. Gastric MALT may need H. pylori eradication.

stem: A 39-year-old woman with Sjögren’s has weakness, serum potassium 2.6 mmol/L, a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis and urine pH 6.5. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis from primary aldosteronism
options.B: Small-fibre neuropathy
options.C: Levamisole-adulterated cocaine
options.D: Distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis due to tubulointerstitial nephritis
options.E: Diuretic-induced hypokalaemia with metabolic alkalosis

explanation: Tubulointerstitial nephritis typically causes distal RTA, with inability to acidify urine, hypokalaemia and nephrocalcinosis. Glomerulonephritis is less common and often related to cryoglobulinaemia. Normal anion gap acidosis with hypokalaemia: distal (type 1) RTA (urine pH >5.5; SjD, SLE, PBC, amphotericin, lithium, toluene); proximal (type 2) RTA (bicarbonate wasting, Fanconi syndrome: myeloma, tenofovir, ifosfamide, Wilson’s); diarrhoea (urine anion gap negative); ureteric diversion; acetazolamide. TIN with distal RTA can cause hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, nephrocalcinosis, stones and osteomalacia. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and Fanconi syndrome also occur. TIN occurs early; GN (MPGN from cryoglobulins) occurs later and signals lymphoma risk. Potassium citrate or bicarbonate. GC (± MMF, rituximab) for active TIN with declining eGFR. Renal biopsy if eGFR is falling or there is proteinuria or haematuria.

stem: A woman with Sjögren’s has burning feet with normal nerve conduction studies. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Adhesive capsulitis
options.B: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy
options.C: Inclusion-body myositis
options.D: Small-fibre neuropathy
options.E: Tarsal tunnel syndrome

explanation: Small-fibre neuropathy is a recognised extraglandular feature and is confirmed by skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density. Sensory ganglionopathy also occurs. Burning feet: small-fibre neuropathy (SjD, sarcoid, diabetes or prediabetes, alcohol, HIV, amyloid, Fabry disease, B12 deficiency, coeliac disease, chemotherapy) vs large-fibre length-dependent neuropathy (abnormal NCS), tarsal tunnel syndrome, erythromelalgia (myeloproliferative), sensory ganglionopathy (non-length-dependent, ataxic). Sensory ganglionopathy is characteristic of SjD: asymmetric sensory ataxia with pseudoathetosis and areflexia, from dorsal root ganglion injury. Exclude paraneoplastic anti-Hu ganglionopathy (small cell lung cancer) and cisplatin. Other neurology: trigeminal neuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex (cryoglobulins), autonomic neuropathy, myelitis or NMOSD (AQP4-IgG), white matter lesions. Small-fibre neuropathy: confirm with skin biopsy (reduced intraepidermal nerve fibre density) or QSART; treat with neuropathic analgesia, with IVIG in selected immune cases. Ganglionopathy responds poorly (IVIG, rituximab).

stem: What are the typical clinical features of inflammatory myopathy, and which rash is characteristic of dermatomyositis?

options.A: Symmetrical small-joint synovitis with morning stiffness over an hour
options.B: Asymmetric distal weakness with sparing of facial muscles
options.C: A malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, with photosensitivity
options.D: Subacute, symmetrical proximal weakness with raised muscle enzymes; Gottron’s papules and a heliotrope rash are characteristic of dermatomyositis
options.E: Painless proximal weakness without any skin involvement, typical of all subtypes

explanation: Extramuscular involvement includes ILD, dysphagia, myocarditis and arthritis. Skin disease may precede or dominate muscle involvement (clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis). DM rash mimics: SLE (spares the knuckles), psoriasis (scalp), seborrhoeic dermatitis, rosacea, contact dermatitis, drug eruption (hydroxyurea DM-like eruption), photosensitivity reactions, flagellate erythema from bleomycin or shiitake mushrooms. Pathognomonic DM signs: Gottron’s papules and sign, heliotrope rash. Characteristic: V-sign, shawl and holster signs, facial erythema, flagellate erythema, itchy scalp, inverse Gottron’s (palmar), periungual erythema with ragged cuticles. Late: poikiloderma, calcinosis. Skin can precede weakness by 3–6 months. Prominent myalgia suggests another diagnosis. Use CDASI to measure skin activity. Photoprotection matters (UV triggers skin and muscle flares).

stem: A patient with suspected inflammatory myositis has a normal CK. Does this exclude myositis?

options.A: A normal CK does not exclude myositis; review weakness, other enzymes, MRI, EMG, antibodies and biopsy
options.B: Yes; a normal CK makes myositis very unlikely regardless of other features
options.C: Yes, provided EMG is also normal
options.D: No, but only if the patient also has a rash
options.E: Yes, in patients over 60 years of age

explanation: normal CK does not exclude myositis; review weakness, other enzymes, MRI, EMG, antibodies and biopsy Clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis (especially anti-MDA5) and longstanding disease may have normal CK. CK is normal in about 20% of DM. Aldolase can be raised with a normal CK in perimysial or fascial disease. AST and ALT are usually muscle-derived, so check GGT before blaming methotrexate. EMG shows a myopathic pattern with fibrillations; a normal EMG does not exclude IIM. CK is reliable for activity in IMNM, partly in ASyS, and not in DM or IBM.

stem: A patient with suspected inflammatory myositis needs a muscle biopsy. Which investigation best guides biopsy site selection?

options.A: MRI of the sacroiliac joints using inflammatory sequences
options.B: MRI of the thighs with STIR (fat-suppressed) sequences
options.C: Cross-sectional vascular imaging such as PET-CT, CTA or MRA
options.D: Plain radiographs of the affected limb
options.E: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis

explanation: STIR MRI shows active muscle oedema and avoids sampling end-stage or unaffected muscle. If EMG is used, the contralateral muscle should be biopsied to avoid needle artefact. Target an affected but not end-stage muscle (deltoid, biceps, vastus lateralis), avoiding recently needled muscles. A biopsy is not always needed: a typical clinical picture plus an MSA (DM rash with anti-TIF1γ; anti-HMGCR with typical IMNM) may suffice. Biopsy when antibodies are negative or discordant, when IBM, dystrophy or metabolic myopathy is possible, or when the response is poor. Sarcoplasmic MxA is highly specific for DM (ENMC criteria).

stem: At diagnosis of inflammatory myositis, what should be assessed?

options.A: Genetic testing for muscular dystrophy in every patient
options.B: Muscle strength, CK, lung function and HRCT, swallowing, cardiac involvement and malignancy risk
options.C: HLA-B27 status alone, without any organ-specific assessment
options.D: A single CK measurement alone, without functional or organ assessment
options.E: Joint ultrasound alone, without any assessment of lung or cardiac involvement

explanation: Extramuscular disease drives prognosis, and antibody profile guides risk stratification. At diagnosis: MMT-8, CK, PFTs with DLCO plus HRCT (for all), swallowing assessment (SLT), troponin I, ECG and echo (CMR if suspected), an extended myositis antibody panel, cancer screening stratified by risk, bone health, CV risk and vaccination. Severe features: MRC <3 proximally, dysphagia or aspiration, falling FVC or nocturnal hypoventilation, rapid progression, rhabdomyolysis, cardiac involvement.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has Gottron’s papules, periungual erythema, painful palmar papules, digital ulcers and rapidly worsening breathlessness. CK is normal and HRCT shows rapidly progressive ground-glass change and consolidation. Which antibody is most likely?

options.A: Anti-histone
options.B: Anti-Jo-1
options.C: Anti-SRP
options.D: Anti-TIF1-gamma
options.E: Anti-MDA5

explanation: Anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis is often clinically amyopathic with cutaneous ulceration and carries a high risk of rapidly progressive ILD with high mortality. Early intensive combination immunosuppression is used. RP-ILD in a CTD: anti-MDA5, ASyS with acute exacerbation, SLE pneumonitis or DAH, PJP, CMV, COVID-19, drug pneumonitis, acute exacerbation of fibrotic ILD. Anti-MDA5 skin clues: palmar papules, painful digital ulcers or skin necrosis, alopecia, oral ulcers, arthritis, little weakness. Ferritin and KL-6 are raised. Pathogenesis involves intense type I IFN, macrophage activation and lung vasculopathy. Early mortality from RP-ILD is 30–60%. An emergency: pulse GC plus two more agents immediately (the Japanese triple regimen of high-dose GC, tacrolimus and IV cyclophosphamide; or rituximab, MMF, IVIG or tofacitinib). Add PLEX if refractory. Monitor for CMV and PJP (give prophylaxis). Track ferritin and KL-6. Refer early for lung transplant.

stem: A 49-year-old woman has proximal weakness, non-erosive arthritis, cracked hyperkeratotic skin on the radial borders of her fingers, Raynaud’s phenomenon and basal crackles. Which antibody is most likely?

options.A: Anti-MDA5
options.B: Anti-SRP
options.C: Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70)
options.D: Anti-Jo-1
options.E: High-resolution CT chest

explanation: Antisynthetase syndrome (anti-Jo-1, PL-7, PL-12 and others) features myositis, ILD, mechanic’s hands, Raynaud’s, arthritis and fever. ILD determines prognosis and may dominate. Antisynthetase antibodies: Jo-1 (commonest; myositis plus ILD), PL-7 and PL-12 (lung-dominant, little myositis), EJ, OJ, KS, Zo, Ha. Arthritis occurs in up to 90%, is symmetric and non-erosive, and can sublux (“floppy thumb” in about 19% of Jo-1). ACPA, RF and Ro52 can be positive. ILD is usually NSIP or OP. The model is lung-first (smoking or inhaled triggers in HLA-DRB1*03:01 carriers). Test the extended myositis panel in any “seronegative RA” with ILD, mechanic’s hands or raised CK. Treatment is driven by the lung: GC plus MMF, azathioprine or tacrolimus; methotrexate for arthritis without significant ILD; rituximab or IV cyclophosphamide for severe or progressive ILD (RECITAL showed similar efficacy, with fewer adverse events for rituximab).

stem: A 67-year-old man presents with a heliotrope rash, shawl sign and proximal weakness. Anti-TIF1-gamma is positive. What is the most important next step?

options.A: Topical steroid treatment for the skin alone, without systemic assessment
options.B: Enhanced malignancy screening, including CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, with age-and sexappropriate tests
options.C: Genetic counselling only, since this is a familial condition
options.D: Reassurance, since TIF1-gamma is not associated with malignancy in adults
options.E: Immediate high-dose immunosuppression alone, without any cancer screening

explanation: Anti-TIF1-gamma and anti-NXP2 in adult dermatomyositis confer high cancer risk. Screening is repeated over the first 3 years, when risk is greatest. Cancer risk by group: | Group | Cancer risk | |—|—| | Anti-TIF1γ (adult DM) | very high (20–50%) | | Anti-NXP2 (adult) | moderate to high | | Seronegative DM or IMNM | high | | SAE, Mi-2 | intermediate | | HMGCR | uncertain or modest | | SRP, ASyS, overlap, MDA5 (Western) | low | | IBM, juvenile | not raised | About a quarter of adults with IIM develop cancer within 3 years either side of onset (up to 30% in DM). High-risk features: age >40, male sex, dysphagia, skin necrosis or ulceration, rapid onset, refractoriness, TIF1γ, NXP2, seronegative disease. Lower risk: ILD, Raynaud’s, arthritis, antisynthetase antibodies. Tumours can express mutated TIF1 genes, making the myositis paraneoplastic. IMACS screening: a basic panel for standard risk; basic plus enhanced (CT neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis; tumour markers; mammography; pelvic and TV ultrasound; FOB) for moderate risk; enhanced panel annually for 3 years for high risk, with FDG-PET if negative. Nasoendoscopy for South-East Asian patients (nasopharyngeal carcinoma). Re-screen at flare or refractoriness. Treat the cancer first. IVIG spares GC without oncological concern.

stem: In juvenile dermatomyositis, which antibody is most strongly associated with calcinosis?

options.A: Anti-MDA5
options.B: Anti-Jo-1
options.C: Anti-Sm
options.D: Anti-NXP2
options.E: Anti-histone

explanation: Anti-NXP2 is associated with calcinosis and more severe muscle disease. Early, effective disease control reduces calcinosis risk. JDM accounts for up to 4 per million children per year. Antibodies include TIF1γ (the commonest in JDM, but not cancer-associated in children), NXP2 (calcinosis, severe weakness, GI vasculopathy), MDA5 (ILD, arthritis, ulcers) and Mi-2. Calcinosis occurs in 20–40% overall, more with delayed treatment. Aggressive early control: pulse methylprednisolone with methotrexate (first line), then IVIG, MMF, rituximab or JAK inhibitors. Calcinosis has no validated treatment (options: intensify immunosuppression, sodium thiosulfate, bisphosphonates, diltiazem, surgery). Photoprotection.

stem: A 70-year-old man on atorvastatin for 3 years has progressive proximal weakness. CK is 8,500 U/L and weakness persists 3 months after stopping the statin. Biopsy shows necrotic fibres with minimal inflammation. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.A: Inclusion-body myositis
options.B: Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy; immunosuppression such as glucocorticoids with IVIG and/or methotrexate
options.C: Hypothyroid myopathy; thyroid replacement alone
options.D: Toxic statin myopathy; reassurance since it will resolve within weeks of stopping
options.E: Relapsing polychondritis

explanation: Anti-HMGCR myopathy persists after statin withdrawal and needs immunosuppression; IVIG is particularly effective. Statins should be avoided thereafter. Statin-related muscle disease: toxic self-limited myopathy (improves within weeks of stopping; HMGCR negative) vs anti-HMGCR IMNM (persists or progresses after stopping; HMGCR positive; HLA-DRB1*11:01). Also hypothyroidism (which raises statin myopathy risk), interacting drugs (fibrates, macrolides, ciclosporin), and an unmasked metabolic myopathy. Stop statins and never restart. Use PCSK9 inhibitors or ezetimibe for lipids. GC plus IVIG at induction, plus methotrexate or another DMARD. IVIG can be used early or even first-line. CK tracks activity and guides tapering. Younger anti-HMGCR patients recover more slowly and may mimic a dystrophy. Zilucoplan failed in phase 2; FcRn blockers are under study.

stem: A 38-year-old woman has rapidly progressive severe proximal weakness, dysphagia, CK 15,000 U/L and an arrhythmia. Biopsy shows necrotising myopathy with minimal inflammation. Which antibody is most likely?

options.A: Anti-Jo-1
options.B: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT
options.C: Thyroid function tests
options.D: Anti-SRP
options.E: Anti-MDA5

explanation: Anti-SRP is associated with severe necrotising myopathy, dysphagia and cardiac involvement, often needing early combination therapy. Anti-SRP (about 5% of IIM): acute aggressive proximal weakness, very high CK, early atrophy, dysphagia, cardiac involvement and sometimes ILD; no rash or arthritis. It is often steroid-refractory. IMNM antibodies are directly pathogenic (complement-mediated), and titres track CK and strength. Aggressive early therapy: GC plus IVIG plus early rituximab, then MMF or tacrolimus; PLEX in case reports. Cardiac monitoring.

stem: A 72-year-old man has 3 years of slowly progressive finger flexor and quadriceps weakness, falls, dysphagia, a mildly raised CK and positive anti-cN1A antibodies. What is the likely diagnosis and how does it respond to treatment?

options.A: Antisynthetase syndrome, which responds well to early immunosuppression
options.B: Anti-HMGCR necrotising myopathy, which improves rapidly with IVIG
options.C: This is likely inclusion body myositis, which responds poorly to immunosuppression; management is supportive
options.D: Polymyositis, which typically responds well to glucocorticoids alone
options.E: A statin-induced toxic myopathy that will resolve within weeks

explanation: IBM typically affects people over 50 with asymmetric deep finger flexor and quadriceps weakness. Biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles. Exercise, falls prevention and swallowing management are key. Distal or asymmetric weakness: ALS (fasciculations, UMN signs), myotonic dystrophy, distal myopathies, FSHD (scapular winging, facial weakness), multifocal motor neuropathy, CIDP, sporadic late-onset nemaline myopathy (paraprotein). IBM: over 45, male; insidious asymmetric weakness of the deep finger flexors and quadriceps; falls in 40–70%; dysphagia (cricopharyngeal) in 40–60%; CK <15× ULN. Diagnosis is often delayed by 3–5 years. Anti-cN1A is present in 30–50% but also occurs in Sjögren’s and SLE. It is associated with T-LGL leukaemia and Sjögren’s. Strength falls by 3.5–17% per year, but life expectancy is near normal. There is no approved disease-modifying drug. Use exercise, falls prevention, orthoses (knee brace, AFO), OT, SLT, and IVIG, cricopharyngeal dilatation or myotomy for dysphagia. Avoid long-term GC (they lower CK but do not help strength). Failed trials: bimagrumab, arimoclomol, ulviprubart (anti-KLRG1). A sirolimus trial is ongoing.

stem: What is the first-line treatment for active dermatomyositis or polymyositis, and how does it change with severe weakness and dysphagia with aspiration risk?

options.A: NSAIDs and physiotherapy alone, reserving glucocorticoids for severe cases
options.B: Methotrexate alone, without any glucocorticoid at all, even in severe disease
options.C: Topical steroids alone, since the disease is considered primarily cutaneous
options.D: IV immunoglobulin alone, without any glucocorticoid, used as first-line treatment
options.E: High-dose glucocorticoids with an early steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate); severe disease needs IV methylprednisolone pulses with IVIG

explanation: and an early steroid-sparing agent IVIG, rituximab or calcineurin inhibitors are used for refractory or severe disease, and cyclophosphamide for severe ILD. IVIG has proven efficacy in dermatomyositis and is useful for dysphagia. Speech and language therapy swallowing assessment is essential, and respiratory muscle weakness needs monitoring. Prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day (40–60 mg), tapering after about 6 weeks according to response, to 10–20 mg by 6 months and ideally ≤5 mg. Continue a DMARD for ≥2 years after remission. Methotrexate is not contraindicated in ILD, but MMF or tacrolimus is preferred when ILD dominates. IVIG (2 g/kg every 4 weeks) carries a thromboembolism risk, so hydrate and infuse slowly. Supportive: PJP prophylaxis with high-dose GC plus a second agent (especially in ILD or anti-MDA5); specialist exercise programme (safe even in active disease); bone health; vaccination. Skin: photoprotection, topical steroids or tacrolimus, HCQ (drug rash is more common in DM), methotrexate, MMF, IVIG, JAK inhibitors. Refractory disease: rituximab (RIM trial missed its primary endpoint, but most patients improved), abatacept, cyclophosphamide, JAKi or brepocitinib, CAR-T trials. Failure to improve at 4–6 months: consider wrong diagnosis (dystrophy, Pompe), IBM, steroid myopathy (normal CK, no MRI oedema), damage (fat on MRI), hidden cancer, non-adherence.

stem: A patient with active polymyositis has a raised troponin T without chest pain or ECG change. Which test best distinguishes cardiac from skeletal muscle origin?

options.A: Serum myoglobin
options.B: Troponin I
options.C: Serum IGF-1
options.D: CK-MB alone, without troponin
options.E: Repeat troponin T in 24 hours without further testing

explanation: Troponin T and CK-MB can be released from regenerating skeletal muscle, whereas troponin I is cardiac-specific. A raised troponin I warrants assessment for myocarditis. A raised troponin I warrants ECG, echo and CMR (T2 oedema, LGE), with Holter monitoring. Treat myocarditis with intensified immunosuppression (pulse GC, IVIG) and cardiology input. Screen all adults with troponin I, ECG and echo; IIM also raises atherosclerotic risk.

stem: What is the significance of myositis-associated antibodies (such as anti-PM/Scl, anti-Ku and anti-U1-RNP) compared with myositis-specific antibodies?

options.A: They are more specific than myositis-specific antibodies for predicting malignancy
options.B: They indicate a worse prognosis than myositis-specific antibodies in all cases
options.C: They indicate overlap connective tissue disease features rather than a specific myositis subtype
options.D: They are mutually exclusive with myositis-specific antibodies and never coexist
options.E: They define distinct myositis subtypes, just as myositis-specific antibodies do

explanation: Myositis-specific antibodies (Jo-1, MDA5, SRP, HMGCR, TIF1-gamma, Mi-2, NXP2) define clinical phenotypes, whereas associated antibodies suggest overlap syndromes. MAA associations: anti-PM/Scl (SSc overlap, ILD, calcinosis, mechanic’s hands; good muscle response); anti-Ku (SSc or SLE overlap, arthritis); anti-U1-RNP (MCTD); anti-Ro52 (worse ILD when combined with Jo-1 or MDA5). Overlap myositis is treated by the dominant organ: IVIG and GC for muscle, MMF or rituximab for ILD, methotrexate or biologics for erosive arthritis, CCBs and PDE5 inhibitors for Raynaud’s.

stem: A patient has suspected GCA: new temporal headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and CRP 82 mg/L without visual symptoms, or transient monocular visual loss in the past 24 hours. What is the immediate glucocorticoid regimen?

options.A: Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily, titrated up only if symptoms persist
options.B: Without visual symptoms: prednisolone 40–60 mg daily immediately with urgent fast-track referral.
options.C: Delay glucocorticoids until ultrasound or biopsy confirms the diagnosis
options.D: No glucocorticoids until ophthalmology has excluded other causes of headache
options.E: IV methylprednisolone for all patients regardless of visual symptoms, as a precaution

explanation: With evolving visual loss or amaurosis fugax: IV methylprednisolone 500 mg–1 g daily for up to 3 days, then highdose oral prednisolone, with same-day ophthalmology High-dose glucocorticoids are started the same day when GCA is strongly suspected, without waiting for investigations; specialist assessment should follow within days, and ultrasound and biopsy remain informative early in treatment. If IV treatment is not immediately available for visual symptoms, oral prednisolone 60 mg should be given at once. Established blindness rarely recovers, so protecting the other eye is the goal. New headache over 50: GCA vs intracranial mass or haemorrhage, cervicogenic headache, migraine (new over 50 is atypical), TMJ disorder or dental pain, trigeminal neuralgia, glaucoma, herpes zoster (pre-eruptive), sinusitis, AAV involving the temporal artery, crowned dens syndrome, medication-overuse headache, hypertension or PRES. Visual loss with a swollen disc and normal CRP suggests non-arteritic AION. Symptoms improve within 24–72 hours of GC. CRP normalises in 1–2 weeks (ESR in 2–4 weeks). Routine pulses without ischaemic features are not recommended. Avoid more than 60 mg/day.

stem: A patient with suspected GCA was started on glucocorticoids yesterday. What should happen to diagnostic testing, and when and how should temporal artery biopsy be done?

options.A: Stop glucocorticoids until biopsy is performed, to preserve test sensitivity
options.B: Delay the biopsy for at least 4 weeks to allow the inflammation to settle first
options.C: Proceed urgently with ultrasound and/or biopsy, never withholding treatment to preserve test sensitivity; biopsy ideally within 2 weeks of starting glucocorticoids
options.D: A negative biopsy performed at this stage reliably excludes a diagnosis of GCA
options.E: Biopsy is no longer useful once glucocorticoids have started, so it should not be done

explanation: Sensitivity declines with time on steroids but remains useful in the first days. Confirming the diagnosis matters because treatment is prolonged and toxic. Skip lesions cause false negatives, so an adequate length is needed, and a negative biopsy does not exclude GCA, particularly large-vessel disease. Biopsy sensitivity is 60–80% (it shrinks to about 0.7 cm after fixation; still useful up to 4 weeks). Contralateral biopsy adds little. Steroids reduce ultrasound yield after 1–2 weeks and PET yield after a few days. High probability plus positive imaging needs no further test. Low probability plus negative imaging makes GCA unlikely. Use biopsy when imaging is unavailable, equivocal, or negative despite high suspicion.

stem: In a fast-track GCA clinic, what is the first-line imaging test for suspected cranial GCA?

options.A: Ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries
options.B: MRI of the brain with contrast
options.C: CT angiography of the aorta
options.D: Temporal artery biopsy, before any imaging
options.E: FDG-PET/CT as the routine first test

explanation: A non-compressible halo sign supports GCA, with accuracy comparable to biopsy in experienced hands. FDG-PET, CT or MR angiography assess large-vessel involvement. Halo sign mimics: atherosclerosis (calcified plaques, older people), AAV involving the temporal artery, amyloid, and operator error (excess compression or gain). FDG-PET/CT is best for large-vessel and aortic disease and PUO; modern scanners also detect cranial arteries. Highresolution cranial MRI shows mural enhancement. CTA or MRA images the aorta and its branches.

stem: A 72-year-old woman has arm claudication, constitutional upset and a raised CRP, but no headache or jaw claudication and normal temporal arteries. Could this be GCA?

options.A: No, since normal temporal arteries exclude GCA
options.B: No, because jaw claudication is required for the diagnosis
options.C: No, limb claudication always indicates peripheral arterial disease instead
options.D: No, since CRP elevation without cranial symptoms suggests an alternative diagnosis
options.E: GCA can present with large-vessel (extracranial) disease without cranial symptoms

explanation: Large-vessel GCA causes limb claudication, bruits, pulse or blood pressure asymmetry and aortitis. Imaging of the aorta and branches (ultrasound, PET-CT, CT or MR angiography) is used. Aortitis and large-vessel vasculitis: GCA, Takayasu (<40), IgG4-related periaortitis, Behçet’s, Cogan’s syndrome, relapsing polychondritis, SpA (aortic root), sarcoid, Erdheim–Chester (“coated aorta”), infection (syphilis, TB, Salmonella, Staphylococcus: mycotic aneurysm), isolated aortitis (found at surgery), radiation. Atherosclerosis can mimic it on imaging. Baseline aortic imaging (CT, MRA or PET) in all patients with GCA, and surveillance every 1–2 years with largevessel involvement or risk factors. Control BP and stop smoking.

stem: How should glucocorticoids be tapered once GCA is controlled, and what is added for a patient who relapses twice below 15 mg daily?

options.A: Taper to 7.5 mg/day within 1 month, stopping by 6 months regardless of relapse
options.B: Add etanercept, a TNF inhibitor, specifically for relapsing polymyalgia disease
options.C: Increase prednisolone indefinitely rather than adding any steroid-sparing agent
options.D: Stop glucocorticoids abruptly as soon as the CRP level normalises
options.E: Taper to 15–20 mg/day within 2–3 months, aiming to stop within 12–18 months; for relapsing disease add tocilizumab, with upadacitinib or methotrexate as alternatives

explanation: Initial prednisolone 40–60 mg/day is tapered to 15–20 mg/day within 2–3 months. The 2025 EULAR recommendations aim to stop glucocorticoids within 12–18 months (the 2018 version targeted 5 mg/day or less after 1 year). Tocilizumab increases sustained remission and reduces cumulative glucocorticoid dose. The 2025 EULAR recommendations reserve adjunctive therapy (tocilizumab, or the JAK inhibitor upadacitinib) for relapsing or refractory disease or high glucocorticoid-toxicity risk, with methotrexate as an alternative. TNF inhibitors are ineffective in GCA. Relapses occur in 40–60%, usually below 10–15 mg or within 2 years, most often as PMR or headache. A rising CRP alone is not a relapse. Tocilizumab and upadacitinib suppress CRP and ESR, so judge activity clinically and by imaging. With tocilizumab or upadacitinib, a 26-week taper to zero is standard. Tocilizumab is usually given for 1 year (sometimes 2), and relapse after stopping is common. Minor relapse: return to the last effective dose (or add 5–10 mg), then taper again; add or switch a steroid-sparing agent. Major relapse (ischaemic symptoms or progressive aortitis): 40–60 mg (pulses if visual), plus tocilizumab or upadacitinib. Remember JAKi cautions in older patients with CV or VTE risk. GC toxicity affects about 85% of those on long courses.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with newly diagnosed GCA has no history of cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease. Should low-dose aspirin be started?

options.A: Yes, in all patients, given the inflammatory and thrombotic risk of GCA
options.B: Yes, but only for the first month of treatment
options.C: Not routinely; antiplatelet therapy is reserved for other established indications
options.D: No; aspirin is specifically contraindicated with glucocorticoids in GCA
options.E: They are not used routinely, because harms outweigh limited long-term benefit

explanation: Evidence of benefit is limited and bleeding risk is increased on glucocorticoids. Gastroprotection and bone protection should be considered. Use aspirin only for usual CV indications, adding a PPI if combined with GC. Some clinicians use short-term aspirin for critical cranial ischaemia. Other measures: bone protection from day 1, BP, glucose, eye and mood checks, PJP prophylaxis with high doses plus other immunosuppression, vaccination, a steroid card. Follow up at weeks 0, 1–2, 3 and 6, then months 3, 6, 9 and 12.

stem: A patient being treated for PMR develops jaw claudication. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Continue the current prednisolone dose and review again in 4 weeks
options.B: Urgent assessment for GCA, with high-dose glucocorticoids if it is suspected
options.C: Add a steroid-sparing agent without reassessing for GCA
options.D: Arrange dental review before any other action, since jaw claudication suggests dental disease
options.E: Begin high-dose glucocorticoids urgently and arrange rapid assessment

explanation: Patients with PMR should be asked about headache, scalp tenderness, jaw or tongue claudication and visual symptoms at every review. At every PMR review, ask about headache, scalp tenderness, jaw or tongue claudication, visual symptoms and limb claudication. Poor response or relapse of PMR should prompt imaging for large-vessel GCA (ultrasound of axillary arteries, PET-CT).

stem: What initial glucocorticoid dose is recommended for PMR (new bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain, 90 minutes of stiffness, ESR 58, no GCA features), and how should it be tapered after a complete response?

options.A: Prednisolone 60 mg daily, tapering by 10 mg weekly regardless of response
options.B: Prednisolone 5 mg daily, increasing only if there is clearly no treatment response
options.C: Methotrexate as first-line, with glucocorticoids reserved for non-responders
options.D: Prednisolone 15 mg daily (up to 25 mg if needed); reduce to 10 mg/day within 2 months, then by 1 mg every 4 weeks, aiming to stop within about a year
options.E: Prednisolone 40 mg daily, stopping it abruptly once all symptoms have resolved

explanation: The 2025 EULAR recommendations advise 15–25 mg/day initially, and the 2026 BSR guideline describes a typical starting dose of 15 mg, increased to a maximum of 25 mg if response is inadequate. Very low (≤7.5 mg) or very high (>30 mg) starting doses are avoided. A brisk response is expected within 1–2 weeks; EULAR advises that a steroid trial should not be used as a diagnostic test. EULAR advises tapering to 10 mg/day within the first 2 months and aiming to stop within a year, while the 2026 BSR guideline describes a standard taper over 9–12 months, with faster options for those at high toxicity risk under closer review. Expect ≥70% global improvement within 1 week and a normal CRP within 3–4 weeks. Use the lower end of the dose range with comorbidity or diabetes and the higher end with high relapse risk. A single IM methylprednisolone injection (e.g. 120 mg every 3 weeks, tapering) is an alternative. NSAIDs have little role. The EULAR course notes typical duration is 1–2 years, with about a third needing longer low-dose treatment.

stem: Under the 2026 BSR PMR guideline, what bone-protection principle applies to people starting glucocorticoids?

options.A: Osteosarcoma arising in pagetic bone
options.B: Offer calcium and vitamin D alone, without a bisphosphonate
options.C: Offer a bisphosphonate unless contraindicated
options.D: Offer a bisphosphonate only after a fragility fracture has occurred
options.E: Offer bone protection only to patients already classified as high-risk on FRAX

explanation: The 2026 BSR guideline recommends bone protection for all people with PMR starting glucocorticoids, with bone health review (and DXA) at diagnosis. A bisphosphonate is the usual choice unless contraindicated, guided by individual fracture risk and local pathways. Bone protection: calcium, vitamin D and a bisphosphonate (per BSR, for all starting GC unless contraindicated). DXA at diagnosis where available. Monitor BP, glucose, weight, mood and cataracts. Give a steroid card and sick-day rules.

stem: Which features are required to classify polymyalgia rheumatica, and what does shoulder ultrasound typically show?

options.A: Age 40 or over, unilateral shoulder pain and normal inflammatory markers
options.B: Age 50 or over, bilateral shoulder aching and raised CRP and/or ESR, plus sufficient additional points; ultrasound typically shows subdeltoid bursitis and biceps tenosynovitis
options.C: Any age at all, bilateral hip pain alone, regardless of CRP or ESR result
options.D: Age 50 or over with unilateral shoulder pain only, regardless of CRP level
options.E: Age 50 or over with bilateral shoulder pain but entirely normal CRP and ESR

explanation: Additional points come from morning stiffness over 45 minutes, hip pain or limited movement, absence of RF/ACPA, absence of other joint involvement and characteristic ultrasound findings. Ultrasound findings add to classification and help distinguish PMR from mimics. The 2025 EULAR recommendations stress that classification criteria should not be used to diagnose individual patients. 2012 EULAR/ACR scoring: morning stiffness >45 minutes, 2 points; hip pain or limited range, 1; absence of RF and ACPA, 2; no other joint pain, 1; ultrasound (≥1 shoulder plus ≥1 hip abnormal), 1; both shoulders abnormal, 1. The threshold is ≥4 without ultrasound (sensitivity 68%, specificity 78%) or ≥5 with ultrasound. Distal features occur in 25–50% (peripheral synovitis, CTS, RS3PE-like oedema). PET shows interspinous bursae, ischial tuberosities and shoulders. Work-up: FBC, U&E, LFTs, bone profile, CK, TSH, glucose, SPEP and FLC, RF and ACPA, vitamin D, urinalysis, chest radiograph. A normal CRP should prompt reconsideration.

stem: A patient with PMR relapses during taper, sometimes repeatedly (for example a 66-year-old woman with peripheral arthritis and ESR 70 at diagnosis who has relapsed twice). How should relapse be managed, and what steroid-sparing treatment is appropriate?

options.A: Stop glucocorticoids immediately and start methotrexate alone
options.B: Increase glucocorticoids indefinitely without adding any steroid-sparing agent
options.C: Return to the last effective dose and taper again more slowly; for repeated relapse add methotrexate 7.5- 10 mg weekly, with an IL-6 receptor inhibitor for refractory disease
options.D: Switch to a TNF inhibitor specifically for its steroid-sparing effect in this condition
options.E: Adult-onset Still’s disease; start an IL-1 inhibitor (such as anakinra) or an IL-6 inhibitor, ideally early after diagnosis

explanation: Relapses are common, especially in the first year. Return to the last effective dose and taper over 4–8 weeks back to the dose at which relapse occurred. The 2026 BSR guideline advises discussing a relapse with rheumatology and referring after a second relapse or 18 months of glucocorticoids. Repeated relapse should prompt steroid-sparing therapy and reassessment of the diagnosis. Methotrexate is considered early in those at high relapse risk, with relapse or with glucocorticoid toxicity. For people who cannot taper glucocorticoids, both the 2026 BSR and 2025 EULAR recommendations support an IL-6 receptor antagonist; EULAR prefers sarilumab for relapsing or refractory PMR (NHS access depends on commissioning). TNF inhibitors are not effective. Relapse affects 30–50%. High-risk features: female sex, ESR >40, peripheral arthritis. SAPHYR: sarilumab gave higher sustained remission with a 14-week taper than placebo with a 52-week taper. SEMAPHORE and PMR-SPARE: tocilizumab improved GC-free remission, including in early PMR. JAK inhibitors are under study. Treat symptoms, not an isolated CRP rise. Look for largevessel GCA in relapsing PMR.

stem: A patient labelled as PMR has an atypical course: partial response to prednisolone 15 mg with wrist and MCP synovitis; very high inflammatory markers with weight loss and a poor steroid response; or true proximal weakness with CK 2,400 U/L. What should be done?

options.A: Continue the same prednisolone dose without further investigation
options.B: Increase prednisolone to 30 mg daily without reconsidering the diagnosis
options.C: Assume large-vessel GCA alone, without considering any other possible mimic
options.D: Arrange malignancy screening alone, without considering infection or other mimics
options.E: Reconsider the diagnosis and investigate mimics: late-onset RA, infection, malignancy, large-vessel GCA, and inflammatory myopathy if weakness and a raised CK are present

explanation: hypothyroidism and drug-induced myopathy An incomplete response, age under 60, prominent peripheral arthritis or systemic features should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. PMR causes pain and stiffness, not true weakness, and CK is normal; weakness with a raised CK points to myopathy. PMR mimics include malignancy, infection (including endocarditis), late-onset RA, CPPD, myopathy and endocrine disease. Category Mimics elderly-onset RA (especially Inflammatory seronegative), RS3PE, SpA, CPPD (pseudo-PMR), myositis, vasculitis (LV-GCA, AAV), ICI-PMR myeloma, lymphoma, paraneoplastic Malignancy solid tumours septic arthritis, endocarditis, spinal Infection infection, TB hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, Endocrine and osteomalacia, statin myopathy metabolic bilateral cuff disease, adhesive capsulitis, Mechanical cervical spondylosis, OA, fibromyalgia (normal CRP) Parkinson’s disease (rigidity) Neurological Red flags: age <60, chronic onset, no shoulder involvement, normal or extremely high markers, prominent systemic features or weight loss, erosive peripheral arthritis, neurological signs, poor response to 15–25 mg within 1–2 weeks. Tests: RF and ACPA, ultrasound of the hands; SPEP and FLC, CT or PET-CT for malignancy and LV-GCA; blood cultures and echo; CK, TSH and myositis antibodies; vitamin D, calcium and PTH. Refer to specialist care if atypical, under 60, steroid-dependent or refractory.

stem: A young woman has left arm claudication, a 30 mmHg inter-arm systolic difference, a subclavian bruit, raised CRP and MRA showing subclavian wall thickening and stenosis. What distinguishes Takayasu arteritis from GCA, and what treatment is recommended alongside glucocorticoids?

options.A: Takayasu affects the aorta and major branches in younger women usually under 40; add a glucocorticoid- sparing agent such as methotrexate or azathioprine from the outset
options.B: Takayasu spares the pulmonary arteries entirely, unlike GCA; no steroid-sparing agent is needed
options.C: Takayasu occurs only in patients over 60, unlike GCA; glucocorticoids alone are sufficient
options.D: GCA and Takayasu are distinguished by ANCA status, and both are treated with glucocorticoids alone
options.E: Takayasu is distinguished from GCA by a positive temporal artery biopsy; treat with glucocorticoids alone

explanation: Both are granulomatous large-vessel vasculitides. Takayasu arteritis needs combined therapy; tocilizumab or TNF inhibitors are used for refractory disease. Elective revascularisation is performed in remission unless ischaemia is critical. Subclavian or aortic stenosis in a young person: Takayasu vs fibromuscular dysplasia, thoracic outlet syndrome (positional, cervical rib), atherosclerosis (risk factors), radiation arteritis, IgG4-related disease, Behçet’s, Cogan’s, sarcoid, infection (TB, syphilis), congenital coarctation, mid-aortic syndrome (NF1, Williams syndrome), Marfan or Loeys-Dietz (aneurysmal). Numano types I–V describe distribution (from arch branches to the whole aorta). Pulmonary artery involvement and coronary ostial lesions occur. Hypertension is common and often missed because of subclavian stenosis. Induction: prednisolone 40–60 mg/day, tapered, plus methotrexate, azathioprine, MMF or leflunomide. Refractory: tocilizumab, TNFi (infliximab, adalimumab); JAKi are emerging. CV protection: aspirin or statin per risk; strict BP control (measure on an unaffected limb). Revascularisation: stent or bypass in inactive disease (restenosis is higher when active); bypass lasts longer than stenting. Monitoring: MRA, CTA or PET (markers can be normal when active).

stem: A 29-year-old man of Turkish origin has recurrent oral and genital ulcers and erythema nodosum-like lesions. What is required for classification of Behçet’s disease under the International Study Group criteria?

options.A: Recurrent genital ulceration alone, without any additional feature required
options.B: Recurrent oral ulceration at least 3 times in 12 months, plus two of: genital ulcers, eye lesions, skin lesions or positive pathergy test
options.C: A positive pathergy test alone is sufficient for classification
options.D: HLA-B*51 positivity alone, without any clinical feature
options.E: Recurrent oral ulceration alone, with no additional criterion needed

explanation: Recurrent oral ulceration is mandatory in this classification. Behçet’s is a variable-vessel vasculitis affecting eyes, vessels, nervous system and gut. ICBD criteria (≥4 points, more sensitive): oral ulcers 2, genital ulcers 2, ocular lesions 2; skin, neurological, vascular and pathergy 1 each. Oral ulcers are not mandatory under ICBD. Pathergy is positive in up to 60% in Turkey, the Middle East and Japan, but rarely in northern Europeans. HLA-B51 is present in 50–60% (vs about 15% of controls) and supports but does not establish the diagnosis. There is no diagnostic test, so the diagnosis is clinical. Check FBC (cyclic neutropenia), B12, folate, ferritin, coeliac serology, HSV swabs, syphilis serology and HLA-B51. Ophthalmology screening and a vascular assessment if symptomatic.
