stem: A patient with Behçet’s has recurrent oral and genital ulcers without major organ involvement. What is the first-line treatment, and what is used if oral ulcers persist despite topical treatment and colchicine?

options.A: Colchicine with topical treatments first; for refractory ulcers, apremilast (randomised trial evidence) or a TNF inhibitor
options.B: High-dose systemic glucocorticoids as first-line, continued long-term
options.C: Topical treatment alone, with no role for colchicine
options.D: Rituximab as first-line, ahead of colchicine or topical treatment
options.E: Methotrexate as first-line, with glucocorticoids avoided entirely

explanation: Colchicine prevents recurrent mucocutaneous lesions, especially erythema nodosum and genital ulcers. Apremilast reduced oral ulcers in a randomised trial (RELIEF), and the 2025 EULAR recommendations advise apremilast or a TNF inhibitor when mucocutaneous disease is refractory to, or intolerant of, colchicine. Chronic systemic glucocorticoids should be avoided. Topicals: steroid mouthwash and creams, sucralfate, local anaesthetics. Further escalation: azathioprine, interferon-α, TNFi; thalidomide as a last resort (teratogenic, neuropathy). Arthritis: colchicine first, then IA steroid, then azathioprine, IFN-α or TNFi. Other points: stopping smoking can paradoxically worsen oral ulcers. Pregnancy often improves Behçet’s, and colchicine can continue. Emerging: IL-17 or IL-23 blockade (secukinumab, ustekinumab) for mucocutaneous disease; tocilizumab for refractory eye or neurological disease; JAKi.

stem: How should Behçet’s posterior uveitis or retinal vasculitis be treated, and how does management change when it is sight-threatening?

options.A: Topical steroids alone are sufficient for posterior uveitis, since it rarely threatens sight
options.B: Observation alone, since Behçet’s uveitis typically resolves spontaneously without treatment
options.C: All Behçet’s uveitis needs systemic immunosuppression, not glucocorticoids alone; sight-threatening disease needs high-dose glucocorticoids with infliximab
options.D: Glucocorticoids alone, without any steroid-sparing agent, are sufficient even for sight-threatening disease
options.E: IL-1 blockade alone, without any glucocorticoids, for sight-threatening disease

explanation: Sight-threatening posterior segment disease needs urgent ophthalmology-led treatment. The 2025 EULAR update increasingly favours monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies (especially infliximab) for eye involvement, both for induction and maintenance. Azathioprine, ciclosporin or interferon-alpha remain options for less severe posterior disease. Retinal vasculitis: Behçet’s (occlusive, veins and arteries, hypopyon), sarcoid (periphlebitis, “candle-wax drippings”), TB (Eales disease), syphilis, toxoplasmosis, CMV or ARN (herpes viruses; exclude before immunosuppression), SLE or APS, GPA, PAN, Susac syndrome (BRAO, deafness, corpus callosum lesions), MS (intermediate uveitis, periphlebitis), intraocular lymphoma masquerade. Isolated anterior uveitis can be treated topically, with systemic azathioprine in young men with poor-prognosis features. Avoid ciclosporin in neuro-Behçet’s (it is neurotoxic and can induce neuro-BD). Arrange regular ophthalmology review. Adalimumab is licensed for noninfectious posterior uveitis (VISUAL I/II).

stem: A 31-year-old man with Behçet’s disease develops an acute femoral DVT. Pulmonary artery aneurysm has been excluded. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Anticoagulation alone, without any accompanying immunosuppressive treatment
options.B: Thrombolysis given as first-line treatment, given the acute clinical presentation
options.C: No specific treatment is needed here beyond simple compression stockings
options.D: Glucocorticoids with an immunosuppressant, preferably a monoclonal anti-TNF antibody or azathioprine; anticoagulation only if bleeding risk is low
options.E: High-dose anticoagulation alone, since pulmonary artery aneurysm has been excluded

explanation: Thrombosis in Behçet’s is driven by vessel wall inflammation. The 2025 EULAR recommendations advise glucocorticoids with immunosuppressives, preferably anti-TNF antibodies, continued as maintenance. Anticoagulants may be added only if bleeding risk is low and pulmonary artery aneurysms have been excluded, because rupture can be fatal. Thrombosis in Behçet’s is inflammatory, with an adherent thrombus, so immunosuppression prevents recurrence and anticoagulation alone adds little. Venous disease is the commonest vascular form (superficial thrombophlebitis, DVT, Budd–Chiari, IVC thrombosis, CVST). Pulmonary artery aneurysms present with haemoptysis and are lethal. Arterial or pulmonary artery aneurysm: high-dose GC plus cyclophosphamide, infliximab if refractory. Embolisation is preferred to open surgery. Operate urgently on symptomatic peripheral aneurysms under immunosuppression (anastomotic aneurysm risk). Parenchymal neuro-BD: high-dose GC plus azathioprine or TNFi (preferred for severe disease). GI disease: 5-ASA or azathioprine; TNFi or thalidomide for severe disease; surgery for perforation or bleeding. CVST: GC with short anticoagulation (after excluding PAA). Mortality comes mainly from PAA, Budd–Chiari, CNS and major vessel disease in young men. vasculitis

stem: How does the Chapel Hill consensus nomenclature primarily classify vasculitis?

options.A: By the presence or absence of ANCA positivity alone
options.B: By the specific autoantibody profile associated with each disease
options.C: By the predominant size of vessel involved, with additional aetiological categories
options.D: By age at onset alone, with no reference to vessel size
options.E: By the organs involved alone, regardless of vessel calibre

explanation: Large-vessel (Takayasu, GCA), medium-vessel (PAN, Kawasaki), small-vessel (ANCA-associated and immunecomplex) and variable-vessel (Behçet’s, Cogan’s) categories are recognised. Category Diseases GCA (>50), Takayasu (<50) Large PAN (no GN, ANCA-negative), Kawasaki Medium Small: ANCA MPA, GPA, EGPA Small: anti-GBM, cryoglobulinaemic, IgA vasculitis, HUV immune complex Behçet’s, Cogan’s Variable Single-organ cutaneous leucocytoclastic angiitis, PACNS, isolated aortitis lupus, rheumatoid, sarcoid, RP vasculitis Systemic disease HCV cryoglobulinaemia, HBV-PAN, Probable syphilitic aortitis, drug-associated cause (hydralazine, PTU, levamisole), cancer Chapel Hill is a nomenclature, not diagnostic criteria. Large and medium vessels do not involve capillaries or venules.

stem: A patient with suspected small-vessel vasculitis needs ANCA testing. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: A clinical diagnosis alone, without any laboratory testing
options.B: Indirect immunofluorescence alone, without antigen-specific immunoassays
options.C: ANCA testing in anyone with unexplained systemic symptoms, regardless of clinical features
options.D: Antigen-specific immunoassays for PR3-ANCA and MPO-ANCA as the primary test
options.E: A single ANCA test is sufficient regardless of clinical suspicion

explanation: High-quality PR3 and MPO immunoassays are the preferred screening tests. Test only with compatible features (pulmonary–renal syndrome, RPGN, mononeuritis, ENT destruction, scleritis, palpable purpura). Use high-quality PR3 and MPO immunoassays; IIF is optional. Request anti-GBM in parallel for RPGN or DAH.

stem: Which ANCA specificity is most strongly associated with GPA, and which features best distinguish GPA from MPA?

options.A: MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA) in GPA, with granulomatous disease more typical of MPA
options.B: ANCA status does not help distinguish GPA from MPA at all
options.C: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) in GPA; GPA more often has granulomatous ENT or lung disease with PR3-ANCA whereas MPA usually has MPO-ANCA without granulomas
options.D: GPA and MPA are distinguished by complement levels, not ANCA specificity
options.E: PR3-ANCA occurs equally often in GPA and MPA, so it does not help distinguish them

explanation: MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA) predominates in MPA, renal-limited vasculitis and ANCA-positive EGPA. These are patterns rather than absolute rules, and both cause pauci-immune necrotising glomerulonephritis and alveolar haemorrhage. Destructive midline nasal disease: GPA vs cocaine-induced midline destructive lesion (often PR3 or anti-elastase positive), NK/T-cell lymphoma, invasive fungal sinusitis, TB, leprosy, leishmaniasis, syphilis, sarcoidosis, IgG4-RD, relapsing polychondritis (cartilage only, no mucosal destruction). GPA: PR3 in 65–75%, MPO in 10–20%, ANCA-negative in about 10% (more often limited ENT disease). MPA: MPO in 60–80%, PR3 in about 10%, negative in 10–20%. EGPA: ANCA-positive in 30–40% (MPO).

stem: How should a low-positive MPO-ANCA without vasculitic features, or a rise in ANCA in a patient with vasculitis in remission (asymptomatic, normal urinalysis), be interpreted?

options.A: A rising ANCA titre alone should always trigger pre-emptive treatment escalation
options.B: ANCA alone neither diagnoses vasculitis nor justifies escalation; assess clinical phenotype and alternative causes, monitoring more closely in remission
options.C: A low-positive result always indicates smouldering, clinically active vasculitis requiring treatment
options.D: Only indirect immunofluorescence should ever be used to confirm the ELISA result
options.E: Any positive ANCA mandates urgent immunosuppression regardless of symptoms

explanation: ANCA can be positive in infection (including endocarditis), drug exposure and other inflammatory disease; testing is most useful when a compatible syndrome exists. A rise or reappearance of ANCA modestly increases relapse risk (especially in PR3 and renal disease) but is an imperfect predictor. ANCA positivity without AAV: infective endocarditis (often PR3, with low complement), TB, HIV, hepatitis C, IBD and PSC (atypical p-ANCA), autoimmune hepatitis, drugs (hydralazine, PTU, minocycline, levamisole, allopurinol), anti-GBM disease, SLE, RA, cystic fibrosis. In remission with rising ANCA: review every 1–3 months with urinalysis, creatinine and symptoms. Consider early retreatment only when the clinical relapse risk is high (PR3, prior relapses), as a shared decision.

stem: What is induction therapy for organ- or life-threatening GPA or MPA (for example PR3-GPA with RPGN, creatinine 240, haemoptysis and sinus disease), and which trial supports rituximab?

options.A: Oral glucocorticoids alone at standard dose, without rituximab or cyclophosphamide
options.B: Methotrexate with glucocorticoids, reserving rituximab for relapse only
options.C: Glucocorticoids (IV pulses then the reduced-dose PEXIVAS taper) with rituximab or cyclophosphamide; rituximab was non-inferior and better in relapsing disease (RAVE)
options.D: Rituximab maintenance alone, without any induction-phase glucocorticoids given first
options.E: Azathioprine combined with glucocorticoids used as first-line induction therapy

explanation: Organ-or life-threatening GPA or MPA needs urgent induction with rituximab or IV cyclophosphamide. The 2025 BSR recommendations prefer rituximab for relapsing disease, and it is a first-line option particularly in PR3-ANCA disease and when fertility preservation matters. Oral prednisolone follows the reduced-dose (PEXIVAS) taper to 5 mg/day by 4–5 months, which is as effective as standard dosing with fewer infections. Avacopan can be considered to spare glucocorticoids. Pulmonary–renal syndrome: AAV, anti-GBM disease (or double-positive), SLE, cryoglobulinaemia, IgA vasculitis, TTP, catastrophic APS, infection (Legionella, leptospirosis, hantavirus, endocarditis), pulmonary oedema with AKI, PE with renal infarct. Rituximab: 375 mg/m² weekly × 4, or 1 g × 2 two weeks apart (RAVE, RITUXVAS). Cyclophosphamide: IV 15 mg/kg (adjusted for age and renal function) at weeks 0, 2 and 4, then every 3 weeks for 3–6 months (CYCLOPS). Some centres combine rituximab with low-dose IV cyclophosphamide for severe GN. Adjuncts:-PJP prophylaxis: co-trimoxazole for ≥6 months after the last rituximab or cyclophosphamide dose.-Screening: HBV, HCV, HIV, TB, Strongyloides; baseline IgG.-Vaccines: before rituximab.-Protection: bone, PPI, VTE prophylaxis (high risk when active), ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria.-Fertility: preservation before cyclophosphamide.-Bladder cancer: surveillance for haematuria once disease is inactive.

stem: A 49-year-old woman has new GPA limited to sinus disease and nasal crusting, with no renal or other organthreatening involvement. Which induction regimen is most appropriate?

options.A: Cyclophosphamide with glucocorticoids as first-line, reserved for all new GPA
options.B: High-dose glucocorticoids alone, without any steroid-sparing agent
options.C: Methotrexate alone, without rituximab as even an alternative
options.D: A rituximab maintenance regimen alone, without an induction phase
options.E: Rituximab with glucocorticoids, with methotrexate or mycophenolate as alternatives

explanation: Cyclophosphamide is reserved for organ-or life-threatening disease. For non-organ-threatening disease, EULAR recommends glucocorticoids with rituximab, and the 2025 BSR recommendations allow methotrexate or mycophenolate, with a lower glucocorticoid regimen (LoVAS-style) considered. Non-organ-threatening disease: GC plus rituximab is preferred. Methotrexate (if eGFR >50) or MMF are alternatives with higher relapse rates. Co-trimoxazole can be an adjunct in limited ENT disease (it reduces relapse and S. aureus carriage). Nasal douching and ENT care.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with MPA has a creatinine rising to 420 micromol/L due to active crescentic glomerulonephritis. Which adjunct may be considered?

options.A: Apremilast
options.B: Disseminated gonococcal infection
options.C: Avacopan
options.D: An IL-17 inhibitor
options.E: Plasma exchange

explanation: Plasma exchange may be considered when creatinine exceeds 300 micromol/L due to active glomerulonephritis. It did not reduce death or end-stage kidney disease overall in a large trial and is not used routinely, including for alveolar haemorrhage alone. PEXIVAS showed no overall benefit of PLEX for death or ESKD. A later meta-analysis suggested a reduced 12-month ESKD risk with high creatinine. PLEX remains mandatory for anti-GBM double positivity. For DAH with hypoxaemia it is an individual decision.

stem: A patient with newly diagnosed severe MPA also has poorly controlled diabetes and osteoporosis. Which agent may be used with rituximab or cyclophosphamide to substantially reduce glucocorticoid exposure?

options.A: Avacopan
options.B: Plasma exchange
options.C: Methotrexate
options.D: -2.5 or lower
options.E: Felty syndrome

explanation: Avacopan, an oral C5a receptor antagonist, was non-inferior for remission at 26 weeks and superior for sustained remission at 52 weeks compared with a prednisolone taper. LFTs need monitoring. ADVOCATE: avacopan (30 mg twice daily for 52 weeks) was non-inferior for remission at 26 weeks and superior for sustained remission at 52 weeks, with better eGFR recovery (especially at low eGFR) and lower GC toxicity. Monitor LFTs (hepatotoxicity, rare vanishing bile duct syndrome). It is a CYP3A4 substrate, so watch for interactions.

stem: After rituximab-based induction, a patient with GPA is in remission. Which maintenance strategy is most appropriate?

options.A: Rituximab maintenance for 24-48 months after remission induction
options.B: Methotrexate maintenance alone, continued indefinitely without a defined endpoint
options.C: No maintenance therapy is needed once remission is achieved
options.D: Cyclophosphamide maintenance, continued for 24-48 months
options.E: Rituximab with glucocorticoids continued indefinitely at induction dose

explanation: The 2025 BSR recommendations prefer rituximab (500-1000 mg every 4-6 months) for maintenance for 24-48 months, with azathioprine or methotrexate as alternatives and mycophenolate if these are unsuitable. Glucocorticoids may be withdrawn within 6-12 months. MAINRITSAN: rituximab was superior to azathioprine. MAINRITSAN-3 showed fewer relapses with extended rituximab. Relapse risk is higher with PR3, ENT or lung disease, prior relapse, persistent ANCA and S. aureus carriage. Rituximab 500 mg every 6 months (or 1 g every 4–6 months) for 24–48 months, longer in high-risk patients. Check IgG before each dose (IVIG if low with infections). Major relapse: treat as new disease, preferring rituximab. Minor relapse: increase GC and optimise maintenance.

stem: A patient with GPA develops increasing stridor due to subglottic stenosis. What is the best immediate approach?

options.A: Reassurance, since subglottic stenosis rarely progresses to airway compromise
options.B: Increase systemic immunosuppression alone, without any ENT or respiratory input
options.C: Urgent airway assessment with ENT and respiratory input, alongside disease-directed treatment
options.D: Immediate tracheostomy, without any attempt at local or systemic treatment
options.E: Await outpatient ENT review, since this is rarely urgent

explanation: Subglottic stenosis can threaten the airway and may not track systemic markers; it often needs local procedures as well as immunosuppression. Stridor or hoarseness in a rheumatology patient: GPA subglottic stenosis; relapsing polychondritis (laryngotracheal chondritis or tracheomalacia); RA cricoarytenoid arthritis; amyloid; post-intubation stenosis; angioedema (ACE inhibitors, HUV, C1-inhibitor deficiency); vocal cord palsy (aortic aneurysm, mediastinal mass); SLE; Behçet’s. Flow–volume loop, CT of the airway, laryngoscopy. Intralesional steroid injection with dilatation (laser or balloon); tracheostomy for critical stenosis. Stenosis can progress despite systemic remission.

stem: What proportion of EGPA patients are ANCA-positive, what is a leading cause of death, and what treats relapsing non-organ-threatening EGPA that relapses below 10 mg prednisolone?

options.A: About 30–40% are ANCA-positive (usually MPO); cardiac disease is a leading cause of death. Mepolizumab or benralizumab treat relapsing, steroid-dependent disease
options.B: Over 90% are ANCA-positive (usually PR3); renal failure is the leading cause of death
options.C: EGPA never involves the heart, unlike GPA and microscopic polyangiitis do
options.D: Oral corticosteroids alone are used for relapsing disease, with no role for biologics
options.E: ANCA status does not correlate with any clinical phenotype at all in EGPA

explanation: ANCA positivity is associated with glomerulonephritis, neuropathy and purpura; ANCA-negative disease more often features cardiac and lung involvement. ECG, troponin, echocardiography and cardiac MRI are performed at diagnosis. Rheumatology SCE — 5-option SBA 110 Anti-IL-5/IL-5R therapy reduces relapses and glucocorticoid exposure and is recommended by the 2025 BSR recommendations for non-life-or organ-threatening EGPA and for maintenance. Severe EGPA is treated with glucocorticoids plus cyclophosphamide, or rituximab if cyclophosphamide is unsuitable. Hypereosinophilia: EGPA vs hypereosinophilic syndrome (FIP1L1-PDGFRA, tryptase, B12, T-cell clonality), parasites (Strongyloides serology before steroids), ABPA, drug reaction (DRESS), chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, eosinophilic fasciitis, lymphoma (Hodgkin, T-cell), adrenal insufficiency, mastocytosis, IgG4-RD. Mepolizumab 300 mg SC every 4 weeks (MIRRA). Benralizumab 30 mg SC every 4 weeks was non-inferior to mepolizumab in MANDARA, with more patients stopping GC. REOVAS: rituximab was not superior to conventional therapy in EGPA but is commonly used. Maintenance after severe disease: azathioprine, methotrexate, MMF or rituximab, with or without anti-IL-5. Asthma and sinus care: inhaled therapy and ENT management of polyps. Cardiac EGPA needs aggressive immunosuppression plus heart failure therapy.

stem: A 32-year-old woman has retiform purpura with necrosis of both earlobes, arthralgia, neutropenia and very high titre MPO-ANCA, with PR3-ANCA also positive. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Levamisole-adulterated cocaine
options.B: Polyarteritis nodosa
options.C: Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis
options.D: Felty syndrome
options.E: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis

explanation: Levamisole-contaminated cocaine causes cutaneous vasculopathy, neutropenia and dual ANCA positivity, often with anti-elastase and antiphospholipid antibodies. Management centres on stopping cocaine. Retiform purpura or necrosis: levamisole, cryoglobulinaemia (type I), APS or CAPS, calciphylaxis, cholesterol emboli, warfarin or heparin necrosis, purpura fulminans (protein C deficiency, meningococcaemia), ecthyma gangrenosum, vasculitis (PAN, AAV). Levamisole-cocaine causes retiform purpura (ears, cheeks), neutropenia or agranulocytosis, very high MPO with PR3 (dual positivity), anti-elastase, aPL, low complement, and occasionally GN. Cocaine cessation (with addiction services) and wound care. GC or immunosuppression only for organ-threatening disease. Recurrence follows re-exposure.

stem: A man has testicular pain, mononeuritis multiplex, livedo, hypertension and renal and mesenteric microaneurysms on angiography, ANCA-negative and HBsAg-positive. What distinguishes PAN from AAV, and how is HBV-PAN treated?

options.A: PAN causes glomerulonephritis identical to MPA; HBV-PAN is treated with prolonged immunosuppression alone
options.B: PAN affects medium-sized arteries, causing microaneurysms and infarction without glomerulonephritis; HBV-PAN is treated with antivirals plus short-course glucocorticoids
options.C: PAN affects small vessels and capillaries, causing pulmonary haemorrhage
options.D: HBV-PAN is treated with long-term glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide, deferring antivirals
options.E: PAN and AAV are distinguished only by ANCA status, with identical vessel involvement

explanation: HBV-associated PAN is immune-complex mediated. Prolonged immunosuppression promotes viral replication, so antivirals (entecavir or tenofovir) are combined with brief glucocorticoids and plasma exchange. PAN causes neuropathy, skin lesions, renal artery aneurysms and mesenteric ischaemia; glomerulonephritis and lung haemorrhage point to small-vessel vasculitis. Other microaneurysm causes: segmental arterial mediolysis, fibromuscular dysplasia, endocarditis (mycotic), vEDS, DADA2 (young, lacunar strokes, livedo), cocaine or amphetamines, atrial myxoma emboli, hairy cell leukaemia-associated PAN. Feature PAN MPA small (± Vessels medium arteries medium) MPO in 70– ANCA negative 90% absent (infarcts, GN RPGN renovascular hypertension) DAH, ILD Lung spared Microaneurysms yes rare HBV link yes Rheumatology SCE — 5-option SBA 111 no uncommon (20–30%) Relapse common Idiopathic PAN: non-severe disease, GC ± methotrexate or azathioprine; severe disease (FFS ≥1: neurological, renal, GI, cardiac), GC plus cyclophosphamide then maintenance. Cutaneous PAN (often post-streptococcal): NSAIDs, colchicine, dapsone, short GC. DADA2: TNF inhibitors. Screen all PAN patients for HBV.

stem: A patient with suspected medium-vessel vasculitis has abdominal pain out of proportion to examination and a rising lactate. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Urgent colonoscopy as the first investigation, before any imaging
options.B: Immediate high-dose glucocorticoids alone, without surgical input
options.C: Urgent surgical and medical assessment for mesenteric ischaemia, alongside vasculitis treatment
options.D: Observation with serial examination over 24 hours
options.E: Oral antibiotics alone, pending stool culture results

explanation: Bowel ischaemia is life-threatening and requires urgent imaging and surgical input. Urgent CT angiography, surgical review and pulse GC. Bowel ischaemia, perforation, gallbladder or appendix infarction and pancreatitis can all occur in PAN. GI involvement scores in the FFS. Consider cyclophosphamide.

stem: A 57-year-old woman has palpable purpura, arthralgia, peripheral neuropathy and low C4. Type II cryoglobulins are present and hepatitis C RNA is positive. Disease is mild without organ threat. What is the first-line treatment?

options.A: Rituximab monotherapy, deferring antiviral treatment
options.B: Direct-acting antiviral therapy for hepatitis C
options.C: High-dose glucocorticoids alone, without any antiviral or immunosuppressive agent
options.D: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor
options.E: Interferon-based antiviral therapy as first-line

explanation: Mild to moderate HCV-associated cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis often responds to viral eradication. Severe disease may need rituximab, with glucocorticoids and/or plasma exchange, alongside antivirals. HCV accounts for 70–90% of mixed cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis. Cryoglobulins are found in 40–60% of chronic HCV, but only 5–15% become symptomatic. Meltzer triad (purpura, arthralgia, weakness) is present in only 25–30% at diagnosis. Organ involvement: skin 70–90% (orthostatic purpura, ochre pigmentation, malleolar ulcers); joints 40– 80%; painful axonal sensory neuropathy 20–60%; MPGN 20–35% (a major adverse prognostic factor); lymphoma 5– 10%. Mechanism: the HCV E2 protein binds CD81 on B cells, with t(14;18) and BAFF promoting clonal RFproducing B cells. Severity Treatment DAAs (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 Mild to moderate weeks, or glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks; SVR >95%) Severe (GN, rituximab ± moderate GC, then or with ulcers, motor DAAs neuropathy) Life-threatening PLEX + IV methylprednisolone + rituximab; DAAs as soon as feasible Vasculitis persists or relapses after SVR in 10–20% (autonomous clone, lymphoma), so give rituximab. Screen for HBV before DAAs (reactivation risk). Rituximab can complex with cryoglobulins (serum sickness), so with a high cryocrit use PLEX first or a lower dose. Interferon regimens are obsolete. Low-grade splenic marginal zone lymphoma may regress after HCV eradication.

stem: A 52-year-old man has palpable purpura over the legs, abdominal pain and arthralgia after an upper respiratory infection. Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits. What is the most important follow-up investigation?

options.A: Serial urinalysis for blood and protein, blood pressure and renal function
options.B: Skin biopsy repeated at 3 months to confirm resolution
options.C: Abdominal CT to look for underlying malignancy
options.D: Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70)
options.E: Faecal occult blood testing alone

explanation: Adults with IgA vasculitis more often develop significant nephritis than children. Renal biopsy is needed for significant proteinuria or impaired function. Palpable purpura: IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis, AAV, drug hypersensitivity vasculitis (antibiotics, NSAIDs, allopurinol), infection (meningococcaemia, gonococcaemia, endocarditis, hepatitis B or C), SLE or RA vasculitis, HUV, paraneoplastic vasculitis (haematological malignancy), Schamberg’s disease (non-palpable), scurvy (perifollicular). Take a deep punch biopsy within 24–48 hours for H&E and direct IF (IgA). IgA vasculitis features purpura on the legs and buttocks, arthritis, abdominal pain (intussusception in children) and IgA nephritis. Adults have a worse renal prognosis and more often an underlying cause (malignancy, infection, IBD). Supportive care for mild disease. GC for GI or severe disease. Nephritis is managed like IgA nephropathy (RAAS blockade, GC; MMF or cyclophosphamide for crescentic disease). Monitor urine for at least 6 months (children) and longer in adults.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has urticarial lesions lasting more than 24 hours that leave bruising, with arthralgia, low C3, C4 and C1q, and anti-C1q antibodies. Which diagnosis best fits, and what associations should be sought?

options.A: Chronic spontaneous urticaria, with no further investigation needed
options.B: Schnitzler syndrome, requiring a search for monoclonal IgM
options.C: Adult-onset Still’s disease, requiring ferritin and a search for an evanescent rash
options.D: CAPS, requiring NLRP3 genetic testing
options.E: Hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis; associations include SLE and obstructive lung disease

explanation: Individual urticarial vasculitis lesions persist beyond 24 hours, may burn or hurt and leave pigmentation. The hypocomplementaemic form overlaps with SLE and can cause COPD-like lung disease, angioedema, glomerulonephritis and uveitis. Urticaria with systemic features: urticarial vasculitis (normocomplementaemic or hypocomplementaemic), Schnitzler syndrome (monoclonal IgM, fever, bone pain), CAPS (neutrophilic urticaria from childhood), adult-onset Still’s (evanescent rash), SLE, serum sickness, chronic spontaneous urticaria (lesions <24 hours, no bruising, antihistamine-responsive). Skin biopsy (leucocytoclastic vasculitis). Mild disease: antihistamines, dapsone, colchicine, HCQ. Systemic disease: GC plus MMF or azathioprine; rituximab, omalizumab, anakinra or canakinumab for refractory disease. Screen for SLE, HCV, malignancy and COPD (HUV causes early emphysema; avoid smoking).

stem: A patient with systemic vasculitis develops acute foot drop from mononeuritis multiplex. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Physiotherapy and an ankle-foot orthosis alone, without any change to immunosuppression
options.B: Urgent assessment and treatment of active vasculitic neuropathy, because prompt therapy may prevent permanent deficit
options.C: Observation with serial nerve conduction studies over several months
options.D: Oral glucocorticoids alone, without reassessment of systemic therapy
options.E: Referral for elective nerve decompression surgery

explanation: New motor neuropathy indicates organ-threatening disease. Nerve conduction studies and, where needed, nerve biopsy support the diagnosis. Mononeuritis multiplex is a stepwise, asymmetric painful neuropathy in multiple named nerves (foot drop, wrist drop). Causes: PAN (60–70%), EGPA (45–75%), MPA, GPA, cryoglobulinaemia, RA vasculitis, SLE, Sjögren’s, sarcoid, diabetes, HIV, HNPP, leprosy, lymphoma (neurolymphomatosis), amyloid. NCS show an axonal multifocal pattern. Combined sural nerve and muscle biopsy (sural plus peroneus brevis) increases yield. Induction as for severe vasculitis. Neuropathic pain treatment, AFO or splints and physiotherapy. Recovery is slow (months).

stem: A previously well man has a hot swollen knee and fever. Which organism most commonly causes native joint septic arthritis in adults, and what is the initial management if he has no prosthesis, MRSA risk or penicillin allergy?

options.A: Neisseria gonorrhoeae; start IV ceftriaxone empirically in all adults
options.B: Coagulase-negative staphylococci; start oral flucloxacillin alone
options.C: Mycobacterium tuberculosis; await culture before any antibiotic
options.D: Staphylococcus aureus; aspirate the joint and take blood cultures, then start IV flucloxacillin
options.E: Streptococcus pyogenes; start IV benzylpenicillin alone

explanation: Empirical flucloxacillin is used for adults without risk factors; clindamycin if penicillin-allergic, vancomycin if MRSA risk, and a third-generation cephalosporin for older or frail patients or suspected gonococcal or Gram-negative infection. Gonococcus is considered in young sexually active adults, and Gram-negative organisms in the elderly, immunosuppressed and people who inject drugs. Kingella is a cause in young children. Acute hot joint: septic arthritis; crystal arthritis (gout, CPP; can coexist); reactive arthritis; haemarthrosis (trauma, anticoagulants, haemophilia, PVNS/TGCT); inflammatory arthritis flare; Lyme disease; viral arthritis; acute rheumatic fever; cellulitis or bursitis mimicking a joint; osteomyelitis near the joint; Charcot joint; SONK or insufficiency fracture. Fever is present in about 60%. Blood cultures are positive in about 50%. CRP, ESR and WCC support but cannot rule out infection. Procalcitonin and synovial lactate may help. Inoculate synovial fluid into blood culture bottles. Screen for the source (skin, urine, endocarditis); do gonococcal NAAT if relevant. Use ultrasound for hip effusion and guided aspiration, and MRI for osteomyelitis or abscess. Hold biologics and JAKi. Early physiotherapy once controlled.

stem: A hot swollen native knee has a synovial fluid white cell count of 80,000/mm³ with 90% neutrophils. Which interpretation is safest?

options.A: Gram stain and bacterial culture
options.B: Septic arthritis is a major concern; send cultures and treat urgently if clinical suspicion is high
options.C: Staphylococcus aureus; aspirate the joint and take blood cultures, then start IV flucloxacillin
options.D: A count below 50,000/mm³ reliably excludes septic arthritis
options.E: This cell count is diagnostic of gout and excludes infection

explanation: High cell counts with neutrophil predominance raise concern for infection, but no cut-off is perfectly diagnostic and crystal arthritis can overlap. WCC guide: non-inflammatory 200–2,000; inflammatory 2,000– 50,000; septic usually >50,000 with >90% neutrophils (but lower in early, partially treated, gonococcal, TB or immunosuppressed cases). Crystal arthritis can exceed 50,000. Crystals do not exclude infection. Synovial glucose is low and lactate high in sepsis.

stem: A patient with suspected septic arthritis is hypotensive and tachycardic. What is correct regarding aspiration and antibiotics?

options.A: Aspirate and await results before starting any antibiotic, since cultures must not be compromised
options.B: Treat the hypotension alone first, deferring cultures and antibiotics until stable
options.C: Give oral antibiotics only, since IV access may be difficult in shock
options.D: Delay antibiotics until surgical review confirms the diagnosis
options.E: Take blood and joint cultures rapidly if feasible, but do not delay antibiotics and resuscitation

explanation: In sepsis, resuscitation and antibiotics take priority. In stable patients, aspiration before antibiotics improves culture yield. Sepsis-6 within the hour: cultures, IV antibiotics, fluids, lactate, oxygen, urine output. Image-guided aspiration as soon as feasible, without delaying antibiotics. Urgent orthopaedic washout. Consider an MRSA-active agent in healthcare-associated cases.

stem: What is the role of joint washout in septic arthritis, and how long should antibiotics continue in uncomplicated S. aureus native-knee infection that improves rapidly after washout?

options.A: Washout is never needed at all if blood cultures happen to be positive
options.B: Washout may be needed for large joints, purulent fluid or failure to improve; about 2 weeks of targeted therapy is non-inferior to 4 weeks after drainage
options.C: Intra-articular antibiotics should be given at the time of washout
options.D: A full 6 months of antibiotics is required regardless of surgical drainage
options.E: Washout is only indicated for prosthetic joint infection, never native joints

explanation: Daily needle aspiration, arthroscopic washout or open debridement are used depending on joint, response and organism; the hip usually needs surgery. Older guidance advised about 2 weeks IV followed by 4 weeks oral, without trial evidence. Randomised data now support shorter targeted courses after surgical drainage in uncomplicated native-joint infection, with early switch to oral therapy (OVIVA showed oral is non-inferior to IV in bone and joint infection). Bacteraemia, osteomyelitis, prostheses and resistant organisms need longer treatment. Intra-articular antibiotics cause chemical synovitis and are not used. Monitor clinical response, CRP and repeat aspiration. Physiotherapy to restore range. Recheck the diagnosis if there is no improvement (TB, fungi, crystals).

stem: A patient develops a painful, warm, swollen knee after total knee replacement, either 9 months later (clinically stable) or 2 weeks after surgery with wound erythema and fever but a well-fixed implant. What is the first action, and which strategy suits early infection?

options.A: Start empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately in both scenarios, before any aspiration
options.B: Assume aseptic loosening in both scenarios, since the implant is stable
options.C: Treat this as gout without any joint aspiration, given the recent surgery
options.D: Proceed directly to two-stage revision surgery in both clinical scenarios
options.E: Urgent orthopaedic referral for aspiration before antibiotics; early postoperative or acute haematogenous infection with a stable implant suits DAIR (debridement, antibiotics, implant retention)

explanation: Antibiotics before aspiration reduce culture yield and can compromise decisions on debridement, implant retention or revision, so they should, where possible, be withheld until aspirate and intraoperative samples have been taken. Chronic or late infections usually need one-or two-stage revision in a specialist MDT. Painful prosthesis: PJI vs aseptic loosening (X-ray cannot separate them), instability, periprosthetic fracture, metallosis or ALVAL (metal-on-metal), crystal arthritis in the replaced joint, referred hip or spine pain, CRPS, haemarthrosis. DAIR (with exchange of mobile parts) suits infection with symptoms <3–4 weeks, a stable implant and a susceptible organism. One-stage revision suits a known susceptible organism with good soft tissues. Two-stage revision is for difficult or unknown organisms or poor soft tissue. Suppressive antibiotics when surgery is impossible. Prevention: optimise diabetes, skin, weight and smoking; decolonise S. aureus; perioperative prophylaxis; DMARD timing; avoid IA steroid within 3 months before surgery.

stem: A 23-year-old sexually active woman has migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis of the wrist and a few painless pustules on her hands. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?

options.A: Reactive arthritis following a recent gastrointestinal infection
options.B: Secondary syphilis, requiring only a single dose of penicillin
options.C: Still’s disease, requiring high-dose glucocorticoids
options.D: Brucellosis, requiring prolonged combination antibiotics
options.E: Disseminated gonococcal infection; IV ceftriaxone, with testing for other STIs and partner notification

explanation: The arthritis-dermatitis-tenosynovitis triad is characteristic. Blood, synovial fluid and mucosal site cultures with NAAT should be taken. Arthritis with dermatitis and tenosynovitis: DGI vs meningococcaemia, ReA, secondary syphilis, infective endocarditis, HBV prodrome, Lyme disease, Still’s disease, Sweet’s syndrome, sarcoid. Two patterns: the triad of migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis and painless pustules; or purulent mono-or oligoarthritis without skin lesions. Risk factors: women (asymptomatic mucosal infection), menstruation or pregnancy, MSM, terminal complement deficiency (C5– C9), eculizumab, HIV. Mucosal NAAT and culture are positive in about 80%; synovial culture in about 50%. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily, switching after improvement for ≥7 days in total. Get culture sensitivities (resistance is rising). Test for chlamydia, HIV and syphilis, and treat partners. Recurrent neisserial infection warrants a CH50 check.

stem: How is Lyme disease treated: erythema migrans (a 12 cm expanding lesion with central clearing 2 weeks after positive)?

options.A: Erythema migrans should not be treated until serology confirms the diagnosis
options.B: Erythema migrans requires IV ceftriaxone as first-line, before any oral option
options.C: Lyme arthritis should be treated with NSAIDs alone, without antibiotics
options.D: A single dose of doxycycline is sufficient for both erythema migrans and Lyme arthritis
options.E: Erythema migrans: treat clinically with doxycycline for 21 days without serology. Lyme arthritis: doxycycline for 28 days

explanation: Erythema migrans is diagnostic of Lyme disease and should be treated without serology, which is often negative early in infection; amoxicillin is an alternative. A small reaction appearing within 48 hours of a bite is usually a hypersensitivity reaction, not erythema migrans. Arthritis persisting after antibiotics may be post-infectious and is managed with anti-inflammatory treatment. Lyme arthritis is a large-joint mono-or oligoarthritis (often a big knee effusion with little pain). Synovial WCC is 10,000– 25,000. IgG is almost always positive. Synovial PCR is positive in most untreated cases. About 10% of US patients have antibiotic-refractory arthritis (HLA-DR-linked). Manifestation Treatment doxycycline 10–21 days (amoxicillin, EM cefuroxime) Facial palsy, doxycycline or IV ceftriaxone 14–21 meningitis, days radiculitis IV ceftriaxone if high-degree block, Carditis otherwise oral doxycycline doxycycline 28 days (amoxicillin in Arthritis young children and pregnancy) second 28-day oral course or IV Persistent arthritis ceftriaxone 2–4 weeks; then NSAIDs, IA steroid, DMARDs, synovectomy Prevention: tick avoidance and checks. Single-dose doxycycline within 72 hours of a high-risk bite in highincidence areas.

stem: A 64-year-old man with diabetes has severe progressive thoracolumbar back pain, fever and raised CRP. MRI shows discitis with adjacent endplate oedema. Blood cultures are negative and he is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Image-guided biopsy for culture (including mycobacteria) before antibiotics
options.B: NSAIDs
options.C: Start empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately, without a biopsy
options.D: Repeat blood cultures only, with no imaging-guided biopsy
options.E: Treat empirically for spondyloarthritis with NSAIDs and physiotherapy

explanation: A microbiological diagnosis guides prolonged antibiotic therapy. TB, Brucella and fungi should be considered. Urgent surgery is needed for cord compression or instability. Spondylodiscitis organisms: S. aureus, streptococci, Enterobacterales, TB (Pott’s), Brucella (lumbar, older men), Salmonella, fungi (Candida in IVDU). Mimics: Modic type 1 change, erosive osteochondrosis, Andersson lesion (AS), SAPHO, metastasis, destructive spondyloarthropathy of dialysis, CPPD or gout of the spine. Blood cultures (positive in 50–70% of pyogenic cases); CTguided biopsy (repeat if negative) with TB PCR, fungal and Brucella cultures. Echo for S. aureus or streptococci. Six weeks of targeted therapy (longer for undrained abscess or implants). Surgery for neurological deficit, instability or a large abscess. MRI lags clinical improvement, so follow clinically and with CRP.

stem: A 30-year-old man from Pakistan has thoracic back pain, night sweats and weight loss. MRI shows destruction of two adjacent vertebral bodies with a large paraspinal abscess and relative disc sparing. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Spinal tuberculosis (Pott’s disease)
options.B: Metastatic spinal disease from an undiagnosed primary tumour
options.C: Discitis from Staphylococcus aureus
options.D: Brucellosis; combination antibiotics for at least 6 weeks
options.E: Transient osteoporosis of the hip

explanation: Spinal TB typically affects the thoracic spine with anterior vertebral destruction, subligamentous spread, early disc preservation and large cold abscesses. Pott’s disease: thoracic predominance, anterior vertebral destruction, subligamentous spread, skip lesions, early disc preservation, large calcified cold (psoas) abscesses, gibbus deformity. 10–40% of spinal infections in endemic areas. CT-guided biopsy (AFB, GeneXpert, culture, histology). Standard anti-TB therapy for 9–12 months. Surgery for cord compression, instability or deformity. Screen for HIV. Notify public health.

stem: A patient with RA has fever, a new murmur, anaemia, positive blood cultures, purpura and haematuria. Which condition can mimic systemic vasculitis here?

options.A: Infective endocarditis
options.B: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
options.C: Multiple myeloma
options.D: Development of MALT lymphoma
options.E: Systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus nephritis

explanation: Endocarditis causes immune-complex disease, glomerulonephritis and positive autoantibodies including ANCA and RF. Infection must be excluded before immunosuppression. Endocarditis can cause immune-complex GN, low complement, positive RF, PR3-ANCA (or MPO), splinters, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes and Roth spots, emboli, arthralgia, back pain and discitis, and septic arthritis. Three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics, echo (TOE if TTE is negative), modified Duke criteria. Never start immunosuppression for “vasculitis” until endocarditis is excluded. Culture-negative endocarditis: consider Bartonella, Coxiella (Q fever), T. whipplei and HACEK organisms; consider Libman–Sacks endocarditis in SLE or APS.

stem: In a patient with an organ-threatening rheumatic presentation and high clinical suspicion, confirmatory tests are still pending. Which principle is safest?

options.A: Wait for all confirmatory tests before starting any treatment
options.B: Treat based on the single most likely diagnosis only
options.C: Delay treatment until a tissue diagnosis is obtained
options.D: Treat urgently while obtaining investigations in parallel
options.E: Treat only after excluding every alternative diagnosis

explanation: Vision-threatening GCA, pulmonary haemorrhage, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, septic arthritis and airway compromise all need time-critical treatment. Time-critical presentations:-GCA with visual symptoms: IV methylprednisolone.-DAH or pulmonary–renal syndrome: pulse GC + rituximab or cyclophosphamide ± PLEX; test anti-GBM.-RPGN: pulse GC, biopsy within days.-Septic arthritis: aspiration then antibiotics.-Airway threat (RP, GPA): ENT and ICU.-Scleroderma renal crisis: captopril.-CAPS: triple therapy.-MAS: GC + anakinra.-Cauda equina syndrome: MRI and decompression.-Fractured ankylosed spine: CT and immobilise.-Neutropenic sepsis: antibiotics within 1 hour.-Adrenal crisis: hydrocortisone 100 mg.-Methotrexate toxicity: folinic acid.

stem: A patient with inflammatory arthritis taking a JAK inhibitor develops sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. Which diagnosis must be considered first?

options.A: Pulmonary embolism, alongside other acute cardiopulmonary causes
options.B: Chondrocalcinosis
options.C: An interstitial lung disease flare, given the patient’s inflammatory arthritis
options.D: Apremilast
options.E: Pleuritic pain from the underlying inflammatory arthritis alone

explanation: JAK inhibitors are associated with venous thromboembolism, particularly in those with additional risk factors. CTPA, D-dimer (often raised in inflammation), leg ultrasound. Anticoagulate and stop or switch the JAKi (switch to a biologic; avoid JAKi re-exposure after VTE). Other JAKi emergencies: zoster (including disseminated), serious infection, MACE. Assess VTE risk before starting: prior VTE, cancer, immobility, obesity, oestrogen therapy.

stem: A primary school teacher develops sudden symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis two weeks after children in her class had ‘slapped cheeks’. RF is weakly positive. What is the most likely diagnosis and course?

options.A: Early rheumatoid arthritis; start methotrexate without delay
options.B: Parvovirus B19 arthropathy; self-limiting, confirm with IgM
options.C: Reactive arthritis following a recent infection, requiring NSAIDs for months
options.D: Hepatitis B prodrome, requiring antiviral therapy
options.E: Rubella arthritis, requiring long-term DMARD therapy

explanation: Adults with parvovirus B19 often present with an acute symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis mimicking RA, sometimes with transient RF or ANA positivity. Most cases settle within weeks, and NSAIDs suffice. Serology avoids unnecessary DMARD therapy. Infection in pregnancy carries a risk of fetal anaemia and hydrops. Acute symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis in an adult: parvovirus B19, rubella or recent vaccination, HBV prodrome (urticaria, raised ALT), HCV, HIV seroconversion, EBV or CMV, chikungunya or other alphaviruses after travel, early RA, SLE (parvovirus can mimic it: rash, cytopenias, positive ANA, low complement), Still’s, sarcoid, ReA, PSRA or ARF. Check parvovirus IgM (positive for up to about 3 months) or PCR. Use NSAIDs and reassure (most settle within weeks, sometimes months). Check rubella immunity and inform obstetric services if pregnant or in contact with pregnant women (risk of fetal hydrops and loss, especially before 20 weeks). Aplastic crisis can occur in haemolytic anaemias.

stem: A 38-year-old man with untreated HIV infection has bilateral painless parotid swelling, dry eyes and mouth, and a circulating CD8+ lymphocytosis. Anti-Ro and anti-La are negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Diffuse infiltrative lymphocytosis syndrome (DILS)
options.B: Primary Sjögren’s disease, with anti-Ro positivity expected
options.C: Sarcoidosis with Heerfordt syndrome
options.D: Lymphoma infiltrating both parotid glands
options.E: Mumps parotitis, requiring supportive care alone

explanation: DILS is a CD8+ T-cell infiltrative disorder in HIV that mimics Sjögren’s disease. Unlike primary Sjögren’s, it is usually autoantibody negative, involves more prominent parotid swelling and may infiltrate other organs. It improves with effective antiretroviral therapy. DILS: bilateral parotid enlargement, sicca, CD8+ lymphocytosis (>1,000/µL), lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis, nephritis, hepatitis, neuropathy, aseptic meningitis; anti-Ro and anti-La negative. It is less common in the ART era. Antiretroviral therapy; GC for organ-threatening infiltration. Exclude lymphoma. Other HIV rheumatology: HIVassociated arthritis, ReA, severe PsA, painful articular syndrome, myopathy (including zidovudine), osteonecrosis, IRIS-triggered autoimmunity.

stem: A 42-year-old woman returns from Réunion with fever, a maculopapular rash and severe, disabling symmetrical polyarthralgia of the hands, wrists and ankles. Four months later she still has persistent hand arthritis. Which infection is most likely?

options.A: Disseminated gonococcal infection
options.B: Complex regional pain syndrome
options.C: Development of MALT lymphoma
options.D: Chikungunya virus
options.E: Enthesitis-related arthritis

explanation: Chikungunya, an Aedes-transmitted alphavirus, causes intense acute polyarthralgia. A substantial minority develop chronic inflammatory arthritis that can mimic seronegative RA. Chronic disease is managed with NSAIDs, short courses of steroids and sometimes methotrexate. Dengue arthralgia is not usually prolonged. Chikungunya: abrupt fever, severe symmetric polyarthralgia of the hands, wrists and ankles, periarticular oedema and rash. Chronic arthritis develops in 25–40% and can mimic RA or SpA. RT-PCR in the first week, IgM after 5–10 days. Analgesia and NSAIDs (only after excluding dengue, because of bleeding risk), short GC for subacute disease, methotrexate for chronic inflammatory arthritis. Other alphaviruses: Ross River (Australia), Sindbis, Mayaro, O’nyong-nyong.

stem: A 54-year-old man has a 6-year history of migratory, seronegative large-joint arthritis that worsened after starting a TNF inhibitor. He now has diarrhoea, weight loss, low-grade fever and lymphadenopathy. What is the most appropriate diagnostic test?

options.A: Serum ACE level and a chest radiograph for sarcoidosis
options.B: Colonoscopy with random biopsies for inflammatory bowel disease
options.C: Duodenal biopsy for PAS staining and T. whipplei PCR
options.D: Stool culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin testing
options.E: Increase the TNF inhibitor dose, since the diarrhoea suggests inadequate disease control

explanation: Whipple’s disease often starts with years of migratory arthritis before gastrointestinal symptoms. Immunosuppression, particularly TNF inhibition, can unmask or accelerate it. Diagnosis is by PAS staining and T. whipplei PCR of duodenal tissue. Treatment is ceftriaxone followed by prolonged co-trimoxazole, or doxycycline with hydroxychloroquine. Whipple’s disease mostly affects middle-aged white men. Prodromal migratory non-destructive arthritis can precede GI symptoms by years. Other features: weight loss, diarrhoea, fever, lymphadenopathy, hyperpigmentation, culture-negative endocarditis, uveitis, and CNS disease (oculomasticatory myorhythmia is pathognomonic). Red flag: worsening after TNFi or other immunosuppression. Duodenal biopsy (PAS-positive foamy macrophages) with T. whipplei PCR. Saliva or stool PCR alone is not diagnostic (healthy carriers). Do a CSF PCR in all cases. Treat with ceftriaxone for 2 weeks then co-trimoxazole for 12 months, or doxycycline plus HCQ for 12 months (with lifelong doxycycline in some). Watch for IRIS early in treatment.

stem: How is acute rheumatic fever classified under the revised Jones criteria in a high-incidence community (for example ankle monoarthritis, fever 38.2 °C, ESR 35 and a raised ASO), and how is recurrence prevented?

options.A: Only the original single-tier Jones criteria apply here, regardless of population risk level
options.B: Fever and arthralgia alone, without any other supporting criteria, are sufficient for diagnosis
options.C: Monoarthritis never counts towards the Jones criteria at all, in any population studied
options.D: ASO titre alone, without any supporting clinical criteria, confirms the diagnosis outright
options.E: In moderate/high-risk populations, monoarthritis counts as a major criterion, and fever ≥38°C plus ESR ≥30 count as minor criteria; prevent recurrence with IM benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks

explanation: The revised Jones criteria lowered the thresholds for moderate/high-risk populations: monoarthritis or polyarthralgia can count as major criteria, and fever ≥38 °C and ESR ≥30 count as minor criteria. Older texts describe only the single criteria set. Echocardiography is recommended for all suspected cases to detect subclinical carditis, and septic arthritis should still be excluded in monoarthritis. Secondary prophylaxis is the most effective way to prevent recurrent ARF, which drives progression of valve disease. Duration depends on severity, typically at least 10 years after the last episode or into adulthood (age 21), and longer (to 40 or lifelong) with moderate or severe carditis. Oral penicillin or erythromycin are less effective alternatives. Diagnosis requires evidence of preceding GAS infection plus 2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor criteria (recurrence: 2 major, 1 major and 2 minor, or 3 minor). Major criteria: carditis (clinical or echo), arthritis, chorea (Sydenham’s; may occur alone), erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules. Low-risk thresholds: polyarthritis only, fever ≥38.5 °C, ESR ≥60 or CRP ≥3 mg/dL. Eradicate GAS (penicillin). High-dose aspirin or NSAIDs for arthritis (a dramatic response is typical; little response suggests another diagnosis). GC for severe carditis, plus heart failure care. Treat chorea with haloperidol, valproate or carbamazepine.

stem: A man with active pulmonary TB develops a sterile symmetrical polyarthritis that settles with antituberculous therapy. What is this condition?

options.A: Rheumatoid arthritis triggered by TB infection
options.B: Poncet’s disease (reactive tuberculous arthritis)
options.C: Look for an underlying malignancy
options.D: Septic arthritis requiring synovial biopsy and culture before treatment
options.E: Add an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor

explanation: Poncet’s disease is a sterile reactive polyarthritis associated with active TB elsewhere, and it resolves with TB treatment. Direct tuberculous arthritis is usually a chronic monoarthritis of a large weight-bearing joint with positive synovial biopsy or culture. Pyrazinamide can cause hyperuricaemia and arthralgia. Arthritis in TB: Poncet’s (sterile reactive polyarthritis), direct TB arthritis (chronic monoarthritis), TB dactylitis, spinal TB, drug-induced (pyrazinamide hyperuricaemia and gout; isoniazid drug-induced lupus; rifampicin and fluoroquinolone tendinopathy), and BCG-induced ReA after intravesical therapy. Standard anti-TB therapy; NSAIDs for symptoms. Poncet’s resolves with treatment. Exclude septic TB arthritis with synovial biopsy if monoarticular.

stem: A 40-year-old shepherd who drinks unpasteurised goat’s milk has undulant fevers, night sweats and unilateral buttock pain. MRI shows unilateral sacroiliitis with an adjacent effusion. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?

options.A: Ankylosing spondylitis; start a TNF inhibitor
options.B: Spinal tuberculosis (Pott’s disease)
options.C: Brucellosis; combination antibiotics for at least 6 weeks
options.D: Septic sacroiliitis from Staphylococcus aureus; IV flucloxacillin
options.E: Transient osteoporosis of the hip

explanation: Brucellosis commonly causes sacroiliitis, spondylitis and peripheral arthritis. Combination antibiotic therapy is needed to prevent relapse, and spondylitis requires longer courses. The laboratory must be told, because Brucella is a significant hazard to laboratory staff. Brucellosis is acquired from unpasteurised dairy, animal contact (farmers, vets, abattoirs) or laboratories, mainly in the Mediterranean, Middle East, Central Asia and Latin America (B. melitensis). Features: undulant fever, sweats, hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenias. Osteoarticular disease occurs in about a third: unilateral sacroiliitis (young), lumbar spondylitis (older; “Pedro Pons” anterior epiphysitis), large-joint arthritis, bursitis. Prolonged blood cultures (biohazard: warn the laboratory), PCR, serology (SAT ≥1:160; cross-reacts with Yersinia). Doxycycline plus rifampicin for 6 weeks, or doxycycline plus an aminoglycoside for the first 1–2 weeks. Spondylitis needs ≥3 months. Special regimens apply in pregnancy and children.

stem: A 72-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation has an INR of 2.6 and a painful knee effusion from CPPD. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Low-dose colchicine prophylaxis during initiation and titration
options.B: Immediate factor VIII replacement with rest, ice and analgesia
options.C: Urgent management for suspected septic arthritis while cultures are pending
options.D: Proceed without stopping warfarin if the INR is in range
options.E: Avoid aspiration altogether while anticoagulated

explanation: The risk of significant bleeding after joint aspiration or injection in therapeutically anticoagulated patients is very low. Interrupting anticoagulation risks thrombosis. The INR should be checked and be within the target range (generally up to about 3). Use a fine needle and apply pressure afterwards. Use a fine needle, apply firm pressure for 5 minutes, and consider ultrasound guidance. DOACs: no need to stop for most joint procedures (time the procedure at the trough if worried). Antiplatelets: continue. Haemophilia: aspirate only with factor cover. For an INR above about 3–3.5, defer elective procedures or seek haematology advice.

stem: After a knee steroid injection, which feature most strongly suggests iatrogenic septic arthritis rather than a post-injection flare?

options.A: Mild pain persisting beyond a week without fever
options.B: A low-grade temperature on the day of injection only
options.C: Macrophage activation syndrome
options.D: Worsening beyond 48 hours with fever and systemic upset
options.E: Erythema at the injection site within the first hour

explanation: A post-injection flare (a crystal-like reaction to the steroid ester) starts within hours and settles within 48-72 hours. Iatrogenic infection is rare and usually develops days later with worsening pain and systemic features. Urgent aspiration for culture is needed if sepsis is suspected. Worsening after injection: post-injection crystal flare (onset within hours, settles in 48–72 hours, afebrile); iatrogenic septic arthritis (days later, worsening, fever); underlying crystal or inflammatory flare; haemarthrosis; steroidinduced rapid chondrolysis or “rapidly progressive OA” (weeks to months); missed fracture or AVN. Ice and analgesia for a flare. Urgent aspiration for culture if sepsis is suspected. Use aseptic no-touch technique and avoid injecting through infected or broken skin.

stem: A 58-year-old man with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes is to have a subacromial injection of methylprednisolone 40 mg. What advice is most appropriate?

options.A: Avoid the injection entirely, since diabetes is an absolute contraindication
options.B: No specific precautions are needed, since this is a local injection only
options.C: Reduce the insulin dose by half before the injection, as a precaution
options.D: Monitor glucose closely for several days; adjust insulin if needed
options.E: Delay the injection until HbA1c is rechecked in 3 months

explanation: Intra-articular and soft-tissue corticosteroids are absorbed systemically and commonly raise blood glucose for up to several days in people with diabetes. Patients should monitor glucose and have a plan to adjust treatment. Larger doses and multiple sites increase the effect. Advise checking capillary glucose 4 times daily for 2–5 days and give a correction-dose plan. Expect larger rises with higher doses, multiple sites and long-acting preparations. Extended-release triamcinolone (microsphere) causes less glucose rise. Consider a lower dose or an alternative (e.g. physiotherapy) if control is poor. Warn about facial flushing and transient BP rise.

stem: After a twisting injury, a 27-year-old skier has a tense knee effusion. Aspiration yields blood with fat globules floating on the surface. What does this finding indicate?

options.A: Triamcinolone hexacetonide
options.B: An intra-articular fracture (lipohaemarthrosis)
options.C: ACL rupture, without any bony injury
options.D: A bleeding disorder such as haemophilia
options.E: Simple synovitis from a meniscal tear, without fracture

explanation: Fat globules in a haemarthrosis indicate marrow fat released through an intra-articular fracture, such as a tibial plateau fracture. A horizontal-beam lateral radiograph may show a fat-fluid level, and CT defines the fracture. Acute haemarthrosis without fat suggests ACL rupture, patellar dislocation or a bleeding disorder. Acute traumatic haemarthrosis: ACL rupture (the commonest in adults), patellar dislocation, osteochondral fracture, peripheral meniscal tear, intra-articular fracture (fat globules, lipohaemarthrosis). Atraumatic haemarthrosis: anticoagulation, haemophilia or von Willebrand disease, PVNS/TGCT, Charcot joint, CPPD or Milwaukee shoulder, haemangioma, scurvy, Ehlers–Danlos. Horizontal-beam lateral radiograph (fat–fluid level), CT for the fracture, MRI for ligaments. Orthopaedic referral.

stem: A 69-year-old woman with severe knee osteoarthritis is on the waiting list for total knee replacement, expected in 6 weeks. She asks for an intra-articular corticosteroid injection for pain. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Proceed with the injection now, since timing before surgery makes no difference to infection risk
options.B: Avoid steroid injection within about 3 months of arthroplasty
options.C: Injection is absolutely contraindicated at any time before joint replacement
options.D: Arrange urgent aspiration first to exclude infection before any injection
options.E: Proceed with the injection, since exercise alone has already failed

explanation: Large cohort studies show that intra-articular corticosteroid in the months before hip or knee replacement increases the risk of periprosthetic infection, and most surgeons avoid injections within 3 months of surgery. Analgesia and physiotherapy should be optimised instead. More generally, the same joint should not be injected more often than about every 3 months. Optimise analgesia (topical or oral NSAIDs with gastroprotection), physiotherapy and prehabilitation, weight loss, a walking aid. Genicular nerve block or RFA may bridge selected patients. If an injection is unavoidable for severe symptoms, discuss timing with the surgeon (most defer surgery by ≥3 months).

stem: A 4-year-old girl has oligoarticular JIA affecting one knee. ANA is positive and her eyes are white and asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate eye management?

options.A: No screening is needed since the eyes are currently asymptomatic
options.B: Regular slit-lamp screening by ophthalmology at frequent intervals (for example every 3 months)
options.C: Screening only if uveitis symptoms develop
options.D: Annual screening only, regardless of ANA status or age of onset
options.E: Screening is only required once methotrexate is started

explanation: Young-onset ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA carries the highest risk of chronic anterior uveitis, which is asymptomatic and can cause cataract, glaucoma and band keratopathy. Uveitis occurs in 10–20% overall (up to 30% in early-onset ANA+ oligoarthritis): chronic, non-granulomatous, often bilateral, white and painless. About 90% develops within 4 years of onset and up to 10% precedes arthritis. Complications: synechiae, band keratopathy, cataract, glaucoma, macular oedema, amblyopia. Screening intervals: | Risk | Group | Frequency | |—|—|— | | High | oligo, RF-neg poly, psoriatic or undifferentiated; ANA+; onset <7; duration ≤4 years | every 3 months | | Medium | same subtypes but ANA-, older onset or longer duration | every 6 months | | Low | systemic, RF+ poly, ERA | yearly (urgent review for red eye) | Treatment: topical GC plus mydriatics. If steroid-dependent (>2 drops/day beyond 3 months) or poor prognostic signs, add methotrexate (SC). If uncontrolled, add adalimumab (SYCAMORE roughly halved treatment failure). Then infliximab, tocilizumab, abatacept, JAKi. Avoid etanercept (ineffective and associated with new uveitis). Stopping adalimumab after 1 year of control led to frequent recurrence (ADJUST), so withdraw cautiously.

stem: A 13-year-old boy has heel pain with Achilles enthesitis, asymmetrical lower-limb oligoarthritis and an episode of painful red eye. HLA-B27 is positive. Which JIA category is most likely?

options.A: Scheuermann’s disease
options.B: Juvenile psoriatic arthritis
options.C: Enthesitis-related arthritis
options.D: Systemic JIA
options.E: Oligoarticular JIA, extended course

explanation: ERA typically affects boys over 6 with enthesitis, lower-limb arthritis, HLA-B27 and symptomatic acute anterior uveitis. Some develop axial disease later. Adolescent heel pain with arthritis: ERA vs Sever’s disease (calcaneal apophysitis), Osgood–Schlatter or Sinding-Larsen–Johansson (knee), reactive arthritis, IBD arthropathy, stress fracture, osteoid osteoma, CRMO, tarsal coalition. Features: lower-limb large joints, tarsitis, heel enthesitis, sacroiliitis in adolescence (juvenile SpA). Uveitis is acute, symptomatic, unilateral and recurrent. NSAIDs first. TNFi or secukinumab for sacroiliitis or enthesitis. Methotrexate does not treat axial disease. Physiotherapy.

stem: A 7-year-old with polyarticular JIA needs methotrexate. What is the usual dose and route?

options.A: 20-25 mg/m² weekly, by mouth only
options.B: A fixed dose of 7.5 mg weekly regardless of body size
options.C: 2.5 mg three times weekly, by mouth
options.D: Daily low-dose oral methotrexate rather than weekly dosing
options.E: 10-15 mg/m² weekly, with subcutaneous administration preferred at higher doses

explanation: Folic acid reduces adverse effects. Anticipatory nausea is a common practical problem in children. Use methotrexate for polyarthritis from the start, or for oligoarthritis that persists or relapses after injections, extended oligoarthritis, uveitis or poor prognostic features. Manage nausea with SC dosing, antiemetics, distraction and taste-masking, and consider “methotrexate intolerance severity score” assessment. Leflunomide is an alternative. Escalate to a biologic after about 3 months of inadequate response, or early in high-risk disease (RF/CCP+, hip, cervical spine or wrist involvement, erosions).

stem: A 6-year-old with oligoarticular JIA has an active knee effusion. Which intra-articular corticosteroid is preferred?

options.A: Methylprednisolone acetate
options.B: Triamcinolone hexacetonide
options.C: Hydrocortisone acetate
options.D: An IL-17 inhibitor
options.E: Betamethasone, given its shorter duration of action

explanation: Triamcinolone hexacetonide has the longest duration of effect. Sedation or anaesthesia may be needed in young children, and extra-articular leakage can cause subcutaneous atrophy. US-guided injection where possible, under sedation, nitrous oxide or local anaesthesia. Remission lasts months in most knees. Risks: subcutaneous atrophy, periarticular calcification, transient Cushingoid features if multiple joints are injected. For oligoarthritis, IA steroid comes first, then methotrexate if persistent or recurrent, then a biologic if refractory.

stem: A boy with systemic JIA develops persistent fever, hepatosplenomegaly and confusion, with ferritin rising to 12,000 µg/L while platelets, ESR and fibrinogen fall. What is the diagnosis, and what is first-line treatment?

options.A: Sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation; broad-spectrum antibiotics alone
options.B: Macrophage activation syndrome; high-dose glucocorticoids with IL-1 blockade (anakinra), adding ciclosporin or other agents if refractory
options.C: Simple viral hepatitis with reactive hepatosplenomegaly
options.D: Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome; anticoagulation and plasma exchange
options.E: Lymphoma; urgent oncology referral and biopsy

explanation: Rising ferritin with falling platelets, ESR and fibrinogen, and raised transaminases, triglycerides and D-dimer, characterise MAS, a form of secondary HLH. Infection must be sought in parallel. MAS is life-threatening and requires urgent intensive treatment, often with critical care input. Sepsis or DIC, primary HLH (perforin, UNC13D and similar), EBV-HLH, malignancy-associated HLH (lymphoma, leukaemia), Kawasaki, TTP, drug reaction (DRESS), MIS-C, SLE-associated MAS. 2016 classification: a febrile patient with known or suspected Still’s and ferritin >684 ng/mL plus any 2 of platelets ≤181, AST >48, triglycerides >156 mg/dL (1.76 mmol/L) and fibrinogen ≤360 mg/dL. Supportive: soluble CD25, CXCL9, haemophagocytosis on marrow. Ferritin:ESR ratio >21 favours MAS over active Still’s. Overt MAS occurs in about 10% of Still’s (subclinical in 30–40%), at onset, during flares or with infection (EBV). IV methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/day, maximum 1 g, × 3) plus high-dose anakinra, with ciclosporin as an adjunct. Emapalumab (anti-IFN-γ) is FDA-approved for MAS in Still’s when GC fail (monitor for CMV). Rescue: ruxolitinib or etoposide. Supportive: blood products, treat triggers, ICU.

stem: A 3-year-old boy has 6 days of fever, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, red cracked lips, a polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy and oedema of the hands. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Oral antibiotics for presumed streptococcal infection
options.B: IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin, ideally within 10 days of fever onset
options.C: Oral prednisolone alone, without IVIG
options.D: Supportive care only, since the illness is usually self-limiting
options.E: IL-1 blockade (canakinumab or anakinra)

explanation: Kawasaki disease is treated to reduce coronary aneurysm risk; corticosteroids are added in high-risk patients. Echocardiography is needed at diagnosis and follow-up. Prolonged fever with rash and conjunctivitis in a child: Kawasaki vs MIS-C (post-COVID; GI symptoms, shock, myocarditis, older children), scarlet fever, staphylococcal or streptococcal toxic shock, measles, adenovirus, EBV, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, DRESS, systemic JIA, leptospirosis, Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Fever ≥5 days plus ≥4 of 5: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis; oral changes (red cracked lips, strawberry tongue); polymorphous rash (often perineal); extremity changes (oedema, then periungual peeling at 2–3 weeks); cervical node ≥1.5 cm. Incomplete Kawasaki (infants): use laboratory features (CRP, albumin ≤3 g/dL, anaemia, ALT, platelets ≥450 after day 7, WCC ≥15, sterile pyuria) plus echo. Coronary aneurysms occur in 15–25% untreated and 4–5% treated. It is the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in high-income countries. IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin (moderate to high dose until afebrile, then 3–5 mg/kg for 6–8 weeks). Primary adjunctive GC for high risk (Kobayashi score, infants, aneurysms at diagnosis). IVIG resistance (10–20%): second IVIG, GC, infliximab, ciclosporin or anakinra. Giant aneurysms (≥8 mm): anticoagulation plus aspirin. Echo at diagnosis, 1–2 weeks and 4–6 weeks. Defer live vaccines for 11 months after IVIG.

stem: An 11-year-old girl has 4 months of pain in the distal femur and clavicle, with normal blood counts and mildly raised CRP. MRI shows multifocal bone marrow oedema. Biopsy excludes infection and malignancy. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.A: High-dose bisphosphonate therapy as first-line
options.B: BRAF V600E mutation analysis
options.C: Broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed multifocal osteomyelitis
options.D: Look for an underlying malignancy
options.E: NSAIDs

explanation: Chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis is autoinflammatory. Bisphosphonates or TNF inhibitors are used for refractory or vertebral disease. Multifocal bone pain in a child: CNO or CRMO vs bacterial osteomyelitis (usually unifocal, fever), leukaemia (cytopenias, LDH, night pain), lymphoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, Ewing’s sarcoma or neuroblastoma metastases, hypophosphatasia, scurvy (restricted diets, autism), SAPHO (adolescents), Majeed syndrome (LPIN2, with dyserythropoietic anaemia), DIRA (IL1RN). CNO sites: metaphyses of long bones, clavicle, vertebrae and pelvis, symmetric and recurrent. Associated with psoriasis, PPP, acne and IBD. Whole-body MRI maps silent lesions. NSAIDs first. For refractory disease or vertebral involvement (collapse risk): bisphosphonates (pamidronate) or TNFi, with methotrexate or sulfasalazine for some. Monitor with whole-body MRI. musculoskeletal problems

stem: A tall 19-year-old man has an aortic root Z-score of 3.1 and bilateral ectopia lentis, with no family history and genetic testing pending. Can Marfan syndrome be diagnosed under the revised Ghent nosology?

options.A: Aortic root Z ≥2 plus ectopia lentis is diagnostic
options.B: Autosomal dominant COL5A1 or COL5A2 variants
options.C: Diagnosis requires a positive FBN1 genetic test regardless of clinical features
options.D: Lofgren syndrome
options.E: Aortic root Z-score alone, without any other feature, is sufficient

explanation: The revised Ghent nosology replaced the older 1996 criteria (which older texts still describe). It gives cardinal weight to aortic root dilatation and ectopia lentis, and their combination is diagnostic once Loeys-Dietz, Shprintzen-Goldberg and vascular EDS features are excluded. The systemic score is used when one cardinal feature is missing. Marfanoid habitus: Loeys–Dietz, vEDS, Shprintzen– Goldberg syndrome (craniosynostosis, intellectual disability), homocystinuria, familial thoracic aortic aneurysm syndromes (ACTA2, MYH11), congenital contractural arachnodactyly (Beals; FBN2, crumpled ears), Stickler, MEN2B, Klinefelter syndrome. Revised Ghent nosology (without family history): 1. Aortic root Z ≥2 plus ectopia lentis. 2. Aortic root Z ≥2 plus a causal FBN1 variant. 3. Aortic root Z ≥2 plus systemic score ≥7. 4. Ectopia lentis plus an FBN1 variant known to cause aortic disease. Systemic score items include wrist and thumb signs (3), pectus carinatum (2) or excavatum (1), hindfoot deformity, pneumothorax, dural ectasia, protrusio acetabuli, reduced upper-to-lower segment ratio with increased arm span, scoliosis or kyphosis, reduced elbow extension, facial features, skin striae, myopia >3 dioptres, and MVP. β-blockers or ARBs (losartan); annual echo (with MRI or CT of the whole aorta); prophylactic aortic root surgery (typically at about 5.0 cm, or lower with risk factors); avoid contact and isometric sports and fluoroquinolones; ophthalmology review; pregnancy counselling (dissection risk, especially if root >4.0–4.5 cm); screen first-degree relatives.

stem: A 14-year-old tall boy with long limbs and mild learning difficulty has inferonasal dislocation of both lenses. He recently had an unprovoked DVT. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency)
options.B: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome
options.C: Marfan syndrome, given the tall stature and lens dislocation
options.D: Rotator cuff-related shoulder pain
options.E: Loeys-Dietz syndrome

explanation: Homocystinuria produces a marfanoid habitus with downward (inferonasal) lens dislocation, intellectual disability and thrombosis. In Marfan syndrome, lenses usually dislocate upward and intellect is normal. Plasma total homocysteine is diagnostic, and many patients respond to pyridoxine. Homocystinuria vs Marfan: downward (inferonasal) vs upward (superotemporal) lens dislocation; intellectual disability vs normal intellect; arterial and venous thrombosis; osteoporosis; malar flush. Inheritance is autosomal recessive (CBS). It is included in UK newborn screening. Plasma total homocysteine. Pyridoxine trial (about half respond). Methionine-restricted diet, betaine, B12 and folate. Thromboprophylaxis around surgery and pregnancy. Avoid nitrous oxide anaesthesia (it raises homocysteine).

stem: A 22-year-old woman has joint hypermobility, a bifid uvula, widely spaced eyes and tortuous arteries on CT angiography. Her father died of aortic dissection at an aortic diameter of 4.2 cm. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Antisynthetase syndrome
options.B: Felty syndrome
options.C: Adhesive capsulitis
options.D: Loeys-Dietz syndrome
options.E: Takayasu arteritis

explanation: Loeys-Dietz syndrome is caused by variants in TGF-beta pathway genes (TGFBR1/2, SMAD3, TGFB2/3). It features hypertelorism, bifid uvula or cleft palate, and widespread arterial tortuosity and aneurysms. Dissection occurs at smaller aortic diameters than in Marfan syndrome, so surveillance and surgical thresholds are lower. Loeys–Dietz features: hypertelorism, bifid uvula or cleft palate, arterial tortuosity and aneurysms throughout the body, craniosynostosis, club foot, translucent skin, early dissection, and allergic or GI eosinophilic disease. Image head to pelvis. Aortic surgery thresholds are lower (about 4.0–4.5 cm). ARB or β-blocker; annual MRA from head to pelvis; early surgery; specialist pregnancy care; genetic counselling (AD).

stem: A 28-year-old woman with genetically confirmed vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (COL3A1) attends clinic. Which management principle is most appropriate?

options.A: Routine catheter angiography for surveillance imaging
options.B: Elective prophylactic aortic surgery at routine intervals
options.C: Non-invasive imaging, avoid elective arterial procedures, consider celiprolol
options.D: Encourage isometric strength training to build vascular resilience
options.E: Aggressive surgical management of any arterial aneurysm found

explanation: Vascular EDS carries a risk of arterial, bowel and uterine rupture, and invasive procedures are hazardous because of tissue fragility. Celiprolol reduced arterial events in a randomised trial. Pregnancy is high risk and needs specialist planning. vEDS features: thin translucent skin with visible veins, extensive bruising, characteristic face (thin lips and nose, prominent eyes), acrogeria, hypermobility of small joints only.
