It causes arterial dissection or rupture, bowel perforation (sigmoid), uterine rupture in pregnancy, pneumothorax, and carotid–cavernous fistula. Median survival is about 50. Celiprolol (BBEST trial). Non-invasive imaging (avoid catheter angiography). An emergency card. MDT care. Avoid isometric exertion and contact sports. Plan pregnancy in a specialist centre (delivery planning; consider caesarean). Surgery is hazardous (tissue friability), so manage conservatively where possible. Genetic counselling.

stem: A 30-year-old man has hyperextensible, velvety skin, widened atrophic ‘cigarette-paper’ scars over his shins and generalised joint hypermobility. His mother is similarly affected. Which genetic basis is most likely?

options.A: Autosomal dominant COL5A1 or COL5A2 variants
options.B: Disseminated gonococcal infection
options.C: 3 points; he meets the criteria
options.D: Prosthetic joint infection
options.E: Autosomal recessive TNXB variants

explanation: Classical EDS is autosomal dominant and is usually caused by COL5A1/COL5A2 variants. Some tables wrongly list it as recessive. Classical-like EDS (TNXB) is recessive, and hypermobile EDS has no identified gene and is diagnosed clinically using the 2017 criteria. Classical EDS: marked skin hyperextensibility, wide atrophic “cigarette-paper” scars, easy bruising, molluscoid pseudotumours and subcutaneous spheroids, generalised hypermobility, hernias, prolapse. Major criteria are skin hyperextensibility with atrophic scarring plus GJH. Diagnosis needs genetic confirmation. Wound care with careful layered suturing and longer suture retention, protective padding for shins, physiotherapy, vitamin C (some advocate it for bruising), and screening echo for aortic root dilatation (occasionally present).

stem: A 25-year-old woman has had seven low-trauma fractures since childhood. She has blue-grey sclerae and early conductive hearing loss, and her height is normal. Her father has a similar history. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Non-accidental injury
options.B: Idiopathic juvenile osteoporosis
options.C: Hypophosphatasia
options.D: Osteogenesis imperfecta type I (COL1A1 null allele)
options.E: Osteogenesis imperfecta type III

explanation: OI type I is the mildest and most common form. It is autosomal dominant, with blue sclerae, hearing loss beginning in early adulthood and near-normal stature. Bisphosphonates reduce fracture rates in children, and adults need audiology review and fracture-risk management. Recurrent childhood fractures: OI vs non-accidental injury (a key safeguarding differential; metaphyseal corner fractures, posterior rib fractures, fractures of different ages), idiopathic juvenile osteoporosis, hypophosphatasia, rickets, Menkes disease (copper), immobility, GC, leukaemia. Sillence types: | Type | Severity | Features | |—|—|—| | I | mild, commonest | blue sclerae, hearing loss (20s–30s), near-normal stature | | II | perinatal lethal | multiple fractures in utero | | III | progressively deforming | short stature, dentinogenesis imperfecta, grey sclerae | | IV | moderate | normal or grey sclerae, variable | | V | IFITM5 | hyperplastic callus, interosseous membrane calcification | Recessive forms involve CRTAP, LEPRE1 and others. Children: IV bisphosphonates (pamidronate, zoledronate) reduce fractures and bone pain. Intramedullary rodding for deformity. Adults: audiology (stapes surgery or hearing aids), fracture-risk management (bisphosphonates, teriparatide or denosumab with specialist input), dental care, physiotherapy. Setrusumab (anti-sclerostin) is in trials.

stem: A 13-year-old overweight boy has a 3-week limp and pain in the left knee. On examination, the left hip rotates externally when it is passively flexed, and internal rotation is reduced. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Reassurance and discharge, since the knee X-ray is normal
options.B: Urgent AP and frog-leg hip radiographs; same-day orthopaedic referral
options.C: MRI of the knee alone, without hip imaging
options.D: Physiotherapy alone, without any imaging
options.E: Education with a progressive gluteal tendon loading exercise programme

explanation: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis often presents with referred knee pain in overweight adolescents. Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion is characteristic. Delay risks further slippage and avascular necrosis. Treatment is surgical fixation. Limp with knee pain in an adolescent: SUFE (overweight, aged 10– 16, obligatory external rotation on flexion) vs Perthes disease (aged 4–8, AVN of the femoral head), septic arthritis or osteomyelitis, transient synovitis (younger), JIA, osteosarcoma (distal femur, proximal tibia), Osgood–Schlatter, patellofemoral pain, osteochondritis dissecans, stress fracture. Always examine the hip in knee pain. Risk factors: obesity, endocrine disease (hypothyroidism, GH therapy, hypogonadism, renal osteodystrophy), Black ethnicity, male sex. It is bilateral in about 20–40% (consider prophylactic fixation of the other side in high-risk cases). Klein’s line on AP film. An “unstable” SUFE (unable to bear weight) carries the highest AVN risk. Make non-weight-bearing immediately and give same-day orthopaedic in-situ screw fixation. Check TFTs if atypical (age <10 or >16, or underweight).

stem: A 13-year-old footballer has 2 months of anterior knee pain after training, with a tender, prominent tibial tubercle. There is no effusion and hip examination is normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Urgent MRI of the knee to exclude osteochondritis dissecans
options.B: Reassure that it is self-limiting; advise load modification and stretching
options.C: Joint aspiration to exclude septic arthritis
options.D: Referral for surgical excision of the tibial tubercle
options.E: Clinically, without imaging

explanation: Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle in active adolescents. It usually settles at skeletal maturity with load management. Enthesitis at multiple sites, or with arthritis or uveitis, should raise the possibility of enthesitis-related arthritis. Anterior knee pain in an adolescent: Osgood– Schlatter (tibial tubercle) vs Sinding-Larsen–Johansson (inferior pole of the patella), patellar tendinopathy, patellofemoral pain syndrome, osteochondritis dissecans, patellar instability, plica, referred hip pain (SUFE), ERA enthesitis, tumour (night pain, swelling). Education and load modification (activity is allowed within pain limits), quadriceps and hamstring stretching, ice, a knee strap, analgesia. Symptoms settle at physeal closure. A persistent ossicle may need excision in adulthood.

stem: A 5-year-old girl has a limp and a painful right hip. Which combination of features most increases the likelihood of septic arthritis rather than transient synovitis?

options.A: Age under 3 years and a normal CRP
options.B: A well-appearing child with normal observations
options.C: Recent viral illness alone, with a normal ESR
options.D: Fever >38.5°C, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40 mm/h, WCC >12 x 10I/L
options.E: Afebrile with a normal WCC and ESR

explanation: Kocher’s predictors (fever, non-weight-bearing, raised ESR and raised WCC), together with raised CRP, increase the probability of septic arthritis. With several present, urgent ultrasound-guided aspiration is required. Transient synovitis typically follows a viral illness, and the child is well and afebrile. Painful hip in a young child: transient synovitis (commonest; aged 3–8, after a viral illness, afebrile, well), septic arthritis, osteomyelitis (proximal femur, pelvis), Perthes disease, JIA, trauma or NAI, leukaemia, discitis (refuses to walk), psoas abscess, appendicitis. Kocher criteria: fever >38.5 °C, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40 mm/h, WCC >12 × 10I/L. Predicted probability of septic arthritis is about 3% with 1 criterion, 40% with 2, 93% with 3 and 99% with 4. Adding CRP >20 mg/L (Caird) improves prediction. Kingella kingae is common under 4 (needs PCR). Ultrasound for effusion, then urgent US-guided aspiration (Gram stain, culture, Kingella PCR) and washout if septic. Transient synovitis: NSAIDs, rest and safety-net advice; review if symptoms persist beyond 1–2 weeks (consider Perthes).

stem: A 7-year-old boy has episodes of leg pain. Which feature would be inconsistent with benign ‘growing pains’ and warrant further investigation?

options.A: Compression ultrasound of the leg
options.B: Bilateral pain confined to the shins, worse at night
options.C: Pain relieved by massage, with a normal examination
options.D: Intermittent pain that resolves completely by morning
options.E: Persistent unilateral pain with a limp and focal bone tenderness

explanation: Growing pains are bilateral, intermittent, nocturnal and leave a normal child by morning. Unilateral or persistent pain, limp, joint swelling, bone tenderness, systemic symptoms or abnormal blood counts suggest infection, malignancy (such as leukaemia or bone tumour) or inflammatory arthritis. Growing pains: aged 3– 12, bilateral, in the shins, calves or thighs (not joints), evening or night, relieved by massage, no limp, normal examination, and well by morning. Reassurance, massage, stretching, simple analgesia. Investigate red flags with FBC and film, CRP and ESR, LDH, X-ray or MRI, and consider marrow examination if blood counts are abnormal (leukaemia can present with bone pain and arthritis before cytopenias). Consider vitamin D deficiency and benign joint hypermobility.

stem: A 17-year-old with a repaired cleft palate has high myopia, a previous retinal detachment, sensorineural hearing loss and early-onset osteoarthritis of the hips. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Marfan syndrome, given the myopia and joint findings
options.B: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome
options.C: Behcet syndrome
options.D: Stickler syndrome (type II collagen disorder)
options.E: Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

explanation: Stickler syndrome is most often due to COL2A1 variants. It combines ocular (high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration, retinal detachment), orofacial (cleft palate, Pierre Robin sequence), auditory and skeletal features, including premature osteoarthritis. Regular ophthalmic surveillance is essential. Stickler syndrome: COL2A1 (type 1; membranous vitreous; commonest), COL11A1 (type 2; beaded vitreous), COL11A2 (non-ocular), and recessive forms. Features: high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration and retinal detachment, cleft palate or Pierre Robin sequence, midface hypoplasia, sensorineural or mixed hearing loss, hypermobility, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, premature OA. Annual ophthalmic review (prophylactic retinopexy or laser to reduce detachment risk); audiology; cleft and airway care; joint protection and early arthroplasty when needed; genetic counselling (AD).

stem: A young woman has daily spiking fevers, an evanescent salmon-pink rash, sore throat, arthritis, neutrophilia and ferritin 8,000 µg/L with infection and malignancy excluded. What is the diagnosis, and what is the next treatment if she remains febrile on prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg?

options.A: Adult-onset Still’s disease; start an IL-1 inhibitor (such as anakinra) or an IL-6 inhibitor, ideally early after diagnosis
options.B: IL-1 blockade (canakinumab or anakinra)
options.C: Systemic lupus erythematosus with serositis
options.D: Lymphoma; refer urgently for biopsy before any immunosuppression
options.E: Reactive arthritis following streptococcal pharyngitis

explanation: Adult-onset Still’s disease is a diagnosis of exclusion, and very high ferritin is supportive but not specific. Systemic JIA and adult-onset Still’s disease are treated as one disease. The 2024 EULAR/PReS recommendations advise starting an IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitor as early as possible after diagnosis to avoid prolonged glucocorticoids, aiming for clinically inactive disease off glucocorticoids by 6 months. MAS must be actively sought. Infection (endocarditis, EBV, CMV, HIV, TB), lymphoma (PET-CT), other malignancy, SLE, vasculitis, DRESS, Schnitzler syndrome, Sweet’s syndrome, Kikuchi disease, and in older patients VEXAS and other monogenic or acquired autoinflammatory diseases. Fever ≥39 °C (quotidian or double-quotidian) with a salmon rash during fever (Koebner phenomenon; atypical persistent pruritic or flagellate lesions occur). Sore throat often precedes fever. Lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and serositis. Neutrophilia >15,000 (≥80% neutrophils), abnormal LFTs in about 75%. Glycosylated ferritin ≤20% plus ferritin >5× ULN gives >90% specificity. IL-18 and S100 are very high. RF and ANA are negative. Yamaguchi criteria (≥5 including ≥2 major, after exclusions; sensitivity 96%); Fautrel criteria (no exclusions needed). Chronic disease causes pericapitate wrist ankylosis. Course: monocyclic (about 30%), polycyclic (about 30%) or chronic articular (35–40%; worst prognosis). Methotrexate for chronic arthritis; TNFi for destructive arthritis. Refractory: switch between IL-1 and IL-6, JAKi. MAS (10–20%; mortality 10–40%): pulse GC plus high-dose anakinra plus ciclosporin; emapalumab. Watch for Still’s lung disease and DRESS-like reactions to biologics.

stem: A young man of Armenian or Mediterranean descent has recurrent 1–3-day episodes of fever with peritonitis and pleurisy, and two MEFV mutations. What is the main goal of lifelong colchicine, and what is done if attacks continue (two a month) with raised SAA despite colchicine 2.5 mg daily taken reliably?

options.A: To reduce flare frequency only, with no effect on amyloidosis risk
options.B: Colchicine prevents AA amyloidosis and reduces attacks; for colchicine-resistant FMF, continue colchicine and add IL-1 blockade
options.C: Switch to high-dose NSAIDs instead of escalating the colchicine dose further
options.D: Add a TNF inhibitor, since IL-1 blockade is considered ineffective in FMF
options.E: Stop colchicine, since IL-1 blockade alone fully prevents AA amyloidosis

explanation: FMF is an autosomal recessive autoinflammatory disease. Colchicine-resistant FMF (persistent attacks or raised inflammatory markers despite the maximum tolerated dose, up to 3 mg/day in adults) should be treated with IL-1 inhibitors added to colchicine, which continues to protect against amyloidosis. Persistently raised SAA signals a risk of AA amyloidosis, so serum amyloid A and urinary protein are monitored. Recurrent fever with serositis: other periodic fevers (TRAPS has longer attacks; MKD infant onset with nodes), acute intermittent porphyria (no fever), recurrent appendicitis or cholecystitis, endometriosis, IBD, hereditary angioedema (abdominal attacks without fever; low C4), SLE, recurrent idiopathic pericarditis. Exon 10 mutations: M694V is the most severe (amyloid risk); E148Q is low-penetrance and of doubtful significance. About 25–30% of patients carry only one mutation. Features: peritonitis (>90%), pleuritis, large lower-limb monoarthritis, erysipelas-like erythema, acute scrotum, exertional leg myalgia, protracted febrile myalgia (responds to GC). Associations: IgA vasculitis, PAN, sacroiliitis. Criteria: Tel-Hashomer or Livneh (adults), Yalcinkaya–Ozen (children). Paediatric colchicine doses: ≤0.5 mg/day under 5, 0.5–1 mg at 5–10 and 1–1.5 mg over 10; adults up to 3 mg/day. Aim for SAA <10 mg/L. Colchicine is safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding (do not stop for conception in either partner). Watch CYP3A4 and P-gp interactions and statins. Confirm adherence first (resistance affects 5–10%). Canakinumab is licensed (CLUSTER), or anakinra. Tocilizumab for AA amyloid refractory to IL-1 blockade.

stem: A patient with long-standing poorly controlled inflammatory arthritis (for example 30 years of RA) develops nephrotic-range proteinuria. What is the least invasive specific investigation, and what is the key management principle for AA amyloidosis?

options.A: Renal biopsy as the first and only test, given the clinical certainty
options.B: Abdominal fat aspirate with Congo red staining (with typing and exclusion of AL); suppress the inflammatory driver and monitor renal function
options.C: Serum amyloid A measurement alone, without any tissue confirmation
options.D: Echocardiography, since cardiac amyloid is the dominant concern here
options.E: Genetic testing for hereditary amyloidosis as the first-line test

explanation: Abdominal fat aspiration is safe and highly specific, though less sensitive than organ biopsy. Typing (immunohistochemistry or mass spectrometry) distinguishes AA from AL amyloid, and serum free light chains and immunofixation are needed to exclude AL. AA amyloidosis results from sustained serum amyloid A elevation; effective control of inflammation can stabilise or improve renal function. Nephrotic syndrome in a rheumatology patient: AA amyloid; AL amyloid (myeloma or MGUS); membranous nephropathy (SLE class V, gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs, HBV, malignancy, anti-PLA2R); minimal change or FSGS (NSAIDs, lupus podocytopathy); diabetic nephropathy; lupus nephritis; cryoglobulinaemic MPGN. Congo red shows apple-green birefringence. Fat pad sensitivity is 70–90% in AA and AL (lower in ATTR). Organs involved: kidney (>90%), GI tract, liver, spleen, adrenals, thyroid; the heart rarely. SAP scintigraphy maps wholebody load. Median survival is now ≥10 years; SAA <4 mg/L gives the best outcome. Treat the cause aggressively. Tocilizumab is especially effective (SAA Rheumatology SCE — 5-option SBA 130 production is IL-6-dependent); also TNFi; IL-1 blockade in FMF, CAPS and TRAPS; treat infection (TB, bronchiectasis, osteomyelitis); siltuximab or tocilizumab for Castleman disease. ACE inhibitor or ARB, diuretics, dialysis, transplant once inflammation is controlled. Eprodisate and anti-fibril antibodies are unproven. Monitor SAA every 1–3 months.

stem: A man in his 60s has submandibular swelling, autoimmune pancreatitis and retroperitoneal fibrosis with storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis and IgG4+ plasma cells on biopsy. What is first-line treatment, and what maintenance is used after a second relapse below 7.5 mg prednisolone?

options.A: Antibiotics alone, since this likely represents chronic sialadenitis
options.B: Cyclophosphamide first-line, reserving glucocorticoids for refractory disease
options.C: Observation only, since IgG4-related disease is usually self-limiting
options.D: Methotrexate monotherapy, without any glucocorticoid
options.E: Glucocorticoids first-line; B-cell depletion (rituximab or inebilizumab) for relapse or steroid sparing

explanation: Glucocorticoids induce remission in most patients. Relapse is common on steroid tapering (40–60% after withdrawal). A phase 3 trial (MITIGATE) showed that inebilizumab (anti-CD19) markedly reduced flares (by about 87%) and steroid exposure, and it became the first treatment approved for IgG4-RD in some regions in 2025. Rituximab is widely used off-label. Conventional steroid-sparing agents have weaker evidence. Serum IgG4 is neither fully sensitive nor specific, so malignancy and mimics must be excluded. Pancreatic cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, lymphoma, multicentric Castleman disease (high CRP, IL-6, anaemia), Rosai–Dorfman, Erdheim–Chester, GPA (orbit, sinus, meninges), sarcoid, SjD (anti-Ro positive, persistent sicca), PSC, infection. IgG4-RD typically affects men aged 50–70; the head and neck phenotype is commoner in women. It is subacute and painless, with rare fever and common atopy. Phenotypes: pancreato-hepatobiliary (sausage pancreas, sclerosing cholangitis); retroperitoneal and aortic; head and necklimited (Mikulicz, Küttner tumour, orbital pseudotumour, Riedel’s thyroiditis, hypophysitis, pachymeningitis); classic Mikulicz with systemic involvement (lung, TIN with low complement). Histology: >10 IgG4+ cells per HPF with an IgG4:IgG ratio >40%. Granulomas or neutrophilic vasculitis argue against it. Serum IgG4 is raised in 60– 80%; >5× ULN is more specific. 2019 ACR/EULAR classification requires ≥20 points. Treat urgently when vital organs are involved: pancreas, bile ducts, kidney, aorta, retroperitoneum with ureteric obstruction, pachymeninges. Asymptomatic lymphadenopathy can be watched. Prednisolone 0.6 mg/kg (30–40 mg) for 2– 4 weeks, then taper over 3–6 months; failure to respond should prompt rethinking the diagnosis. Maintenance: low-dose prednisolone 2.5–5 mg, MMF, azathioprine or methotrexate, rituximab or inebilizumab. Stent biliary or ureteric obstruction. Established fibrosis responds poorly.

stem: A 32-year-old woman has painful bilateral ankle periarthritis, erythema nodosum and fever. Chest radiograph shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis and outlook?

options.A: SAPHO syndrome
options.B: Reactive arthritis following a preceding gastrointestinal infection
options.C: Löfgren’s syndrome; usually self-limiting, treated with NSAIDs
options.D: Tuberculosis with hilar lymphadenopathy, requiring anti-TB therapy
options.E: Lymphoma, requiring urgent biopsy of the hilar nodes

explanation: This acute sarcoidosis presentation usually resolves within 6-24 months. In typical cases biopsy is often unnecessary. Erythema nodosum causes: idiopathic, streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, IBD, drugs (OCP, sulfonamides), TB, Yersinia, Behçet’s, pregnancy, lymphoma, coccidioidomycosis. Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy: sarcoid, lymphoma, TB, histoplasmosis, berylliosis, metastases. Löfgren’s syndrome: acute fever, bilateral ankle periarthritis (periarticular swelling rather than true synovitis), erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. It is associated with HLA-DRB1*03 and has a good prognosis (>90% remit within 2 years). Biopsy is unnecessary in typical cases. NSAIDs; short low-dose prednisolone if severe; colchicine for arthritis. Baseline sarcoid screen: FBC, calcium, creatinine, LFTs, urinalysis, ECG, eye examination, PFTs with DLCO. Repeat chest imaging to confirm resolution.

stem: A patient with sarcoidosis and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy develops a new facial nerve palsy. What is the best approach?

options.A: Reassurance only, since facial palsy in sarcoidosis is always benign and self-limiting
options.B: Observation with no imaging, since the chest radiograph is already known to be abnormal
options.C: Lofgren syndrome
options.D: Refer to ENT alone, without any neurological or CSF assessment
options.E: Urgent assessment for neurosarcoidosis and other causes, as organ-threatening disease may need systemic treatment

explanation: Neurosarcoidosis needs MRI, CSF analysis and exclusion of infection and malignancy. Facial palsy with BHL: neurosarcoidosis vs Lyme disease, TB meningitis, lymphoma, HIV, GPA, Bell’s palsy (coincidental). Bilateral facial palsy suggests sarcoid, Lyme, GBS or HIV. Neurosarcoidosis affects 5–10%: facial palsy (Heerfordt’s syndrome with parotitis and uveitis), aseptic meningitis, hypothalamic and pituitary disease (DI), myelopathy, smallfibre neuropathy. MRI brain (leptomeningeal enhancement) and CSF (lymphocytosis, raised protein, low glucose; exclude TB, fungi and lymphoma by cytology and flow). GC, then add methotrexate, then infliximab early for severe CNS disease; cyclophosphamide in selected cases. Isolated facial palsy often responds to a short GC course.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has recurrent bilateral auricular chondritis sparing the lobules, nasal chondritis and new stridor. What is the most serious complication requiring urgent assessment?

options.A: Necrotising scleritis
options.B: Progressive sensorineural hearing loss alone, without airway risk
options.C: Laryngotracheal involvement with airway stenosis or collapse
options.D: Saddle-nose deformity alone, which is cosmetic rather than life-threatening
options.E: Aortic regurgitation alone, which progresses slowly and rarely needs urgent action

explanation: Relapsing polychondritis can involve the larynx, trachea and bronchi. Dynamic CT and flow-volume loops are needed. Ear inflammation: RP vs infectious perichondritis (Pseudomonas; involves the lobule), trauma, frostbite, cellulitis, insect bite, gout tophus, GPA, VEXAS. Saddle nose: GPA, cocaine, syphilis, leprosy, trauma. Relapsing polychondritis: prevalence 4–9 per million; peak onset 40–60; F:M about 1:1. About 30% have an associated condition (AAV, RA, SLE, Sjögren’s, MDS). Features: auricular chondritis in 85–90% (spares the lobule; cauliflower ear), nasal chondritis (saddle nose), airway disease in about 50% (subglottic stenosis, tracheobronchomalacia; the leading cause of death), eye 50–60%, migratory non-erosive arthritis, costochondritis, cardiovascular disease (AR or MR, aortitis; the second cause of death), audiovestibular damage, GN (poor prognosis). McAdam criteria require ≥3 of 6. Flow–volume loops, dynamic inspiratory and expiratory CT, bronchoscopy, echo, aortic imaging, FDG-PET. Mild disease: NSAIDs, colchicine, dapsone, short GC. Severe disease (airway, eye, heart, kidney, inner ear): pulse GC plus methotrexate, azathioprine or MMF; cyclophosphamide for life-threatening disease. Refractory: TNFi (most data), tocilizumab, abatacept, anakinra, JAKi. Airway management by ENT and respiratory (stent, tracheostomy, CPAP for malacia; intubation is risky). MAGIC syndrome (mouth and genital ulcers with inflamed cartilage) should prompt testing for VEXAS or trisomy 8 MDS.

stem: A 67-year-old man has recurrent ear and nasal chondritis, macrocytic anaemia and neutrophilic skin lesions. Bone marrow shows vacuoles in myeloid and erythroid precursors. Which test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

options.A: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT
options.B: Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70)
options.C: Somatic UBA1 mutation testing
options.D: Bone marrow trephine biopsy alone, without genetic testing
options.E: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing alone

explanation: VEXAS syndrome mainly affects men over 50 and features relapsing polychondritis, neutrophilic dermatosis, vasculitis, thrombosis and macrocytic anaemia or MDS. It is often glucocorticoid-dependent. VEXAS (Vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, Autoinflammatory, Somatic) is caused by somatic UBA1 mutations (p.Met41) and affects about 1 in 4,000 men over 50. Features: relapsing polychondritis (50–60%), Sweet’s-like dermatosis, vasculitis, pulmonary infiltrates, VTE, macrocytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, MDS, steroid dependence. Mortality is about 50% at 5–10 years. UBA1 sequencing (blood or marrow). GC; JAKi (ruxolitinib is the most effective in cohorts); tocilizumab; azacitidine (especially with MDS). Allogeneic HSCT is the only cure. Give VTE prophylaxis or treatment. Consider VEXAS in any older man with RP, unexplained recurrent inflammation, macrocytosis and steroid dependence.

stem: A patient with Raynaud’s phenomenon, puffy hands, inflammatory arthritis and myositis features has hightitre anti-U1-RNP antibodies. Which organ complication needs active surveillance?

options.A: Scleroderma renal crisis, requiring urgent ACE inhibition
options.B: Digital ulceration alone, requiring vascular surveillance
options.C: Pulmonary arterial hypertension and interstitial lung disease
options.D: Cryoglobulinaemic glomerulonephritis, requiring urgent biopsy
options.E: Class IV lupus nephritis, requiring induction immunosuppression

explanation: Mixed connective tissue disease overlaps features of SLE, SSc and myositis. PAH is a major cause of death. UCTD (CTD features with ANA for ≥3 years without meeting criteria; 20–35% evolve within 5 years, mostly to SLE; predictors are dsDNA, Sm, Scl-70, ACA, homogeneous ANA, an SSc capillaroscopy pattern, serositis, cytopenias, low complement). Overlap syndromes (rhupus, scleromyositis with PM/Scl or Ku, antisynthetase). IPAF (ILD with autoimmune features from ≥2 of clinical, serological and morphological domains; a research classification). MCTD: high-titre anti-U1-RNP (anti-U1-70 kDa is most specific); Raynaud’s in >90%, puffy hands, polyarthritis (60–90%; can be erosive), mild myositis, ILD (20–50%; NSIP), PAH (10–25%; the leading cause of death), oesophageal dysmotility, trigeminal neuropathy, aseptic meningitis (sometimes NSAID-triggered). Anti-dsDNA, Sm, Scl-70 and centromere antibodies are absent; their appearance suggests evolution to SLE or SSc. Criteria: Alarcón-Segovia, Kasukawa, revised Japanese. HRCT and PFTs at diagnosis; yearly echo, DLCO and NTproBNP for PAH; RHC if suspected. Early MCTD-PAH may partly respond to immunosuppression plus dual vasodilators. Arthritis and myositis: methotrexate and GC. ILD: MMF first. HCQ for mild disease. In pregnancy, test anti-Ro and aPL and avoid pregnancy with PAH.

stem: A young man has 2-week fever episodes with migratory painful rash over areas of myalgia, periorbital oedema and abdominal pain; his father had similar attacks and developed nephrotic syndrome. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Familial Mediterranean fever, given the recurrent abdominal attacks
options.B: TNF receptor-associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS)
options.C: Cyclical neutropenia, confirmed by serial blood counts
options.D: Lofgren syndrome
options.E: Complex regional pain syndrome

explanation: TRAPS (TNFRSF1A, autosomal dominant) causes prolonged attacks, often over a week, with centrifugal migratory rash over myalgia and periorbital oedema. It carries a risk of AA amyloidosis. IL-1 blockade (canakinumab or anakinra) is preferred for maintenance; monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies can paradoxically worsen it. Cysteine mutations are more severe; R92Q and P46L are low-penetrance and milder. Attacks last >7 days (often 1–3 weeks), with centrifugal migratory myalgia (fasciitis) and overlying erythema, periorbital oedema, conjunctivitis and abdominal pain. AA amyloid occurs in 10–15%. Short GC courses for attacks; IL-1 blockade for maintenance (canakinumab is licensed). Etanercept is partially Rheumatology SCE — 5-option SBA 133 effective. Avoid infliximab and adalimumab (they can paradoxically worsen TRAPS). Colchicine is ineffective. Monitor SAA and urine protein.

stem: A 3-year-old has had recurrent fever lasting 4-6 days since infancy. Episodes are often triggered by vaccination and accompanied by tender cervical lymphadenopathy, diarrhoea, aphthous ulcers and a maculopapular rash. Which test best supports the diagnosis?

options.A: Genetic testing for TNFRSF1A alone, without urinary studies
options.B: Serum IgD level alone, as the definitive diagnostic test
options.C: Urinary mevalonic acid during an attack, with MVK genetics
options.D: A throat swab for group A streptococcus during an attack
options.E: NOD2 genetic testing alone, without any urinary or enzyme studies

explanation: Mevalonate kinase deficiency (formerly hyper-IgD syndrome) begins in infancy, and attacks are often triggered by vaccination. Raised IgD is neither sensitive nor specific, contrary to older descriptions. Urinary mevalonic acid during attacks and biallelic MVK variants confirm it. IL-1 blockade (canakinumab) is effective for frequent attacks. MKD spans HIDS (residual enzyme activity 1–10%) to mevalonic aciduria (<1%: developmental delay, dysmorphism, cataracts). Attacks are triggered by vaccines, infection and stress, with painful cervical nodes, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, aphthae and rash. There is a risk of MAS (and rarely amyloid). On-demand NSAIDs or GC for mild disease; IL-1 blockade (canakinumab licensed per CLUSTER; anakinra on demand) for frequent attacks. Colchicine and statins are ineffective. HSCT for severe mevalonic aciduria.

stem: A young woman has had a non-itchy urticarial rash since childhood with fever, conjunctivitis and progressive sensorineural deafness; her mother is affected. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Long-term antihistamines, since this is a mast-cell-mediated urticaria
options.B: IL-1 blockade (canakinumab or anakinra)
options.C: Avoidance of cold exposure alone, as in familial cold urticaria without further treatment
options.D: X-linked hypophosphataemia; burosumab
options.E: High-dose glucocorticoids alone, without any biologic agent

explanation: Muckle-Wells syndrome is a cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome caused by gain-of-function NLRP3 variants that drive IL-1-beta release. IL-1 inhibition controls inflammation, can stabilise or improve hearing, and prevents AA amyloidosis. The urticaria-like rash is neutrophilic and does not respond to antihistamines. Chronic non-itchy urticarial rash with fever: CAPS, Schnitzler, urticarial vasculitis, AOSD, SLE, cold urticaria (itchy, mast cell-mediated), PLAID (cold urticaria with antibody deficiency). CAPS phenotypes: FCAS (mild; cold-induced; attacks <24 hours); MWS (near-daily rash, deafness, amyloid about 25%); NOMID/CINCA (neonatal onset, chronic aseptic meningitis, papilloedema, deafness, patellar overgrowth, frontal bossing, developmental delay). Somatic mosaicism occurs in up to a third of NOMID and in late-onset adult CAPS. The rash is neutrophilic urticaria and antihistamineresistant. Anakinra (best CNS penetration; escalate the dose in NOMID), canakinumab or rilonacept, started early to prevent deafness and amyloid. Monitor audiometry, eyes and SAA.

stem: A 4-year-old has 4-day fevers every 4 weeks with aphthous ulcers, pharyngitis and cervical adenitis, and is well between episodes. Which response would most support the likely diagnosis?

options.A: Elevated serum IgD, confirming mevalonate kinase deficiency
options.B: Fever resolving promptly after one dose of prednisolone
options.C: A biallelic MEFV mutation on genetic testing
options.D: Persistently raised inflammatory markers between episodes
options.E: Failure to respond to a single dose of glucocorticoid

explanation: PFAPA is the commonest periodic fever syndrome of childhood. Attacks are clock-like, and the child is well between episodes. A single dose of corticosteroid aborts the fever, although it may shorten the interval between attacks. Colchicine or tonsillectomy can reduce recurrence, and it usually resolves by adolescence. Modified Marshall criteria apply. Attacks last 3–6 days every 3–8 weeks with clockwork regularity; the child is well and grows normally between attacks. It usually resolves by adolescence, though adult cases are recognised. Prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg (or 0.5 mg/kg) as a single dose at onset (may shorten intervals). Colchicine prophylaxis (especially in MEFV variant carriers); cimetidine; tonsillectomy (curative in most); anakinra for refractory cases. Eurofever/PRINTO PFAPA criteria help exclude monogenic disease (for example if there are GI symptoms, rash or arthritis).

stem: A 64-year-old man has a chronic non-itchy urticarial rash, recurrent fever, bone pain and a monoclonal IgM paraprotein, unresponsive to antihistamines. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

options.A: Schnitzler syndrome; IL-1 blockade (such as anakinra)
options.B: A biallelic NLRP3 mutation confirming cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome
options.C: Multiple myeloma, requiring immediate chemotherapy
options.D: Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia, requiring rituximab-based chemotherapy
options.E: IL-1 blockade (canakinumab or anakinra)

explanation: Schnitzler syndrome is an acquired autoinflammatory disorder of later life: urticarial rash, monoclonal IgM (or IgG), fever, bone pain and raised inflammatory markers. IL-1 inhibition gives dramatic responses. Patients need monitoring because of the risk of progression to lymphoproliferative disease. Strasbourg criteria: 2 major (urticarial rash plus monoclonal IgM or IgG) plus ≥2 minor (recurrent fever, abnormal bone remodelling or pain, neutrophilic dermal infiltrate, leucocytosis or raised CRP). 15–20% progress to Waldenström’s or lymphoma. Bone scintigraphy or MRI shows increased uptake at the distal femur and proximal tibia. Anakinra gives a dramatic, near-universal response; canakinumab and tocilizumab also work. Long-term haematology follow-up of the paraprotein. Risk of AA amyloid if untreated.

stem: A 9-year-old has livedo racemosa, recurrent fevers, two lacunar strokes and mesenteric aneurysms suggesting polyarteritis nodosa, along with mild hypogammaglobulinaemia. Which test and treatment are most appropriate?

options.A: Genetic testing for NLRP3 alone, treating with IL-1 blockade
options.B: Antiphospholipid antibody testing alone, treating with anticoagulation
options.C: ADA2 enzyme activity and genetics; treat with a TNF inhibitor
options.D: Nerve conduction studies alone, treating with physiotherapy
options.E: ANCA testing alone, treating with cyclophosphamide

explanation: Deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2) causes early-onset PAN-like vasculitis, lacunar strokes, livedo and immunodeficiency. TNF inhibitors are highly effective at preventing strokes, whereas glucocorticoids and conventional immunosuppressants are less effective. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is used for severe haematological disease. DADA2 (AR): early-onset PAN-like vasculitis, lacunar strokes (often before age 5), livedo racemosa, hepatosplenomegaly, hypogammaglobulinaemia, cytopenias including pure red cell aplasia, bone marrow failure. TNF inhibitors (etanercept, adalimumab) prevent strokes. Avoid anticoagulants and antiplatelets after strokes (haemorrhage risk). HSCT for the haematological phenotype. Screen siblings. Consider DADA2 in young or familial PAN, and in Sneddon-like presentations.

stem: A 3-year-old has boggy, painless swelling of the wrists and ankles (tenosynovitis), granulomatous panuveitis and a tan-coloured scaly ichthyosiform rash. A parent had uveitis in childhood. The chest radiograph is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis with uveitis, unrelated to any rash
options.B: Blau syndrome (NOD2-associated granulomatous disease)
options.C: Cystic fibrosis with arthropathy
options.D: Sarcoidosis, adult-type, with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy
options.E: Langerhans cell histiocytosis with skin and bone involvement

explanation: Blau syndrome (and early-onset sarcoidosis) is caused by gain-of-function NOD2 variants. It presents before age 5 with the triad of granulomatous arthritis or tenosynovitis, uveitis and rash, and the lungs are usually spared. Ocular disease is the main threat, and TNF inhibitors are often needed. Childhood granulomatous disease: Blau, CGD, CVIDassociated granulomas, TB, cat-scratch disease, Crohn’s, JIA (non-granulomatous), sarcoid (adult-type is rare in young children). Blau syndrome (familial) and early-onset sarcoidosis (sporadic) are both NOD2 gain-of-function (AD) and present before 5 with a granulomatous triad: boggy synovitis and tenosynovitis with large cystic swelling, panuveitis (sight-threatening), and ichthyosiform or papular rash. Also camptodactyly, fever, vasculitis, hepatic granulomas. The lungs are spared. GC, methotrexate, TNFi (adalimumab or infliximab) for the eyes; ophthalmology surveillance; IL-1 blockade or JAKi for refractory disease.

stem: A 46-year-old Afro-Caribbean woman with lupus pernio has painful swelling of several fingers. Hand radiographs show ‘lace-like’ lytic lesions and cysts in the middle and distal phalanges with intact joint spaces. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: SAPHO syndrome
options.B: Polyarteritis nodosa
options.C: Paget disease of bone
options.D: Reactive arthritis
options.E: Osseous sarcoidosis

explanation: Bone sarcoid usually affects the phalanges, with a lacy lytic pattern, and strongly correlates with chronic cutaneous disease such as lupus pernio. Asymptomatic lesions need no treatment. Painful or destructive disease is treated with glucocorticoids and steroid-sparing agents such as methotrexate, with TNF inhibitors for refractory cases. Lytic phalangeal lesions: sarcoid, enchondroma, gout (punched-out with overhanging edges), hyperparathyroidism (subperiosteal resorption, acroosteolysis), TB dactylitis, metastasis (lung), osteomyelitis, glomus tumour, PsA acro-osteolysis. Bone sarcoid occurs in up to 15% (phalanges with “lacelike” lytic lesions; vertebral or pelvic lytic or sclerotic lesions that mimic metastases on PET or MRI). Muscle granulomas are found in 50–80% at biopsy, usually silently. Joints: acute (Löfgren’s) or chronic, oligo-or polyarticular, sometimes destructive; dactylitis. First line: GC (pulmonary 20–40 mg, taper over 3–6 months; course 6–12 months; relapse in a third). Second line: methotrexate (10–20 mg/week), azathioprine, MMF, leflunomide. HCQ for skin, joints and hypercalcaemia. Third line: infliximab or adalimumab for refractory lung, cutaneous (lupus pernio), cardiac or neurological disease. Not effective: ciclosporin. Efzofitimod missed its phase 3 primary endpoint. JAKi are promising for skin. Biomarkers: ACE is not diagnostic; sIL-2R and chitotriosidase are better activity markers. Prognosis: spontaneous remission in 60– 70%; mortality <5%.

stem: A 44-year-old man with known pulmonary sarcoidosis reports palpitations and an episode of presyncope. ECG shows new first-degree heart block with right bundle branch block. What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.A: Pulmonary function tests alone, without cardiac imaging
options.B: Serum ACE level alone, to guide cardiac risk
options.C: Chest radiograph alone, repeated serially
options.D: Compression ultrasound of the leg
options.E: Cardiac MRI and/or FDG-PET with Holter monitoring

explanation: Cardiac sarcoidosis causes conduction block, ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death, and is under-recognised. New conduction abnormalities need cardiac MRI (late gadolinium enhancement) and/or FDG-PET. Treatment includes immunosuppression and, often, device therapy. ACE levels do not guide management. Cardiac sarcoid is clinically evident in about 5% (up to 25% on imaging or at autopsy): conduction block, VT, sudden death, heart failure. Screen everyone with ECG and symptoms, plus Holter and echo if abnormal. CMR (patchy mid-wall or subepicardial LGE, especially basal septum) and cardiac FDG-PET (after a high-fat, lowcarbohydrate preparation). GC plus an early steroidsparing agent Rheumatology SCE — 5-option SBA 136 (methotrexate); infliximab for refractory disease. ICD or pacing for high-degree block or VT (an ICD is often indicated even if the block recovers). Transplant for end-stage disease.

stem: A man has knee pain, diabetes insipidus, symmetrical long-bone osteosclerosis and ‘hairy kidney’ perirenal infiltration; biopsy shows CD68-positive, CD1a-negative foamy histiocytes. Which molecular test guides treatment?

options.A: BRAF V600E mutation analysis
options.B: NSAIDs
options.C: Clinically, without imaging
options.D: MAPK pathway sequencing only, without BRAF-specific testing
options.E: Look for an underlying malignancy

explanation: Erdheim-Chester disease is a histiocytic neoplasm with symmetrical long-bone osteosclerosis, retroperitoneal and perirenal infiltration and diabetes insipidus. About half of patients carry BRAF V600E and respond to BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib. Others often have MAPK pathway variants treatable with MEK inhibitors. Histiocytoses: LCH (CD1a+, langerin+, Birbeck granules, lytic lesions), Rosai–Dorfman (emperipolesis), multicentric reticulohistiocytosis, IgG4-RD (retroperitoneal fibrosis), retroperitoneal lymphoma. Erdheim–Chester disease: a non-Langerhans histiocytosis (CD68+, CD1a-, S100 variable) with symmetrical diaphyseal and metaphyseal osteosclerosis of the legs, “hairy kidney” perirenal infiltration, “coated aorta”, retroorbital masses, DI, xanthelasma, right atrial pseudotumour and CNS involvement. BRAF V600E is present in about half. BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib, dabrafenib) or MEK inhibitors (cobimetinib) for MAPK-pathway variants. Interferon-α historically. Bone scan or PET for staging.

stem: A woman has a destructive DIP-predominant arthritis and red-brown ‘coral bead’ papules around the nail folds and on the face. What is the diagnosis, and what must be screened for?

options.A: Rheumatoid arthritis, requiring only methotrexate
options.B: Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis; underlying malignancy
options.C: 3 points; he meets the criteria
options.D: Psoriatic arthritis mutilans, unrelated to any systemic screening
options.E: Gout, confirmed by synovial fluid crystals alone

explanation: Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis combines papulonodular skin lesions (histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells) with an aggressive DIP-predominant arthritis that can progress to arthritis mutilans. Around a quarter of cases are associated with malignancy. Treatment includes methotrexate, bisphosphonates and TNF inhibitors. Screen for malignancy (CT chest, abdomen and pelvis; age-appropriate tests; skin biopsy). Treatment: methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, bisphosphonates, TNFi or tocilizumab, GC; treat the tumour. Early aggressive therapy aims to prevent arthritis mutilans.

stem: After intensive weight training, a man develops woody induration of the forearms and calves with a ‘groove sign’, sparing hands and face, with no Raynaud’s and marked eosinophilia. Which investigation best confirms the diagnosis?

options.A: Peripheral blood eosinophil count alone, without tissue sampling
options.B: Deep full-thickness biopsy including fascia
options.C: Skin biopsy of the epidermis alone, without fascia
options.D: Capillaroscopy, since this closely mimics early systemic sclerosis
options.E: MRI of the thighs with STIR (fat-suppressed) sequences

explanation: Eosinophilic fasciitis causes fascial inflammation and thickening with prominent eosinophilia. A deep en-bloc biopsy including fascia, or MRI showing fascial enhancement, confirms it. Most patients respond to glucocorticoids, often with methotrexate. Haematological malignancy is an occasional association. Eosinophilic fasciitis (Shulman syndrome) is often triggered by strenuous exercise and sometimes by statins or checkpoint inhibitors. Rapid woody induration of the limbs (“peau d’orange”, groove sign) spares the hands, feet and face. There is no Raynaud’s, capillaroscopy is normal, eosinophilia and hypergammaglobulinaemia are present, and morphoea coexists in about a third. Associations: aplastic anaemia, lymphoma, MDS. MRI (fascial thickening and enhancement) and fullthickness en-bloc biopsy. GC (often 0.5–1 mg/kg) plus methotrexate early; MMF, IVIG, tocilizumab, JAKi or sirolimus for refractory disease. Physiotherapy for contractures. FBC surveillance for haematological disease.

stem: A 30-year-old man has a 2-year history of recurrent atraumatic swelling of the right knee, with blood-stained aspirates. MRI shows nodular synovial proliferation with low signal and ‘blooming’ on gradient-echo sequences. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Haemophilic arthropathy from an undiagnosed bleeding disorder
options.B: Synovial chondromatosis
options.C: Spinal tuberculosis (Pott’s disease)
options.D: Transient osteoporosis of the hip
options.E: Diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumour (PVNS)

explanation: Tenosynovial giant cell tumour (the current name for PVNS) is a CSF1-driven synovial neoplasm. Haemosiderin deposition gives a characteristic ‘blooming’ artefact on gradient-echo MRI. Treatment is surgical synovectomy. CSF1 receptor inhibitors are now an option for diffuse disease that is not amenable to surgery. Recurrent atraumatic haemarthrosis: TGCT/PVNS, haemophilia or von Willebrand disease, anticoagulation, synovial haemangioma, CPPD, Charcot joint, synovial sarcoma, scurvy. Gradient-echo “blooming” (haemosiderin) also occurs in haemophilic arthropathy. Localised (nodular) vs diffuse TGCT; the knee is the commonest site in diffuse disease. CSF1 translocation causes CSF1 overexpression. X-ray may show erosions or cysts with preserved joint space. Surgical synovectomy (open or arthroscopic), with high recurrence in diffuse disease. CSF1R inhibitors (pexidartinib, with hepatotoxicity; vimseltinib) for disease not amenable to surgery. Radiosynovectomy is an adjunct. Arthroplasty for end-stage disease.

stem: A man being investigated for myelodysplasia develops fever, neutrophilia and tender red plaques; skin biopsy shows a dense neutrophilic infiltrate without vasculitis. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Systemic glucocorticoids, while investigating the marrow
options.B: Colchicine alone, reserving glucocorticoids for refractory cases
options.C: Broad-spectrum antibiotics alone, pending culture results
options.D: Observation alone, since the lesions are expected to resolve spontaneously
options.E: Potassium iodide alone, reserving glucocorticoids for treatment failure

explanation: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) responds quickly to glucocorticoids, with colchicine, dapsone or potassium iodide as alternatives. It may be idiopathic, drug-induced (for example, by G-CSF) or associated with malignancy, especially AML and MDS. VEXAS syndrome should also be considered in older men with Sweet-like lesions and macrocytosis. Neutrophilic dermatoses: Sweet’s, pyoderma gangrenosum, Behçet’s, bowel-associated dermatosis– arthritis syndrome, neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis (Still’s, CAPS, Schnitzler, SLE), erythema elevatum diutinum, infection (cellulitis, mycobacteria), leukaemia cutis. Sweet’s syndrome criteria: abrupt tender red plaques or nodules with a dense neutrophilic infiltrate without vasculitis (major), plus fever, an association (malignancy, infection, IBD, pregnancy, drugs), neutrophilia and raised ESR, and a rapid GC response. Associations: AML, MDS, G-CSF, azacitidine, ATRA, vaccination, IBD, Behçet’s, VEXAS. Prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg (rapid response). Alternatives: colchicine, dapsone, potassium iodide, ciclosporin, IL-1 blockade. Treat the underlying cause, and do FBC, film and marrow examination in older patients. Check for macrocytosis and UBA1 in older men.

stem: A woman with ulcerative colitis has a rapidly enlarging, very painful leg ulcer with a violaceous undermined border that began after minor trauma. What is the key management principle?

options.A: Early surgical debridement to remove necrotic tissue
options.B: Compression bandaging alone, without any systemic treatment
options.C: Topical antibiotics alone, since this likely represents a secondary skin infection
options.D: Avoid debridement (pathergy); give systemic immunosuppression
options.E: Urgent vascular surgery referral for revascularisation

explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis associated with IBD, inflammatory arthritis and haematological disease. Surgical trauma can worsen it through pathergy. First-line treatment for extensive disease is systemic glucocorticoids or ciclosporin, with TNF inhibitors as effective options, particularly with IBD. Leg ulcers in rheumatology patients: pyoderma gangrenosum (IBD, RA, PsA, myeloma or IgA paraprotein, AML, PAPA), vasculitic ulcers (RA vasculitis, PAN, cryoglobulinaemia, AAV), Felty’s leg ulcers, APS or livedoid vasculopathy, calciphylaxis, venous or arterial ulcers, infection (atypical mycobacteria, fungi, ecthyma gangrenosum), malignancy (SCC), hydroxyurea ulcers, Martorell ulcer (hypertensive). PG is a diagnosis of exclusion (Delphi or PARACELSUS criteria). Biopsy the edge to exclude infection and malignancy, and expect pathergy. Local: potent topical steroid or tacrolimus, moist dressings, no sharp debridement. Systemic: prednisolone or ciclosporin (STOP GAP trial showed equivalence). TNFi (infliximab, adalimumab), especially with IBD; IL-1, IL-23 or IL-17 blockade, JAKi or IVIG for refractory disease. Treat the associated disease. Plan any surgery with immunosuppression cover. malignancy

stem: A man with long-standing type 1 diabetes cannot press his palms flat together and has thick, waxy finger skin, without Raynaud’s and with normal capillaroscopy. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: The A1 pulley at the metacarpal head
options.B: Osteosarcoma arising in pagetic bone
options.C: Systemic sclerosis, limited cutaneous subtype
options.D: Diabetic cheiroarthropathy (limited joint mobility)
options.E: Scleredema diabeticorum

explanation: Limited joint mobility in diabetes produces the ‘prayer sign’ and waxy skin thickening from glycation of connective tissue. It is associated with microvascular complications. Absent Raynaud’s, normal capillaroscopy and no autoantibodies distinguish it from systemic sclerosis. Limited hand mobility with thick skin: diabetic cheiroarthropathy vs SSc (Raynaud’s, capillaroscopy, antibodies), scleredema diabeticorum (upper back), Dupuytren’s, palmar fasciitis and polyarthritis (paraneoplastic, rapid onset), eosinophilic fasciitis (spares hands), hypothyroid myxoedema, amyloid, stiff skin syndrome, chronic GVHD. Optimise glycaemic control, stretching and hand therapy. Screen for microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy), which are associated.

stem: A woman with diabetic neuropathy has a warm, swollen, red midfoot, 3°C warmer than the other foot, with no ulcer and normal radiographs. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Oral antibiotics for presumed cellulitis, without any offloading
options.B: Urgent surgical debridement, given the suspicion of deep infection
options.C: Reassurance and routine follow-up in 2 weeks, since radiographs are normal
options.D: Compression bandaging alone, continuing normal weight-bearing
options.E: Acute Charcot foot: immediate offloading in a total contact cast and urgent MDT referral

explanation: Acute Charcot foot can present with normal radiographs. A temperature difference over 2°C in a neuropathic foot should be treated as Charcot until proven otherwise. Immediate offloading prevents collapse and rocker-bottom deformity. MRI shows early bone marrow oedema, and infection is unlikely without an ulcer. Warm swollen neuropathic foot: acute Charcot vs cellulitis, osteomyelitis (usually with an ulcer; forefoot), gout, DVT, fracture, septic arthritis. Other neuropathic arthropathies: tabes dorsalis (knee), syringomyelia (shoulder, elbow), leprosy, alcohol, congenital insensitivity to pain, amyloid neuropathy. Charcot occurs in 0.1–1% of people with diabetes, mostly at the midfoot (Lisfranc), then the ankle. The temperature difference is >2 °C. X-ray progresses through the “6 Ds”: distension, density, debris, disorganisation, dislocation, destruction. Rocker-bottom deformity follows. Total contact cast or removable walker until the temperature difference is <2 °C (often 3–6+ months), then custom footwear. Diabetic foot MDT. Surgery for unstable deformity. Bisphosphonates have limited evidence.

stem: A 49-year-old man has bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, knee pain, increasing shoe and ring size and coarse facial features. Hand radiographs show widened MCP joint spaces and the heel pad is thickened. Which test is most appropriate first?

options.A: Anti-Jo-1
options.B: MRI of both hips
options.C: CT of the chest
options.D: High-resolution CT chest
options.E: Serum IGF-1

explanation: Acromegalic arthropathy causes cartilage hypertrophy with widened joint spaces, then secondary OA. Carpal tunnel syndrome is common. Serum IGF-1 is the screening test (older texts suggested a skull radiograph), confirmed by failure of GH suppression on an oral glucose tolerance test and by pituitary MRI. Acromegaly arthropathy affects about 70%: early joint space widening (cartilage hypertrophy), then premature OA with large osteophytes. Also CTS, Raynaud’s, proximal myopathy, back pain with DISH-like changes and posterior vertebral scalloping, spade-like hands, heel pad >22–23 mm, prognathism, sleep apnoea, cardiomyopathy, colonic polyps. IGF-1 (screen), then OGTT GH suppression (confirm), then pituitary MRI. Transsphenoidal surgery, somatostatin analogues, pegvisomant. Joint changes are only partly reversible.

stem: A 61-year-old woman has 4 months of proximal muscle aching, cramps and weakness, with slow-relaxing ankle reflexes. CK is 1,400 U/L. She is not taking a statin. What is the most important next investigation?

options.A: Anti-Jo-1
options.B: Thyroid function tests
options.C: MRI of both hips
options.D: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT
options.E: Anti-SRP

explanation: Hypothyroid myopathy can mimic inflammatory myositis, with raised CK and proximal weakness, and is reversible with thyroxine. It should be excluded before invasive investigation for myositis. Muscle hypertrophy with stiffness (Hoffmann’s syndrome) is a rare variant. Raised CK with weakness: myositis, hypothyroidism, statin or other drug myopathy (colchicine, HCQ, zidovudine, alcohol), muscular dystrophy, metabolic myopathy (McArdle, Pompe), hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia, rhabdomyolysis, exercise, IM injection, macro-CK, African ancestry (higher baseline CK), cardiac troponin confusion. Hypothyroid myopathy occurs in 30–80% of untreated patients: proximal weakness, cramps, myalgia, slowrelaxing reflexes, CK 2–10× (sometimes higher). EMG is near-normal, MRI shows little oedema, and biopsy shows type II atrophy without inflammation. Hypothyroidism also raises statin myopathy risk. ANA and RF are often positive in autoimmune thyroid disease without CTD. Levothyroxine (myopathy resolves over weeks to months). Recheck CK and strength. Investigate for myositis only if weakness persists when euthyroid.

stem: A 45-year-old man has early large-joint osteoarthritis, disc calcification, blue-black ear cartilage and urine that darkens on standing. Which treatment targets the metabolic defect?

options.A: Allopurinol, to reduce urate-driven cartilage deposition
options.B: A TNF inhibitor
options.C: Colchicine, to reduce pigment deposition
options.D: Nitisinone
options.E: Clinically, without imaging

explanation: Alkaptonuria (homogentisate dioxygenase deficiency) causes ochronosis: homogentisic acid deposits in cartilage, causing pigmentation and premature arthropathy. Nitisinone inhibits an upstream enzyme and markedly lowers homogentisic acid, slowing progression. Alkaptonuria (AR, HGD deficiency): dark urine on standing or alkalinisation, blue-black pigmentation of the ear and scleral cartilage, disc calcification with fusion (mimics AS), early spinal and large-joint arthropathy, tendon rupture, aortic stenosis, renal and prostatic stones. Diagnose with urinary homogentisic acid. Nitisinone (SONIA 2 trial; it raises tyrosine, so use a lowprotein diet and eye monitoring for keratopathy). Joint replacement, physiotherapy, cardiac surveillance.

stem: A 19-year-old man with severe haemophilia A has an acutely painful, warm, swollen right knee after minor trauma. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Aspiration of the joint as the first step, before any factor treatment
options.B: Oral NSAIDs alone, without factor replacement
options.C: Compression bandaging alone, deferring factor replacement until swelling increases
options.D: Observation only, since haemarthrosis in haemophilia typically resolves spontaneously
options.E: Immediate factor VIII replacement with rest, ice and analgesia

explanation: Prompt factor replacement is the key treatment for haemarthrosis in haemophilia. Aspiration is not routine and is done only with factor cover if infection or a tense effusion is suspected. Recurrent bleeds lead to synovitis and haemophilic arthropathy, so prophylaxis is important. Recurrent haemarthroses cause synovitis and haemophilic arthropathy (knees, elbows, ankles), with “target joints” and pseudotumours. X-ray shows epiphyseal overgrowth, squared patella and widened intercondylar notch. Factor replacement or emicizumab prophylaxis, physiotherapy, radiosynovectomy for chronic synovitis, arthroplasty with factor cover. Avoid NSAIDs (use COX-2 cautiously); avoid IM injections. HCV and HIV screening in older patients (historical transfusion).

stem: A teenager with sickle cell disease has fever and a painful swollen tibia. Apart from Staphylococcus aureus, which organism characteristically causes osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease?

options.A: Scheuermann’s disease
options.B: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
options.C: Gram stain and bacterial culture
options.D: An IL-17 inhibitor
options.E: Salmonella species

explanation: Functional hyposplenism and bowel infarction predispose people with sickle cell disease to Salmonella osteomyelitis, although S. aureus remains common. Bone infarction is far more frequent than osteomyelitis, so blood cultures and, where possible, bone or subperiosteal aspirate help guide therapy. Bone pain in sickle cell disease: vaso-occlusive bone infarction (far commoner) vs osteomyelitis (Salmonella, S. aureus), septic arthritis, AVN of the femoral or humeral head, dactylitis (hand–foot syndrome in infants), gout (increased turnover). Blood cultures and MRI (osteomyelitis vs infarct is difficult to separate), with aspirate or biopsy where feasible. Empirical cover for Salmonella and S. aureus (for example a third-generation cephalosporin plus an antistaphylococcal agent). Treat 6 weeks or more.

stem: A 67-year-old man has back pain, weight loss, anaemia, hypercalcaemia, raised creatinine, normal ALP and a vertebral compression fracture. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: Compression ultrasound of the leg
options.B: Whole-body isotope bone scan
options.C: MRI of both hips
options.D: Serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation and free light chains
options.E: Somatic UBA1 mutation testing

explanation: Anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment and bone lesions suggest myeloma. ALP is usually normal and bone scans are often falsely negative, because myeloma lesions are purely lytic. Serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation and free light chains are the key tests, followed by whole-body low-dose CT or MRI. Back pain with hypercalcaemia and anaemia: myeloma, metastases (breast, prostate, lung, kidney), lymphoma or ATLL, hyperparathyroidism with osteoporotic fracture, sarcoid with vertebral fracture, TB spondylitis. CRAB: calcium >2.75 mmol/L (or >0.25 above ULN), renal (creatinine >177 µmol/L or CrCl <40), anaemia (Hb <100 g/L), bone (≥1 lytic lesion ≥5 mm). SLiM: ≥60% marrow plasma cells, FLC ratio ≥100, >1 MRI focal lesion. SPEP + immunofixation + FLC detects >97%. Renal disease is mainly cast nephropathy, plus AL or LCDD and Fanconi syndrome. Whole-body low-dose CT (has replaced the skeletal survey), PET-CT or whole-body MRI, bone marrow with FISH, R2-ISS staging. Urgent haematology referral. Hydrate and avoid NSAIDs and contrast. Bisphosphonate or denosumab for all treated patients. Vertebral augmentation for painful fractures. Daratumumab-based quadruplets; CAR-T and bispecifics for relapse.

stem: A 63-year-old smoker has painful swelling of the ankles and wrists, finger clubbing, and tenderness over the distal tibiae. Radiographs show smooth periosteal new bone along the tibial and fibular diaphyses. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT
options.B: CT of the chest
options.C: MRI of both hips
options.D: Compression ultrasound of the leg
options.E: High-resolution CT chest

explanation: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (clubbing, periostitis and arthropathy) is strongly associated with intrathoracic malignancy, particularly non-small cell lung cancer, and also with chronic lung suppuration and cyanotic heart disease. Bone scintigraphy shows parallel ‘tram-line’ cortical uptake. Symptoms may improve after tumour resection. Secondary HOA causes: NSCLC (commonest), mesothelioma, metastases; bronchiectasis, CF, lung abscess, ILD; cyanotic heart disease, infective endocarditis; IBD, cirrhosis, coeliac disease; thyroid acropachy (Graves’); localised forms (infected vascular grafts, aneurysms). Clubbing without periostitis: the same list. Primary HOA (pachydermoperiostosis; HPGD or SLCO2A1; adolescent boys) features pachydermia, cutis verticis gyrata and hyperhidrosis. Secondary HOA (about 90% of adult cases) is caused by megakaryocyte or platelet clumps bypassing the lung, releasing VEGF and PDGF, plus raised PGE2. Bone pain is worse on dependency and eased by elevation. Synovial fluid is non-inflammatory. Treat the cause (tumour resection can produce dramatic improvement). NSAIDs or COX-2 inhibitors. IV bisphosphonates (pamidronate, zoledronate) for pain. Octreotide or anti-VEGF in refractory cases.

stem: A 79-year-old man develops sudden, symmetrical synovitis of both wrists and hands with marked pitting oedema of the dorsum of both hands. RF and anti-CCP are negative. He improves rapidly on low-dose prednisolone. Which additional step is most appropriate?

options.A: Look for an underlying malignancy
options.B: Nerve conduction studies of both hands
options.C: A further, longer course of oral prednisolone without any screening
options.D: A short course of oral prednisolone
options.E: Anticoagulation, given the pitting oedema

explanation: RS3PE (remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting oedema) typically affects older men and responds well to low-dose glucocorticoids. It can be paraneoplastic, with solid tumours and haematological malignancies reported. A poor steroid response or systemic features should prompt a search for cancer. Elderly-onset symmetrical synovitis with oedema: RS3PE vs PMR with distal oedema (overlapping), elderly-onset RA (ACPA), CPPD, PsA, SpA, paraneoplastic arthritis, DPP-4 inhibitor-associated RS3PE, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, hypothyroidism. Prednisolone 10–15 mg gives a rapid response (taper over months). Screen for malignancy (CT, SPEP, PSA, ageappropriate tests), especially with a poor steroid response, constitutional symptoms or very high ESR. HCQ for steroid sparing. Associated cancers are found in up to about 25%.

stem: A patient on pembrolizumab (for example for melanoma, tumour responding) develops seronegative inflammatory polyarthritis that persists and limits function despite NSAIDs. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Stop the checkpoint inhibitor immediately and start cyclophosphamide
options.B: High-dose glucocorticoids alone, continued indefinitely at induction dose
options.C: Permanently discontinue the checkpoint inhibitor regardless of tumour response
options.D: Glucocorticoids at the lowest effective dose, usually continuing immunotherapy with oncology input, adding a csDMARD or biologic if steroid-dependent
options.E: Observation only, since arthritis from immunotherapy always resolves spontaneously

explanation: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced arthritis is often persistent. Rheumatology input, glucocorticoids at the lowest effective dose and early steroid-sparing csDMARDs are recommended; TNF or IL-6 receptor inhibitors are options for refractory disease. Close collaboration with oncology aims to control arthritis while continuing cancer immunotherapy where possible, and immunotherapy can usually continue for arthritis that is not life-threatening, through shared decision with oncology. New arthritis during cancer therapy: ICI arthritis vs aromatase inhibitor arthralgia, paraneoplastic arthritis, bone metastases, G-CSF bone pain, crystal arthritis (tumour lysis), septic arthritis (neutropenia), BRAF or MEK inhibitor arthralgia. Rheumatic irAEs affect about 5–10% of ICI recipients: RAlike, PMR-like or SpA-like arthritis (usually seronegative, sometimes persisting after stopping the ICI), sicca, myositis (with myocarditis and myasthenia), GCA-like vasculitis, sarcoid-like reactions, lupus-like disease. Anti-CTLA-4 plus anti-PD-1 combinations carry the highest risk. Pre-existing autoimmune disease is not an absolute contraindication, but flares are common. Grade by CTCAE. Grade 1: NSAIDs, IA steroid. Grade 2: prednisolone 10–20 mg. Grade 3–4: 0.5–1 mg/kg, hold the ICI, then steroid-sparing methotrexate, SSZ or HCQ, then IL-6R or TNFi. Check troponin and CK if myalgia or weakness occurs (3M overlap). Screen for HBV, HCV and TB before biologics.

stem: A 59-year-old woman develops rapidly progressive bilateral palmar thickening with flexion contractures of the fingers (‘woody hands’) and an inflammatory polyarthritis. Nailfold capillaroscopy is normal. Which investigation is most important?

options.A: Pelvic imaging and CA-125 (ovarian cancer)
options.B: Nailfold capillaroscopy repeated at 3 months
options.C: Anti-MDA5
options.D: Anti-Scl-70 and anti-centromere antibody testing
options.E: Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibody testing

explanation: Palmar fasciitis and polyarthritis syndrome is a paraneoplastic disorder strongly associated with ovarian carcinoma, and also with other adenocarcinomas. It can precede the diagnosis of cancer and responds poorly to immunosuppression. It can resemble Dupuytren’s disease or scleroderma, but onset is rapid and inflammatory. PFPAS (palmar fasciitis and polyarthritis syndrome): rapid “woody” palmar thickening with flexion contractures, polyarthritis, swollen hands, nodules. It is strongly associated with ovarian cancer, and also pancreatic, breast, lung and gastric adenocarcinoma. It may precede the cancer and responds poorly to immunosuppression. Pelvic and transvaginal ultrasound, CA-125, CT chest, abdomen and pelvis or PET-CT. Treating the tumour may improve the hands. Hand therapy. Other paraneoplastic syndromes to remember: carcinomatous polyarthritis, panniculitis–arthritis–pancreatitis syndrome (lipase, pancreatic acinar carcinoma), Lambert–Eaton (VGCC; SCLC), erythromelalgia (MPN), paraneoplastic Raynaud’s or digital ischaemia.

stem: A woman with inflammatory arthritis plans pregnancy in the next year. What is the best overall plan?

options.A: Switching to a biologic DMARD only after conception is confirmed
options.B: Continuing all current medications unchanged until pregnancy is confirmed
options.C: Stopping all DMARDs now, restarting only after delivery
options.D: Delaying conception until disease activity scores reach zero on current therapy
options.E: Preconception counselling aiming for low disease activity on pregnancy-compatible medicines for several months before conception

explanation: Active disease itself increases risks such as pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and growth restriction, so planned transition to compatible therapy before conception is ideal. Why outcomes go wrong in inflammatory arthritis pregnancy: active disease (the main driver; DAS28-CRP >3.2), prednisolone >7.5 mg, NSAID-related subfertility, unplanned conception on a teratogen, undiagnosed aPL or anti-Ro, unrecognised cervical spine instability (anaesthesia), postpartum flare after stopping treatment. RA improves in about 50–65% (more in seronegative disease) but often with moderate residual activity; 40–60% flare within 3–6 months postpartum. axSpA usually does not improve (worse night pain in the second trimester; 50– 80% flare postpartum). Psoriasis often improves; PsA behaves more like RA. Time to pregnancy is longer with active disease, NSAIDs and prednisolone >7.5 mg/day; methotrexate does not prolong it once stopped. 1. Before conception: treat to remission; switch MTX or leflunomide to sulfasalazine and/or HCQ ± a TNF inhibitor (certolizumab if needed throughout); screen aPL and anti-Ro/La where relevant; folic acid; rubella and varicella immunity; review cervical spine in longstanding RA. 2. During pregnancy: assess activity each trimester with DAS28-CRP (ESR rises physiologically); avoid NSAIDs late; lowest-dose prednisolone or intra-articular steroid for flares. 3. Third trimester: anaesthetic review (cervical spine, hips, lumbar ankylosis). 4. Postpartum: review at 6–12 weeks and restart treatment promptly; breastfeeding does not worsen RA. Disease activity, not the diagnosis, drives risk of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, SGA and caesarean section. A Danish registry linked miscarriage to younger women with recently diagnosed (active) RA. Continuing TNF inhibitors late in pregnancy, or restarting promptly, lowers postpartum flare risk.

stem: Which DMARDs are generally considered compatible with pregnancy?

options.A: Methotrexate at low dose throughout pregnancy, given its long safety record
options.B: Leflunomide without washout, since levels fall naturally in pregnancy
options.C: Hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine and azathioprine
options.D: Mycophenolate mofetil, given its established pregnancy safety data
options.E: JAK inhibitors, given their targeted mechanism and short half-life

explanation: The 2024 EULAR recommendations also list colchicine, ciclosporin and tacrolimus as compatible, and TNF inhibitors can be used throughout pregnancy; prednisolone is tapered to 5 mg/day or less where possible. Sulfasalazine should be given with folic acid 5 mg daily. Not compatible: methotrexate, leflunomide (unless washed out), mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide (except lifethreatening disease after the first trimester), JAK inhibitors, thalidomide, warfarin (switch before week 6), ACE inhibitors and ARBs, endothelin receptor antagonists (bosentan, ambrisentan, macitentan). Limited data: rituximab, tocilizumab, abatacept, anakinra, IL-17 and IL-23 inhibitors, belimumab — use only if no compatible alternative controls disease. Compatible in pregnancy (2024 EULAR and the course agree): HCQ, sulfasalazine (with folic acid 5 mg), azathioprine (≤2 mg/kg), ciclosporin, tacrolimus, colchicine, IVIG, LMWH, low-dose aspirin, prednisolone and TNF inhibitors. Prednisolone target: the source explanation cites tapering to ≤5 mg/day where possible; the EULAR course table gives ≤7.5–10 mg/day. Long-term doses above 10–15 mg/day raise GDM, hypertension, preeclampsia, PROM, infection and preterm birth. Use prednisolone (not dexamethasone or betamethasone) for maternal disease, because placental 11β-HSD2 inactivates most of it. Give stress-dose hydrocortisone at delivery after prolonged use above 5 mg/day. IV methylprednisolone pulses are acceptable for severe flares. Among biologics with limited data, anakinra and rituximab (given before conception) have the most experience. Belimumab may be continued in SLE when needed for disease control; registry data are reassuring. Accidental first-trimester biologic exposure is not a reason to terminate.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with RA on methotrexate 20 mg weekly plans to conceive. When should methotrexate be stopped?

options.A: Immediately upon a positive pregnancy test, with no lead time
options.B: At least 1 month before conception, continuing folic acid
options.C: Before conception, after the post-treatment contraception interval in the product information
options.D: Only after a formal washout procedure with cholestyramine
options.E: There is no need to stop, provided folic acid is continued

explanation: Methotrexate is teratogenic and is stopped before conception; UK (BSR) guidance advises at least 1 month before, replaced by a compatible drug, and continuing folic acid. Inadvertent first-trimester exposure warrants stopping, high-dose folic acid and specialist fetal assessment. Timing advice varies: BSR — stop ≥1 month before conception; 2024 EULAR and the EULAR course — stop 1–3 months before. Many clinicians use 3 months as the cautious figure. Continue high-dose folic acid (5 mg daily) through the first trimester. Methotrexate is teratogenic and abortifacient (aminopterin or methotrexate embryopathy: craniofacial, limb and CNS anomalies; miscarriage). This is why pregnancy is its absolute contraindication. Relative contraindications or cautions include moderate renal impairment (dose reduction), heavy alcohol use, significant liver disease, active serious infection, and pre-existing significant lung disease; older age alone is not a contraindication. Severe renal impairment (eGFR <30) is usually treated as a contraindication. Plan the switch (sulfasalazine, HCQ, TNF inhibitor) and confirm control before stopping contraception. Inadvertent exposure: stop the drug immediately; folic acid 5 mg; early fetal assessment and detailed anomaly scan; report to a pregnancy registry; switch to a compatible drug to prevent flare. Absolute malformation risk with low-dose MTX exposure is about 6–10% vs a background of 3–4%, often lower than patients fear — exposure is not by itself an indication for termination.

stem: A 34-year-old man with PsA on methotrexate 15 mg weekly asks whether he must stop it before trying for a baby. What is the correct advice?

options.A: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.B: Switch to leflunomide, which is considered safer for male fertility
options.C: Reduce to 7.5 mg weekly but continue trying to conceive
options.D: At least 1 month before conception, continuing folic acid
options.E: Stop methotrexate now and wait 3 months before trying to conceive

explanation: The 2024 EULAR recommendations state that men trying to conceive may continue methotrexate at 25 mg/week or less; data show no increase in miscarriage or malformations. Cyclophosphamide is the main drug where paternal exposure is a concern (dose-related irreversible infertility). Male subfertility in rheumatic disease: sulfasalazine oligospermia, cyclophosphamide gonadotoxicity, active inflammation, erectile dysfunction (vascular disease, depression, drugs), hypogonadism from chronic glucocorticoids or opioids, varicocele, Behçet’s epididymoorchitis, mumps orchitis, unrelated female-partner factors. Paternal exposure — EULAR course summary: Drug Advice for fathers Stop ≥3 months before Cyclophosphamide conception; offer sperm banking Can be continued (2024 Methotrexate EULAR: ≤25 mg/week); no increase in miscarriage or malformations Mycophenolate Can be continued Azathioprine, HCQ, TNF Can be continued inhibitors, most biologics Can be continued; reversible Sulfasalazine oligospermia (recovers ~3 months after stopping) Limited data, no harm signal JAK inhibitors (2024 EULAR suggests considering a switch) Thalidomide Condoms required Reassure for most drugs. If conception is delayed beyond 12 months on sulfasalazine, perform semen analysis, consider switching, and investigate both partners. Offer sperm banking before cyclophosphamide.

stem: A 31-year-old woman on leflunomide wishes to conceive within 6 months. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Stop leflunomide and perform cholestyramine washout, confirming low plasma levels, while switching to a pregnancy-compatible DMARD
options.B: Continue leflunomide unchanged, since teratogenicity data are reassuring
options.C: Stop leflunomide and simply wait 2 years without any washout procedure at all
options.D: Switch directly to methotrexate while leflunomide washout is completed
options.E: Continue leflunomide and simply avoid conception until it is naturally cleared

explanation: The active metabolite persists for up to 2 years. Washout is cholestyramine 8 g three times daily for 11 days, with two plasma levels below 0.02 mg/L 14 days apart. Teriflunomide (active metabolite) has enterohepatic recirculation and can persist for up to 2 years. Washout: cholestyramine 8 g three times daily for 11 days (alternative: activated charcoal 50 g four times daily for 11 days), then confirm two plasma levels <0.02 mg/L at least 14 days apart. Switch to a compatible DMARD during or before washout. Use effective contraception until levels are confirmed. Cholestyramine reduces absorption of other drugs (including oral contraceptives), so use additional contraception during washout. The EULAR course notes that leflunomide can be continued until conception if washout is started promptly once pregnancy is confirmed; exposed pregnancies with prompt washout show no excess malformations, so the old 2-year wait without washout is no longer needed. This is a more permissive approach than many UK practices, which still prefer pre-conception washout.
